First, write out six versions of the word, each starting at a different letter and wrapping round to the beginning when it reaches the end: \(\mathtt{banana}\), \(\mathtt{ananab}\), \(\mathtt{nanaba}\), \(\mathtt{anaban}\), \(\mathtt{nabana}\), \(\mathtt{abanan}\). These are the word's cyclic rotations: the same six letters, each time in a different order. (As permutations of the positions, they are the six powers of one, \(\sigma = (0\;1\;2\;3\;4\;5)\) in cycle notation: \(\sigma^0\), the identity, is the word itself, and \(\sigma^k\) starts it \(k\) letters in. Stacked in the order \(\sigma^0\) to \(\sigma^5\), each row is the one above shifted one letter: a circulant matrix, strictly its mirror image, since a circulant matrix shifts each row to the right. Sorting those same rows alphabetically shuffles them into what is called the Burrows–Wheeler matrix, which Seward's square is.) Then sort the six rotations alphabetically and stack them as rows:

Sorting the rotations into the Burrows–Wheeler matrix

In order each row shifted one letter Sorted alphabetically the Burrows–Wheeler matrix b a n a n a σ0 a n a n a b σ1 n a n a b a σ2 a n a b a n σ3 n a b a n a σ4 a b a n a n σ5 each row is the one above with its first letter moved to the end 0 1 2 3 4 5 a n a n a n a n b n n n a n a b a n a n σ5 a b ab… < an… a n a b a n σ3 a n a b anab… < anan… a n a n a b σ1 a a… < b… b a n a n a σ0 b b… < n… n a b a n a σ4 n a b nab… < nan… n a n a b a σ2 nanaba, the last one left banana, σ⁰, lands in row 3 a circulant matrix, mirrored Left, the rotations of banana built in their natural order: each row, σ¹ to σ⁵, is a copy of the one above with its first letter moved to the end. Right, the same rows sorted alphabetically. Before each row moves, the letters it shares with its closest rivals are tinted and the letter that settles the order is outlined: abanan goes first because after a, b comes before n. Each row keeps its label, so the powers end up shuffled, 5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2. The sorted square's first column is shaded green and its last blue; banana, σ⁰, lands in row 3.

Each row now has two numbers. Its row number, on the left, says where sorting put it; its power of \(\sigma\), on the right, says which rotation it is. Sorting scrambled the first but not the second: \(\sigma^5\) and \(\sigma^4\) are still one letter apart round the word, even though they now sit in rows 0 and 4. Recovering that relationship from the row numbers alone is what decoding comes down to.

Read down the last column of the sorted rows, and it spells \(\mathtt{nnbaaa}\). The original \(\mathtt{banana}\), \(\sigma^0\), is in row 3, counting from zero. The transform keeps just those two things, the last column and the row number, and stores nothing else. It doesn't make the block smaller; the reordered letters compress better in bzip2's later stages, for a reason that comes below.

How can a decoder get \(\mathtt{banana}\) back from only \(\mathtt{nnbaaa}\) and 3? Each of Seward's algorithms answers that question in a different way.

Seward names the pieces with letters, following Burrows and Wheeler's 1994 report A Block-sorting Lossless Data Compression Algorithm. On the same square:

Seward's names for the pieces

0 a b a n a n 1 a n a b a n 2 a n a n a b 3 b a n a n a 4 n a b a n a 5 n a n a b a F first column: aaabnn L last column: nnbaaa M every rotation of S, sorted: N × N letters, N = 6 S the block: banana I its row: 3 Stored by bzip2: L and I. Everything else here, the decoder has to work out. The square of sorted rotations again, with each symbol pointing at what it names. In bzip2, N can be up to 900,000.

So the decoder is given \(L\) and \(I\) and must produce \(S\). The square has been a way to understand the transform, but the decoder never builds it, and that matters for everything that follows. For a block of a million bytes, \(M\) would be a million rows of a million letters: a terabyte. The decoder keeps only \(L\), one byte a row, and whatever it needs to find its way from one row to the next. None of Seward's algorithms builds \(M\); what separates them is how much of that navigation they store, and in what form. That is the space in his space–time tradeoff.

Why only \(L\) is stored. Of the square's two outer columns, bzip2 keeps only the last:

  • \(F\) is the letters of the word in sorted order, so the counts alone fix it. A decoder holding \(L\) can rebuild \(F\) by counting, so it is never sent.
  • \(L\) holds the letter that comes before each row's opening, with the rows sorted by what follows. Letters before similar text tend to repeat (in English, \(\mathtt{he}\) is often preceded by \(\mathtt{t}\)), so \(L\) has long runs, which bzip2's later stages compress well.

Moving backwards through the word. Look again at row 3, \(\mathtt{banana}\). Move its last letter to the front and you get \(\mathtt{abanan}\). That is another rotation of the word, so it is already in the square, at row 0. Do the same to \(\mathtt{abanan}\) and you get \(\mathtt{nabana}\), at row 4. Each move steps one letter backwards through the word, treating its end as joined to its beginning, as on a ring:

Stepping backwards round the word

each row reads clockwise 0 1 2 3 4 5 row 3 row 0 row 4 row 1 row 5 row 2 b a n a n a Each move starts the reading one letter earlier row 3 reads from position 0 banana row 0 reads from position 5 abanan row 4 reads from position 4 nabana row 1 reads from position 3 anaban row 5 reads from position 2 nanaba row 2 reads from position 1 ananab Each row's last letter, in L, is the letter just before its start: a, n, a, n, a, b, which is banana read backwards. banana written round a circle, positions numbered from the top. Every row of the square reads the word clockwise from one letter (green), so its last letter (blue) is the one just before its first. Moving that last letter to the front starts the reading one letter earlier, so the walk steps anticlockwise: rows 3, 0, 4, 1, 5, 2. Row Move its last letter to the front Lands on row 3: \(\mathtt{banana}\) \(\mathtt{a} + \mathtt{banan}\) 0: \(\mathtt{abanan}\) 0: \(\mathtt{abanan}\) \(\mathtt{n} + \mathtt{abana}\) 4: \(\mathtt{nabana}\) 4: \(\mathtt{nabana}\) \(\mathtt{a} + \mathtt{naban}\) 1: \(\mathtt{anaban}\)

The letters moved, \(\mathtt{a}\), \(\mathtt{n}\), \(\mathtt{a}\), are each row's last letter, in \(L\), and they spell \(\mathtt{banana}\) backwards from its end. So a decoder could recover the whole word from \(L\) alone, starting at row \(I\), if it knew where each move lands. Seward records the landing rows in \(T\), the "transformation vector": here \(T[3] = 0\), \(T[0] = 4\) and \(T[4] = 1\). As a permutation of the rows, \(T = (3\;0\;4\;1\;5\;2)\): one cycle through all six, so following it from row 3 visits every row once before coming back, reading the whole word on the way.

The \(\sigma\) labels on the square show why: rows 3, 0, 4, 1, 5, 2 hold \(\sigma^0, \sigma^5, \sigma^4, \sigma^3, \sigma^2, \sigma^1\), so each step of \(T\) counts the power down by one. Stacked in that order, \(\mathtt{banana}\), \(\mathtt{abanan}\), \(\mathtt{nabana}\), …, each row is the one above shifted one letter to the right: a circulant matrix in the strict sense. Following \(T\) rebuilds it row by row, undoing the sort. \(T\) is the one-letter step back, \(\sigma^{-1}\), written in row numbers instead of powers (conjugated by the sort, in group-theory terms). (Read down the square, those powers, 5 3 1 0 4 2, are what string algorithms call the suffix array: the compressor computes it by sorting, and the decoder never has it.)

His theory section, "a more detailed exposition of Algorithm D in §2 of [1]", puts it in symbols:

\[ M[j, N-1]\; M[j, 0..N-2] = M[i, 0..N-1] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T[j] = i. \]

The left-hand side is row \(j\) with its last letter moved to the front; \(T[j]\) is the row where that lands.

Which row to land on. The moved letter becomes the first letter of the landing row, so the landing row is one of those that start with it in \(F\). But \(\mathtt{banana}\) has three \(\mathtt{a}\)s, so three rows start with \(\mathtt{a}\). Moving the \(\mathtt{a}\) off the end of row 3 lands on row 0, not row 1 or 2; how could a decoder know that without the square?

Up to now the three \(\mathtt{a}\)s have looked identical. To tell them apart, label each by where it falls in the word: \(\mathtt{b}\;\mathtt{a}_1\;\mathtt{n}_1\;\mathtt{a}_2\;\mathtt{n}_2\;\mathtt{a}_3\). The labels are only for following the letters; nothing in bzip2 stores them. This way of making the matching visible is borrowed from Ben Langmead's lecture slides on the transform. Langmead also wrote Bowtie, a DNA read aligner that uses the same correspondence to search a genome rather than to decompress it. Rows 3, 4 and 5 end in \(\mathtt{a}_3\), \(\mathtt{a}_2\) and \(\mathtt{a}_1\), and rows 0, 1 and 2 start with \(\mathtt{a}_3\), \(\mathtt{a}_2\) and \(\mathtt{a}_1\): the same occurrences, in the same order. This preserved order is what makes inversion possible, and the sort is why it holds. Rows 3, 4 and 5 are in that order because of what comes before their last \(\mathtt{a}\): \(\mathtt{banan} < \mathtt{naban} < \mathtt{nanab}\). Moving the \(\mathtt{a}\) to the front puts those same letters right behind it, where they decide the order again:

Why the a’s keep their order

Rows ending in a the Burrows–Wheeler matrix, last column L Rows starting with a the same matrix, first column F 0 a3 b a1 n1 a2 n2 1 a2 n2 a3 b a1 n1 2 a1 n1 a2 n2 a3 b 3 b a1 n1 a2 n2 a3 4 n2 a3 b a1 n1 a2 5 n1 a2 n2 a3 b a1 0 a3 b a1 n1 a2 n2 1 a2 n2 a3 b a1 n1 2 a1 n1 a2 n2 a3 b 3 b a1 n1 a2 n2 a3 4 n2 a3 b a1 n1 a2 5 n1 a2 n2 a3 b a1 b a1 n1 a2 n2 n2 a3 b a1 n1 n1 a2 n2 a3 b banan… < naban… < nanab… b a1 n1 a2 n2 a3 n2 a3 b a1 n1 a2 n1 a2 n2 a3 b a1 a3 a2 a1 a3 a2 a1 a3, a2, a1 down L a3, a2, a1 down F The square twice, its a’s and n’s labelled by where they fall in banana. Left, rows 3, 4 and 5 end in a; what comes before that a (tinted) puts them in order. Each moves its a to the front, carrying the tinted letters one place right, and lands on rows 0, 1 and 2 on the right, in the same order. So the a’s run a3, a2, a1 down both L and F.

The same goes for the two \(\mathtt{n}\)s, and for every letter of any block: the first \(\mathtt{a}\) in \(L\) (row 3's) lands on the first row starting with \(\mathtt{a}\) (row 0), the second on the second, and so on.

So the matching can be worked out from \(L\) and a count of each letter. Because \(F\) is sorted, its letters occur in runs, three \(\mathtt{a}\)s, one \(\mathtt{b}\) and two \(\mathtt{n}\)s, and those counts describe it completely, much like run-length encoding. Seward calls the count table \(C\); once the counts are accumulated, it says where each letter's run begins in \(F\). The decoder's whole path, from what is stored back to the word:

What the decoder rebuilds

L nnbaaa C a3 b1 n2 F aaabnn T 4 5 3 0 1 2 S banana count expand match walk L is used again to match each byte to its occurrence in F; the walk starts at row I = 3 Each arrow is a step explained in the rest of this section: counting, expanding the counts into F, matching occurrences to get T, and the walk.

Walking \(T\). Row \(T[j]\) starts with the byte row \(j\) ends with, which comes just before row \(j\)'s first byte in \(S\). So \(F[T[i]]\) precedes \(F[i]\). The decoder has \(L\), not \(F\), but \(L[k] = F[T[k]]\), and substituting gives a relation in \(L\) alone:

\[ L[T[k]] \text{ immediately precedes } L[k] \text{ in } S. \]

\(L[I]\) is the last byte of \(S\), so starting at \(I\) and following \(T\) gives \(S\) from the end:

Decoding banana by following T

row visited byte read 3 a → 0 n → 4 a → 1 n → 5 a → 2 b j L[j] T[j] 0 n 4 1 n 5 2 b 3 3 a 0 4 a 1 5 a 2 S, written from the end 0 1 2 3 4 5 a Step 1: row 3, emit L[3] = a into S[5]; next row T[3] = 0 n Step 2: row 0, emit L[0] = n into S[4]; next row T[0] = 4 a Step 3: row 4, emit L[4] = a into S[3]; next row T[4] = 1 n Step 4: row 1, emit L[1] = n into S[2]; next row T[1] = 5 a Step 5: row 5, emit L[5] = a into S[1]; next row T[5] = 2 b Step 6: row 2, emit L[2] = b into S[0]; done S = banana, recovered by following T from row I = 3 Across the top, the rows the walk visits and the byte it reads at each. Below, each step reads the byte in L at the current row, writes it into S from the end, and moves to the row T names. Every jump depends on the entry just read, which is why the walk is one dependent load after another.

That is \(\mathtt{banana}\) backwards, and it is the whole inner loop of the inverse transform: load the entry at \(p\), emit a byte, jump where it says. Where each jump lands depends on the content of \(S\), not on the last jump. In a million-byte block that is a million loads from places the cache has no reason to hold.

To write \(S\) forwards, Seward assumes the compressor reverses each block before sorting. bzip2 doesn't, which a footnote calls "a design flaw"; by the manual's account, "the bzip2 format was frozen before I properly and fully understood the performance consequences". Its decoder builds the links the other way instead, writing \(i\) into slot \(s\) where Seward would set \(T[i] = s\) (tt[cftab[uc]++] |= i << 8), and following that \(T^{-1}\) emits \(S\) forwards. mibz2 does the same, so its navigation table holds \(T^{-1}\): each entry points forwards, to the row whose string starts one byte later in \(S\).

Building \(T\) from counts. Since the \(k\)-th \(c\) in \(L\) lands on the \(k\)-th row starting with \(c\), Seward can state the rule directly: "if \(c\) occurs \(k\) times in \(L[0..j]\) and \(L[j] = c\), then \(T[j]\) must be \(i\), where \(i\) is the position of the \(k\)-th \(c\) in \(F\)."

T matches each L byte to the same occurrence in F

L[j] F[i] j = 0 n2 a3 i = 0 j = 1 n1 a2 i = 1 j = 2 b a1 i = 2 j = 3 a3 b i = 3 j = 4 a2 n2 i = 4 j = 5 a1 n1 i = 5 T[0] = 4 T[1] = 5 T[2] = 3 T[3] = 0 T[4] = 1 T[5] = 2 With the occurrences labelled, each link joins a letter in L to itself in F: L[3] is a3, which is F[0], so T[3] = 0. The links never cross within one letter, which is why counts are enough to rebuild T.

The \(c\)'s in \(F\) form one bucket. Turning the counts in \(C\) into running totals gives where each bucket starts: \(C[c]\) becomes the number of bytes smaller than \(c\) (for \(\mathtt{banana}\), a 0, b 3, n 4). So

\[ T[j] = C[c] + k - 1, \qquad c = L[j], \]

and one scan of \(L\) with a running count per byte value builds \(T\). Within each byte value the links increase with \(j\). Every BWT has this ordering, and our compact table depends on it.

items.title: 2. Making inversion fast: basis, bw94 and mergedTL
items.text:
"How fast can inversion be?" Three algorithms, each refining the last, answer it.

basis is the theory written out: count, build \(T\), walk. It reads \(L\) three times and keeps \(L\) (one byte a row) and \(T\) (four) alive: \(5N\) bytes.

bw94, named for Burrows and Wheeler's report, merges the first two passes by recording \(T'[i]\), the number of earlier occurrences of \(L[i]\), while counting. That is \(T\) without its bucket's start, \(T[i] = T'[i] + C[L[i]]\), and the walk adds the start back. Two passes, still \(5N\) bytes.

mergedTL comes from looking at bw94's walk, which reads \(L[p]\) and \(T'[p]\) at the same arbitrary index: "Unless both \(T\) and \(L\) fit in the machine's cache, this could cause two (capacity) misses per iteration." So it packs both into one 32-bit word, limiting \(N\) to \(2^{24}\):

\[ U[i] = 256 \cdot T'[i] + L[i]. \]

The name is literal: \(T\) and \(L\), merged. Each step unpacks the byte with a mask and the link with a shift, which costs instructions, "but the near-halving of the cache miss rate is potentially valuable". The table is also a byte a row smaller: \(4N\).

What one row costs, bit by bit

0 bits 8 16 24 32 bits bw94 T′[i] T′[i], displacement in its bucket array 1 L[i] L[i] array 2: a second line mergedTL U[i] T′[i], 24 bits L[i] one word: U = 256·T′ + L indexF A[i] low 16 bits of T[i] 4 byte: binary search in C bzip2, mibz2 tt[s] i such that T[i] = s, 24 bits L[s] the link reversed indexF's 20 bits sit in two arrays: 16 in one, and a 4-bit nibble packed two to a byte in another. bw94 keeps T′ and L in separate arrays, so a step can miss twice. mergedTL packs both into one word. indexF keeps only T, in 20 bits, and finds the byte from the counts. bzip2 and mibz2 pack the byte with the reversed link.

bzip2 uses mergedTL, with the reversed link stored as an absolute position, so its walk needs no \(C[c]\) addition. Its manual credits the change with a real gain: "Single array implementation of the inverse BWT. This significantly speeds up decompression, presumably because it reduces the number of cache misses."

items.title: 3. Spending less memory: indexF and the count trees
items.text:
"Can we reduce memory use whilst retaining useful decompression speed? Interestingly, yes." The relation in \(F\), \(F[T[i]]\) precedes \(F[i]\), needs only \(T\) to walk. If the decoder reads the output bytes from \(F\) instead of \(L\), it needs \(L\) only while it builds \(T\), so \(T\) can be written over it. \(F\) needn't be stored either: it is sorted, so the 256 running totals in \(C\) describe it, and \(F[p]\) is the byte whose bucket contains \(p\). "No free lunch, alas": finding it is a binary search in \(C\).

indexF, named for indexing into \(F\), keeps \(T\) alone in \(N\) 20-bit words (so \(N \le 2^{20}\)): a 16-bit array plus a nibble array, \(2.5N\) bytes. It starts the walk at \(T[I]\), because reading \(F\), the byte \(L[I]\) is found at \(F[T[I]]\). bzip2 ships it as -s, "a modified algorithm which only requires 2.5 bytes per block byte … albeit at about half the normal speed", with the search as BZ2_indexIntoF. What it gives up:

  • A search per byte, eight or nine comparisons where mergedTL has a mask. The 1 KB of counts stays in cache, so the search costs instructions, not misses, and since the next position is \(A[p]\) alone, a processor can overlap it with the next load.
  • Two arrays again. The 20-bit entry is split between the 16-bit array and the nibbles, so a step can touch two cache lines, the cost mergedTL removed.
  • A cap of \(2^{20}\) bytes per block, which bzip2's 900,000-byte maximum fits.

The trees. "It is instructive to ask just how little storage we can get away with": \(L\) and the counts alone. Any \(T[j]\) is \(C[c]\) plus the number of \(c\)'s before \(j\) in \(L\), but counting them means scanning \(L\), \(O(N)\) a step and \(O(N^2)\) in all: "absurdly inefficient". Seward buys speed back with 256 binary trees of partial counts, one per byte value. Each node counts its byte in an aligned power-of-two segment of \(L\), an empty subtree costs nothing, and a node budget sets how deep the trees grow. To count the \(c\)'s up to \(j\), descend \(c\)'s tree, adding the left child's count whenever \(j\) lies to the right, and scan \(L\) only for the last segment. The FM-index, published the year before, asks the same question of \(L\) to search text without decompressing it, and answers it with counts stored every so many rows and a scan between them.

A count tree answers a rank query

[0, 8) · 3 [0, 4) · 1 [4, 8) · 2 [2, 4) · 1 [4, 6) · 2 [0, 2) · none [6, 8) · none n 0 n 1 b 2 a 3 a 4 a 5 6 7 L padding How many a's in L[0..4]? Right at the root (+1 from [0, 4)), left to [4, 6), off the tree: scan L[4..4] (+1). Two. The tree for byte a over L = nnbaaa, padded to 8 positions. Counting the a's up to position 4 takes one left-child count and a one-byte scan, so T[4] = C[a] + 2 − 1 = 1.

tree stores a node in three 32-bit words. treeopt packs a node into 54 bits, two words, and a leaf into one, fitting nearly twice as many nodes in the same space, which halves the scans. With \(L\), tree-1M and treeopt-1M take \(2N\) bytes and treeopt-500k \(1.5N\).

items.title: 4. The space–time tradeoff
items.text:
The machine was a 400 MHz AMD K6-III with 128 MB of memory and a 256 KB second-level cache. Blocks were at most 10⁶ bytes, 1 MB, and each was inverted ten times. He tested six files of at least a megabyte, four of them from the Canterbury Corpus. The last column says what each shares with mibz2's own benchmark corpora:

File MB What it is Closest in mibz2's corpora bible 4.05 The King James Bible: English prose text, though ours is the crate's own source code, repeated, so more redundant world192 2.47 The CIA World Factbook, 1992: an English record per country Wikidata's subject matter, though not its JSON format ecoli 4.64 The E. coli genome: four letters, a, c, g and t, and notoriously hard to compress No counterpart. Its tiny alphabet is the case the tree algorithms handle best kennedy 1.03 An Excel spreadsheet, full of long runs of one byte runs, and at the extreme onebyte netscape 7.68 Netscape Navigator 4.75: x86 machine code records, binary and structured bashtgz 1.71 bash 2.04's source, gzipped: already compressed, so close to random random

Each algorithm's memory for a 1 MB block, and how fast it inverted each file, in MB/s. The fastest on each file is in bold, and mergedTL is the fastest on every one:

MB bashtgz bible ecoli kennedy netscape world192 Mean basis 5.0 1.54 1.72 1.53 2.46 2.32 1.65 1.86 bw94 5.0 1.58 1.77 1.57 2.54 2.41 1.69 1.93 mergedTL 4.0 2.49 2.76 2.48 4.72 3.51 2.65 3.10 indexF 2.5 1.20 1.36 1.30 1.71 1.67 1.31 1.43 tree-1M 2.0 0.032 0.211 0.325 0.099 0.044 0.207 0.153 treeopt-1M 2.0 0.059 0.301 0.342 0.167 0.099 0.298 0.211 treeopt-500k 1.5 0.032 0.218 0.339 0.100 0.036 0.198 0.154

The paper gives these numbers only as tables. Plotting each algorithm's average speed against its memory shows the space–time tradeoff between them:

Seward's measured speed–memory choices

0 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 working memory, MB for a 10⁶-byte block (Table 1) average rate, MB/s (Table 3) mergedTL 3.10 indexF 1.43 bw94 1.93 basis 1.86 the three tree variants, 0.15–0.21 Each algorithm's average rate over the six files against its memory, from Seward's Tables 1 and 3, on a 400 MHz K6-III in 2001. The paper gives the numbers as tables; the plot is ours.

It isn't a smooth curve on which each saved byte costs speed. mergedTL is "on average 61% and 67% faster than bw94 and basis respectively, at the same time using less memory": it beats both on both axes, by changing how the next link is read. indexF runs at 46% of its speed in 62.5% of its memory. Below that, half a byte a row less costs a factor of seven.

Seward then asks why. Simulating the K6-III's cache with cacheprof, his own profiler, he counted what each does per byte of bible. bw94 runs 18 instructions, with 9 memory references and 1.63 cache misses; mergedTL runs 20 instructions, with 8 references and 0.88 misses. So mergedTL does 11% more work and takes 54% as many misses. 89.4% of those misses are the walk's reads of \(U[p]\), and 78.6% of those reads miss, because \(T\) holds "a completely arbitrary permutation" that the decoder "is obliged to traverse". Seward concludes that "there appears to be no way to avoid a miss rate approaching one per \(L\)-byte", and mergedTL is "a realistic upper bound on inversion performance".

kennedy inverts nearly twice as fast as bashtgz because its long runs make \(T\) point each row at its neighbour, which is usually already cached; random input sets the floor near 2.5 MB/s. And the tree algorithms vary 10:1 across files, against mergedTL's 1.9:1, because a small alphabet such as ecoli's four letters lets a few deep trees shorten every scan.

bzip2 itself decompresses bible at 67% of mergedTL's inversion rate, while also doing its Huffman and move-to-front decoding, so "no amount of re-engineering of bzip2 can increase its decompression speed much further". The paper ends on a caveat:

Such observations only hold true whilst cache sizes are much smaller than block sizes. Future growth in cache sizes may invalidate such findings.

items.title: 5. Four blocks sharing one cache
items.text:
The K6-III's cache held 256 KB, against mergedTL's 4 MB for one block. Our workstation has a 20 MiB last-level cache, and a full bzip2 block, up to 900,000 rows at 4 bytes each, needs a 3.6 MB table. Read literally, the caveat has come true.

Caches against tables, then and now

0 MB 5 MB 10 MB 15 MB 20 MB 2001 K6-III cache 256 KB one block's table 4 MB: about 16 times the cache 2026 workstation cache 20 MiB one block's table 3.6 MB four blocks' tables 14.4 MB: 0.7 of the cache One scale, in megabytes. In 2001 one block's table was far larger than the cache; today one fits several times over, but four take most of it. Table sizes are computed for full blocks, not measured cache occupancy.

Two things kept Seward's sentence true anyway. A modern core keeps many misses in flight if it is given independent loads, so mibz2's walk advances 32 separate pieces of the chain in turn and runs 8.6 times as fast as one chain.

And a decoder doesn't invert one block at a time. Four workers keep four tables live, 14.4 MB before any of their other buffers, in one cache they all share, and decoding with four costs more CPU time per byte than decoding with one: the workers finish sooner together, but compete for the memory system on the way. With the cache divided between blocks, caches are again much smaller than the tables being walked.

On Seward's axes a smaller table is a step down in speed. With four blocks sharing a cache, it also leaves more of the cache to the other three. Could the same links be stored in much less space, and would the lighter memory load make up for the extra work of reading a compressed entry? The first valid comparison answers both ways at once. The compact walk costs 14.85% more CPU time on one core and 15.95% less with four workers walking together. That result is about this traversal, measured on its own; what it means for the whole decoder is still open.

items.title: 6. A smaller table, a busier lookup
items.text:
The census of the navigation table found that most of its links follow simple patterns. An earlier format built on that, FOR-14, packed 14-bit offsets into fixed records. It halved the table, but extracting the packed bits made each step so much longer that the walk lost even with four workers, where it took 1.45 times as long as the ordinary walk.

Compact30 keeps each offset directly addressable instead. Its name means thirty rows per record, not thirty-bit pointers. A 64-byte record, aligned to a cache line, holds thirty 16-bit offsets and a 4-byte header. In an ordinary record the header carries a base position and the byte the thirty rows all output, and a row's next position is the base plus its offset. A group of rows that start with different bytes, or whose next positions are too far apart for 16-bit offsets, is stored instead as a RAW group: thirty full 4-byte entries, padded to 128 bytes.

One ordinary compact30 record

30 offsets, one per row30 × 2 bytes = 60 bytes H4 B Next position = the base in H + this row's offset H also holds the byte the record's rows output. Thirty rows in one cache line. RAW groups, segment starts and parking are handled outside this ordinary case.

On the measured corpus that brings the table from 4 bytes per row to 2.164, 45.9% less: about 1.95 MB for a full block instead of 3.6 MB, and 7.79 MB instead of 14.4 MB for four blocks at once.

Read against Seward's paper, the record combines three of its ideas. Its offsets rest on the ordering that makes \(T\) cheap to build: within one byte's bucket the links increase with the row, so a group's links are a base plus small offsets, smallest where the byte's occurrences in \(L\) sit close together, as in kennedy's runs. In Wikidata's blocks they usually do: about 77% of a full block's rows fall in 32-row groups that each come from a single run in \(L\). The header's byte is indexF's idea, emitting from \(F\) so that the walk needs no \(L\), with one byte stored per group in place of a search. And keeping the header and the offset in one cache line is mergedTL's. At 2.164 bytes a row, the record sits between treeopt-1M and indexF on Seward's memory axis, and aims at mergedTL's speed.

The step costs more, though. An ordinary compact30 step compiles to 21 instructions and four data loads; the conventional step is 16 instructions and three loads. Two of compact30's loads, the offset and the header, are both addressed from the current row, so neither waits for the other, but they are still two loads where the conventional step needs one. The walker's journal has the annotated disassembly.

So the question is which matters more when several cores share the machine: the extra instructions, or the smaller table.

items.title: 7. Timing the walk on one core and on four
items.text:
The comparison times two versions of the same traversal and assembly. The control walks mibz2's 4-byte table; compact30 walks its records with the same 32-lane walk. Every walk's output was checked byte for byte against the decoder's.

Only the walk is timed. Before each walk, the control builds its table with the decoder's own builder, while compact30 copies in records made beforehand by a reference builder, so the comparison measures how fast each prepared table is walked, not what it costs to build. The two preparations may also leave different data in cache.

The protocol used one corpus of 434 blocks (207 million rows) and 20 paired rounds, on one pinned core or four. With four, each worker prepared its next block, all four started walking together, and none checked its output until all had finished, with blocks dealt so that each worker had about the same number of rows. CPU cost is the threads' own CPU time, summed, per row. Completion time is the time from the first walk's start to the last walk's end in each step, summed over the steps. Neither is the decoder's elapsed time.

Conventional Compact30 Compact30 ÷ conventional (95% interval) CPU time per row, one core 1.221 ns 1.402 ns 1.148 (1.147–1.149) CPU time per row, four workers 2.055 ns 1.727 ns 0.840 (0.838–0.843) Completion time per pass, four workers 114.45 ms 97.97 ms 0.856 (0.852–0.860)

The intervals describe variation across the twenty rounds, on one machine and one corpus. Before the run, the protocol fixed what would justify building a direct constructor: the upper end of the four-worker CPU ratio at most 0.865, and of the completion ratio at most 1.02. The upper ends were 0.843 and 0.860. The analysis and an independent reconstruction from the individual walks agree on every figure.

CPU time per row, one core and four workers

CPU nanoseconds per row · lower is better 00.51.01.52.0 One coreFour workers 1.2211.4022.0551.727 ConventionalCompact30 Each walking thread's CPU time, summed and divided by rows. Building the tables is not included.

The gain is spread across the workload. All 230 full-sized blocks were cheaper with compact30 at four workers, taking each block's average over the rounds, and compact30 used less CPU in 1,138 of the 1,140 full-sized four-worker steps. These are checks within one experiment, on blocks that repeat each round, not independent trials. The 204 short blocks were slower with compact30, but together they hold 8,324 rows, 0.004% of the total.

The run also had to show that the four walks started together, within 2% of each step's length. An earlier complete run failed that check, because waking sleeping workers delayed some walks by tens of microseconds, and it doesn't count. This run used a spinning start barrier instead, with nothing else changed; its worst start skew was 0.023%.

items.title: 8. Four workers cost the conventional walk far more
items.text:
From one core to four workers, the conventional walk's CPU cost per row rises from 1.221 ns to 2.055 ns, 68% more. Compact30's rises from 1.402 ns to 1.727 ns, 23% more. Both run under the same four-worker conditions, and the conventional table pays much more for them.

FOR-14 showed the same pattern earlier: from one block to four, the conventional walk's cost per row rose 56% and FOR-14's only 8%. Its smaller table removed most of the four-worker penalty, but each of its steps started 1.40 ns per row behind, three times what it saved. Compact30's step is cheap enough to come out ahead.

The obvious explanation is the table's size. Four conventional tables take about 14.4 MB, four compact30 tables about 7.79 MB, and the test machine's four cores share a 20 MiB last-level cache with everything else the workers use. Smaller tables could mean fewer evictions and less contention for memory, and they could also change address-translation costs.

Navigation tables for four full blocks

Conventional14.4 MB Compact307.79 MB One full-sized block per worker · table sizes, not cache occupancy The tables' sizes on the measured corpus. How much of each stays in cache, and how much memory traffic each causes, was not measured.

That explanation hasn't been tested. The run recorded no cache-miss or memory-controller counters, and the two arms prepared their tables differently before each walk, which by itself could change what is in cache when the walk starts. The size difference makes the cache explanation credible; it doesn't measure it.

The result also stops short of the decoder. A decoding worker doesn't spend all its time walking tables: it also reads input, reconstructs the last column, builds the table, assembles segments and writes output. Some of its walks run alone, and others overlap two or three neighbours rather than all four. So compact30's 14.85% loss on one core matters as much as its gain at four, and how much of a whole decode runs under four-way contention hasn't been measured.

items.title: 9. The table still has to be built
items.text:
The records in this comparison came from a reference builder that first computes every row's successor in a full-sized temporary array, then converts the result into compact30 records. That kept construction out of the measurement, but a decoder can't afford it. A direct builder has to produce the records from the block's last column and its byte counts, without the temporary array.

It also has to compete with the decoder's current builder, which places every row in one counting-sort pass and writes runs of sixteen equal bytes sixteen entries at a time. Compact30's builder has to write group headers, check offsets against the 16-bit limit, and move groups to RAW, and still stay close to that.

The traversal result sets the budget. A rough planning model puts the decoder's current table building at 0.592 CPU-seconds per decoded GB, and the traversal with its assembly at 1.847. If b and w are compact30's building and traversal costs as fractions of today's, the saving is about 0.592 × (1 − b) + 1.847 × (1 − w) CPU-seconds per GB, and the target is at least 0.25.

If the four-worker traversal ratio carried over to the decoder, a builder costing the same as today's would save about 0.295 CPU-seconds per GB. The builder could be up to 7.5% slower than today's at the central estimate, or 6.7% using the conservative end of the interval. That is a budget conditional on the traversal gain surviving inside the decoder, built on approximate phase costs; meeting it would justify the next test, not settle the question.

The next step is a design for that builder, set out in the constructor brief. Its main difficulty is already clear. Groups that straddle two bytes' rows can be found from the byte counts before any row is placed, but a group whose offsets turn out too wide is only known when its last row lands, and has to move to RAW then. The builder has to produce exactly the records tested here, and the first measurements will be whether it does and what it costs. After that, a whole-decoder comparison can show how much of the four-worker gain survives in practice.

For now, a smaller navigation table has beaten the conventional one in a controlled four-worker traversal while losing on a single core. That is a strong reason to study the memory contention behind it, and a concrete budget for building the table.

Research records: Traversal protocol and the runs behind it · This result's records · Independent reconstruction · Compact30 walker · FOR-14 trial.

items.title: An autonomous agent team
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The last post was about compact30, my effort to give the decoder's navigation table a smaller representation. Four agents did the research behind it, but until today they could only work together if I copied each one's messages to the next by hand.

This post is about how they now pass work between themselves through the repository: who does what, how a message gets from one agent to another, and what I learnt from running it: an afternoon, a first full cycle, and then a first night with nobody watching. That night produced real gains, and one ordinary mistake that taught me the most: a message can be sent, and recorded as sent, without ever being delivered.

items.title: Call on mibz2: cutting instructions from bzip2 decoding with an autonomous swarm
items.text:
Each of four agents does one part of the research. A GitHub doorbell lets them hand work to each other directly, without me acting as their message bus.

4 November 2026, revised 5 November · 20 min read · Meta

items.title: 1. A tale of four agents
items.text:
The Coordinator is Claude Code. It writes the code for each change in the plan, compiles it, runs the tests and keeps the results. When a result is ready it posts a checkpoint: a comment saying what was built and which commit holds the evidence.

The Guardian and the Researcher both read every checkpoint, looking for different things. The Guardian checks the result against the research charter: which gates it passes, what work can follow, and what has to come to me. The Researcher looks at the reasoning: whether the argument holds, whether something else explains the numbers, whether there's a better direction, and whether the Guardian has got it right.

The Optimiser works on the instruction counts themselves. It reads the source, the compiled listings and the execution counts, works out transformations that remove instructions, and keeps the ledger of what each one saves. Its proposals are what the Coordinator builds next.

The Guardian, the Researcher and the Optimiser all run Astra, a model I use through ChatGPT, each as a ChatGPT Work task with its own reasoning-effort setting. What separates them is what they're responsible for, not the model. The roles, and the branch each one owns, are written down in ROLES.md. To reproduce the setup, these are the settings:

Role Runs as Model Reasoning effort Started by Coordinator Claude Code session Claude, as configured for the session High a subscription to the shared channel, #145, and the PRs it follows Guardian ChatGPT Work task, Compact30 (W) Guardian Astra Extra High a new comment in its inbox, #161 Optimiser ChatGPT Work task, Compact30 (W) Optimiser Astra Ultra a new comment in its inbox, #160 Researcher ChatGPT Work task, Compact30 (W) Researcher Astra Extra High a new comment in its inbox, #162

Each Astra agent's instructions live in the repository as its agent spec, beside ROLES.md. SPEC.md holds what the three have in common: how a run goes, from the inbox comment to the receipt, the work and the review, and the reasoning behind that design. SPEC.OPTIMIZER.md, SPEC.GUARDIAN.md and SPEC.RESEARCHER.md each say only what that agent's work is. A task's prompt in ChatGPT is a single sentence pointing at its two files at one pinned commit. So an agent's behaviour changes only by a commit to its spec and a new pin, both of which stay in the record. SPEC.md also holds the one command that loads a new pin into all three tasks.

The team: three Astra agents and Claude Code, joined by one repository

Astra · ChatGPT Workeach role is an event-triggered task, started by a comment in its own inboxGuardianapplies the charter's gatesto every checkpointExtra HighOptimisersearches the listings forinstructions to cutUltraResearcherquestions the reasoningbehind every checkpointExtra HighThe repositorymessages are pull-request comments · each agent keeps its state on its own branch · every claim pins a commitCoordinator · Claude Codeimplements and tests each change,then posts it as a checkpoint Claude Code builds each change and posts a checkpoint. The Guardian checks it against the rules and the Researcher checks the reasoning, while the Optimiser hunts for more instructions to cut. All four work through the same repository.

items.title: 2. Every result is a commit
items.text:
A checkpoint points at a commit, never at a branch, because a branch keeps moving. The commit holds the source and its baseline, the compiled listings, the toolchain, the test records, the execution counts and the arithmetic that ties them together. Reports and scripts go in files, and the comment links to them.

That lets a reader check a claim rather than take it on trust. If the Optimiser predicts that a change will remove a load from the inner loop, the checkpoint shows whether the compiled code actually lost it, whether setup got more expensive, whether a caller picked up a spill, and how often each path runs.

Each agent writes only to its own branch: the Coordinator to the implementation branches, the others to their reports, decision logs and ledgers. Every file has one author, and a review never edits the code it reviews. Each agent also keeps its working state on its branch, which is why a fresh run can pick up exactly where the last one stopped.

items.title: 3. Comments as messages, events as the clock
items.text:
The agents talk in comments on pull requests. Each comment starts with a short header:

FROM: coordinator
TO: guardian
RE: prototype 2 @ 29dd071f8787a28560a7a081fd7ac0ef13991466
TYPE: CHECKPOINT

FROM: names the sender, since every agent posts from the same account. TO: records who it's for, RE: pins the commit, and TYPE: says what kind of message it is. The protocol has six types:

Type Means CHECKPOINT a result at a pinned commit, ready to assess REVIEW an assessment, with its evidence on the sender's branch PROPOSAL an idea to consider; not permission to build it DECISION a decision the sender is allowed to make ACK what was received, and what happens next ESCALATION something only I can decide

The messages travel through draft PRs that are never merged. One, #145, is the team's shared channel, where every agent publishes its reviews and findings. Each Astra agent also has a quiet inbox of its own, where it receives work: #160 for the Optimiser, #161 for the Guardian and #162 for the Researcher. Each experiment has a PR of its own too.

Here is what that looks like on GitHub. Every comment comes from my account, lmmx, and the small badge on the avatar shows which app posted it: Claude's mark for the Coordinator, ChatGPT's for the Astra agents. The header is the only thing that says which agent wrote it.

Three agents, one account: a checkpoint from the Coordinator, the Guardian's review of it, and the independent reviewer's report, all on #145. Read the whole exchange

The originals: the checkpoint, the Guardian's review and the independent review.

A new comment is also what wakes the agents up. Each Astra agent is a Work task subscribed to new comments on its own inbox and nothing else, so the filtering happens before a run starts. The inbox is the address: every comment in it is for its agent. The Coordinator posts each checkpoint to the inbox of every agent that should act on it, so a checkpoint for the Guardian and the Researcher is two comments, one in each inbox. Each run fetches its comment, reads from the header who sent it and what kind of message it is, and does the work. It commits a receipt to its own branch first, then its progress as it goes, and publishes its REVIEW on #145. The Coordinator subscribes to #145, so a reply reaches it within seconds.

This keeps each agent's attention on its own work. An inbox carries only messages meant for its agent, so the other agents' reviews, CI results and pull requests never start a run there. An investigation that takes a quarter of an hour runs to the end undisturbed, and everything it finds still comes back to one place.

One cycle: a checkpoint to two inboxes, two reviews, the next step

1 · Checkpointa result at a pinned commit,posted to each reader's inbox2 · Guardianapplies the gates,posts a REVIEW on #1452 · Researchertests the reasoning,posts a REVIEW on #1453 · Next stepthe Coordinator wakes,acts on both reviewseventeventMeanwhile · Optimiserworks on briefs from its own inbox, #160; once implemented, its proposals become new checkpoints Each arrow is a pull-request comment. A checkpoint goes to the inbox of each agent that should act on it, and each review comes back on the shared channel, #145, where it wakes the Coordinator. No Astra agent polls, and nothing goes through me.

items.title: 4. A receipt for every message
items.text:
Before doing any work, a run checks its cursor: a file on its branch listing the comments it has already handled. Then it loads what it needs, does the work, posts its result, and adds the comment to the cursor. If several comments arrive at once, each is checked separately. For technical reviews the key also includes the PR, the candidate's commit and a hash of the evidence, so a repeated request can't be mistaken for a revised candidate.

The cursor answers "have I already done this?" for the next run, and it lets me trace every message to what came of it. Two cases it doesn't cover on its own: a run that posts its result but stops before saving the cursor, and two runs of the same agent at once. Recording the result's commit and comment ID makes the first recoverable. I haven't tested either case yet.

A review queue in the repository lists what is waiting on whom. Work that depends on a pending review waits for it, and everything else goes ahead.

items.title: 5. What a message can authorise
items.text:
The research charter sets out what is authorised: the representation, the reference builder, the baselines, and for each prototype a registered design, acceptance criteria and a fixed number of attempts. Inside that, the Coordinator implements and tests without asking me, and the Guardian makes the decisions delegated to it. Anything that widens the work, such as a new prototype, new unsafe code or integration into production, needs me.

So the rule is: a message in the repository can narrow what's allowed, but only I can widen it, and only in the Coordinator's session. A finding can put a prototype on hold. A proposal can suggest something new, but nobody acts on it unless it's already authorised or I say so. Charter amendments are approved the same way, and every review cites the charter revision it applied.

This matters because every agent posts through my GitHub account, as the screenshots in section 3 show, so FROM: guardian names a role without proving who wrote it. The repository also limits who can comment, and the channel PRs are locked. Before the Guardian went live it was tested on exactly this: it was sent forged requests for things only I can approve, and turned both of them down.

items.title: 6. Reproducible, independent review
items.text:
The main figure for compact30 counts the instructions executed by the whole table builder and everything it calls, weighted by how often each path runs on the corpus. Setup, fallbacks, callers, callees and extra memory operations all count, and a saving that only moves work elsewhere is charged where the work lands. Correctness needs its own evidence: byte-identical output against the reference builder, safety arguments for release builds, Miri checks for undefined behaviour, and mutation tests that break an invariant on purpose to show the tests notice.

Reviewers treat the implementer's write-up as a set of claims to check, and work the figures out again from the source, listings, counters and test records. Before prototypes are combined, the charter also asks for one review by an agent that has seen none of the discussion. The ongoing Researcher can't do that: it has followed the work, and it suggested some of the tests. So it started a fresh helper whose only input was a pinned brief, and recorded exactly what that helper was given. A fresh run on its own wouldn't have been enough: the point is that the reviewer never saw the discussion.

items.title: 7. What running it looks like
items.text:
The first afternoon taught me what to expect. Mostly it comes down to patience, and knowing where to look.

Runs are long and quiet. A Work task can spend anything from a minute to a quarter of an hour on one message: the Researcher's revision of this post took about sixteen minutes, most of it reading the record and testing drafts on simulated readers. Between runs, a task's page just shows that it has worked. That means it is waiting for its next comment, not that it has stalled.

Each run has room to finish. Its inbox receives nothing else while it works, and the Coordinator sends an agent its next brief only after the last one has been published. A run commits a receipt first and its progress as it goes, so if one ever stops part-way, a short resume in its inbox picks it up from its last commit.

Watch the repository, not the task pages. Every message ends in a receipt: a cursor commit on the agent's own branch, then a REVIEW on #145 that cites it. A message with a receipt but no review is in progress. One with neither, while the agent's branch is still, gets a resume, once.

When an agent starts a helper of its own, I ask it to keep its run open until the helper has published, and to record both the launch and the result. The independent reviewer was set up this way, with its settings and inputs written to the repository before it began.

Keeping things moving is the Coordinator's job. When the record goes quiet, it checks the receipts, works out who has the next step, and posts the checkpoint that starts it. No Astra agent runs on a timer. On the first night the Coordinator's session had one, waking it every quarter of an hour to re-read its mode note; otherwise it too wakes on events. Nothing sits waiting for me.

items.title: 8. What a shared message board got wrong
items.text:
The design above is the second one. The first put every message on one PR, #145, and let every agent read the whole board. It looked simple, and over the evening of 4 November it went wrong in five ways.

Every event woke every agent. Each Work task started on any comment in the repository, fetched it, and decided for itself whether it was addressed. A review from one agent, a CI result, a preview bot's comment or a merged PR started a run in all three, and nearly all of those runs ended straight away with "not for me".

A new run displaced the one in progress, and nothing caught the loss. The automation keeps one current run per task. When an event arrived while a long run was still working, the new run took its place, and the earlier one stopped without an error, a partial result or any record of what it had read. There was no dead-letter queue to catch it. That evening six briefs to the Optimiser went this way. Each run started and began reading, and each was overtaken within two or three minutes: by the other agents' reviews of the same checkpoint, by a bot, or by a merge. None of them committed anything. From outside, it simply looked as if the Optimiser had gone quiet.

A dead-letter queue is the post office's room for letters that can be neither delivered nor returned. A message system keeps one so that a failed message is set aside where someone can find it. The first design had none, so a displaced run left no trace.

Routing by header was brittle. Each agent decided from TO: and TYPE: lines whether a comment was meant for it, sometimes by exact string. A checkpoint naming two agents had to be worded exactly right for both, and a message that failed the test was dropped without trace.

Noise spent the wakes. Every one of those runs counts against a task's use of the automation, and on a busy board most of them went on comments the agent then ignored.

The connector added friction. The Astra agents reach GitHub through ChatGPT's GitHub connector, not a shell with git as the Coordinator has. Their runs hit errors such as a call missing its repository argument, or "no usable execution environment". Each was recoverable, but each one lengthened a run, and a longer run was more likely to be overtaken. The task settings also can't show their subscriptions back, so the only way to confirm where an agent listens is to watch where it wakes.

The inboxes fix all five. An agent's subscription now covers its own inbox and nothing else, so the only events it sees are its own work, and there's nothing to filter by header. With nothing else arriving, a long run finishes. A receipt is committed first, so a stopped run leaves a trace that a one-line resume can pick up. The wake budget goes on work. And each agent's instructions are an agent spec at a pinned commit, so what each one does can be read in the repository, not inferred from a task page.

They also bring a failure of their own: when the address is the mechanism, a message sent to the wrong address fails without a sound.

items.title: 9. Trust, but verify
items.text:
In the inbox design a comment in #160 wakes the Optimiser, and the same comment on #145 wakes nobody but the Coordinator. That is what keeps each agent's attention on its own work.

A checkpoint that looked dispatched. On the night of 4–5 November the Coordinator ran the research with nobody watching. At 06:03 UTC it sent the Optimiser a brief in #160, and the review came back at 06:12. At 07:38 it posted the next brief, reporting that the fused post-walk pass (#183) had been rejected, to #145 instead, and at 08:21 an addendum to the same place. Both had the right header and the right TO:, the first pinned its commit, and GitHub accepted both. Then the Coordinator waited for a review that couldn't come.

I found it at my morning check, by looking at what had happened rather than at what had been reported:

  • the two comments were on #145;
  • the Optimiser's inbox had received nothing since 06:03;
  • its task's run history showed no run since 06:12.

The Coordinator had intended to dispatch an assignment, and GitHub had confirmed that a comment was posted. Neither fact established that the Optimiser had received the work. Correctness of intent and correctness of record both held. Correctness of effect didn't.

The recovery didn't need me as a message bus. I pointed out the discrepancy. The Coordinator re-sent both messages as one checkpoint in the right inbox at 08:31, said so in that message, and logged the mistake in the channel log. The Optimiser's run started from that comment, its cursor marked the brief finished, and its review came back at 08:48, proposing the next build. The work had sat at the wrong address for 53 minutes. Once the error was visible, the system recovered by its own means: a corrected checkpoint in the right inbox, and a review back on #145.

A guard that guarded nothing. At 08:26 the Coordinator squash-merged #185, naming the commit it expected as the PR's head, so that the merge would be refused if anything had been pushed after CI tested it. It passed c32ba5db3b0f…: the first eight characters of the real head, c32ba5db9df8…, padded out to forty with characters it made up. The merge went through anyway. The right commit merged, since nothing had been pushed after it. But the check the Coordinator relied on to merge only the commit CI had tested had checked nothing. A short prefix had been refused on an earlier merge, which was why the check seemed to work. The Coordinator noticed when it read the head back, fourteen seconds after merging.

Both mistakes have the same shape: an agent's report of its own action is a claim, like any other claim in this project, and it needs an observable effect behind it. The research already works that way, since every result pins a commit that a reviewer can check. The coordination didn't. The answer isn't for me to watch more closely. It's small, deterministic checks on the few actions whose effects matter, so that a route is computed rather than remembered, and a posted message or a merge is read back rather than assumed. The Coordinator still runs them on itself, so they narrow this failure rather than remove it.

Check What it compares Status route an assignment's destination: the role's inbox, or, while it is busy, staged on #145 as TYPE: QUEUED required before each assignment; none posted since it landed verify the posted comment, read back by ID: its PR, its header, the only assignment in flight required after each; replayed, it fails the 07:38 misroute and passes the 08:31 dispatch head-sha a merge's expected head against the PR's exact 40-character head, before the merge and, with --merged, after it before: since #186; after: since #190; rejects #185's SHA audit every message on #145 and the inboxes since the inbox cutover in use at each session start and wake-up; in its tests, the 120 comments up to 08:49 give exactly the two misroutes the tripwire each new comment on #145 or an inbox, checked by a GitHub Actions workflow that runs independently of the Coordinator in use as a record: a failing check on #145's head until the next commit there; no event for the Coordinator

The first four are one stdlib script, coord.py, added in #186, and the repository's CLAUDE.md says when the Coordinator runs each one. The script only reads: it never posts, edits or deletes. The tripwire can't stop a misroute, only report it. It never edits, moves or re-posts a comment, and never dispatches anything itself, so it can't create work of its own.

QUEUED marks work that must wait its turn. While a role is busy, its next brief is set down on #145, and the Coordinator carries it to the role's inbox once the role is free.

The tripwire needed the same treatment as everything else. A workflow started by a comment runs only from master, so each version could be tested only after it merged. The Coordinator tested each one with a deliberate, labelled misroute on #145, and each test found something that the code and its unit tests hadn't.

A check run is one line in a pull request's list of checks. GitHub gathers a workflow's runs into a suite, and the Coordinator hears only when a whole suite finishes.

  • The first was classified correctly, and then its warning couldn't be posted: #145 is locked, and the Actions bot can't comment on a locked conversation.
  • The second raised a failing check run on #145 instead. The check showed red, but nothing woke the Coordinator.
  • The third made its check run start in progress and then fail, to reopen the suite. The suite stayed green and sent no event: a GitHub Actions suite follows its workflow run, not check runs added to it.

One of these tests refuted a claim that had already merged: #188 went in saying its check run would wake the Coordinator, and its test showed within a minute that it didn't.

So the tripwire is a record, not an alarm. It leaves a failing check on #145's head commit, independently of the Coordinator, and the check shows on #145 until the next commit to the channel branch. The Coordinator finds the misroute itself, by running audit at the start of each session and every time it wakes.

The merge guard needed the same treatment, and got it only while this post was being checked. A reviewing agent pointed out that GitHub refuses a mismatched head, and it does: a merge of #139 was refused with a 409 on 2 November. The guess had never reached GitHub. The merge tool takes the expected head as expectedHeadSha, and the Coordinator had been passing it as sha, a name the tool doesn't have and drops without a word. The prefix refused earlier had met the tool's own format check, under the right name. Read back, eight merges between 02:12 and 09:36 had passed the head that way, among them an earlier guess on #167 and four merges made after head-sha existed. Each merged its PR's final head, so nothing wrong landed, but none was checked. head-sha had checked the value; nothing had checked that the value reached the merge. #190 adds the missing step: the SHA goes in expectedHeadSha, and head-sha --merged reads the merge back and passes only if the PR merged at exactly that head.

Three gaps remain. The checks are run by the Coordinator on itself: CLAUDE.md says when, but nothing outside its session makes it run them, and the tripwire, the one check outside it, can only leave a mark. The Coordinator can't see the Astra tasks' run history; it infers a run from receipts in the cursors, which route reads. And a brief that was delivered but never started, one with no receipt half an hour after it was posted, is still caught only by the Coordinator noticing a quiet record (section 7). A mechanical check for it would close the loop from sent to started. It isn't built.

items.title: 10. Where it stands
items.text:
The channel log records each step. The trigger was first tested on the Guardian: a comment started its run, it published an assessment, and its review woke the Coordinator. The first real cycle followed on a checkpoint covering two prototypes. The Guardian's run started nine seconds after it was posted, checked both prototypes against the gates, and asked for the independent review.

That review came back while this post was being finished. The Researcher launched the isolated reviewer, and its report arrived as a comment on the channel. Both prototypes pass on correctness and safety, and so does v3's finaliser. Two things need fixing before anything is combined: some changed paths still need their own execution counters, and both prototypes remove the same instruction, so their savings overlap. That is the next checkpoint.

On 5 November the redesigned setup ran its first full round:

  • The Optimiser ranked the whole decoder's candidates from its inbox. It put P87, a production-shaped change that writes the walk's output over a buffer it has already consumed, first.
  • The Coordinator built P87 and registered a decision rule before measuring it.
  • The Guardian and the Researcher reviewed that rule from their inboxes before the benchmark finished. The Guardian's review changed it.
  • The change made the four-worker Wikidata decode 2.2% faster in one run, and favourable but inconclusive in a second, with 6.8% less memory and no slower row. It merged.

Then all three agents took their next assignment under the new specs:

  • each woke only on its own inbox;
  • each committed a receipt within a minute or two, and published its review on #145;
  • the Guardian also moved itself onto its current operating spec.

The first reviews under the new design corrected the Coordinator's write-up before it was published.

The rest of that night was the first long test. At 02:52 UTC, at my instruction, the Coordinator's mode note was amended to tell it to fan out hard on the hard research, and to do tests, CI and documentation itself rather than spend agents on them. From then until my morning check it ran with nobody watching. Only the Optimiser was in the loop: the Guardian and the Researcher received no work after 00:36.

The Coordinator's Claude Code workflows put several agents on one question at once. In one, three agents mined an old CI sweep, modelled each runner's per-core miss resources and built a walk keyed on SMT co-residency, and three sceptics each refuted part of that work. Another reviewed the fused post-walk change through three lenses, one of them a differential of about 14,600 valid and corrupt inputs against master, which found no divergence. The workflows' own records stay in the Coordinator's session; the journal keeps what they found. Every decoder change that reached a pull request still went through the CI benchmark, under a decision rule registered before its first run, without review by the Guardian or the Researcher.

Five decoder changes merged. Two trimmed the move-to-front stage (#170, #172). #171 staged the walk's output through one tile, for a four-thread wall 5% to 14% faster over five runs. #180 widened the window of blocks in flight, for 8% to 10% in three runs, at a cost of 4% to 6% more CPU and 8 MB more memory. The Coordinator weighed that in the journal and accepted it, noting that the extra CPU still has to be measured in wikidata-pq's pipeline, where the decoder shares its cores. #181 removed the deferred flags that #171 had carried with it: the decoder ran about 4% more instructions and still got faster. That fits the reading that the walk is bound by memory requests in flight rather than by instructions, though no hardware counter has shown it. The benchmark history, which chains each merge's own paired run, now puts the four-thread Wikidata wall at 0.75× its value at #69 (95% band 0.69–0.82), against 0.85× before #180. The chain assumes that a change measured on one runner holds on another.

As much again was tested and rejected. The 32 KiB tile, 1024 offsets a lane, filled the whole of Zen 4's L1D and ran 23.5% slower even at one thread (#177, #178). The fused post-walk pass (#183) halved the simulated cache misses after the walk, but the four-thread wall wasn't shown to follow: neither PR run was faster there beyond noise, though the fusion alone was, by 1.5%. October's four-copy win for a walk keyed on SMT co-residency reversed on today's staged walk. Split condition variables were rejected on a count of wasted wakes before anything was built.

Each is written up in the journal with its runs. The walk round had already redirected the work: since the 06:03 checkpoint the Optimiser has ranked candidates by the memory traffic of four workers on two SMT cores, not by instruction counts, and the fused pass and split condition variables were its first and third picks. Their failures narrowed the search to the walk's random reads and its table's footprint. The next build the Optimiser proposed is a retest of compact30's smaller table under today's staged walk, though its own prior on it is weak.

So the work moves without me relaying it. When a message went to the wrong address, the record showed it, and the Coordinator corrected it without my carrying anything across, though it took me to notice. Now the Coordinator reads each message and each merge back rather than assume they landed, and a misroute leaves a failing check on #145 that the Coordinator didn't write. Whether all of this makes the research faster will keep showing in the benchmark history.

If you want to set up something similar:

  • give each agent its own inbox, and one shared place to publish;
  • have each run commit a receipt before it works, and its progress as it goes;
  • point every message at an exact commit;
  • wake agents with events rather than timers, and keep those events few;
  • keep every agent's instructions in the repository at a pinned commit;
  • write down what a message is allowed to authorise;
  • decide what an independent reviewer gets to see;
  • check effects, not reports: read every message back where it should have landed, and every merge back after it lands.

My own part is choosing the scope and making the decisions the charter keeps for me.
