items.title: 2.4 Why this might reduce work
items.text:
A single induction step manipulates the terminal intervals' lengths, order relations and word references. It does not traverse each row of the interval being removed.

Let \(S\) count elementary induction steps. For the original right-end construction, the Wikidata research census reported:

Quantity Value Run density \(r/n\) 0.0722 Induction steps per run \(S/r\) 1.812 Induction steps per row \(S/n\) 0.1309

Approximately 131,000 induction steps per million BWT rows, for this recorded Wikidata workload and the right-end schedule, not a general complexity bound.

This is where the original performance hypothesis comes from. We replace approximately one permutation transition per output byte with substantially fewer, more regular interval operations, followed by grammar expansion.

There are important limits. An adversarial text such as \((ab)^ka\), whose BWT has only two runs, can take linearly many (\(O(n)\)) elementary right-end steps. The journal identifies a possible division rule for batching repeated subtraction, but that is not part of the current Cells kernel. This accelerates induction itself: a repeated-winner sequence such as \(17-3-3-3-3-3=2\) can be represented by \(17=5\cdot3+2\), provided its word, order and marker updates are composed exactly. The connection is to Zorich-style acceleration, distinct from choosing a different induction schedule or optimising the conventional table walker.

There are also alternative induction orders with fewer steps. The journal found one reaching approximately \(1.279r\) steps versus \(1.812r\) at the right end. Choosing those steps cheaply is itself an unresolved algorithmic problem. Fewer transformations do not guarantee lower total construction cost.

Source: MONODROMY mathematical construction, §§1–5.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 3. The reconstruction program produced by induction
items.text:
The crucial second compression happens in the words.

Initially, each interval has a one-byte word. As induction proceeds, the algorithm creates rules of the form

\[ N_k\longrightarrow U_iU_j. \]

Rather than copying the contents of \(U_i\) and \(U_j\) every time, it can retain their identities and lengths.

The resulting structure is a straight-line program, a directed acyclic grammar with exactly one derivation for each nonterminal.

For example, an illustrative grammar could be

\[ \begin{aligned} U_0&\to \texttt{a},\\ U_1&\to \texttt{b},\\ U_2&\to U_0U_1,\\ U_3&\to U_2U_2,\\ U_4&\to U_3U_2. \end{aligned} \]

The root \(U_4\) expands to six bytes, but the description contains reusable references to smaller words.

A word identity does not identify its occurrence

A word identity does not identify its occurrenceThe illustrative grammar expands U4 to ababab. Highlight the b at expansion offset 3, distinct from b at offsets 1 and 5. Rotating there yields bababa; repetition to 10 bytes yields bababababa.One definition; several occurrencesU₀ = a U₁ = bU₂ = U₀U₁ = abU₃ = U₂U₂ = ababU₄ = U₃U₂ = abababExpansion offsets (not BWT row IDs)a0b1a2b3a4b5Start at marked offset 3: bababaRepeat / truncate to 10: bababababa The source grammar, expanded exactly. The highlighted offset illustrates output phase; it is not numerically equated with orig_ptr, and this toy grammar is not claimed to be a particular LF cycle. Equal bytes and equal subwords can occur at distinct positions. A real decoder must obtain the marked occurrence from its induction invariant.

This is not an output-compression format being added to bzip2. It is an intermediate reconstruction program. Its purpose is to replace expensive permutation navigation with cheaper grammar construction and memory copying.

The MONODROMY journal makes a stronger structural observation about the right-end construction: its grammar corresponds to a Lyndon-related decomposition of the reconstructed text. That helps explain why these particular concatenations arise, although the decoder's correctness does not require us to implement a general Lyndon-factorisation library.

items.title: Recovering the correct BWT origin
items.text:
It is insufficient to construct just any cyclic rotation of the text.

The decoded output must begin at the phase specified by orig_ptr. For periodic inputs, the selected permutation cycle can also be shorter than \(n\).

The original mathematical construction has a marked-point invariant. One particularly useful implementation replaces the marked row with a singleton letter and propagates a marker through the grammar.

When induction terminates, the marker identifies a path through the grammar to that original row.

This gives both:

  1. The correct permutation cycle to reconstruct.
  2. The position at which to rotate its word to produce the required output.

For a cycle of length \(p\), the output is the correctly rotated cycle repeated and truncated to \(n\) bytes.

The marker has to identify a particular occurrence or trajectory, not merely the contents of a word. Two equal grammar words may represent different return destinations.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: Converting the grammar into actual bytes
items.text:
The reconstruction phase must still emit \(n\) bytes. No induction theorem eliminates that work.

The original research writer uses short inline words and longer grammar rules. It finds suitable output positions for rule expansions, expands factors, and uses copies from already materialised occurrences.

Long factors, repeated occurrences, the marked path and the final cyclic rotation require careful handling. These are not incidental implementation details: they determine both memory safety and the actual number of writes.

A previous writer version left certain marked-spine bytes unwritten—the marked spine is the grammar path carrying the selected occurrence. The corrected implementation includes targeted long-factor tests and independent review of the writer-safety finding F01. That episode is a useful reminder that the grammar representation and its output schedule are separate correctness problems.

At the end of the process, the original RLE1 decoding and CRC obligations remain.

This gives us a complete theoretical pipeline:

From run intervals to verified output

From run intervals to verified outputFive transformations: run records, weighted interval exchange, induction grammar, cycle-word reconstruction, RLE1 and CRC output. Each arrow changes the representation rather than transporting a message.Run representation of Lbyte values · lengths · orig_ptrWeighted interval exchangetop / bottom orders · lengths · wordsInduction and grammarcompose returns · preserve the markCycle-word reconstructionexpand · position · copy · repeatRLE1, CRC and outputdecode byte runs · verify checksum Structural pipeline, not a timing or scale diagram. The grammar replaces permutation navigation; it does not remove output stores, run-length decoding (RLE1), or checksum (CRC) verification.

This is the central theoretical approach. Everything in the later labelling, surgery, first-return and performance experiments concerns how to represent or execute some part of this pipeline more economically.

items.title: 4. How the Cells algorithm implements that mathematics
items.text:
The early research considered a fairly direct representation: two doubly linked orders of interval records, with each step updating links and creating one grammar rule.

That representation was correct, but fairly expensive. The important implementation advance was Cells.

Instead of continually modifying linked records, Cells processes the two orders from their right-hand ends, creates a permanent record for each consumed interval piece, and leaves surviving portions in a small amount of register state.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: A cell is a completed piece of the induced map
items.text:
A cell contains the information needed for the represented interval piece: its width, word identity and relationships to its position in the other order.

Each step creates one cell corresponding to the shorter terminal overlap. Once written, the cell itself does not need to be repositioned or repeatedly patched.

The algorithm maintains two fronts:

  • The last currently unconsumed interval in top order.
  • The last currently unconsumed interval in bottom order.

For each front it carries the remaining length, word, predecessor information and the location where its next cell belongs in the other order.

This makes a substantial difference to the inner loop.

The original linked-order construction needed to maintain the connections of changing objects. The Cells construction instead uses promised slots: when an interval still has an unconsumed remainder, a location is reserved for its next completed piece. That allows the current cell's references to be finalised without later traversing a chain of displaced objects.

The central induction work is essentially:

Read terminal letters A and B from the two orders.

While the marked component is not closed:
    s = min(remaining_length(A), remaining_length(B))
    N = concatenate(word(A), word(B))

    Construct the completed cell of width s.
    Write its top- and bottom-order records.

    Consume s from both active terminal portions.
    Keep any winning remainder in register state.

    When a front is exhausted, read its predecessor.
    When a component closes, retain or discard it
    according to whether it contains the marked row.

Recover the marked cycle's grammar root.
Expand its word in the required origin phase.

That is a structural summary, not a substitute for the implementation's equal-length, closure and buffer-boundary logic.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: The physical representation
items.text:
The implemented research design uses two arrays of 24-byte slots, holding the two orders. It also has a small-word arena, a longer-rule arena and writer-position storage.

References within the principal buffer are 32-bit offsets, rather than separately allocated Rust objects with full pointers.

That matters because a graph of heap-allocated nodes would introduce additional allocation, pointer loading and cache-line traffic. Cells is deliberately laid out to avoid much of that.

The protected #365 implementation records the explicit bound

\[ \boxed{\begin{gathered} \text{Kernel buffers}\leq\\ 48R+84B+4{,}528+4G\text{ bytes} \end{gathered}} \]

where:

  • \(R\) is the record count used for allocation;
  • \(B\) is the permitted number of cells;
  • \(G=64\) in debug/Miri and zero in release.

The coefficient \(48R\) corresponds to two 24-byte order records per initial record. The \(84B\) term covers additional slots, word/rule storage and writer positions.

In production admission, the cell budget is bounded by

\[ B\leq\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{25}\right\rfloor. \]

The implementation also refuses high-density inputs before induction, checks the marked-letter floor (the number of letters after splitting out the marked row, minus one), and checks the cell budget before every cell.

On refusal, it calls the existing Segmented inversion path. This is not a loss of correctness; it is an attempt to prevent pathological induction costs.

These bounds describe the experimental Cells kernel's allocated working storage, not total decoder RSS. They exclude existing fallback scratch, input/output buffers, allocator metadata and fixed kernel state. Buffers also retain their high-water capacity across blocks.

items.title: Why 24-byte slots and a common buffer matter
items.text:
This is where the algorithm starts becoming a physical-computing design rather than just a combinatorial one.

The slots are fixed-width and reached through offsets in contiguous allocations. A completed cell is generally written in two places determined by the two orderings, so this is not a purely sequential array algorithm. Nevertheless, those destinations are often knowable before the step that writes them.

The research implementation prefetches information approximately 12 slots ahead of the current frontier. On its original research machine, that change reduced a cell's observed time from roughly 9.8 ns to 7.2–7.7 ns in the tested samples. These were the same ten sampled Wikidata blocks, one run per variant on the shared research container; the journal warns of roughly 10% run-to-run variation, and the intermediate variants were not committed. This is a historical observation, not a portable prefetch-distance or speed guarantee.

This is a direct example of mathematical structure informing microarchitecture: because the induction determines future slot destinations, the implementation can request the associated cache lines before they are needed.

The 24-byte layout is a logical packing choice; it is not a promise that every record is contained within one cache line. Explicit unaligned accesses are part of the implementation's safety argument.

The 16-byte short-word representation is another deliberate choice. Frequently used small words can be stored as bytes, while longer words remain grammar references.

Source: Cells safety and layout argument.

Layout and bound record.

items.title: 5. What physically happens in memory and the cache hierarchy
items.text:
It is useful to distinguish the idealised algorithmic objects from their actual storage and access patterns.

Object Physical representation Main cost or concern Conventional inverse table Contiguous 32-bit entries, \(4n\) bytes Dependent and irregular reads during traversal BWT run input Compact byte/length records Sequential scanning, conversion and record coalescing Cells interval orders Two arrays of 24-byte slots Reads and writes through two orderings; prefetchability Cells short words Inline bytes in an arena Small writes and short copies Longer return words Grammar rules referring to earlier words Grammar-node creation, traversal and output copies Delimiter first-return state Interval records, frontier and completed pieces Boundary splitting, lookups and metadata Phrase dictionary/hash cons Word IDs, child references, hash-table slots Lookup traffic, growth, allocation and retained metadata Final output Byte buffers for BWT inversion, RLE1 and writer stages Unavoidable output plus any additional copies

items.title: The key distinction: bytes resident versus bytes accessed
items.text:
The original research journal estimated a Cells live working set of several megabytes for a large Wikidata block, potentially larger than the conventional permutation table.

That sounds counterintuitive if we're expecting compression to save memory.

But its intended advantage was not necessarily a smaller total allocation. It was a more favourable pattern of accessing that allocation.

For a conventional permutation table, successive accesses within a chain depend on previously loaded destinations. If the next entry misses private cache, execution can stall waiting for the appropriate line.

With Cells, the principal operations include fixed-size records, short-word writes, prefetchable order fronts and eventual output copies. These can offer more predictable memory traffic and more opportunity for overlap.

That distinction showed up in the journal's instrumented analysis: on selected Wikidata blocks, Cells used fewer instructions and substantially fewer simulated private-cache misses than the conventional build-plus-walk path.

However, simulated misses on one machine are not measurements of L1/L2/L3 residency on the i9 workstation, and certainly not proof of equal behaviour with several decoder workers contending for the shared last-level cache.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: A cache-level interpretation
items.text:
Access patterns through the memory hierarchy

Access patterns through the memory hierarchyConceptual list of registers, L1, private L2, shared L3 and DRAM with possible data accesses. No sizes, timings, measured residency or cache hit guarantees are encoded.Possible access targets—not residencyRegistersactive lengths, words and offsetsL1hot slot fields and short wordsPrivate L2hot parts of order / grammar arraysShared L3 / LLCarenas and table; competing workersDRAMmisses, allocation and buffers Conceptual hierarchy only: these are possible access targets, not measured or guaranteed residency. Equal box widths deliberately encode no cache capacity. Independent lanes can hide dependency latency; prefetch and copies may change exposure, but actual cache traffic and concurrency effects require measurement.

There are several points where the implementation choices could change cache behaviour substantially:

First, slot width and locality. Reducing two 24-byte records to smaller fields could reduce the number of cache lines touched, but may require additional loads or arithmetic. It is not automatically worthwhile.

Second, prefetch distance. Twelve slots ahead was empirically useful for the initial Cells loop. A different CPU or changed frontier schedule might favour a different distance.

Third, grammar locality. A tightly packed grammar can be much cheaper to traverse than Python objects linked through dictionaries. But even a compact grammar can incur expensive random lookups and repeated expansion.

Fourth, concurrent decoder workers. A working set that behaves well alone can create pressure on shared cache and memory bandwidth when many block decoders operate concurrently. The high-water allocations matter as well as the live logical records.

Fifth, the writer. A sequential copy is not free, but it can exploit memory bandwidth and cache-line locality in a way that a dependent permutation walk cannot. The number of copies, intermediate buffers and actual stores still determine whether that is advantageous.

These are hardware-performance hypotheses, not equivalent descriptions of the same algorithmic count.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: What is stored on disk?
items.text:
During ordinary decoding, the compressed bzip2 file is the persistent input; the interval exchange, permutation table, grammar and output scratch are in-memory structures, not disk-backed databases.

The research infrastructure is different. It persists frozen corpora or their hashes, exported run streams, immutable schedules, source identities, operation counters, validation logs and experiment reports to GitHub branches or retained artifacts.

For example, PR #371 retained compressed input/run evidence and the result of its single block attempt. That material is for reproducibility and independent verification. The candidate constructor was not permitted to obtain its answer from a precomputed oracle path.

So the proposed performance gain is primarily about CPU instructions, cache latency, memory traffic, allocation and reconstruction work—not reducing disk seeks. Any end-to-end file-reading effect is a separate measurement question.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 6. The second algorithm: delimiter-based first returns
items.text:
This is where the last two days' mathematical experiments diverged from the original right-end Cells algorithm.

Instead of always inducing on a progressively shorter prefix \([0,m)\), suppose we retain a set of rows

\[ K=\{i:L[i]=c\} \]

for some chosen delimiter byte \(c\).

Define the first-return map

\[ F_K(x)=\pi^{t(x)}(x), \]

where \(t(x)\) is the smallest positive integer for which \(\pi^{t(x)}(x)\in K\).

Between two consecutive retained rows, the original permutation emits a string. We store that string as a return word.

The resulting representation consists of a smaller permutation on the retained rows, together with words describing the excursions between them.

Unlike the right-end method, the retained set is not generally a contiguous interval. The constructor must determine the correct return itineraries by propagating intervals through the LF run map and splitting them where their trajectories diverge.

First returns to a separated section

items.title: The practical constructor
items.text:
The experimental delimiter constructor works approximately as follows:

  1. Find the delimiter intervals among the input runs.
  2. Initialise a frontier of interval fragments, each carrying its source-anchor identity, current interval coordinates and accumulated return-word reference.
  3. Apply LF's translation to a fragment.
  4. If its image crosses run or delimiter boundaries, split it into fragments with uniform return behaviour.
  5. When a fragment reaches a delimiter interval, record its first-return destination and word.
  6. Assemble the resulting token-level permutation, recover the marked cycle and expand its return words.

The experimental representation also exploits the fact that delimiter-separated phrases admit a useful lexicographic token ordering. The tests verify when the induced map agrees with the token-BWT construction.

That property is conditional. Arbitrarily adding the original row to the retained set, for example, can destroy the token-order correspondence even though the first-return map remains mathematically valid.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: What happened on real data?
items.text:
PR #371 tested one frozen Wikidata block:

Quantity Observed Original LF rows \(n\) 899,931 Maximal LF runs 51,184 Delimiter intervals 679 Delimiter rows 135,716 Constructor interval visits \(E\) 124,080 Completed phrase pieces \(Q\) 6,133 Grammar nodes \(H\) 70,559 Constructor plus residual token visits 259,796

The output bytes, origin, selected cycle, token permutation, RLE1 result and CRC agreed with the reference.

The traversal count was approximately 71% below \(n\). That is meaningful evidence that a smaller return-level description exists for this block.

However, it is not evidence of a 71% reduction in CPU time.

The constructor still represented trajectories covering all 899,931 rows in its weighted accounting. It also performed approximately 5.69 million binary-search comparisons, and residual reconstruction involved 1.66 million grammar visits.

Most decisively, the Python implementation's live metadata was at least 23.5 MB, against the experiment's \(4n\), or 3.6 MB, limit.

It therefore failed its predeclared memory criterion.

The conclusion was not that first returns cannot work. It was that this representation did not earn a compiled performance experiment.

Frozen block result and accounting.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: Why this is genuinely a different design choice
items.text:
With Cells, the question is:

Can we reduce the complete interval exchange quickly enough that a grammar of its selected cycle is cheap to construct?

With delimiter first returns, it is:

Can we choose a small retained section whose return words are inexpensive to construct and whose token-level permutation is inexpensive to traverse?

Both produce grammars, but their construction costs arise in different places.

Cells concentrates effort in right-end length comparisons and permanent cells. Delimiter first returns concentrate effort in fragment propagation, boundary splitting, return-word accumulation, dictionary construction and token traversal.

It is entirely possible for one to win on an input where the other loses.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 7. Why we investigated labelling and combinatorial surgery
items.text:
We were looking for ways to make the construction of these compressed descriptions cheaper.

This was the connection with de Mourgues's work on reduced/boosted dynamics, labelling and combinatorial surgery.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: The labelling hypothesis
items.text:
If a portion of a permutation changes, perhaps we can retain stable identities for the unaffected pieces rather than renumber their positions repeatedly.

The thesis's labelling method preserves information about where distinguished edges attach as combinatorial transformations change the surrounding permutation. The repository study could not directly retrieve the thesis PDF; it checked the author's first paper, §3.4 and second paper, §§2 and 5. The thesis remains the historical reference, while those papers and the pinned experiment delimit what was directly verified.

An LF implementation could use a related idea to preserve interval identities, return-word occurrences and the marked origin.

But the thesis's combinatorial equivalence is not itself an equivalence of weighted LF maps with emitted words. That additional structure must be preserved explicitly.

PR #369 found small counterexamples to naive edge deletion and positional lifting. Exact first-return construction requires the proper interval refinements.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: The surgery hypothesis
items.text:
Suppose a current return map is \(F\), and we remove a set \(D\) containing no consecutive points of the \(F\)-orbit:

\[ D\cap F(D)=\varnothing. \]

For a surviving point \(x\), the new first-return map is

\[ F'(x)= \begin{cases} F(F(x)),&F(x)\in D,\\ F(x),&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The emitted word is the concatenation of the transitions actually taken.

That is an exact local contraction. For interval fragments sharing the same itinerary, it becomes composition of translations and concatenation of word references.

Our hoped-for optimisation was to apply many such changes locally while retaining the rest of the representation.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: What the experiments revealed
items.text:
PR #370 tested an implementation maintaining the two orders through treaps.

It preserved the correct destinations, words, marked origin and final coalescing.

It also reduced sorting comparisons from 406,949 to 99,440 and eliminated 105,708 persistent coordinate writes.

But it introduced approximately 883,875 pointer writes and 893,297 tree-size writes, together with considerable allocation and metadata.

We had eliminated coordinate rebuilding but created a more expensive maintenance problem. Here the evidence is the counted metadata work, not a native runtime comparison.

PR #372 then evaluated the alternatives against the saved traces. Its preferred comparator was no longer a general dynamic tree, but a compact global-array rebuild.

A potential hybrid remains:

\[ \text{Choose between } \begin{cases} \text{batch-local update},\\ \text{global compact rebuild} \end{cases} \]

according to how much of the representation actually changes.

In a chunked representation with chunk capacity \(b\), \(D\) dirty chunks, \(R\) total records and \(S\) distinct interior cuts, local maintenance might pay roughly \(O(bD+S)\) work versus \(O(R+S)\) for a global pass, excluding common selection and other overheads. Here \(S\) counts cuts, not the induction steps of §2.4.

The essential unknown is \(D\), the distribution of dirty chunks in both interval orders. Sparse deletions do not imply cheap local updates.

PR #372 did not have that incidence measurement, so it did not authorise another implementation.

This is where our optimistic idea stands: mathematically sound, potentially useful, but currently unpriced well enough to justify another backend.

Contraction counts and semantics; saved-evidence pricing.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 8. The next promising representation problem: grammar allocation and output
items.text:
PRs #371–372 also exposed a different opportunity.

The real-block phrase constructor had 70,559 live grammar nodes, but only 2,716 distinct expanded dictionary words across 6,133 completed pieces.

Constructing each distinct word once, rather than repeatedly expanding shared DAG content, could eliminate 103,233 grammar visits in the recorded dictionary-building phase.

Further savings may be possible by reusing those expanded words directly while writing output, rather than expanding the same grammar through every token occurrence.

But that changes both the CPU and memory trade-off.

For example, a hypothetical compact native representation for #371 might use 32-bit indices for grammar nodes, interval identifiers and child references.

The operation counts suggest such a representation is worth understanding, but ordinary hash-table growth remains problematic.

At a 75% hash-table load threshold, doubling from 65,536 to 131,072 slots while both tables are live creates a temporary allocation peak. In the specified model, that alone brings the accounted working set above the original \(4n\) limit.

There are alternatives: preallocation, segmented tables, fixed-capacity arenas, separate construction and expansion lifetimes, and so forth. Each requires its own construction and allocation-cost accounting.

The unresolved question is not simply whether the final grammar is small. It is whether we can construct and use it without a larger, more expensive temporary representation.

This is an area where physical layout is particularly relevant. The lifetime of the hash-cons table, the grammar node arena, completed interval records and expanded dictionary buffers may matter as much as their individual sizes.

Grammar expansion and temporary-allocation model.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 9. What actually happened from 10–12 November
items.text:
Here is the recent work separated by purpose. The PRs are not successive versions of one decoder kernel.

Work What it established Consequence MONODROMY Cells research Endpoint induction can generate reconstruction grammars, with an indicative inversion-stage advantage Build an opt-in real-decoder version PR #365 Correctness, bounded admission, fallback and writer safety; no convincing whole-decoder speedup Defer deployment pending attribution PR #367 Most Wikidata rows qualify for Cells; admission dilution alone does not explain the stage-to-decoder discrepancy Measure the actual decoder phases PR #369 Reduced/boosted-style LF lifting needs exact refinement and more than positional labels Reject naive reduction PR #370 Labelled local contraction is exact, but dynamic-tree maintenance is expensive Reconsider representation PR #371 Real-block first returns substantially reduce counted visits but exceed metadata budget Revise memory/grammar construction PR #372 Compact rebuilding is a stronger comparator; dictionary reuse has concrete potential Prefer existing decoder diagnostic before another backend PR #366 Prepared a separate frozen one-core diagnostic and incorporated the reviewed accounting correction Await deliberate integration and readiness PR #373 Prepared the matched live-reader Cells diagnostic, with source correspondence and phase instrumentation Correct review finding, reconcile checks, then evaluate readiness
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: The important discrepancy we have been pursuing
items.text:
The original Cells research measured an inversion-stage ratio around 0.82–0.86× the existing run-record inversion path on its Wikidata test environment.

But the subsequent opt-in production-style benchmark did not reproduce that advantage: the reported Wikidata one-thread whole-decoder ratio was approximately 1.000, while some other inputs were considerably slower.

Those measurements have different scopes, implementations, hardware and cache conditioning. They cannot be compared as if one were simply a timed subroutine inside the other.

The #367 census established that 196 of 431 Wikidata blocks were admitted, representing approximately 84.1% of rows. That makes a pure admission-rate explanation insufficient.

Other candidates remain: the production writer's different copy operations, source-layout differences, cache conditioning, instrumentation effects, or costs elsewhere in the decoder.

These are precisely the alternatives that the current diagnostic is intended to distinguish.

Admission census and comparison limits.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 10. Where the live diagnostic fits
items.text:
The prepared #373 harness uses the actual reader and reconstructs an experimental decoder from the corrected #365 source, with observation hooks compiled either in or out.

The measurement plan has four arms:

Hooks off Hooks on Existing baseline Baseline, uninstrumented Baseline, instrumented Experimental Cells Cells, uninstrumented Cells, instrumented

The frozen design specifies ten balanced pairs on each of Wikidata, pattern and onebyte: 120 eventual measured decodes, plus nine untimed/oracle checks.

The instrumented build records exclusive costs for stages such as scanning, run-front construction, ordering, induction, writing, fallback and finishing, together with the reader and complete-decode spans.

This is valuable because it provides a way to separate several possibilities.

If Cells is slower even within a matched inversion-stage comparison, attention should return to its implementation and memory behaviour.

If Cells wins inside inversion but the total decoder does not, the issue may be other stages, instrumentation or integration effects.

If the instrumented and uninstrumented comparisons differ materially, the phase attribution itself may be misleading.

The harness explicitly guards against counting inclusive inversion time again as if it were an additional exclusive stage. Matching off/on conclusion categories would not establish equal effect sizes or causal savings in the uninstrumented build. For example, Cells/baseline ratios of 0.9 with hooks off and 0.45 with hooks on could both qualify as faster under the frozen interval rule. Detailed stage attribution describes the instrumented path, whose observation overhead must still be considered.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: 11. Where further interventions would be most useful
items.text:
I would keep five questions distinct, because they correspond to different kinds of possible progress.

A. Which induced map do we want?

The right-end Cells construction and delimiter first-return construction are two choices of section. Neither dominates the other mathematically or computationally.

An intervention here would concern the inducing set or the order of reductions: for example, choosing boundaries that avoid later fragmentation or repeated winner steps.

B. What is the minimum reconstruction information?

We need to preserve exact destinations, emitted words, return times and the original marked occurrence. But it is still open whether we can represent these with substantially less metadata or fewer transient structures.

An intervention here concerns the semantics of the intermediate representation: what needs to be stored and what can be inferred or shared.

C. How should we maintain that representation?

Linked orders, permanent cells, packed arrays, treaps and chunked arrays are distinct implementations of related mathematical state.

Here we need to price writes, lookups, allocations, cache misses, cross-order indices, coalescing and rebuild costs. Local contraction remains interesting, but a compact global pass is currently the comparison it must beat.

D. How should we execute the reconstruction program?

This includes grammar expansion, dictionary reuse, output scheduling, origin rotation and RLE1/CRC work. A small grammar is no use if traversing it repeatedly costs more than following the original permutation.

The possible direct dictionary-output savings identified in #372 belong here.

E. Where does the actual decoder spend time?

Before making another substantial implementation investment, we need the matched Cells diagnostic. It determines whether the principal issue is mathematical construction, the native port, the writer, surrounding decoding stages or runtime conditioning.

This is the immediate experimental priority.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: My overall assessment
items.text:
The central theoretical programme remains coherent:

\[ \boxed{\begin{gathered} \text{LF interval exchange}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{induced return maps}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{compact word program}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{exact text} \end{gathered}} \]

The theory explains why it is possible to replace row-level permutation traversal with transformations on run intervals and symbolic words.

The engineering programme is to make every stage of that replacement cheaper than the computation it eliminates.

We have already demonstrated important parts of this: exact induction, correct origin preservation, compact symbolic programs, and favourable operation counts in selected circumstances. We have also found costly representations that should not be deployed.

My preference is to maintain both mathematical lines—endpoint Cells and phrase-level first returns—as distinct research possibilities, while using the present diagnostic to guide the next implementation investment. I would not rule out novel induction schedules, better local contraction or more compact grammar construction; I simply wouldn't assume their benefits without charging their full costs.

The next decisive result is not another proof of correctness. It's a trustworthy explanation of why the research inversion advantage has not yet appeared in full decoding. Once we have that, we can decide intelligently whether to improve the mathematics, change the storage representation, reorganise the writer, or focus on the surrounding decoder.

Research records: original technical report and internal reading notes; mathematical construction and historical timings; reduced/boosted counterexamples; de Mourgues’s thesis, §§4.1.4–4.1.5 and Chapter 5; live diagnostic plan.
path: A new way back from the BWT

items.title: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The last post followed Cells, one of mibz2's ways of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) that bzip2 applies to each block of text. Cells does not decode one position at a time. It works on intervals: at the start, each interval is a run of equal bytes in the BWT's output, which the decoding moves as a whole to a new place. In the block aab, for example, the BWT's output is baa, and its intervals are one b and two as. As the decoding goes on, intervals shrink and join.

Cells tracks every interval in two orders at once: where it lies, and where it is moved to. The code calls an interval a letter, and keeps a small record for it, a slot, in each of the two orders. Until now, both slots held the same two pieces of information: the interval's length, and a reference to the text it stands for. This post shows why the second copy was never needed, and what mibz2 0.3.3 gained by removing it.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references
items.text:
mibz2 tracks each run of equal bytes in two orders, and a run's entry in the second shrinks from 20 bytes to 8 by pointing to the first.

15 November 2026 · 12 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.3.3 (changelog)
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: The idea in brief
items.text:
Cells works through each of its two orders from one end, the order's front, so each front reaches every letter once. That gives every letter two visits, one per order.

A letter's length and text reference are read only at the first of its two visits, and a short proof shows that the top order's slot always holds them at that moment. Call the two orders top and bottom. If the top front reaches the letter first, the details are read from the top slot, and the bottom slot's copy is never used. If the bottom front reaches it first, the top front has not got there yet, so the top slot has not been touched and still holds the details. Either way, the top slot is enough.

So 0.3.3 keeps the details in the top slot only. The bottom slot shrinks from 20 bytes to 8: it keeps its link to its neighbour, and a pointer to the letter's top slot. Here is what that gives, and what it costs:

  • 30% less memory for the slots, counted on the benchmark's Wikidata corpus, and about a fifth less for the rebuild's whole working area, which also holds the text itself.
  • A faster decoder at four threads on both test machines, and at one and two threads on one of them. On a 10-core Intel desktop, 0.3.3 took 6.5% less wall time than 0.3.2 at four threads, and about 4% less at one and two. On the project's 2-core CI runner it took 4.2% less at four threads; at one and two threads the change was within noise.
  • The price is an extra memory read. On 53.7% of slot reads, the processor must read the bottom slot to learn where the top slot is before it can read the details. That could have cost more than it saved; on these measurements it did not.
  • More threads can now usefully decode a block each. mibz2 switches from giving each thread a block of its own to having threads share blocks at a fixed thread count, the team threshold. After 0.3.3, a block per thread was faster up to nine threads on the desktop, and the change moving the threshold to ten threads is released in mibz2 0.3.4. That shift is the work of every improvement to Cells so far, not of this change alone.

Section 1 builds the two orders from a three-byte example, and shows why each letter needs a slot in both. Sections 2 to 4 show the new layout, why it is safe, and what the extra read costs. Sections 5 to 7 give the measurements: memory, speed, and the team threshold.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 1. Why does every letter need two slots?
items.text:
bzip2 compresses each block of text after rearranging it with the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). The BWT sorts all the rotations of the block and keeps the last byte of each, which tends to put equal bytes next to each other. To decompress, the decoder must undo that rearrangement.

Take the block aab. Sorted, its rotations are aab, aba and baa. The BWT's output is their last bytes: baa. Sorting the output gives aab, the first bytes of the same rotations. Number the sorted rotations 0 to 2 and call them rows. The decoder knows which byte of the output goes with which byte of the sorted list, because equal bytes keep their order. The output's first a is the sorted list's first a, its second a is the second, and b is b. This pairing is called LF, and following it from row to row spells out the block backwards, one byte per step. From row 0, read b and go to row 2; read a and go to row 1; read a. That is the usual way to decode, one position at a time.

LF has a pattern that Cells uses. The output baa falls into runs of equal bytes: one b, then two as. Within a run, consecutive rows go to consecutive rows, so each run moves as a whole. Name the runs B and A. In the output they lie in the order B, A. Where LF sends them, in the sorted list, they lie in the order A, B.

The block aab: the same two runs, in two orders

Top orderthe runs as they lie in the outputBottom orderthe same runs where LF sends themrow 0row 0row 1row 1row 2row 2bBa aAa aAbBoutputbaasortedaabAB Worked by hand: the BWT’s output baa above, the same bytes sorted below. Each band joins a run to the rows LF sends it to. The bands cross because the runs swap places: B, A on top; A, B below.

Each run is one of the intervals, a letter. The code calls the runs as they lie in the output the top order, and the same runs where LF sends them the bottom order. There are still only two letters, A and B; each has a place in both orders. Each letter has a length, the number of rows it covers, and a word, the text those rows stand for. At the start, A covers two rows and its word is a; B covers one row and its word is b.

Cells rebuilds the text by shrinking this picture rather than walking it. Each step compares the letters at the two fronts, the right-hand ends of the orders: here, A on top and B below.

Rebuilding aab in two steps

StartAa2 rowsBb1 rowThe fronts are A on top and B below.Step 1Aa1 rowBab1 rowA is longer, so it gives up one row, row 2.B’s path ran through row 2, so B’s word takesin its a.Step 2A+Baab1 rowEqual lengths: the step joins them. The oneword left is the block. Worked by hand, as in the earlier post on Cells. Each box is a letter, as wide as the rows it covers, with its word inside..

Each word can be checked against the LF walk above. From row 0, B's path reads b, then a, before it reaches a row that is still kept: that is ab read forwards. The full cycle reads aab. The earlier post on Cells works this example through as an animation. On a real block, a letter that covers one row can have a word thousands of bytes long. A step's result is called a cell, and it takes the place of the letters it was made from. Long words are not copied: a word made by joining two others is stored as a rule that names those two.

To find the letter at each front, and a letter's place in the other order, Cells keeps each order as a chain of slots, one per letter. Before 0.3.3, both of a letter's slots had the same five 4-byte fields:

Field What it holds Previous slot the slot before this one in its order Length how many rows the letter covers Word length and word offset the letter's text reference: how many bytes of text its word has, and where they, or its rule, are kept Partner the same letter's slot in the other order

The letter's length and its word's length are different things: in the example, B's length is one row after step 1, while its word is two bytes long. The previous-slot link and the partner say where a slot sits: next to which slot in its own order, and opposite which slot in the other. The length and the word describe the letter itself, and they were stored in both slots.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 2. What changed in 0.3.3?
items.text:
The top slot stays exactly as it was. The bottom slot keeps only two fields: its previous-slot link, and its partner, which is the letter's top slot. The length and word are no longer stored there; when the bottom front needs them, it reads them from the top slot.

A letter’s two slots, before and after 0.3.3

BeforeTop slot20 Bbefore4 Blength4 Bwordlength, offset · 8 Bpartner4 BBottom slot20 Bbefore4 Blengthcopywordcopy of the top’spartner4 Bamber: the same length and word, stored twiceAfter, in 0.3.3Top slot20 B, unchangedbefore4 Blength4 Bwordlength, offset · 8 Bpartner4 BBottom slot8 Bbefore4 Btop slot4 Bgone12 B no longer storedlength and word read from herePer letter, both orders0.700 of the memory before40 B → 28 B The layout as src/cells.rs documents it, drawn to scale: every field is a 4-byte offset or length, and the word is its length and offset, read together as one 8-byte load. Amber marks the fields the bottom slot used to repeat. After the change, the bottom slot’s second field is the letter’s top slot, and the green arrow is the read that replaces the copy.

Each letter used to cost 40 bytes of slots, 20 in each order. It now costs 28: 20 on top and 8 below. That is 0.700 of the slot memory before, and it matches the count on the Wikidata corpus exactly (section 5).
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 3. How do we know the top slot still has the details?
items.text:
Cells reuses slots as it goes: when a letter is used up, its slots are overwritten with the new cell. So a fair worry is that the bottom slot might point at a top slot that has already been overwritten.

The answer is a property of Cells' steps. It is proved in the project's analysis of which stored bytes are ever read, a write-up still under review, which also checked it against every slot read on the Wikidata corpus without a single exception:

A letter's details are read once, at whichever front reaches it first. Its slot in the other order is then overwritten by the letter's own first cell without being read.

That leaves two cases.

Whichever front reaches a letter first, its top slot is intact

Case A: the top front reaches X firstX’s details are read from its top slot.TopBottom…DCX · 20 B…X · 8 BABtop frontbottom frontCase B: the bottom front reaches X firstThe top front is still behind X: its top slot is intact.TopBottom…X · 20 BCD…ABX · 8 Btop frontbottom frontpartner link between X’s two slotsgreen: where X’s length and word are read Conceptual: one letter, X, with a slot in each order. Each order is read from its right-hand end, its front; each step uses up letters at the fronts, so the fronts move leftwards. Green marks where X’s length and word are read. In both cases they are read once, and from the top slot.

In the first case, the top front reaches the letter first. The details are read straight from the top slot. The bottom slot's old copy would never have been read, because the letter's first cell overwrites it.

In the second case, the bottom front reaches the letter first. The top front has not reached the letter yet, so nothing has overwritten its top slot. Cells follows the bottom slot's partner field, reads the length and word from the top slot, and goes on.

So at the one moment the details are read, the top slot holds them in both cases. In the first, it is the slot being read; in the second, the top front has not yet reached it. That is why the copy can always live on the top side, without knowing in advance which front will arrive first. The bottom slot cannot go altogether, though. The bottom order still needs its own chain of links, and each letter still needs a way to its place in the other order. Those two fields are the slot's own state, not copies.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 4. What does the saving cost?
items.text:
Before, reading a bottom slot gave everything at once. Now the processor reads the bottom slot to learn which top slot to go to, and only then can it read the length and word. The second read's address depends on the first read's result. Such a dependent load cannot start until the first has finished, which limits how much work the processor can overlap.

The change's own count on the Wikidata corpus found 32.0 million slot reads, of which 17.2 million come from the bottom front. So 53.7% of slot reads gain a dependent load.

This had gone wrong before. An earlier layout with 16-byte slots added one dependent load per letter read and cost 4.4% more processor time at four threads. Three things make this one cheaper:

  1. The bottom slot's link and partner arrive together in one 8-byte read.
  2. The top slot it leads to is the one the same step writes the new cell into, so that memory is needed anyway.
  3. The decoder already prefetches: it asks for a slot several steps before it reaches it, so the slot is in cache by then. It now reads the bottom slot 12 steps ahead and prefetches the top slot it names. Six steps ahead, it prefetches the letter's text too.

The extra read is also off the chain that finds the next slot: the next bottom slot's address comes from the same 8-byte read as the partner. The change was therefore expected to pay mostly when several threads compete for memory, and to break about even on one thread.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 5. How much memory does it remove?
items.text:
The count is from the change's pull request, on the benchmark's Wikidata corpus. Of its 431 blocks, Cells takes 196; the others go to mibz2's ordinary decoder.

The rebuild’s memory, before and after, on the Wikidata corpus

Slot bytes, both ordersbefore: 443.6 MB310.5 MB · ×0.70064-byte lines of the working areabefore: 9.64 M7.56 M · ×0.784Working area per block, medianbefore: 2.90 MiB2.27 MiB Counted, not timed: #414’s count over the 196 blocks Cells decodes, at one thread. The working area is the slots, the words’ text and the rules; only the slots shrink.

The slots shrink by exactly the 40-to-28 ratio. The whole working area also holds the words' text and their rules, and those are unchanged. So the working area shrinks by less: it takes 21.6% fewer cache lines, and the median block's goes from 2.90 MiB to 2.27 MiB.
path: Removing duplicated interval lengths and text references

items.title: 6. How much faster is the decoder?
items.text:
Two measurements compare 0.3.3 with 0.3.2, decoding the same Wikidata corpus. Both are paired: each round runs both versions in alternation, and the figure is the change in wall time with its 95% interval.

Wall time, 0.3.3 against 0.3.2, decoding the Wikidata corpus

CI runner, 2 cores1 thread−1.4%2 threads−1.2%4 threads−4.2%Intel desktop, 10 cores1 thread−4.1%2 threads−3.9%4 threads−6.5%−10%−8%−6%−4%−2%0%+2%+4%← less wall time with 0.3.3 Measured: 10 paired rounds on each machine. The CI runner is an AMD EPYC 9V45 with 4 virtual CPUs on 2 cores; the desktop is an Intel i9-10900K with 10 cores. Each mark is the change in wall time with its 95% interval; green where the interval excludes no change. The desktop’s record gives ratios, 0.3.2 ÷ 0.3.3: 1.043, 1.040 and 1.070 at one, two and four threads; the chart shows each as the share of wall time saved, 1 − 1/ratio.

The desktop's record gives ratios of wall times, which the chart converts to the project's usual form, the share of wall time saved. At four threads the desktop also used about 7% less processor time.

The desktop run also measured 8, 10, 12, 16 and 20 threads, and nothing changed there. 0.3.3 shares blocks between threads from six threads up, so at those counts it did not use Cells at all. As expected, the gain is clearest with several blocks decoding at once. The desktop shows a gain at one and two threads too; the CI runner does not.

items.title: 7. Why does this move the team threshold?
items.text:
mibz2 decodes a file's blocks in parallel in one of two ways. With few threads, each thread takes a block of its own and decodes it with Cells; these threads are workers. With many threads, threads share blocks in teams, which split one block's work between them. Teams cost more coordination, but they keep fewer blocks in memory at once. The thread count where mibz2 switches from workers to teams is the team threshold. It was set at six threads on 28 October, and not measured again until after 0.3.3.

Every saving in a worker's memory makes it cheaper to run more workers side by side. So after 0.3.3 the project measured the two directly on the same desktop: a block per thread against the shipped decoder, which used teams from six threads.

A block per thread against teams, on the Intel desktop after 0.3.3

Below 1 the workers are faster; green where the 95% interval is wholly below 1. The record gives no interval at ten threads. CPU is the same ratio for processor time; the last column is peak memory, teams → workers.

Workers were faster at every count from six to nine threads, taking 13.9% less wall time at six and 3.6% less at nine. At ten threads the shipped decoder runs three teams of three, so nine threads decode blocks, and it stays ahead: workers took 15.3% longer. Workers also use more memory, since more blocks are in flight: 133 to 188 MB at six to nine threads, against 65 to 81 MB for the teams. At nine threads they used 12.4% more processor time. That is over the project's 10% limit on extra processor time for such a move, so the choice went to the maintainer. He chose workers below ten threads, where each thread has a physical core of its own, and teams from ten. The change is released in mibz2 0.3.4.

This run measures Cells as it is now, after every improvement since 0.3.0, including slot recycling in 0.3.2 and the smaller bottom slots in 0.3.3. It shows that today's Cells beats the teams up to nine threads on this machine. It does not show how much of the shift is due to the bottom slots alone: no run compared the two layouts at six to nine threads.

items.title: What it teaches
items.text:
The change began from a question about the algorithm, not the machine: when is each stored value actually read? Once the answer was "exactly once, at the first front to arrive", the layout followed. It is not ordinary deduplication, because the slots are rewritten all the time. What makes it safe is that the one remaining copy is guaranteed to be intact at the one moment it is read.

The same question applies wherever a structure keeps two views of the same item. If only one view's copy is ever read, the other can become a pointer. Whether that pays then depends on the extra read, which here was cheap because the memory it reaches was needed anyway.

The change and its count are in mibz2 PR #414. The CI and desktop measurements are in the 0.3.3 release notes, and the desktop run's record is #420. The team threshold's change is PR #425.

items.title: The free closure of an induction
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The width of an induction, the previous post, looked at mibz2's experimental decoder for bzip2. It found that the decoder can hold about a third as much at its busiest moment if it takes its free steps first. A free step is a step of the rebuild that erases one boundary between pieces of the block and creates none. That post also reported that the free steps always reach the same end point, whatever order they run in. This post is about that end point: why the order doesn't matter, how it was proved and checked, and what it allows a decoder to do.

The recap. bzip2 sorts the rotations of each block and stores the last byte of each, the last column; each sorted rotation is a row. To decode, mibz2 follows a map called LF from row to row, reading one byte per move, which spells the block out backwards. A run is a stretch of equal bytes in the last column, and LF moves each run's rows together, as one interval. A new way back from the BWT introduced Cells, the decoder that works on those intervals instead of on rows. Each of its steps cuts some rows out of the map, and lets the interval whose rows used to land there jump straight over them. The code calls each interval a letter, and the bytes its jump reads, in text order, its word. A step happens at a coincidence: a boundary where one letter's rows end and another letter's landing place ends too. Every letter starts with a one-byte word, and when the last step is done, a word spells the whole block.

The width post in brief. The width of a rebuild is the most letters with a word longer than one byte that it holds at once. Cells always steps at the right-hand end of the map. Its width is about 0.32 r at the median on Wikidata, where r is the number of runs in the block. Taking free steps first cuts that to about 0.08–0.11 r. On every block, the peak stayed within the number of letters left once the free steps run out.

The theorem. Take free steps in any order until none is left. You always reach the same letters, with the same words, after the same number of steps. The one exception is a cycle of the map that closes completely during the free steps. It takes no further part, and two orders can leave it in different places, with its word rotated. No real block closes its cycle that early.

Why it matters. Call the state where the free steps run out the free closure. Because the order doesn't matter, it is a property of the block, not of the algorithm that found it. On the 233 large blocks of the Wikidata benchmark it leaves 0.185 r letters at the median, and takes 0.896 r steps to reach. Those are counts, and they are now facts about each block: no cleverer order of free steps can change them. The proof is by hand, and a program checked its every case on 10.7 million pairs of steps, with no exception.

What it allows, and what it doesn't yet. A decoder may take free steps in whichever order is cheapest to find. Free steps on different letters may go to different threads and still meet at the same state. So one block's rebuild can be split between threads, and it is proved to stay correct. No such decoder has been built or timed.

Section 1 works one free step on a four-byte block. Section 2 takes its two free steps in both orders. Section 3 gives the proof's shape, and section 4 the machine check. Section 5 separates what is proved from what is counted. Section 6 says what a decoder could do with it, and section 7 what is open.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: The free closure of an induction: where free steps come to rest
items.text:
The steps that cost mibz2 no bookkeeping can be taken in any order and still meet at one end point, now proved to belong to the block itself.

15 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 1. What does one step do?
items.text:
Suppose you want to compress the four bytes abac. Their four rotations, sorted, are abac, acab, baca and caba, so the last column is cbaa. It has three runs, c, b and aa, so the rebuild starts with three letters. Call them Y, Z and X:

Letter Its rows (top) LF sends them to (bottom) Word Y, the run c row 0 row 3 c Z, the run b row 1 row 2 b X, the run aa rows 2–3 rows 0–1 a

The figure draws each letter twice. The top strip shows where its rows sit in the last column. The bottom strip shows where LF sends them, and the shaded band joins the two. The numbers above the strips count boundaries between rows, so boundary 4 is the end of row 3.

One free step on the column of abac

Before: X and Y end at boundary 401234topbottomY · cY · cZ · bZ · bX · aX · aAfter the step at 4: row 3 is cut01234topbottomcutcutY · acY · acZ · bZ · bX · aX · a Computed by a program that steps the column exactly as the checker in section 4 does; not drawn by hand. Top strip: each letter’s rows. Bottom strip: where LF sends them. Each box shows the letter and its word. Grey boxes are rows the step has cut.

Two things end at boundary 4. In the top strip, X's rows 2–3 end there. In the bottom strip, so does Y's landing place, row 3. That makes boundary 4 a coincidence, and a step can be taken there. Y's one row lands on row 3. Row 3 belongs to X, which sends it on to row 1. So row 3 is only a stopover on Y's way. The step cuts row 3 out, and Y now jumps from row 0 straight to row 1. Its jump reads c and then a. LF runs backwards through the text, so in text order its word grows at the front: c becomes ac, which is indeed in abac. X loses the row, and keeps row 2, which still goes to row 0.

The step is free because of where Y now lands. Its new landing place starts a boundary at 1 in the bottom strip. The top strip already had a boundary at 1, between Y's row and Z's. So the step erased the boundary at 4 and created none that wasn't already there. A step that is not free, a paid step, would put a boundary at a new place, and some later step would have to remove it. A step between two letters of the same length is always free, since one letter simply takes over the other's place.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 2. Does the order matter?
items.text:
The column has a second free step available at the start. At boundary 2, Z's row 1 ends in the top strip. X's landing place, rows 0–1, ends there in the bottom strip. Here Z is the shorter piece, so row 1 is cut. X's row 3 used to land on row 1 and go on with Z to row 2. Now it jumps straight to row 2. That one row splits off from X and becomes Z, with the word ba.

Both steps are free, and they share a letter: X. Each one changes X's length, so neither leaves the other's starting point untouched. The figure takes them in both orders.

Two free steps, two orders, one state

Start: free steps at 2 and 401234Y·cY·cZ·bZ·bX·aX·aStep at 4 firstY·ac; X shrinks01234cutcutY·acY·acZ·bZ·bX·aX·aStep at 2 firstZ·ba; X shrinks01234cutcutY·cY·cX·aX·aZ·baZ·baEither order: one staterows 1 and 3 cut01234cutcutcutcutY·bacY·bacX·aX·astep at 4step at 2then at 2then at 4In each state: upper strip top, lower strip bottom Computed, as in the figure above. Green lines mark the free steps available in each state. Taking the step at 4 first and then the one at 2, or the other way round, gives the same letters, places and words: X at row 2 with the word a, and Y at row 0, landing on row 2, with the word bac.

The left path makes Y's word ac first, and then the step at 2 puts b in front of it. The right path makes Z's word ba first, and then the step at 4 hands Y the whole of ba followed by its own c. Either way, Y ends with bac and X with a. In the language of rewriting systems this is a diamond, or a square. Two steps leave one state, and one step on each side brings them back together.

The tiny block goes on to its end. After the diamond, X and Y form a cycle of two letters, each landing on the other's rows, and one more free step closes it whole. A program tried every one of the twelve orders in which the free steps of cbaa can be taken. All twelve take three steps. Each ends with one letter whose word is abac, acab, baca or caba: the same cycle, read from different starting points. That is the exception in the theorem. On a four-byte block the whole text closes during the free steps. On the Wikidata blocks, where the free steps stop at about a fifth of the runs, none did. bzip2 stores with every block the row of the original rotation, which says where to start reading in any case.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 3. Why does it hold for every block?
items.text:
Two diamonds on one example prove nothing in general, so the proof goes through a classical result. Newman's lemma, from 1942, says that a system of rewriting steps has a single end point from every start if two things hold.

  1. Termination. No sequence of steps goes on forever. Each free step erases one boundary and creates none, and a block has only finitely many boundaries, so this holds.
  2. Local confluence. Whenever two steps are available in the same state, there is some way to continue from each of them so that both reach the same state again.

Termination is what lets the second, local condition decide the global answer. Without it, two paths could keep diverging forever, each step of the way looking reconcilable.

So the proof takes any two free steps available together, at boundaries c₁ and c₂, and shows that they can be brought back together. It rests on two facts. First, a free step touches only its own two letters, and removes no boundary but its own. Second, the place where a free step's shorter letter lands always lies strictly inside the longer letter's interval, so it can never be the other step's coincidence. Then two steps relate in exactly one of four ways:

  1. No letter in common. Neither step changes anything the other reads, so each stays free after the other, and the two orders give the same state.
  2. One shared letter X, whose rows end at c₁ and whose landing place ends at c₂. This is the case of abac, and the hard one. Each step can be one of three kinds: the letter above wins (it is longer), the letter below wins, or the two are equal. That gives nine combinations of kinds for the pair. The table below shows which can happen.
  3. One shared letter, the other way round. This is case 2 with the steps' names swapped.
  4. Both letters shared. The two letters form a cycle of two, and either step closes it. The two results differ only in where the closed letter lies and in which rotation of its word it holds. That is where the theorem's exception comes from.

In case 2, X is the upper letter at c₁, over Y, and the lower letter at c₂, under Z. Rows compare X with Y at c₁, and columns compare X with Z at c₂:

At c₁ ↓ / at c₂ → Z longer X longer equal X longer than Y impossible square; Y and Z equal impossible Y longer than X square impossible square equal square impossible square

The four impossible combinations fail for one reason. For both steps to be free, one of them would have to land strictly inside a letter's interval in the other strip, where no boundary can be. The five squares are each written out in both orders in the proof, and each reaches the same letters, places and words. abac is the square in the top row. X has two rows, so it is longer than Y and longer than Z. Y and Z have one row each, as forced.

A last detail settles the step count. Every square closes with one step on each side, and the closing cycles of case 4 need none. So any two complete paths of free steps have the same length, not only the same end point.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 4. How was it checked?
items.text:
The proof was checked against a program that steps every short column exhaustively. It covers every column over 2 letters up to length 14, and likewise over 3, 4 and 5 letters up to lengths 9, 7 and 6. On each column it follows three random complete paths of free steps. At every state along every path, it takes every ordered pair of free steps available, classifies it by case and kinds, and runs both orders. It checks that the two orders reach the same state. In case 4 it checks instead that one step closes a cycle, and that the two agree up to its rotation.

The results, over 10.7 million ordered pairs. Same state counts the pairs whose two orders reach the same state, and closed cycle the case 4 pairs that agree up to rotation:

Alphabet, longest Pairs Same state Closed cycle (case 4) Exceptions 2 letters, 14 4,322,196 4,042,698 279,498 0 3 letters, 9 3,434,430 3,129,050 305,380 0 4 letters, 7 1,741,700 1,531,570 210,130 0 5 letters, 6 1,164,480 991,358 173,122 0

In every alphabet, the combinations of kinds that occur are exactly the ones the proof allows. Case 2 shows its five squares, and case 3 their mirror images. Case 4 shows only the three combinations that close a cycle. None of the four impossible combinations was ever seen. Rerun for this post, the program gives the same counts.

Before the proof, a separate count had run the free steps to the end under different orders and compared the results directly. No two orders ever disagreed, on 404,677 short columns under ten orders each, or on the 233 Wikidata blocks and four blocks of prose. On every real block the results were equal exactly, with no closed cycle to allow for.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 5. What is proved and what is counted
items.text:
The research record labels each statement as proved by hand, or counted (exact for the data it ran on, but no more). For this result:

  • Proved: free steps in any order reach one end point, up to closed cycles. A program checked every case on 10.7 million pairs of steps.
  • Proved: every complete path of free steps has the same number of steps.
  • Proved: after the free closure, no step adds a letter.
  • Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks under three orders: before reaching the closure, free-first orders never held more long words than the closure has letters.
  • Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks: the closure leaves 0.185 r letters and takes 0.896 r steps, at the median.

The two counted figures are now properties of each block, so their spread across blocks is a spread across text, not across algorithms. The Wikidata corpus is an extract of a Wikidata dump. Its blocks here are the 233 with at least 65,536 rows, and each figure is divided by that block's own r.

items.title: 6. What could a decoder do with it?
items.text:
Everything in this section is a consequence of the theorem, not a measurement.

Any order is correct. The cost of a free-first decoder is in finding its free steps. It needs a worklist of ready steps. An earlier count priced that worklist at about 150 instructions a run on one thread, against 115 for Cells' sweep from the right-hand end. The theorem says a decoder may take its free steps in whatever order its worklist yields them: a stack, a sweep, or batches. The end point, the step count and the bound on width hold for all of them. So a worklist can be designed for speed alone.

Splitting one block between threads. Two free steps on different letters commute. So free steps can be handed to different threads, and they reach the same state as on one thread. The condition is that each thread's step writes only its own two letters' records. That is a way to split one block's rebuild that is proved correct, which matters for how mibz2 uses many cores. It decodes blocks in parallel either with each thread on a block of its own, or with teams of threads sharing a block. On a 10-core Intel desktop at ten threads, a block per thread took 1.040 times the teams' wall time in the latest run. Its 95% interval is 1.019 to 1.061 (the run's report). The working explanation, not yet measured directly, is that each thread's live state competes for the shared cache. A smaller live state, and a proved way to share one block's free steps, both bear on that.

A bound fixed by the block. After the closure, no step adds a letter. So from the closure on, a decoder that takes free steps first never needs more live letters than the closure has. That is about 0.19 r on Wikidata, against the r slots Cells reserves today. Before the closure, the bound held on every block counted.

No free-first decoder has been built. A first decoder that keeps the untouched one-byte letters implicit, and writes a letter only when its word first grows, has been built with Cells' right-end order and is being measured. None of it has been timed yet.

items.title: 7. What is still open?
items.text:
Which steps does the closure leave? Only equal steps remove letters, and a block's rebuild makes exactly r − 1 of them. So the closure's letter count is 1 plus the number of equal steps that can only become ready after a paid step. Saying which equal steps those are, from the block's runs, would describe the closure without running it. That is the next question.

One block on many cores, by rounds. A different route also reaches the end of a rebuild: repeatedly cut the map down to the rows where runs branch, all at once. It collapses a whole Wikidata block to between 2 and 560 letters in 5 to 18 such rounds, and the work within a round is independent. Cells' right-end order, by contrast, has a chain of 93 dependent rounds at the median. As counted, though, each round walks every row it removes, so its work grows with the rows rather than the runs, which is the cost Cells exists to avoid. Whether a round can be computed on letters and their words alone has not been tested.

Is width a cutwidth? The width post links width to the cutwidth of a graph: line up its vertices, cut between any two, and count the edges that cross. Whether the width of a rebuild is exactly a cutwidth of the block's cycle of rows, bundled by runs, is a conjecture.

The record of the rounds count is #440.
