items.title: 1. What does a worker do, and what do the workers share?
items.text:
Who does what in mibz2's parallel decoder

Scanner · one thread, in stream orderreads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbolsWorkers · each finishes one block on its ownworker 1worker 2worker 3worker 4move-to-front, inverse BWT, run-length step, checksumkitchen: cooks, each making a whole dishShared L3 cache, 20 MiBkitchen: the one worktop they all useReader · in stream ordertakes the finished blocks and hands out their bytes Conceptual. The thread names are the code's (src/parallel.rs); the kitchen labels are an analogy. In the kitchen, each cook prepares a whole dish at a station, and all of them spread their ingredients on one worktop; more cooks crowd it. The analogy stops at eviction: a cook's ingredients never vanish from a worktop, but a worker's data does leave the cache and has to be fetched again from main memory.

mibz2's parallel decoder (src/parallel.rs) has three kinds of thread. The scanner reads the compressed stream in order; a block's end is only known once its Huffman-coded symbols have been read, so this scanner reads them one block after another. Each worker then finishes one block on its own: the move-to-front step, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform, a run-length step and the block's checksum. The reader takes the finished blocks back in order and hands out their bytes. The decoder lets up to four blocks a worker be in flight at once, in one window shared by all of them: 28 blocks for seven workers.

Blocks decode independently, so more workers means more blocks at once. But the workers are not independent: they run on cores that share one L3.

The test machine's caches: private L2s, one shared L3

core 1L2core 2L2core 3L2core 4L2core 5L2core 6L2core 7L2core 8L2core 9L2core 10L2each L2: 256 KiB, private to its coreL3 · 20 MiB, shared by all ten coresevery worker's 2.1 MB footprint meets the others heremain memoryfar larger, several times slower to reach The test machine. The L1 caches, per core and smaller still, are left out. A worker's footprint is about eight times its core's L2, so it lives in the shared L3.

Each core has its own 256 KiB level-2 (L2) cache. Behind them sits the 20 MiB L3, shared by all ten. A lazy-letters worker rebuilding a 900 kB block has a footprint of about 2.1 MB: the size of what the kernel stores for the block, an estimate of the memory it reuses while it decodes. It is a proxy for the worker's working set, not a measurement of what it occupies in the LLC. That is far more than the L2, so the footprints meet in the L3.

Working set, footprint and occupancy

A working set is the data a program reuses over some window of time. A footprint is an estimate of its size. Occupancy is how much of a shared cache a worker actually holds at a moment, which depends on the other workers. The standard tools for the first are reuse (stack) distances, introduced by Mattson et al. (1970), and the miss-ratio curves built from them; Qureshi and Patt (2006) use such curves to divide a shared LLC between programs. A curve from one trace is an approximation for a given replacement policy, not the exact miss count of every cache and schedule. mibz2 hasn't measured one yet.

Workers filling the shared L3

Workers: 7

4 workers8.4 of 21.0 MB · 40%7 workers14.7 of 21.0 MB · 70%8 workers16.8 of 21.0 MB · 80%10 workers21.0 of 21.0 MB · 100%0.70.8 Drag the slider to change the number of workers; the text below the bar says what the measurements show at that count. Each green block is one worker's footprint, about 2.1 MB for a lazy-letters worker on a 900 kB block, in the test machine's 20 MiB (21.0 MB) L3. This is capacity accounting, not a model of the misses: footprints overlap and change while a block decodes, and the cost rises smoothly as they grow, with no cliff at 100%. The dashed lines are the teams policy's 0.7 of the L3 and the fitted optimum's 0.8.

items.title: 2. Why are fewer workers faster?
items.text:
Three explanations suggest themselves. The clock: fewer busy cores may each run faster. Idle time: with more workers than the processors can keep busy, some wait. The cache: each worker slows the others by evicting their data. The hardware counters at 10 threads tell these apart. They count per byte of output, against 10 workers.

Fewer workers, cheaper bytes: the work is the same, the shared-cache misses fall

per byte of output, against 10 workers0.40.60.81.0678910decoding workers, at 10 threadsinstructions, 10 workers: 1.000instructions, 9 workers: 0.995instructions, 8 workers: 0.988instructions, 7 workers: 0.982instructions, 6 workers: 0.977instructions 0.977L2 misses, 10 workers: 1.000L2 misses, 9 workers: 1.001L2 misses, 8 workers: 1.013L2 misses, 7 workers: 1.029L2 misses, 6 workers: 1.039L2 misses 1.039cycles, 10 workers: 1.000cycles, 9 workers: 0.966cycles, 8 workers: 0.860cycles, 7 workers: 0.752cycles, 6 workers: 0.672cycles 0.672L3 misses, 10 workers: 1.000L3 misses, 9 workers: 0.924L3 misses, 8 workers: 0.653L3 misses, 7 workers: 0.521L3 misses, 6 workers: 0.403L3 misses 0.4030.7520.521 Measured on the test machine at 10 threads, one copy of the Wikidata extract, 10 repetitions under perf stat, pinned one thread a core. L3 misses are the last-level cache's load misses. The clock (cycles over reference cycles) was 1.326 at every count, so the cycles are not falling because the cores slowed or sped up.

The clock is ruled out first: cycles over reference cycles, which measures the clock against its base rate, is 1.326 at every worker count. The work is the same: instructions per byte fall by under 2% from 10 workers to 7. The private L2 caches see about the same traffic, with L2 misses up about 3%. What changes is the shared cache. From 10 workers to 7, LLC misses per byte fall 48%, and cycles per byte fall 25%. The fall is smooth: an earlier prediction of a cliff, once the footprints fit, was refuted by exactly this shape.

Lost parallelism against cheaper bytes. The wall time is the cycles each byte costs, divided by how many processors are working on the bytes. At 10 workers each worker's CPU utilisation is 0.763, so 7.63 processors' worth are working; at 7 workers it is 0.925, 6.48 processors' worth. That is 15% less processing power. The cycles per byte fell 25%. So the wall time is \(0.752 / 0.849 \approx 0.886\) of what it was, against 0.885 measured.

Why this bookkeeping proves nothing by itself

When the clock is flat, cycles per byte divided by the CPUs at work equals the wall time almost by definition, so any cause would balance this sum. The evidence for the cache comes from the counters' pattern instead.

The evidence comes in three tiers. Observed: with fewer workers, the LLC misses per byte and the cycles per byte both fall, while the instructions, the clock and the private-cache traffic stay about the same. Supported: interference for the LLC's capacity contributes materially to the cost. Under investigation: what the rest is made of. A counters run has since measured the latency of loads that hit in the L3 falling from about 91 cycles to 65 as workers go from 10 to 7, which fits queueing in the L3 and the ring that links it to the cores; but it missed that hypothesis's predicted size, and traffic to main memory was not measured, so main memory isn't ruled out (notes, section 2).

Interference, not (as far as we can tell) coherence

The workers decode independent blocks and don't write to each other's block data, so the main effect is interference in a shared cache's capacity and the paths to it. They do share a queue, hand-offs and allocator state, so some coherence traffic exists. Nothing in the counters points to it as the explanation, but they don't rule it out either.

items.title: 3. A model of what the workers share
items.text:
The model takes the smallest of a few bounds, each counted in workers:

\[m = \min(N,\ W_{L3},\ 0.80\,N,\ W_{\mathrm{ser}}).\]

\(N\) is the logical CPUs the process may use; SMT enters through each worker's cost, not through this cap. \(W_{L3}\) is a cache bound, summed over LLC-sharing domains \(d\) (one on this machine) as \(\sum_d \min(N_d,\ 0.8 \times L_d / F)\), with \(N_d\) a domain's logical CPUs, \(L_d\) its LLC size and \(F\) the footprint: about 7.9 on this machine. \(0.80\,N\) is a CPU bound, and \(W_{\mathrm{ser}}\) a serial bound, how many workers the scanner can keep fed, added after the small-block test of section 4. This is a resource-constrained heuristic: each bound is estimated separately and the smallest taken, and the resources interact. Predicting performance from shared-cache contention has a literature of its own; Xu, Chen, Dick and Mao (2010) is the closest to this approach.

The cache bound. At 10 threads, the cycles per byte with \(W\) workers fit \(c(W) = a + b\,W^2\) with \(a \approx 0.42\) and \(b \approx 0.0068\). These are normalised costs: the measured cycles per byte at 10 workers, about 23, count as 1. The fit is not forced through that point, and gives \(c(10) = 0.422 + 0.0068 \times 100 = 1.102\). A refined form, \(c(W) = a + b\,W\,W_{\mathrm{run}}\) with \(W_{\mathrm{run}}\) the workers running at once, removes most of that residual (it gives 0.983); the quadratic is the simpler illustration. \(a\) is an extrapolated intercept, and the square is a fit: exponents from 1.5 to 2.5 fit these points about as well. If every worker is kept busy, the wall time goes as \(a/W + b\,W\), smallest at \(\sqrt{a/b} \approx 7.9\), where the footprints fill about 0.8 of the L3. The 0.8 is a fitted constant, and the bound is a modelled throughput optimum, not a hard ceiling.

The CPU bound. A worker with a processor to itself has a CPU utilisation of 0.93; the rest of the time it waits on the pipeline. The scanner and reader use about \(0.16\,W\) processors, and a fully subscribed set of processors leaves about \(0.125\,N\) idle, a residual idle capacity whose cause isn't established. Solving \(0.93\,W = N - 0.16\,W - 0.125\,N\) gives \(0.80\,N\).

One worked example, and the tie-break. At 8 threads, the bounds give \(m = \min(8,\ 7.9,\ 6.4) = 6.4\), so the candidates are 6 and 7. At 10 threads, \(m = \min(10,\ 7.9,\ 8.0) = 7.9\), with candidates 7 and 8. The rule chooses between them on the fitted cost, and within 1% it takes the smaller. That tie-break was fitted to these two counts, not predicted: on the cost curve below, 8 workers cost \(0.10715\) against 7's \(0.10789\), 0.7% cheaper, and at 8 threads the model puts 6 and 7 level. The measured bests are 7 (8 was 1.9% slower) and 6 (7 was 5% slower). A separate, more conservative rule, sizing the footprints to 0.7 of the L3 as mibz2's teams policy does for its tables, also gives 7 at 10 threads; it is a different rule, not the fit rounded.

The fitted cost prefers 8 workers; the measured wall time prefers 7

Solid: the measured wall time at 10 threads against 10 workers (figure 1). The two needn't agree point by point, since the measured wall also includes the workers' CPU utilisation; the point is that the fit's cheapest whole count is 8, while the run's is 7.

The rule at two thread counts: bounds, the rule's pick and the measured best

10 threads (N = 10)logical CPUs10cache bound7.9CPU bound8bounds give 7.9; fit puts 8 within 0.7% of 7rule picks 7 · measured best 78 threads (N = 8)logical CPUs8cache bound7.9CPU bound6.4bounds give 6.4; fit puts 6 and 7 within 1%rule picks 6 · measured best 6 Modelled, from measured inputs. The rule then chooses between the whole numbers either side on the fitted cost, taking the smaller within 1%, a tie-break fitted to these two counts. The measured bests are from figure 1.

The same rule gives 5 workers at 6 threads and 3 at 4, and pinned runs found 5 and 3 best there, on the older (eager) kernel. The 8-thread result was already known when the CPU bound was written. All these points below 10 threads were pinned, which section 5 shows matters more than the model allowed.

The contention–parallelism trade-off. At the fit's optimum, the contention-associated overhead \(b\,W^2\) equals the base cost \(a\), so it is half the total; for a general exponent \(p\) it is \(1/p\) of the total. At 7 workers the fit puts it at about 44% of the cost. That is a modelled cost share, not a measurement: it doesn't say how much time any other change could recover, and with other exponents it ranges from about 34% to 60%. The derivation, its sensitivity and what is known about the overhead's make-up are in the notes.

items.title: 4. The test that failed: smaller blocks
items.text:
The test that could fail was the same file compressed with bzip2 -3, whose blocks are a third the size. Each worker's footprint shrinks with its block, to about 0.38 of its size at -9, so the cache bound moves from about 8 to about 22. Frozen beforehand: the trim disappears, and the best count at 10 threads is 9 or 10, with 7 workers no better than 0.98 of 10 workers' time. The three-bound model of the time agreed, predicting 9 workers, with 7 slower than 10.

Smaller blocks, a smaller gain, the same best count

wall time at 10 threads, against 10 workers (lower is faster)0.901.00678910decoding workers6 workers: 0.9227 workers: 0.8858 workers: 0.9029 workers: 0.98210 workers: 1.0006 workers: 0.9877 workers: 0.9788 workers: 0.9879 workers: 0.99210 workers: 1.000-9: 7 workers, 0.885-3: 7 workers, 0.978bzip2 -9bzip2 -34 workers at -3:1.343, off the chart Measured on the test machine at 10 threads, the process limited to one hardware thread a core, 10 paired rounds a point; bars are 95% intervals over the rounds, on one machine. The -9 curve is the first 10-thread run (figure 1); the -3 curve is the same Wikidata extract recompressed with 300 kB blocks. Each point is against 10 workers on the same file.

The best count stayed at 7, so the prediction failed. At 10 threads, 9, 8, 7 and 6 workers took 0.992, 0.987, 0.978 and 0.987 of 10 workers' time, and 4 workers took 1.343. The gain fell from about 12% to 2%, and 7 workers at 0.978 (0.973, 0.983) leave "no better than 0.98" borderline. Part of the model held up. Contention did shrink with the footprint: comparing slopes over the same worker counts at both block sizes, the contention term's exponent in the footprint comes out between 1.85 and 2.23, near the 2 it has in \(W\). But a sharper test, whether misses depend only on how full the cache is, failed at 3 workers: they were 34% below its prediction. That suggests contention depends on how many workers run at once as well as on their footprints.

What sets 7 at -3 is a hypothesis: the scanner. Part of its work, and the reader's, is paid once a block, and a -3 file has three times as many blocks a byte. An occupancy trace showed the workers idle waiting on the scanner 28% of the time at -3 against 5% at -9, and throughput in the timed runs stayed near 2.5 GB/s from 6 workers to 10. But that trace came from a run that failed its own memory-ledger check and was not pinned like the timed runs, so it suggests the serial bound \(W_{\mathrm{ser}}\) without establishing it. The bound was added after the data, so it needs its own frozen test.

Every other frozen prediction, met and failed, is scored in the notes' ledger. Selected:

items.title: 5. What shipped, and what the model still needs
items.text:
Status on 17 November 2026. mibz2 0.5.4, released today, trims its workers on the test machine in two modes. Pinned to one logical CPU on each of exactly as many cores as threads, it runs 7 lazy-letters workers at 10 threads, 6 at 8, and 5 and 3 eager workers at 6 and 4 threads. Unpinned, it runs 7 lazy-letters workers from 10 threads, at 0.873 of 10 workers' time, and changes nothing below. It recognises the machine from its present and online CPUs. It is not the model: no general selector has shipped.

The two modes differ because the pinned gains below 10 threads did not transfer to the full machine. Every sweep of 10 threads or fewer ran pinned, so the workers shared their cores with the scanner, the reader and the main thread, and a worker fewer freed a core for them. Unpinned, those threads have CPUs of their own: at 8 threads 6 workers took 1.000 of 8's time, and at 4 threads 3 took 1.214 of 4's. That implicates competition for the CPU, the effect the CPU bound is meant to capture, but it doesn't rule a cache benefit in or out. A net ratio can hide both: a cache saving to 0.96 of the cycles and a parallelism loss of 1.0417 multiply to 1.000. So the pinned 6- and 8-thread points can't calibrate cache contention alone, and they come out of the contention fit. At 10 threads the gain survives unpinned, at 0.873, and the counters support interference in a shared resource, with the exact mechanism unresolved. (0.5.3 had read the machine through the process's affinity set, which a pinned 10-thread run limits to 10 logical CPUs, so its trim fired only unpinned; 0.5.4 fires in both.) Beyond the cores, 0.5.3's release run measured about 6.5% less wall time than 0.5.2 at 12 to 20 threads, with about 25% less processor time and 22% lower peak memory. 0.5.4 admits only the two configurations above: a 10-CPU mask spread over five cores' hardware threads, say, gets the old plan. Whether a general model should read topology machine-wide or through the affinity set is still open.

Two LLC-sharing domains: the limit is summed per domain

domain 1corecorecorecoreits own L3workers here compete heremin(its CPUs, 0.8 × L3 ÷ F)domain 2corecorecorecoreits own L3workers here compete heremin(its CPUs, 0.8 × L3 ÷ F) Conceptual: a processor with two LLC-sharing domains, as on many AMD chips (one per core complex, or CCX) or a two-socket server. F is a worker's footprint. The cache bound is the sum of each domain's bound, each capped by its logical CPUs, provided the workers are spread across the domains.

The same question arises on processors with several LLC-sharing domains: many AMD chips have one per core complex (CCX), and a two-socket server at least one per socket. Workers compete for an LLC only within their domain, though they still share main memory, so the cache bound sums over the domains the process may use, each capped by its own logical CPUs \(N_d\). The current l3_bytes() reads one file, the first processor's cache/index3/size. The planned fix finds the cache whose level is 3, groups the CPUs in the affinity set by the LLC they share (shared_cpu_list), and gives each worker a soft affinity to a domain. On a free GitHub runner with 2 cores, 4 logical CPUs and one 32 MiB L3, the rule gives 3.2 and so 3 or 4 workers; those runs are pending, and the notes list the three results that would refute the model there.

The design is to detect once, decide once and then decode: read the logical CPUs, the LLC-sharing domains and the block size at startup, pick the count, and keep it, without tuning mid-stream, since streams are often short, timings noisy, and output timing should stay repeatable.

The chain, in short: a sweep found that fewer workers decode faster on the test machine; the counters pointed to the shared cache; a model of the cache, the processors and the scanner reproduces the counts it was fitted to, with a fitted tie-break; its first test at a new block size refuted its best count while its contention term roughly held; and an unpinned run showed that the gains below 10 threads don't transfer beyond pinning, where CPU competition is implicated, while the 10-thread gain survives, with its exact mechanism unresolved. A measured count describes the machine and the affinity it was measured with. A modelled count can be checked anywhere, and has to be.

Research records:

  • The calibration record: the sweep and the model
  • Verdicts: 8 against 9 workers past the cores, 7 against 8 past the cores, with counters, within the cores, with counters and the clock, the confirming run with held-out files, the low-thread sweep, the bzip2 -3 run
  • Release: 0.5.3 and its scaling run; the unpinned run; 0.5.4
  • The model's records: the rule as a spec, its scope, the -3 scoring, the miss-cost run scored
  • The technical notes, with every other record

items.title: Raising the knee
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Ten days ago, mibz2's problem was that giving its bzip2 decoder more work at once could make it slower. The decoder processes a compressed file in independent blocks, so it can decode several simultaneously. But each block has its own data structures, and those structures compete for the processor's shared cache. More blocks promise more parallelism while making each block more expensive. Past a certain point the extra cost wins. The throughput curve bends over: the scaling knee.

The default decoder once dealt with that risk by stopping at a fixed number of decoding teams. It could avoid a fall, but only by declining to use the extra threads. Since then, mibz2 has changed both how it reconstructs a block and how many workers it starts. Version 0.5.4 puts the result in view. Our test machine is a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K, with 20 logical CPUs and a 20 MiB level-3 cache that all ten cores share). On it, ten requested threads decode a 210 MB Wikidata sample in 0.102 seconds, the fastest median in the release sweep. The knee is still there, but it has been raised and softened. It is raised because the best point has moved from eight threads to ten, the machine's physical-core count. It is softened because asking for more now costs little or nothing. In 0.4.0 and 0.5.0, 12 to 20 threads took 11–18% longer than the best point. In 0.5.4's release sweep they take 4–5% longer by the medians, but that sweep pins ten threads and gives twelve or more the whole machine. With placement held constant, 10, 12 and 20 threads decode in the same time, to within half a per cent. It is not straightened: the extra hardware threads add nothing yet. At 12 to 20 requested threads 0.5.4 runs seven active workers, not twelve or twenty. Memory bandwidth is close to binding there: the plateau moves 75% of the memory traffic the machine can sustain, but that is not yet a hard ceiling.

Throughput against threads, five releases on the test machine

0.00.51.01.52.0124810121620threads asked forGB of output a secondpinned, one CPU a corewhole machine0.2.4 (6 November)0.5.0: the fall at its deepest0.5.10.5.30.5.4: best at 10 Measured on the test machine: the median of 10 paired rounds per point, decoding an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump to 209.7 MB of output. Each release is taken from its own release-scaling run (0.2.4 from 6 November; 0.5.0, 0.5.1 from 16 November; 0.5.3, 0.5.4 from 17 November). The runs pin 10 threads or fewer to one CPU a core, and give 12 threads or more the whole machine.

The result is a flatter default curve, not the disappearance of the knee or of contention. The decoder now starts fewer workers than threads in the measured configurations where extra workers made decoding slower. In effect, 0.5.4 caps its workers at the number that pays off: seven, from ten requested threads. The cost of competing for the cache remains; it is now part of the plan rather than a surprise in the benchmark. Here is how we reached that result, what the release run establishes, and what the plateau still leaves open.

items.title: Raising the knee: scaling throughput to the limit of physical cores
items.text:
mibz2 0.5.4 now speeds up until all ten physical cores of its test processor are busy, then holds level on the whole machine up to twenty threads.

17 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.4 (changelog)

items.title: 1. What was the knee?
items.text:
A bzip2 file is made of blocks that can be decoded independently. mibz2 has two ways to spend its threads. In a team, several threads share the work of one block. With workers, each thread decodes a block of its own. The second arrangement can keep more cores busy, but it also puts more blocks' working data in the shared last-level cache (the L3 on the test machine).

The first scaling investigation measured the trade-off directly. On the test machine, each additional block in progress slowed the others. Three teams of three decoded faster than four teams of two. Version 0.2.5 adopted that smaller number of teams and gained about 9% at ten threads against 0.2.4, in two registered runs.

Levelling off is not the same as falling

The old shipped curve mostly levelled off: version 0.2.4 ran four teams of two from eight requested threads upwards, instead of allowing concurrency to keep growing. The falling side of the knee was visible when experiments forced too many blocks to run at once. The policy avoided that fall by leaving extra threads unused. It had contained the problem, not made more concurrency productive.

The kernel changed next. Cells reconstructed the text from compact rules rather than the old row-by-row navigation table. Lazy letters then kept working state for only the letters that needed it, reducing the amount each worker touched. Those gains reached the workers, which ran below ten threads, but not the teams, which still ran from ten. So by 0.5.0 the shipped curve really did fall: eight threads ran eight workers, ten or more ran three teams of three, and 12 to 20 threads took 16–18% longer than 8. In 0.5.1, workers with lazy letters displaced teams at ten threads and above. What was now faster than teams could still become slower if too many workers ran together. That was the next knee to control.

What mibz2 runs at each thread count, release by release

Where a cell has two counts, the first is the plan when the process is pinned one CPU a core, which is how the release-scaling runs measure 10 threads or fewer, and the second the plan on the whole machine.

items.title: 2. What does the new curve look like?
items.text:
The release-scaling benchmark decodes the same Wikidata sample on the test machine at each requested thread count. It reports the time to produce about 210 MB of output. Lower is better. These are the medians from the 0.5.3 and 0.5.4 release runs:

threads requested 0.5.3, seconds 0.5.4, seconds 1 0.387 0.385 2 0.244 0.241 4 0.148 0.144 8 0.110 0.105 10 0.115 0.102 12 0.107 0.106 16 0.107 0.106 20 0.106 0.108

The runs of ten threads or fewer are pinned one logical CPU per physical core; the higher counts use the whole machine. The paired version comparisons preserve placement within each count.

The shape matters more than the last decimal place. In 0.5.3, asking for ten threads made the decoder slower than asking for eight. At twelve and above it recovered. In 0.5.4, ten threads are the fastest point, while twelve to twenty sit between 0.106 and 0.108 seconds. Across eight to twenty threads that is 1.95–2.06 GB/s of decoded output. Twenty is still about 5% slower than ten by these medians. As the box below explains, most or all of that is a change of placement, not of thread count.

The paired comparison is stronger evidence for the version change than the medians alone. Across ten paired rounds, 0.5.3 took 1.123 times 0.5.4's wall time at ten threads (95% interval 1.094–1.152), or about 11% less elapsed time in 0.5.4. At eight threads the ratio was 1.045 (1.038–1.053). The new version also used less processor time and peak memory at those counts. At one, two and twelve to twenty threads, the release comparison detected no change. The apparent improvement at four threads was too small to resolve from the run's variation.

These comparisons show a real improvement at eight and ten threads. They do not by themselves establish that ten is statistically faster than every other count within 0.5.4; the table shows the median ordering, not paired confidence intervals between different thread counts. The figure below gives those within-release comparisons against eight threads, for selected releases since 0.2.4. It leaves out 0.2.5 to 0.3.3. The history between was not one continuous fall. In 0.2.5, ten threads took 0.918 of eight threads' wall time (95% interval 0.910–0.927).

The decline past ten is a change of placement

Paired round by round within 0.5.4's run, the higher counts took longer than ten threads:

The knee diagnostic did hold placement constant: it ran every count on the whole machine, in one session. Its medians, in seconds, with the interquartile range for four copies:

items.title: 3. Why did ten threads dip, and what fixed it?
items.text:
The ten-thread regression in 0.5.3 was a placement mistake in the planner. Version 0.5.3 tried to recognise the test machine from the CPUs the process was allowed to use. With the process pinned to ten CPUs, it no longer recognised the full machine and declined to apply its seven-worker limit. It started ten workers, with forty blocks allowed in flight.

How the release runs place their threads

The release harness pins runs of ten threads or fewer to one logical CPU per physical core. At ten requested threads, the process may use CPUs 0–9: one logical CPU from each physical core. Its workers, scanner and reader share that set. Runs of twelve threads or more may use all 20 logical CPUs. Pinning is how mibz2 runs under taskset or in a container limited to some CPUs; the whole machine is how it usually runs.

Unpinned, 0.5.3 did apply the limit: a later check of production on the whole machine found it building seven workers in all six runs. That check, run after 0.5.3 shipped, also timed seven workers against ten directly, with the counts set explicitly, and seven took 0.873 of ten workers' time (95% interval 0.866–0.880). The release benchmark's ten-thread dip was therefore not evidence that the seven-worker idea failed. It was evidence that the intended plan had not run.

Version 0.5.4 separates the two questions. It identifies the machine from all present and online CPUs, but still reads the process's affinity to decide which measured plan applies. Pinned to ten cores, it now starts seven lazy-letters workers, with 28 blocks in flight. Pinned to eight, it starts six, and pinned to six and four it trims one worker as well. Those three pinned trims did not carry over to the whole machine: in the same check, six workers at eight threads took 1.000 of eight workers' time, the six-thread trim was no faster, and the four-thread trim took 1.21 times as long. Competition for CPUs with the decoder's scanner and reader, which share the workers' cores when the process is pinned, is implicated, so 0.5.4 applies those trims only when pinned. The ten-thread trim holds in both modes; why exactly it pays is not settled.

The machine-wide check is cached once per process. An early release check caught repeated hardware discovery adding overhead to short decodes; that was fixed before 0.5.4 shipped. The result is a narrower policy than a universal formula: it applies to the test machine and its tested placement modes, not automatically to every ten-core processor.

items.title: 4. Does the plateau mean memory bandwidth is full?
items.text:
Nearly, but not yet. The plateau uses 75% of the memory bandwidth the machine can sustain, and every worker past seven adds traffic faster than it adds output.

With ten workers reduced to seven, the worker-count study found about half as many last-level-cache misses per decoded byte and 25% fewer cycles per byte. Instructions and clock frequency stayed approximately level.

At ten workers, each was busy about 76% of the time; at seven, each was busy about 92%. The smaller group offered less aggregate worker time, yet it decoded each byte much more cheaply. That is why removing workers can make a parallel program finish sooner. The utilisation arithmetic alone does not establish the cause; the cache counters supply the evidence for interference.

A diagnostic run on the plateau itself rules out the simplest alternatives. Decoding four copies of the sample on the whole machine, the workers compute 93–95% of the time at every thread count, so no serial stage, such as the scanner that reads the file or the reader that hands bytes back in order, is starving them. What rises with the workers is memory traffic. Counted at the memory controller, reads and writes come to 7.5 bytes for every byte of output at four workers, 11.0 at seven and 12.4 at eight.

More workers, more memory traffic for every byte decoded

The analogy: each worker is a cook at one shared worktop, the 20 MiB L3 cache.Whatever does not fit on the worktop is fetched from the pantry, main memory.More cooks crowd the worktop, so every dish needs more trips to the pantry.051015202512345678910workers decoding at oncebytes moved per byte of output7.511.012.413.9, pinned24.222.7current decoder: memory reads + writes (17 November)older decoder: memory reads + writes (14 November)older decoder: memory reads only Measured on the test machine at the memory controller, reads and writes per byte of output. Green: the current decoder, decoding four copies of the Wikidata extract, in the knee repeat with the memory-controller counters of 17 November (the whole machine, except the hollow point, pinned). Amber: an older decoder that held a slot for every letter of a block, over 15 repeated decodes of the single Wikidata sample a reading (memory-controller run, 14 November). The two runs used different decoders and workloads, so they are drawn side by side, not joined. The first knee diagnostic counted only reads that missed the L3, 6.9, 11.0 and 12.7 bytes at 4, 7 and 8 workers, close to the green totals. The analogy stops where caches differ from kitchens: data is not used up, it is copied in 64-byte lines.

It is tempting to read the two-gigabyte-per-second plateau as a DRAM bandwidth limit, so we measured it. A repeat of the diagnostic with the memory controller's own counters found the seven-worker plateau moving 24.8 GB/s of DRAM traffic: 11.0 bytes per output byte, of which 7.0 are reads and 4.0 writes. A separate test that streams memory as fast as it can reaches 33.1 GB/s on the same counters, so the plateau runs at 75% of the measured ceiling. On an older version of the Cells kernel, on 14 November, the same counters measured 22.7 and 24.2 bytes per output byte at eight and ten workers. The decoder has roughly halved its DRAM bytes per output byte since.

More workers push the traffic up faster than the output. Eight workers reach 83% of the ceiling at 12.4 bytes per output byte, and ten pinned workers 85% at 13.9, and both decode more slowly than seven. So bandwidth is close to binding, and every worker past seven spends it on traffic rather than output. It is not the hard ceiling at seven: the registered rule called bandwidth the limit only at 80% of the ceiling or more, and 75% leaves the question open.

At the plateau: how close is memory traffic to its ceiling?

7 workers: 24.8 GB/s, 75%10–20 threads, whole machinereads 15.8writes 9.08 workers: 27.4 GB/s, 83%8 threads, whole machine10 workers: 28.2 GB/s, 85%10 threads, pinnedmeasured ceiling, 33.10102030GB a second of DRAM reads and writes, four copies of the sample Measured on the test machine, decoding four copies of the Wikidata extract (knee repeat with the memory-controller counters, 17 November). Each bar is DRAM reads plus writes counted at the memory controller, the median of 10 rounds, with idle traffic subtracted. The ceiling is measured too: the best median of a separate test that streams memory as fast as it can (ab stream, its scale kernel), read on the same counters. At 7 workers the decoder writes 2.27 GB of output a second; at 8 and at 10 pinned workers it is slower than at 7, while moving more memory traffic.

There is another reason to be precise about the word plateau. At twelve to twenty requested threads on this machine, 0.5.4 still runs seven decoding workers. The decoder is not starting twelve, sixteen or twenty competing workers; the plan has capped the number of blocks being decoded simultaneously. A nearly flat result there means the planner has kept the most expensive part of the curve out of the default path. It does not prove that the hardware would scale if twenty independent decoding workers were set loose.

items.title: 5. How would we straighten the knee?
items.text:
Straightening the knee means a curve that keeps rising past the ten physical cores. The second hardware thread on each core (simultaneous multithreading, which Intel calls hyperthreading) would then add speed. Today it adds none. Three routes could change that. Each is a hypothesis with a measurement that tests it; none is a result yet.

Cheaper bytes per worker. At seven workers, the reads that miss the L3 come to 11 bytes for every byte of output. A smaller hot set per worker would cut that: the store and the tables the kernel keeps for a block. So would less traffic on the output side. One piece of the output side is folding the block's checksum into the final pass. That is an open research arm (#535), and its measured 1.5–3% gain is not yet settled. Fewer bytes moved per output byte raise the number of workers that pays, so more workers, and eventually the second hardware threads, can contribute. With bandwidth close to binding, this is the route that raises the ceiling. The test: bytes per output byte and wall time by worker count, before and after each cut.

Latency hiding with the second hardware threads. The counters run at ten threads measured about 2.2 reads that missed the L3 in flight at once, whenever any were. That is little memory-level parallelism. If the plateau is bound by latency rather than bandwidth, two workers sharing a core can overlap each other's misses: one computes while the other waits. That is the classic case where hyperthreading helps code that waits on memory. The test: the same number of workers placed as pairs on shared cores, against one worker a core.

Helpers on the second hardware threads. The decoder's other threads already gain from spare CPUs. Decoding four copies of the sample with four threads took 0.405 seconds on the whole machine, against 0.535 seconds pinned. Pinned, the scanner, reader and main thread share the workers' cores. The second hardware threads could host prefetch or helper threads that bring the next block's data into cache ahead of the workers. The test: a helper arm against none, at the same worker count, with the misses per output byte counted.

Which first. The memory-controller run in §4 puts the plateau at 75% of the measured bandwidth ceiling, with traffic per byte rising faster than output past seven workers. That makes cheaper bytes per worker the main route: every byte saved per output byte is room for more workers before the ceiling. Latency hiding with the second hardware threads stays open, since a quarter of the bandwidth is still unused at seven workers.

items.title: 6. What comes next for the knee?
items.text:
The other task is to make the planner portable. The measured seven-worker choice is not a general law. The cache model under test correctly recovered some counts on this machine, then predicted the wrong optimum for smaller bzip2 blocks. Other processors have different core counts, cache sizes, cache-sharing domains and memory systems. The right worker count needs to follow those facts, with tests that can prove a proposed rule wrong.

For now the release result is a good one, with a precise boundary. mibz2 no longer punishes a request for more threads with a large fall in throughput on this measured workload and machine. In the release sweep the penalty past the best point is 4–5%, down from 11–18%. With placement held constant, no decline is seen. It gets there by doing less work in parallel, more efficiently. The old knee exposed a bad trade-off between concurrency and interference. Version 0.5.4 runs on the better side of it.

What remains is a flat stretch past the cores to turn into a rising curve, a ceiling to raise, and a policy to generalise. That is a more useful problem than a curve that falls whenever we give it another core.

Research records:

  • The original eight-thread scaling investigation, lazy letters, and the cache-model post with its technical notes
  • 0.5.3's release-scaling run and the pinned ten-thread diagnosis, the unpinned control, the knee diagnostic and 0.5.4's release-scaling run
  • The worker-plan fix, the once-per-process machine read, and the release attribution ledger
  • The recorded runs: release scaling, and on the evidence branch the knee diagnostic (knee/run-20261117T123939Z), the unpinned control (unpinned/run-20261117T130353Z), the counters runs (miss-cost/run-20261117T104648Z) and the memory-controller runs (cells-imc/run-20261114T180428Z and knee/run-20261117T230729Z)

items.title: Technical notes
items.text: ← Cutting the loop open: decoding a block along shared paths

items.title: Technical notes: cutting the loop open
items.text: These notes hold the detail that the main post leaves out to keep its argument moving. They use its notation. \(L\) is the block's last column, of \(n\) rows, and \(f\) is LF. \(S\) is the set of kept rows, with \(m = |S|\) and the primary row \(p\) among them, and \(E = f(S)\) is the set of entrances. After the cut, the rows not kept form \(H\) wide strips, and \(\sigma\) counts the distinct bytes in the block. Every statement here is from the project's proof, checked by the two verifications cited at the end.

items.title: The bundle bound
items.text:
Partition the row line into the \(H\) wide strips and the \(s\) intervals of consecutive kept rows. That makes \(H + s\) pieces, with \(H + s - 1\) internal boundaries. Let \(e\) be the number of intervals of consecutive entrances. The entrance intervals can also be cut wherever the first-column byte changes. Then every entrance in a bundle is reached from a kept row with the same letter, so a bundle has one kept letter as well as one word.

Bound. There are at most \(e + H + s - 1\) bundles. With the byte cuts, there are at most \(3H + \sigma\).

Proof. Represent a gap between two neighbouring entrances by the row on its right. Inside one strip, a gap moves to the gap between the two rows' images, since the strip shifts both by the same amount. This map of gaps is injective, because LF is. Its image lies inside a strip's image, so it never produces a gap inside \(E\), and two distinct entrance gaps start disjoint gap paths. A gap between two different bundles must meet one of the \(H + s - 1\) internal boundaries before both sides reach the same interval of kept rows. Charge it to the first boundary it meets. Since the gap paths are disjoint, each boundary takes at most one charge. Add one bundle for the left end of each entrance interval. Finally, \(E\) is the complement of the strips' images, so it has at most \(H + 1\) intervals, and the byte cuts add at most \(\sigma - 1\); so \(e \le H + \sigma\). Likewise \(s \le H + 1\). Together, \(e + H + s - 1 \le 3H + \sigma\). ∎

Tight cases. Both verifications found columns with one wide strip that attain the bound. The column 110020000011 at threshold 2, with primary 9, has \(H = 1\) and \(\sigma = 3\), and six bundles: \(3 \times 1 + 3\). It attains the finer bound too, with \(e = 4\) and \(s = 2\), since \(4 + 1 + 2 - 1 = 6\). The column abbbbdddaaaaaaaacccddddaabbbcccc at threshold 4, with primary 21, has \(H = 1\) and \(\sigma = 4\), and seven bundles: \(3 \times 1 + 4\). One verification checked the bound on 19,717 run-structured cases, with no violation. On the frozen block, at \(t = 16\), there are 3,204 bundles against \(3 \times 3{,}448 + 89 = 10{,}433\).

items.title: One strip's heights
items.text:
The bound limits the number of bundles, not their heights. Take a single wide strip of \(w\) rows that LF moves by \(d \ne 0\). There are \(\min(w, |d|)\) rows entering it. When \(0 < |d| \le w\), each entering path advances by \(d\) a step until it leaves the strip, so the paths' heights are \(\lfloor w/|d| \rfloor\) and \(\lceil w/|d| \rceil\). These are the quotients of a Euclidean division of \(w\) by \(|d|\).

The two extremes are a shift by one row and an image disjoint from the strip. A shift by one gives one path of height \(w\): a bundle of width 1, so the traced letters \(U\) equal the area \(A\). A disjoint image gives one bundle of width \(w\) and height 1, so \(U = 1\) for \(A = w\). Two twelve-row columns with the same run widths and byte counts, 220021021110 and 110010202221, show both behaviours at threshold 2. In the first the strip's displacement is \(-3\), and three rows cross in parallel for one traced letter. In the second it is \(+1\), and one row takes three steps along the strip.

This is why neither the bundle count nor a small \(H\) bounds \(U\) by a multiple of \(H\). The same holds for the endpoint constructor's step count \(K\) below. It removes a common suffix one step at a time, without dividing, so a thick strip with a small displacement costs about \(w/|d|\) steps.

More kept rows can mean more to trace. On the frozen block, \(U\) falls at every threshold swept, but that is not a rule. The column 110000 with primary 2 has \(f = [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3]\) and two loops, 2 → 0 → 4 → 2 and 1 → 5 → 3 → 1. At \(t = 1\) only the primary is kept. Its one open path, 0 → 4 → 2, traces two letters, and the other loop is never cut. At \(t = 2\) rows 0, 1 and 2 are kept. That cuts the second loop open. The nonempty paths, 4 → 2 and 5 → 3 → 1, are one and two steps long and lie in separate bundles, so \(U\) rises from 2 to 3.

items.title: The two constructors of the open paths
items.text:
The tracer. Start at the leftmost entrance not yet covered, and follow its path through the wide strips. At each strip, and at the final interval of kept rows, note the distance from the path's row to that piece's right-hand edge. Count the starting entrance interval's edge as well. The smallest of these distances is the width of the bundle: every row in it follows the same strips to consecutive exits. Advance by that width and repeat. The tracer needs only the wide strips and the intervals between them.

The endpoint constructor. Build an auxiliary interval exchange on \(m + n\) points: a prefix of \(m\) terminal points, followed by a shifted copy of the \(n\) rows. Its arrows are:

  1. terminal \(k \to m + e_k\), with the empty word;
  2. \(m + x \to m + f(x)\) on the \(H\) wide strips, with their bytes;
  3. \(m + s_i \to i\), with the empty word.

The terminals of each kind join up into intervals, so at most \(3H + 2\) intervals start the exchange. Its first return to the prefix is exactly \(P\), with the words \(w_k\), because the two empty arrows delimit each path. Now remove rows from the right-hand end until only the prefix is left. If the last domain strip is \(X\) and the last image strip is \(Y\), remove the common suffix of their widths. The shorter strip's record keeps the joined word, the reverse word of \(X\) then that of \(Y\). The prefix boundary can never be crossed, and the number of live strips never increases. On the frozen block, at \(t = 16\), the exchange starts from 7,786 intervals and takes 11,215 steps, making 7,334 rules that each join two words. The word dictionary is then expanded by copying the rules already expanded.

Agreement. The two constructors gave identical bundle and word-length counts at \(t = 16\) on all 431 Wikidata blocks and the six prose blocks.

The queued decoder. As the run records arrive, each narrow row appends its kept index to a queue for its byte. Consecutive entries of a queue are then wired to consecutive exits of a bundle. That is the stable sort of the main post's section 2, done during the pass that reads the runs. A packed table, of four bytes per kept row when the row and the word's code fit in one word and eight otherwise, holds each kept row's inverse return and its word. On the frozen block it is 359,496 bytes. Output follows the marked loop, copying each word's bytes forwards.

items.title: The narrow–wide switch cut
items.text:
Colour each arrow narrow or wide, by the run it leaves. A switch row is a row whose incoming and outgoing arrows have different colours. Narrow-to-wide switches are the rows of \(E \setminus S\), and wide-to-narrow switches the rows of \(S \setminus E\). Since \(|E| = |S|\), the two counts are equal:

\[h = |E \setminus S| = |S \setminus E| = m - |E \cap S|.\]

The count can be taken before any word is known, by intersecting two tilings of the row line into runs. On the frozen block at \(t = 16\), \(h\) = 15,278 in both directions, as one verification recomputed. Keeping only the \(2h = 30{,}556\) switch rows, plus the primary if needed, gives a smaller kept system than the 89,874 narrow rows. But its construction traverses those 30,556 arrows one at a time, and traces 58,581 more letters to find the narrow side's words. In the repeated inverse-only measurement, its emitter took 0.511 ms against the queued decoder's 1.018 ms, and its constructor 6.771 ms against 1.857 ms. One verification corrected a detail of the convention. The program reclassifies a wide primary row as narrow before counting, so on 111000 at threshold 2 with primary 0 it finds switch rows \(\{0, 3\}\), not \(\{0\}\).

items.title: What the two verifications checked
items.text:
Both verifications rebuilt the construction from the proof, not from the project's code.

Claim First verification Second verification Restriction lemma proved proved Factorisation, spelling, independence proved; 6,000 random cases against a plain LF walk proved; 30,557 small column and kept-set pairs, at every kept mark Stochastic complement proved, with the closed loops in \(C\) deleted proved, with the closed loops in \(C\) deleted Bundle bound proved; tight; 0 violations in 19,717 cases proved; tight Endpoint constructor proved; step count not recomputed proved Switch identity proved; 15,278 both ways on the frozen block proved; marking convention corrected Frozen-block counts recomputed exactly at \(t\) = 1, 16, 256 checked as recorded at \(t = 16\) Medians over 233 blocks taken from the records re-derived: 88.6689% and 5.4943% Timings not re-run paired ratios recomputed from the raw rounds

The project's own checks, separately, compare each constructor with a plain decoder on 198,790 column, primary and threshold combinations. They also check the destination and word of every kept row's arrow on 26,135 more, and compare complete streams with libbz2.

Sources: the proof, the research journal, the checks, the first verification's record, and the second verification's review and report.

items.title: Cutting the loop open
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Much of mibz2's research is about one stage of bzip2 decoding: turning each block's Burrows–Wheeler transform back into text. A new way back from the BWT showed how the kernel mibz2 ships, Cells, does it by shrinking a map instead of walking it. The mathematical dictionary then named the objects that kernel works with. This post takes the same map apart another way, by cutting its one long loop open, solving the pieces separately and joining them back.

bzip2 stores a block as the last column \(L\) of its sorted rotations, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). Alongside it is the primary row, the row that holds the original text. A map called LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. Following it from the primary row therefore reads the block backwards, one byte a step, until it comes back to the primary row. That trip, the marked loop, is the decoder's loop. When LF is a single loop, as in the example below, the trip visits every row once, but it need not. The periodic text abab has the column bbaa, and its LF makes two loops, 0 → 2 → 0 and 1 → 3 → 1. The marked loop covers only half the rows, yet the decoder still writes the whole block. One lap reads ba backwards, which is ab forwards, and the decoder repeats that spelling up to the block's known length of four bytes, giving abab. A run is a stretch of equal bytes in \(L\). Because LF shifts all of a run's rows equally, the map is a list of shifted blocks of rows (One shift per run).

The loop is slow because each step needs the row that the step before it found. A plain decoder therefore makes up to 900,000 memory reads per block, each waiting on the last. Cells avoids most of them by working on runs rather than rows. It comes in two forms. Eager Cells lays out all its records before it starts. Lazy Cells, by contrast, makes them as it goes, which suits many threads at once (Lazy letters).

The idea of this post is to choose some rows to keep, the primary row among them, and cut the arrow leaving each one. The marked loop then falls into open paths. Each path starts at an entrance, a row whose incoming arrow was cut, and ends at a kept row. Where each path ends, and what it reads on the way, can be found from the uncut arrows alone. What the cut loses is which kept row's arrow went to which entrance, and a stable sort of the kept rows' letters rebuilds that separately. Joining the two gives back the loop, and with it the text.

The first finding is that the loop factorises. The trip from one kept row to the next is the open-path map applied after the stable sort of the kept letters, and neither needs the other's input. This is proved, and the proof has been verified twice, independently. Nor is the operation new. In Markov-chain theory it is the stochastic complement (Meyer, 1989), the chain watched only on the kept states. Here the chain is one permutation with a letter on each arrow, so the complement's infinite sum stops.

The pieces are also few, because the open paths travel in bundles of neighbouring rows. If the rows left on the open paths form \(H\) wide strips (stretches of long runs), there are at most \(3H + \sigma\) bundles, where \(\sigma\) counts the distinct bytes. Few bundles does not by itself mean little work, however.

The choice of rows to keep matters. On Wikidata the cut keeps every run of 16 rows or fewer. On a test block those are 93% of the runs but hold 10% of the rows. Keeping them therefore removes most of the places where neighbouring paths would split, while 90% of the rows stay on open paths.

On Wikidata, one traced letter spells about sixteen. Over the large Wikidata blocks, bundles cover a median 88.7% of each block, and tracing one path per bundle reads 5.5% of it. Yet two blocks of nearly equal run density differ by 66% in that cost. Sixteen is the saving in finding the paths, not in decoding, because the decoder still writes every output byte. It also still builds and walks a table of the kept rows' returns, one entry per kept row.

The decoder built on it, in one decode of the test block, asked for about 40% less additional heap than eager Cells. Over the whole Wikidata benchmark, on one four-CPU cloud virtual machine without SMT siblings, it is 9–21% slower than eager Cells and 7–8% faster than lazy Cells. The test with many blocks competing for cache is still to come.

Each claim below says whether it is proved, counted on the blocks, measured on a machine, or an interpretation that relates it to other work.

Sections 1 to 3 cut, rebuild and join a seven-byte example by hand; section 2 is the key step. Section 4 relates the result to the stochastic complement and to Cells. Sections 5 and 6 count the bundles, in theory and on Wikidata, and section 7 reports the decoder, its table and its costs. The technical notes hold the longer proofs.

items.title: Cutting the loop open: decoding a block along shared paths
items.text:
Snip the decoder's one long loop open and most of each Wikidata block falls into bundled paths, where one traced letter spells about sixteen.

18 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result

items.title: 1. What happens when the loop is cut?
items.text:
The worked example is the seven bytes banana$, where $ sorts before every letter and appears once. (It keeps the example small; bzip2 blocks don't need one.) Sorting its seven rotations gives the table below. The last column, read down, is \(L\) = annb$aa, and the text itself is row 4.

The sorted rotations of banana$, with each row's last byte and its LF arrow:

Row Rotation \(L\) LF 0 $banana a 1 1 a$banan n 5 2 ana$ban n 6 3 anana$b b 4 4 banana$ $ 0 5 na$bana a 2 6 nana$ba a 3

LF comes from \(L\) alone: \(\mathrm{LF}(i) = C[L[i]] + \mathrm{rank}\). Here \(C[c]\) counts the block's bytes smaller than \(c\), and the rank counts the earlier rows that also end in \(L[i]\). Row 5 ends in a; one byte is smaller, and one earlier row ends in a, so \(\mathrm{LF}(5) = 2\). From row 4 the arrows make one loop through all seven rows, and read $ananab: banana$ backwards. Row numbers are places in the sorted table, not in the text, which is why each step must wait for the last.

The stepper below keeps rows 0, 4 and 5 and cuts the arrows leaving them. Only paths are left, because every row has exactly one incoming arrow and a row on a loop already uses it to stay there. An entrance has lost its incoming arrow, so a path that starts there can never join a loop. It must run until the arrows stop, at a kept row. Each press of Next makes one change and says why.

Step through it: cut the arrows leaving the kept rows, then follow each open path

← BackPlayNext →
  1. The loop: the arrows go 4 → 0 → 1 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 3 → 4 and read $ananab, banana$ backwards.
  2. Keep rows 0, 4 and 5. In row order they are exit indices 0, 1 and 2.
  3. Cut the arrows leaving them: 4 → 0, 0 → 1 and 5 → 2. Rows 0, 1 and 2 lose their incoming arrows and become entrances 0, 1 and 2.
  4. Entrance 0 is row 0, a kept row: no steps, exit index 0, no letters.
  5. Entrance 1: row 1 → row 5, reading n. Exit row 5 is exit index 2.
  6. Entrance 2: row 2 → 6 → 3 → 4, reading nab. Exit row 4 is exit index 1.
  7. So P = [0, 2, 1], with the words: none, n and nab. No path joined a loop: each row of a loop already uses its one incoming arrow.
Use Next and Back, or Play. Circles are rows, with their last-column letters; arrows are LF. An amber ring is a kept row, where open paths end; a green dot is an entrance, where an open path starts. Think of the loop as a circular railway with a station at every row: keeping a row makes it a terminus, the track out of it is lifted, and each lifted track's far end becomes the first station of a line. The analogy stops at order: a railway's stations have no ranking, and here the rows' sorted order is what rebuilds the lifted track (section 2).

What exactly is \(P\)? The kept rows are numbered in increasing order, \(s_0, s_1, s_2\) = rows 0, 4, 5, and the entrances likewise, \(e_0, e_1, e_2\) = rows 0, 1, 2. Then \(P(k) = i\) when the path from entrance \(e_k\) ends at kept row \(s_i\). So \(P\) maps entrance indices to exit indices. It is neither a map of text positions nor LF; it records how the open paths connect, in the entrances' and exits' own numbering. Here an entrance's row and its index happen to agree, whereas an exit's need not: exit row 5 is exit index 2.

The three open paths of banana$, with rows and indices kept apart:

Entrance row Entrance index \(k\) Path Exit row Exit index \(P(k)\) Word \(w_k\), in LF order 0 0 0 0 0 none 1 1 1 → 5 5 2 n 2 2 2 → 6 → 3 → 4 4 1 nab

Why each kept row ends exactly one path. A kept row has no outgoing arrow, and every other row on a path has one of each. The stepper's argument, run backwards from a kept row, therefore reaches exactly one entrance. Any loops left over never meet a cut, and play no part in the text read from the primary row.

items.title: 2. Where do the cut arrows go?
items.text:
The paths needed only the arrows that were left. Putting the loop back together also needs the cut arrows: from each kept row, which entrance does its arrow reach? Looking that up row by row would bring back the walk, so the answer comes instead from how LF is built.

LF is a stable sort. It lists the rows by their last letter, keeping equal letters in row order, and each row's arrow points to its place in that list. If every row that is not kept is struck out, what remains is still sorted by letter, ties still in row order. It is therefore the stable sort of the kept letters alone. Let \(v = L[s_0]\,L[s_1]\cdots\) be the short column of kept letters. Then kept row \(s_j\)'s arrow reaches entrance \(e_k\) with

\[k = \mathrm{LF}_v(j),\]

where \(\mathrm{LF}_v\) is the LF rule applied to \(v\). This is the restriction lemma, the key step, because it gives the cut arrows from the kept letters without reading any other row.

For banana$, the kept rows hold a, $ and a, so \(v\) = a$a. Its stable sort puts $ first, then the two as in order, so \(\mathrm{LF}_v = [1, 0, 2]\). The table agrees. Row 0's arrow reaches row 1, which is entrance 1. Row 4's reaches entrance 0, and row 5's entrance 2. Here an entrance's rank and its row agree, by accident; the figure's lower half shows a kept set where they don't.

Restricting a stable sort to some rows gives those rows' own stable sort

last column, in row ordersorted by letter, ties by row(where each row's arrow points)kept letterssorted alonerow 0aj = 0$from row 40row 1nafrom row 01row 2nafrom row 52row 3bafrom row 63row 4$j = 1bfrom row 34row 5aj = 2nfrom row 15row 6anfrom row 26$j = 1=aj = 0=aj = 2=v = a$aLF of v: [1, 0, 2]entrance k for each jGreen: the kept rows 0, 4 and 5 and their arrows. Strike out the grey rows, and the kept letters stay in the same order.Another kept set, rows 0, 4 and 6: each entrance is numbered by its rank k, not its rowsorted listrow 0$j = 1row 1aj = 0row 2arow 3aj = 2row 4brow 5nrow 6nentrancesk = 0k = 1k = 2row 3 is the third entrance: k = 2strike out the grey rows and close upthe gaps: the ranks keep the orderRow 6's arrow (j = 2) reaches row 3. Among the entrances 0, 1, 3 that is rank 2, and LF of v = [1, 0, 2] gives k = 2directly. The stable sort of the kept letters finds ranks, never row numbers: the row is looked up from the rank. Conceptual, on the worked example. Left: the column in row order, with each kept row's index j. Middle: the same rows sorted stably by letter; a row's arrow (LF) points to its place here. Right: the kept letters, sorted on their own. The green entries appear in the same order in both sorted lists, so the short column's LF gives each kept row's entrance. Below: with rows 0, 4 and 6 kept, the entrances are rows 0, 1 and 3. The short column is again a$a, so k is again [1, 0, 2], but k = 2 now means row 3: k is a rank among the entrances, and the rank is all the sort can give.

On its own, \(\mathrm{LF}_v\) has two loops here, 0 → 1 → 0 and 2 → 2. The short column is not a smaller BWT of the text; the open paths are what join its loops. Its stable sort is a counting sort, one pass over the kept letters. On the test block of section 5 it sorts 89,874 letters, against the block's 899,931 rows.

items.title: 3. Stitching the loop back together
items.text:
Each kept row now has a whole trip to the next kept row: the cut arrow, then an open path. In indices, the cut arrow takes kept index \(j\) to entrance \(\mathrm{LF}_v(j)\), and the path then takes that entrance to exit \(P(\mathrm{LF}_v(j))\). So the first return to the kept rows is

\[g(j) = P\big(\mathrm{LF}_v(j)\big).\]

On the way, the trip reads the kept row's own letter \(v[j]\), then the path's word.

The three trips of banana$. Each kept index \(j\) reaches entrance \(k = \mathrm{LF}_v(j)\) and then the next kept index \(g(j)\); the trip reads \(v[j]\) then the word \(w_k\), in LF order, and the decoder writes it reversed:

\(j\) Kept row \(v[j]\) \(k\) Word \(w_k\) \(g(j)\) Written, \(\mathrm{rev}(w_k)\,v[j]\) 0 0 a 1 n 2 na 1 4 $ 0 none 0 $ 2 5 a 2 nab 1 bana

So \(g = [2, 0, 1]\): one loop through the three kept rows. LF reads the text backwards, so to write it forwards the decoder starts at the primary row's index, 1, and follows \(g\) backwards. Each step writes its trip in reverse, as in the table's last column: \(\mathrm{rev}(w_k)\), then \(v[j]\). Going back from 1 to 2 writes bana, from 2 to 0 na, and from 0 to 1 $. Together that is banana$. When the marked loop is shorter than the block, as for abab, the decoder writes this spelling and repeats it until it has written all \(n\) bytes.

Two jobs that never read each other's input, joined at the end

items.title: 4. The same move in Markov-chain theory
items.text:
Keeping only some states and recording the returns between them is an old operation. A Markov chain moves between states at random, and \(M_{xy}\) is the probability of a step from \(x\) to \(y\). With the states split into the kept set \(S\) and the rest, \(C\), and the kept states ordered first, the matrix is

\[M = \begin{pmatrix} M_{SS} & M_{SC} \\ M_{CS} & M_{CC} \end{pmatrix}.\]

Suppose the chain is watched only while it is in \(S\). From one kept state to the next, it either steps straight within \(S\), or it leaves, spends some number \(a\) of steps in \(C\), and comes back. Adding up every such excursion gives the watched chain's matrix:

\[M_{SS} + M_{SC}\Big(\sum_{a \ge 0} M_{CC}^{\,a}\Big) M_{CS}.\]

The term with \(M_{CC}^{\,a}\) covers returns that take \(a\) steps from \(C\) to \(C\) before coming back. Carl Meyer named this matrix the stochastic complement (Meyer, 1989); it is also called the trace chain. In general the sum is infinite. When the chain cannot stay in \(C\) for ever (every state of \(C\) is transient), it converges to \((I - M_{CC})^{-1}\).

LF is a far simpler chain because it is a permutation. Each row of its matrix holds a single 1: every row has one next row, with certainty. Once any loops lying wholly inside \(C\) are deleted, as section 1 did, what remains of \(M_{CC}\) is a set of disjoint paths. A power of it is therefore zero, and the sum stops. Each arrow's letter is then written in place of its 1, and multiplication becomes joining words. The sum then gives each kept row its one return and that return's word. So the factorisation of section 3 is the stochastic complement of LF, with letters on the arrows (proved, and confirmed by both verifications).

The stochastic complement on banana$: each return is one term of the sum

The block from C to C holds two arrows, 2 → 6 and 6 → 3. Its square is the two-step excursion 2 → 3, and its cube is zero. Railway reading: the complement is the timetable printed only for the termini, with each journey's intermediate stations folded into its word.

The formula says what the kept system is, not how to compute it fast: a dense matrix over 900,000 rows would be hopeless. The Markov view says what must result, and LF's strips say how to remove rows cheaply, many at a time (section 5). The restriction lemma says how to reconnect them.

How this relates to Cells (an interpretation from the first verification, not a theorem). Cells also computes first returns. It shrinks LF's interval exchange from the right-hand end (Rauzy–Veech induction), and each surviving interval stands for a longer word. One of the two ways we compute \(P\) (section 7) takes the same right-end steps, but only over the wide strips and the entrances and exits around them. On the frozen block of section 5 that is 7,786 intervals to begin with, where Cells begins with all 51,184 runs. The narrow runs never enter the induction, because the stable sort wires them. Read this way, cutting open splits the interval exchange by run width.

The two approaches side by side, as we read them:

items.title: 5. How many pieces?
items.text:
The construction is worth having only if the open paths can be solved many rows at a time, and the runs make that possible. Suppose the cut keeps the narrow runs, those of at most \(t\) rows (section 6 uses \(t = 16\)), and the primary row. The other rows then form \(H\) wide strips. A strip is a stretch of consecutive rows that LF shifts by one amount, each row reading the same byte. (It is a wide run, or half of one if the primary row splits it.)

Why keep the short runs? The project keeps one 899,931-row Wikidata block as a fixed test case, the frozen block. Of its 51,184 runs, 68.6% are a single row long, yet they hold only 3.9% of the rows. At the other end, runs longer than 256 rows are about 1.0% of the runs, yet hold 73.9% of the rows. These shares come from the cut at \(t = 256\), which leaves 496 wide strips. One of them may be half of a run that the primary row splits, and runs of exactly 256 rows fall on the kept side. So the short runs make most of the boundaries, and the long runs hold most of the text. Left on the open paths, every short run would add edges where the paths split apart. Kept, they go to the stable sort, which wires them in one pass. The open paths are left a few wide strips, which hold most of the rows.

Most runs are narrow, but most rows are in wide runs

runs93.3% narrow6.7% widerows10.0% narrow90.0% widenarrow: runs of 16 rows or fewer, kept and sortedwide: the 3,448 strips left on the open paths Counted on the frozen block, at threshold 16: 89,874 kept rows (narrow runs, plus the primary row) and 3,448 wide strips out of 51,184 runs. The shares are derived from those counts; a strip split by the primary row counts twice, so the wide share of runs is at most 6.7%.

Two neighbouring entrances in the same strip are still neighbours after the step, since the strip shifts both by the same amount. They stay together, strip after strip, until a strip's edge falls between them, or they reach kept rows. A maximal set of neighbouring entrances that pass through the same strips and end at neighbouring exits is a bundle. The records call it a band. A bundle has a width \(b\), its number of rows, and a height \(h\), its number of steps. Tracing one of its paths costs \(h\) steps, and spells all \(b \times h\) of its letters.

A bundle is traced once for all its rows, but a strip that moves a little makes bundles one row wide

Top: a bundle of width 4 and height 2 passing through two strips; in railway terms, a convoy on parallel tracks, surveyed by one train. Bottom: the proof's one-strip example, with w = 6 rows. When a strip moves by d rows with 0 < |d| ≤ w, its paths have heights ⌊w/|d|⌋ and ⌈w/|d|⌉; when |d| ≥ w, each has height one. A shift by one row gives one tall path, a bundle one row wide with nothing to share, and a move clear of itself gives one short, wide bundle. The analogy fails at the edges: a bundle splits wherever a strip's edge or a kept row's falls between its rows.

Two totals describe a cut. The bundled area \(A = \sum_i b_i h_i\) is the number of letters the bundles spell. For a block whose LF is one loop, it is every row not kept, \(n - m\). The traced letters \(U = \sum_i h_i\) are what tracing one path per bundle costs. The ratio \(A/U\) is how many rows travel together, on average, for each letter traced.

The bound (proved). There are at most \(3H + \sigma\) bundles. The proof follows the gap between two neighbouring entrances as it moves with them through each strip. The two sides part only where the gap meets a strip's edge or the edge of a run of kept rows, and no two gaps meet the same edge first. The bound is attained on small columns (notes). Real blocks sit far below it: the frozen block has 3,204 bundles, against a bound of 10,433.

Few bundles is not little work. The bound counts bundles, not their heights. In the figure's lower half, one strip shifted by one row is a single bundle, yet tracing it costs a step for every letter. So \(U\) can scale with the block rather than with \(H\), as can the endpoint steps of section 7. Those are the figures to watch on real data.

items.title: 6. What do real blocks look like after the cut?
items.text:
The threshold sets the balance. Raising \(t\), the widest run kept, keeps more rows for the sort to wire, and leaves fewer, wider strips. On the frozen block that leaves less to trace at every threshold swept, but that is not a rule. Raising \(t\) can cut open a loop the marked one never met, and so add paths to trace; the notes give a six-row case. The frozen block's counts, recomputed independently from the proof:

Run density misses it. Blocks 118 and 176 both have 900,000 rows, and run densities of 0.06348 and 0.06342. Yet block 118 needs 57,626 traced letters and block 176 needs 34,775: 66% more. Their bundled areas are nearly equal, and so are their numbers of wide strips. The difference is in how the bundles break up (counted). Block 118 has 53% more nonempty bundles, while their mean height is only 8% greater. One verification reads this as the narrow runs cutting across the wide strips' paths more often in block 118 (an interpretation). A run count can't see that, whereas how the runs' images overlap can.

items.title: 7. What comes next?
items.text:
Two ways to compute the open paths. The tracer follows one path per bundle and measures each bundle's width as it goes. The endpoint constructor never follows a path. Instead it puts \(m\) terminal points before a copy of the rows, and joins them to the entrances and exits by arrows with empty words. It then removes rows from the right-hand end. Removing a row joins the arrow into it and the arrow out of it into one arrow, with their words joined. The terminals are never removed, so when only they are left, each terminal's arrow is a whole path, with its word. That is \(P\).

The endpoint constructor removes rows from the right until only the paths' ends are left

1. The route of entrance 2terminal 2empty2n6a3b4emptyterminal 1Empty arrows mark the path's two ends;between them are LF's own arrows and letters.2. One splice: row 6 is rightmost, so it goes first2n6a3⇒2na3The arrows into and out of the removed rowbecome one arrow, and their words are joined.3. Only the terminals left: the whole pathterminal 2nabterminal 1P(2) = 1 Conceptual, on banana$, with every row not kept treated as wide. The decoder removes a common stretch of rows from the end of two strips in one step, where the figure removes one row; the joining is the same. Removing rows 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 in turn leaves terminal 2's arrow reading nab to terminal 1, terminal 1's reading n to terminal 2, and terminal 0's empty arrow to itself: P = [0, 2, 1].

The two constructors gave the same bundle counts and traced-letter counts on all 431 Wikidata blocks and the six prose blocks (notes). The decoder below uses the endpoint constructor, and does the stable sort as it reads the runs, by queueing each kept row under its byte.

The decoder so far (measured). Its output has the same length and SHA-256 as libbz2's on the frozen block, the whole Wikidata benchmark and the prose. It rejects a damaged block CRC and a damaged stream CRC. The timings come from a four-CPU cloud virtual machine without SMT siblings. Each round decodes the Wikidata benchmark, 209,700,196 bytes of output, with eager Cells, lazy Cells (both as in mibz2 0.5.5) and the open decoder in turn. The times are medians in seconds, and the open decoder cuts at \(t = 16\). A ratio is the median over the rounds of that round's ratio, and no interval was computed.

Workers (rounds) Eager (s) Lazy (s) Open (s) Open ÷ eager Open ÷ lazy calling thread (11) 0.751 0.972 0.896 1.171 0.918 2 (9) 0.459 0.583 0.543 1.211 0.931 4 (11) 0.336 0.399 0.383 1.091 0.928

The open decoder beat lazy Cells at every worker count and lost to eager Cells at every one; on prose, on one thread, it took 1.455 times eager Cells' time. The figure below puts the wall times beside the two smaller measurements, each on its own scale: they have different units and cover different amounts of work.

Slower than eager Cells, faster than lazy, lighter on memory: three measurements, three scales

Wall time, whole Wikidata benchmarkopen decoder ÷ Cells; below 1 is faster÷ eager÷ lazy0.91.01.11.2calling thread1.1710.9182 workers1.2110.9314 workers1.0910.928Peak additional heap requestedone decode of the frozen block, MB04812eager Cells10.35open decoder6.29Inverse transform of the frozen blockby phase, ms, median of 51 roundsbuild the tablewrite the output02468open decoder1.86 + 1.02switch cut6.77 + 0.51 Measured on one four-CPU cloud virtual machine. Top: the paired wall-time ratios of the table above. Middle: the peak additional heap requested during one fresh decode of the frozen block. Bottom: the inverse transform alone, repeated on the frozen block, split into building the kept rows' table and writing the output; the switch cut is the harder cut described below. The three panels are not comparable with each other.

A cache simulation of the frozen block's decode counted 11% fewer instructions and 27% fewer first-level data-cache misses than eager Cells; those are simulated counts, not times. How much of the wall-time gap comes from building and walking the kept rows' table is not yet measured over the whole decode. Our reading, an interpretation, is that this table is the main cost eager Cells does not pay. The phase measurement shows its size on one block.

Of the switch cut, that kept fewer rows and paid more to find them

A smaller kept system is not always cheaper to build. A harder cut, the switch cut, keeps only the rows where a path switches between narrow and wide runs. On the frozen block its output phase took half as long as the decoder's above. But its build took 3.6 times as long, because finding the narrow side's words meant tracing 58,581 more letters. The smaller system was real, and this way of reaching it was slower.

What comes next. The open decoder holds less per block, and on many cores mibz2's speed has been limited by blocks competing for the shared cache (Modelling the cache). The test that matters is therefore on a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K), at the worker counts where that competition starts, against the release that ships. A run that settles how the test machine's clock behaves under sustained load comes first. Whether the kept system could itself be cut open again is an open question.

The ten-core comparison is queued behind the sustained-load run; this post will be updated with what it finds.

The chain, in three steps. Cutting the arrows that leave the kept rows turns the marked loop into open paths, which the rest of the block determines alone. A stable sort of the kept letters rebuilds the cut arrows, and joining the two gives the exact return to the kept rows. On Wikidata the open paths travel in wide bundles, so tracing 5.5% of each block spells nearly 90% of it.

The general lesson is about where to cut. A chain of dependent steps can be split into paths and a reconnection when the reconnection has a cheap rule of its own, as the stable sort is here. The split is worth making when many starting points share the paths.
