items.title: What decoding pays for
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Over the past two days we built three new ways to undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform, and studied a fourth that describes the text by copies. The aim was a method that does less work than the kernel mibz2 ships. That kernel, Cells, was introduced in A new way back from the BWT. Cutting the loop open then reported one of the new constructions, open return, which cuts LF's loop at chosen rows and decodes along the open paths left. This post sets all of them side by side. It asks what work each one cannot avoid, and why that work is so similar from one construction to the next.

bzip2 stores each block of text as the last column \(L\) of the block's sorted rotations, which is the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). A map called LF sends each row of the sorted table to the row of the rotation one byte earlier, so following LF reads the text backwards, one byte a step. A run is a stretch of equal bytes in \(L\), and LF moves all the rows of a run by the same amount, so the whole map is a list of shifted runs (One shift per run). We write \(n\) for a block's rows and \(r\) for its runs. A Wikidata block has about 900,000 rows and 50,000 runs. Cells works on runs, not rows. It shrinks the map one comparison at a time until a single row is left, recording how to spell the text as it goes. The mathematical dictionary names the objects it keeps.

The structural work of a construction is the number of basic operations it performs on the runs before it writes any output. Every construction must also write the 900,000 output bytes, so the structural work is where they differ by design.

We counted the structural work on all 233 large blocks of mibz2's Wikidata benchmark. Cells and two of the new constructions, adjacent-rank induction and forest-section elimination ("the forest"), do about the same work: 1.78 to 1.93 operations per run at the median. Their counts also rise and fall together from block to block, yet they do not perform the same operations, as a small example shows.

Much of the shared part is explained by one property of the block. We call the place between two neighbouring rows of a run a gap. Followed through LF, a gap's two rows read the same bytes until one of them crosses a run boundary. How long these pairs stay together, counted over the whole block, is the block's boundary-orbit profile. The persistence of boundary-orbit chains explains much of the variation in the structural work done by Cells and the forest. Yet it explains adjacent-rank induction's count poorly.

The obvious ways to lower that work did not lower it where we tried them. Refining the description of the block raised the forest's count on one block, and Wikidata has almost no repeated steps to accelerate. Splitting one block across cores was only modelled, and the model does far more total work. A description by copies of earlier text is far more compact, about 11,000 copies for a 900,000-byte block, but it is written in text positions. The copy routes we tested had to get those positions by walking LF, the walk the other constructions avoid.

Cells is therefore the best-performing formulation tested, although nobody has shown that it is optimal. The open question is whether a gap's separation depth, the number of bytes its two rows read together, can be found without walking its path.

Each figure is labelled as measured or proved, and each reading of it as interpretation. Sections 1 and 2 count the work and compare it, and section 3 builds the profile on a seven-row example. Sections 4 and 5 cover the routes that failed to do less, and section 6 says where things stand.

items.title: What decoding pays for: how long run boundaries persist
items.text:
Three ways of undoing bzip2's block sort spend about two operations per run, and how long run boundaries persist explains much of why Cells and the forest vary.

18 November 2026 · 16 min read · Research result

items.title: 1. How much work does each construction do?
items.text:
Each construction counts a different kind of operation, so the fair comparison divides each count by the block's runs.

  • Cells counts its steps. Each step compares the last stretch of rows in the runs' order with the last stretch in the order after LF, and trims the longer by the shorter. The earlier post works two steps by hand. Our test block is one block of the benchmark, with 899,931 rows and 51,184 runs; Cells takes 92,570 steps on it.
  • Adjacent-rank induction cuts LF's loop at the rows that are smaller than both of their neighbours along the loop, joins the paths between them, and repeats on the shorter loop. Stretches of neighbouring rows that move together are its atoms. It counts its atom visits: 102,233 on the test block, over 12 rounds (the first investigation).
  • Forest-section elimination draws each run as a site. Each slice of a run that LF sends into a single run is an arc, and the test block has 62,138. It keeps a forest of arcs whose inside is fixed by their boundary, and computes the returns through the arcs left over. Then it repeats on that smaller system until one row is left. It counts the arcs summed over its levels: 90,945 (the third investigation).

Over all 233 blocks, the three counts per run look like this:

Three constructions, about two operations per run

1.21.41.61.82.02.2operations per run (count ÷ runs in the block)Cells (ships in mibz2)unit: steps1.837Adjacent-rank inductionunit: atom visits1.929Forest-section eliminationunit: arcs over levels1.778medianmiddle halffull rangetest block Measured: the structural counts of 233 large Wikidata blocks, each divided by the block's runs. The box is the middle half of the blocks, the whiskers the full range, and the triangle the test block. Population coefficients of variation: 4.27% (Cells), 2.66% (adjacent-rank induction) and 3.45% (forest). The units differ (steps, visits, arcs), so the near-equality is a finding, not a definition.

The medians are 1.837, 1.929 and 1.778 per run, and each count varies by only 3–4% across blocks (the synthesis). An independent verification reproduced every figure from the three census files.

Why the alternatives are slower anyway. Equal counts do not mean equal time. Dividing each construction's time on the test block by its count gives about 17–28 ns per Cells step, 270 ns per adjacent-rank visit and 430 ns per forest arc. Cells is a tight loop over flat arrays; the other two use balanced trees, matching and stored recipes. Decoding the whole Wikidata stream on the calling thread of a four-CPU cloud virtual machine, against eager Cells (the form that lays out all its records before it starts):

Construction Full Wikidata stream, calling thread, against eager Cells Open return (Cutting the loop open) 17.1% slower Adjacent-rank induction (its study) 11.5× slower (8.370 s against 0.729 s) Forest-section elimination 15.23× slower (median of paired rounds)

With a pool of worker threads the gaps change. Open return is 21.1% slower with two workers and 9.1% slower with four. Adjacent-rank induction is 7.8× slower with four (2.682 s against 0.345 s). The per-operation figures are quotients of times by counts in different units. They say where the time went, not that cost per operation is the only difference. The forest, for one, also makes 48,647 slab matches on its first level that its arc count omits.

items.title: 2. Is it the same work?
items.text:
The three medians are close. The stronger finding is that the counts move together from block to block: a block that is expensive for Cells is expensive for the forest too.

Cells and the forest rise and fall together, and the profile explains much of what they share

Each dot is one block1.41.41.61.61.81.82.02.0equalforest: arcs over levels, per runCells: steps per runPearson 0.906Correlation left after removing…run density r/n0.859…and the excess proxy (q̃₁ − 1)/r0.393…and the profile's tail−0.061r/n, q̃₁…q̃₈ separately0.3070 Measured, on 233 large Wikidata blocks. Top: Cells' steps per run against the forest's arcs per run. Bottom: the correlation between the two counts' fitted residuals, after removing, by linear regression, the quantities named on each bar. The second bar's term is the historical proxy for the excess (one less than the first historical depth count, per run), and the third bar's is the historical profile's tail, counted with row 0; both are explained in section 3. The per-block points were joined from the Cells census and the forest census; the third and fourth bars come from the profile test, whose per-block profile values are not published.

The Cells–forest Pearson correlation is 0.906. Part of it could be run density, \(r/n\), which differs from block to block. Removing \(r/n\) by regression leaves 0.859, so most of the agreement is about something else in the block. The agreement is weaker for adjacent-rank induction: 0.74 with the forest and 0.68 with Cells.

Of a tempting reading, undone by thirteen bytes

Not the same events. A tempting reading is that the constructions perform the same operations in different clothes. An independent verification refuted that on a 13-byte column, 1111000011100. The forest has a free choice when two arcs have equal width. Reversing only those ties leaves the input, the starting network and the first level's output the same, yet the forest's total goes from 12 arcs to 15. Cells has no such choice, and its count is unchanged. So the shared count is not an event-by-event match but a shared dependence on something in the block, which the next section names.

items.title: 3. What the profile measures
items.text:
The worked example is the seven rotations of banana$, sorted, with their last bytes. Its last column annb$aa has five runs: a, nn, b, $ and aa.

Two neighbouring rows read the same bytes until a run boundary separates them

rowrotationlast byte0$bananaa1a$banann2ana$bann3anana$bb4banana$$5na$banaa6nana$baaamber line: a run boundary121. both read n, go to rows 5, 62. both read a, go to rows 2, 33. n | b: they partdepth 2depth 1 Conceptual, on the worked example. Rows 1 and 2 are neighbours inside the run nn. LF keeps neighbours in one run as neighbours, so the pair moves together until it straddles a run boundary. Read the chain the other way, from the boundary between rows 2 and 3: it pulls back to the gap between rows 5 and 6, then to the gap between rows 1 and 2, and stops there, because the rows LF sends to 1 and 2 (rows 0 and 5) are not neighbours. The profile counts four gaps at depth 0 and one each at depths 1 and 2.

The two rows stay together because, inside a run, LF sends neighbouring rows to neighbouring rows: both end in the same byte, and LF ranks rows with equal last bytes in their original order. So the pair reads the same byte, moves one step, and, if it is still inside a run, does so again. It parts only when it lands on a run boundary. The number of bytes the pair reads together is its gap's separation depth. In banana$, the gap between rows 1 and 2 has depth 2 and the gap between rows 5 and 6 has depth 1. The four gaps that are run boundaries have depth 0.

The boundary-orbit profile counts the gaps by depth. Let \(q_k\) be the number of gaps between neighbouring rows whose rows read exactly \(k\) bytes together. For banana$, \(q_0 = 4\), \(q_1 = 1\) and \(q_2 = 1\).

Why it counts chains. Read backwards, as in the figure, each run boundary starts a chain of gaps. In banana$, the boundary between rows 2 and 3 leads to the gap between rows 5 and 6, and then to the gap between rows 1 and 2. A chain that lasts \(\ell\) steps has exactly one gap at each depth \(0, 1, \dots, \ell\). So \(q_k\) is also the number of chains that last at least \(k\) steps. In banana$ one chain reaches depth 2 and the other three stop at once, which is why \(q_1 = q_2 = 1\). The profile records how long the run boundaries persist when pulled back through LF. This is proved, and checked on all 233 blocks (the chain record).

Why the short tail is the part that matters. Added over every depth from 1 up, the profile is the total length of the chains, and that is always \(n - r\): in banana$, \(q_1 + q_2 = 2 = 7 - 5\). This holds for any block that is not one word repeated, which covers all 233. (In a repeated word such as abab, some gaps lie on loops and belong to no chain.) So the total alone cannot tell apart two blocks with the same rows and runs, though the whole profile can. What separates them is how early their chains die. The short tail, \(\sum_{k=2}^{8} q_k\), counts one gap for each chain still alive at each depth from 2 to 8. In banana$ it is 1: the single chain that outlives its first step.

How the profile meets the forest. The start of the profile is already part of the forest's network. Overlay two ways of cutting the rows into pieces: at the run boundaries, and at the boundaries of the runs' images under LF. Each has \(r - 1\) internal cuts. If \(C\) of the cuts coincide, the overlay has

\[E_0 = 2r - 1 - C\]

pieces, and those pieces are exactly the forest's arcs. This is proved, and it holds on all 233 blocks. The forest's excess is \(E_0 - V_0\), its arcs minus its sites (\(V_0 = r\)). A gap has depth 1 when LF carries it onto a run boundary, and the run boundaries reached that way are the \(r - 1 - C\) that are not also image cuts. So

\[q_1 = r - 1 - C = E_0 - r,\]

the excess. The forest's leftover arcs, its chords, number one more, \(E_0 - r + 1\). In banana$, \(C = 3\) and \(E_0 = 6\), so \(q_1 = 1\) and the forest has 2 chords.

The profile test's convention. The profile test that the fits below come from counted one point more. Row 0 starts a run but sits at no gap, and the test added it at the depth \(d_0\) where row 0's own path first lands on a run boundary. We write that historical profile as \(\tilde q_k = q_k + [k = d_0]\). On 229 blocks \(d_0 = 1\), so \(\tilde q_1\) equals the chord count: 10,955 on the test block, against \(q_1 = 10{,}954\). On the other four, \(d_0 = 2\) and the extra point falls in the tail. The three-byte column 100 shows the same case: there \(\tilde q_1 = q_1 = 1\), while the forest has 2 chords. So the historical \(\tilde q_1\) matches the chords only when \(d_0 = 1\), not by a rule (the check). On the test block, \(\tilde q_2\) to \(\tilde q_5\) equal exactly the excesses of the refined networks in section 4.

On the real blocks the profile decays slowly. The median of \(\tilde q_k/r\) over the 233 blocks falls only from 0.223 at \(k = 1\) to 0.101 at \(k = 8\) (the profile test). After eight steps, there is still about one chain running for every ten runs.

The test. It compared the short-tail sum with the depths fitted one by one. Each count per run was fitted by least squares, with leave-one-out error, using the historical profile:

Model Cells \(R^2\) Forest \(R^2\) Adj.-rank \(R^2\) Residual correlation \(r/n\) and the excess proxy \((\tilde q_1 - 1)/r\) 0.825 0.887 0.529 0.393 the same, plus \(\sum_{k=2}^{8} \tilde q_k/r\) 0.925 0.923 0.557 −0.061 \(r/n\) and \(\tilde q_1, \dots, \tilde q_8\) separately 0.946 0.959 0.570 0.307

From one chain to the fit. The first model already holds run density and the historical proxy for the excess, \((\tilde q_1 - 1)/r\). The exact excess \(q_1\) counts the chains reaching at least one step. On the 229 blocks with \(d_0 = 1\) the proxy equals the exact excess per run, \(q_1/r\), and on the other four it is lower by \(1/r\). The first-depth count includes longer chains, but it cannot tell how long they last. What it cannot see is chains like the one in banana$ that outlive that step, and that is where Cells and the forest still agree. The last column is the correlation between the two counts' fitted residuals, the part of each that the model leaves unexplained. It is 0.393 under the first model. Adding the tail, the chains that persist, takes it to −0.061: about zero. As a separate check, the leave-one-out error falls by 34% for Cells and 17% for the forest. Fitting all eight depths separately fits each count more closely, but leaves 0.307 in common, so the single tail sum accounts for more of what the two share. Adjacent-rank induction stays poorly explained under every model, at \(R^2 \le 0.570\). Its rounds are chosen by local minima of the rows' order rather than by run boundaries, which may be why some other property drives it.

These fits use the historical profile as recorded. On the four blocks with \(d_0 = 2\) its tail holds row 0's extra point, and the fit's excess term, taken as \((\tilde q_1 - 1)/r\), is one gap low. A fit on the internal-gap profile alone has not been run.

So, measured: the persistence of boundary-orbit chains explains much of the variation in the structural work done by Cells and the forest. Our interpretation, not a proof: both pay roughly once for each point on a boundary chain until the chains collide. Cells meets those points in order, and the forest by levels. The profile is fixed by the column \(L\) before any construction runs. It is not an exact accounting of either count, and it gives no lower bound on the work of other constructions.

items.title: 4. Why not do less of it?
items.text:
If the work follows the boundary chains, there are three obvious ways to try to reduce it. None lowered it where we tried it, on evidence of three kinds: a count on the test block, a measurement on Wikidata, and a model.

Refining the presentation. The forest pays for its excess, so the first route describes the block with smaller pieces that have less excess. At depth \(k\), a piece is a stretch of neighbouring rows that pass through the same runs in their first \(k\) steps of LF; at depth 1 the pieces are the runs themselves. The excess does fall, from \(0.21\,r\) to \(0.07\,r\), yet the total work rises:

Smaller pieces lower the excess, and raise the work

0 r1 r2 r3 r4 r12481632depth k: how many steps of run labels each site shares90,945 arcs = 1.78 r208,766 = 4.08 rwork: arcs over all levelsfirst-level excess E₀ − V₀: 0.21 r → 0.07 r Measured on the test block, from the first refinement record: the forest's arcs summed over all its levels (amber), and its first-level excess (steel, dashed), both in units of the block's runs, at depths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 16 and 32. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.

The arcs summed over levels go from 90,945 at depth 1 to 208,766 at depth 32. Part of the reason is proved. Refining by one more step turns every arc of the old network into a site of the new one, \(V_0(k+1) = E_0(k)\). So the sites grow by the old excess, and the first level's arcs by the new one. That the later levels shrink by less is counted at the nine depths tried, not proved (record of the refinement test). Coarser pieces fail the other way, with an excess of about \(r\). So among the presentations tried, runs are best. That is a finding about this block, not a theorem: on the three-byte column 100, refining lowers the total from 5 arcs to 3.

Accelerating repeated steps. When a stretch of the map repeats, one division can stand in for many identical steps, and adjacent-rank induction does exactly this. On an artificial text, \(abcd\) repeated with an end marker, whose column has five runs, it decodes 875,001 bytes about 9.5 times faster than mibz2's shipped route: 0.161 ms against 1.526 ms, over five runs. That route sends so sparse a column to its Segmented decoder, not to Cells. Wikidata, however, has almost nothing to accelerate. Division compresses only repeated passes through one atom, and Cells' census on the test block finds no repeated steps. On the full benchmark adjacent-rank induction is the slower of the two (section 1).

Splitting a block across cores. Cells is one sequential chain of 92,570 steps on the test block: each step reads the state the previous one left. Adjacent-rank induction is more parallel, in a model. A row-by-row model reproduces its 12 rounds exactly, and their combined longest path is 87 row steps: the classical parallel route of contracting a list at an independent set of its points. But the model executes 1,337,701 row steps, \(1.49\,n\), against Cells' 92,570 steps, about \(0.1\,n\). The real decoder routes atoms, not rows; how long that routing runs in sequence was not measured, and no threaded version was built. Meanwhile, one block per thread already fills a ten-core Intel desktop (an i9-10900K), which is limited by memory contention and power at seven to ten busy cores. So the model trades much more work for a shorter path, with no speed-up shown on the test machine. Our reading is that giving another core another block remains the better use of it.

Contracting a list at an independent set is the classical parallel way to shorten a chain. Herein adjacent-rank induction cuts the loop at the rows smaller than both their neighbours, joins the paths between them, and repeats: in the model, a longest path of 87 row steps, bought with 1,337,701 row steps in all, against Cells' 92,570.

items.title: 5. Why not copy earlier text?
items.text:
The fourth route leaves the run network behind. Much of a block repeats earlier text, so the text can be described as literal bytes plus copies, each a pointer back to an earlier stretch of output and a length. This is the idea behind LZ77-style compressors, and decoding a copy is a plain memory copy.

It is compact. Seeded with the 51,184 run-head bytes in text order, a greedy parse covers the rest of the test block with 11,145 copies and 33 single literal bytes. Replaying them is estimated, not timed, at 0.1–0.3 ms a block. The inverse BWT it is set against, the control in that assessment, took about 2.4 ms on the same block in the original investigation; it was not timed again.

It needs text positions. The short parse needs its seed bytes in text order, and the BWT gives its rows in sorted order. With the same seed bytes in sorted order, the parse needs 18,132 copies. The BWT does carry a copy description of its own: neighbouring rows of a run read the same bytes (section 3), so each one can copy from its neighbour. Grouped into phrases, this is a known scheme (Navarro, Ochoa and Prezza, Theorem 7). On the test block it has 51,184 literal bytes and 10,954 copies. But 5,611 of its copies have sources that overlap them or come later in the text. An evaluator that sweeps front to back needs 12,406 sweeps; one that follows the dependencies could order them differently, but was not tried. Putting the copies in text order needs each row's place in the text, and the routes we tested got those places by walking LF. Whether list ranking or another method could recover them more cheaply is open. The obstacle here is a different one from the run network's (the copy-route assessment; its independent reproduction).

All four routes, side by side:

What each route avoids, and what it still pays

Cells (ships in mibz2)avoidsthe row-by-row walk: it trims the map of runspays≈ 1.84 steps per run, in one sequential chaincostthe baseline, about 17–28 ns a stepAdjacent-rank inductionavoidsper-row state; repeats, by divisionpays≈ 1.93 atom visits per run, plus routingcost11.5× (calling thread), 7.8× (4 workers)Forest-section eliminationavoidsfollowing each path's interiorpays≈ 1.78 arcs per run, plus slab matchingcost15.2× slower, calling threadCopies of earlier textavoidsspelling repeats: 11,145 copiespaystext positions: tested routes walk LFcostreplay ≈ 0.1–0.3 ms a block (estimate) A summary of sections 1, 4 and 5. Counts are medians per run over 233 blocks; times are full-stream slowdowns against eager Cells on a four-CPU cloud virtual machine, on the calling thread unless a worker count is named; the copy route's replay is an estimate. Open return, reported in its own post, avoids induction on the narrow runs and is 17.1% slower than eager Cells on the calling thread, 9–21% across the calling thread and two or four workers.

items.title: 6. Where things stand
items.text:
Measured and proved. Three unlike constructions do about 1.8 operations per run on Wikidata, their counts correlate strongly, and they do not process the same events. The identity \(E_0 = 2r - 1 - C\) is proved and holds on every block, and the depth-one count \(q_1 = E_0 - r\) is the forest's excess, one less than its chords. The short tail of the profile, as historically counted, explains much of the variation Cells and the forest share. Refinement raised the work on the test block, acceleration has nothing to act on in Wikidata, and in a model, splitting a block costs far more total work; no threaded version was tested. The copy route is compact, but the routes tested had to walk LF for its text positions.

Not shown. No one has shown that Cells is optimal. The shared count is not a lower bound, and the only proved bounds are the trivial ones: reading the \(r\) runs and writing the \(n\) bytes. Cells is the best-performing formulation tested.

The open question. On our reading, Cells and the forest pay for each boundary chain step by step. Some shortcuts exist: division compresses repeated passes through one atom, and a one-bit test tells when two neighbouring paths spell the same word. But among the methods we measured or costed, learning how long an aperiodic chain runs meant walking it, or pointer jumping after preprocessing of order \(n \log n\). What remains open is whether a gap's separation depth can be found without walking its path. A method that could would attack the work Cells and the forest share.

Next. Two studies are under way: a bounded study of whether steps of different kinds in Cells can be fused into one, and a literature study of these gap chains.

In short: three constructions count about the same work, and much of what they share is how long the run boundaries persist. The ways tried to shorten that work raised it, found nothing to act on, or, in a model, multiplied it. When unlike methods agree on a count, the reason is worth looking for in the input before tuning the methods.

Research records: the synthesis of the four investigations · refinement and parallel depth · the boundary-orbit profile test · the profile's chains and conventions · the adjacent-rank study · the forest's verification · the independent synthesis review and its report · the forest review · investigations one, two and three · the copy route, recovered · the Cells census · the forest census

items.title: Open Returns
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The setting. bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900,000 bytes. For each block it sorts every rotation of the text and stores only the last column of the sorted rows, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), plus the row that holds the original text. Decoding means walking a map called LF, which sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. Each step reads one byte, so the walk spells the block backwards, but each step also needs the row the previous step found. That chain of dependent memory reads is most of the cost of decoding. Repeated letters sit together in the last column as runs, and mibz2's kernels so far, eager Cells and LazyCells, save work by reasoning about runs instead of single rows (A new way back from the BWT, Lazy letters).

What Open does. mibz2 0.5.7 adds a third kernel, Open. It keeps only the rows that sit in short runs, about a tenth of a Wikidata block, and for each kept row works out its return: the next kept row the walk will reach, and the bytes it spells on the way. Decoding then jumps from kept row to kept row, writing whole words at a time. The rows it drops are the ones in long runs, whose neighbouring rows move together under LF like a convoy. Open therefore traces one member of each convoy and the rest of it comes for free: on Wikidata, one traced letter spells about sixteen bytes.

What it bought. 0.5.7 decodes Wikidata 7–11% faster than 0.5.6 from 8 to 20 threads on a ten-core i9, with 23% less peak memory, and Open alone is the cause. The release's only other decoder change affects 6 threads, which this comparison doesn't run, and a test of Open alone against 0.5.6 found the same gain. Below 8 threads nothing changes, because Open runs only on the parallel workers' route.

The gain depends on using Open only where it pays. Open has fixed setup costs, and on text, where runs are short, it is up to 5× slower. Each block is therefore checked first: Open runs only if its run records are between 1/64 and 15% of its rows, the range the existing LazyCells kernel already used. The check is two integer comparisons and adds no new tuned constant.

The result comes from one machine (an i9-10900K) and one workload (a pinned Wikidata sample), and it did not come at the first attempt. The first registered test of Open failed on a badly designed guard rule, and that verdict stands; a second test, with its rule fixed in advance, passed.

The guard rule of the first test compared single estimates with a 2% bound across 39 noisy cells, wherein a change with no effect at all would fail about 97% of the time. Its verdict stands; the second test, registered separately, is the one that adopted Open.

05001,0001,5002,0002,500output MB/s, Wikidata (higher is faster)0.5.7 · 2,3830.5.6 · 2,231+9% at 10 threads124810121620threadspeak memory from 8 threads: 96–107 MB on 0.5.7, against 125–134 MB on 0.5.6 Measured on the i9-10900K: 0.5.7 against 0.5.6 on the Wikidata sample, the median of 10 paired rounds at each thread count (release-scaling/run-20261119T203443Z). The two releases are level up to 4 threads, where Open is not on the route. From 8 threads up, the shaded gap is Open: 2,557 MB/s against 2,356 at 10 threads.

Section 1 works a small example by hand. Section 2 explains the convoys and what they look like in real blocks, and section 3 how the returns are computed without walking. Section 4 covers the gate, and section 5 the road from a research idea to the release.

items.title: Open Returns: decoding a block from a tenth of its rows
items.text:
mibz2 0.5.7 decodes Wikidata up to 11% faster on ten cores by keeping a tenth of each block's rows and letting the rest travel together in convoys.

19 November 2026 · 10 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.7 (changelog)

items.title: 1. How can a decoder skip nine rows in ten?
items.text:
The 13 bytes bananabandana make a small example. Sorting their rotations and reading down the last column gives nndnbbaanaaaa, with the text itself at row 6. Its runs are nn, d, n, bb, aa, n and aaaa.

On real blocks Open keeps every run of at most 16 rows. In a block this small, that would keep everything, so the toy keeps runs of one row only, plus the start row 6. That keeps rows 2, 3, 6 and 8 and drops the other nine.

the block's last column L, one letter per sorted row (row number below)n0n1d2n3b4b5a6starta7n8a9a10a11a12LF moves the four a-rows 9–12 together, to rows 2–5: a convoykept: a row in a short run (here, of one row), or the start rowdropped: the rows of longer runs, which Open never visits one by oneReal blocks keep runs of up to 16 rows; this 13-row toy keeps only runs of one, so that something is dropped. The worked example. Kept rows are blue; the runs Open drops are grey. The amber arrows are LF on the long run of four a's: rows 9 to 12 go to rows 2 to 5, still side by side, as LF does to any run (section 2).

Following LF from each kept row until it reaches another kept row reads one letter per step. That trip and its word are the row's return:

kept row its letter LF goes through returns to word 6 a 0 (n), 9 (a) 2 ana 2 d – 8 d 8 n 12 (a), 5 (b), 7 (a), 1 (n), 10 (a) 3 nabana 3 n 11 (a), 4 (b) 6 nab

Decoding is now four jumps instead of thirteen steps:

decoding by returns: from each kept row, jump to the next kept row and write the word in between6“ana”2“d”8“nabana”3“nab”, and back to the startfour jumps write ana · d · nabana · nab = anadnabananab,which is the block read backwards: bananabandanaA plain walk would take 13 dependent steps, one per row; the returns take 4. The four returns, chained from the start row. Joined, the words read the block backwards, exactly as a row-by-row walk would. Every byte is still written; what shrinks is the number of dependent jumps and the rows the decoder has to keep.

The words still have to come from somewhere, and in this toy they were found by walking. The point of Open is that on real blocks the words can be built far more cheaply than by walking, because the dropped rows travel in convoys.

items.title: 2. Why do long runs travel together?
items.text:
Within one run, every row holds the same letter, and LF sends consecutive rows with the same letter to consecutive rows. LF therefore moves a run as a block: its rows stay side by side until the convoy reaches a place where the runs around it change, and splits. In the toy, the four a-rows 9–12 arrive together at rows 2–5. The earlier post called these groups bundles; a convoy of width b that travels h steps spells b·h bytes, but finding its route means tracing only one member, h steps.

Long runs make long convoys, and keeping the short runs removes most of the places where convoys would split, so everything else travels through intact. Medians over the 233 large Wikidata blocks in the sample (counts):

a median large Wikidata block's rowskept 11%travels in convoys 89%the convoys' 89%: letters Open traces itself (5.5%), and what they spellspelled for free by the rest of each convoy5.5%≈ 16 bytes spelled per letter traced: convoys are about sixteen rows wide.Prose, by contrast, keeps 68% of its rows: its runs are short, so there is little to drop. Counted, at Open's threshold of 16 rows: medians over 233 large Wikidata blocks and six prose blocks. Wikidata keeps 11.3% of its rows; 88.7% ride in convoys, of which Open traces 5.5% of the block itself. Each traced letter spells about 16 bytes (median 15.9). In prose the convoys are about as wide, but they cover only a third of the block.

That is the whole source of the saving, and also of its limit: a block whose runs are short has little to drop.

items.title: 3. How are the returns found without walking?
items.text:
The returns split cleanly into two independent pieces, a result proved in Cutting the loop open:

  • The kept rows among themselves. The order in which kept rows hand over to each other depends only on their own letters, a stable sort of the kept part of the column. Open builds it as the run records stream in: each kept row joins a queue for its letter.
  • The convoys' routes. Where each convoy enters and leaves the dropped region, and the word it spells, are found by a small auxiliary computation on the long runs alone. It needs at most about three records per long run, however the kept rows are wired. The words are stored as a dictionary of shared pieces, not spelled out per row.

On one test block of 899,931 rows, that meant 89,874 kept rows, an auxiliary problem of 7,786 records solved in 11,215 steps, and 7,334 dictionary rules. The decoder then walks the kept rows' returns and copies words forwards.

Less to hold means less memory traffic. On that block, a full decode asked for 6.3 MB of extra heap against 10.4 MB for eager Cells and 15.4 MB for LazyCells, and in a cache simulation it executed 11% fewer instructions with 27% fewer first-level data-cache misses (measurements).

items.title: 4. Why not use Open everywhere?
items.text:
Because its setup has to pay for itself. Every block was timed both ways, on one thread (census):

corpus blocks Open's time ÷ the existing kernel's Wikidata, admitted 228 0.972 Wikidata, too many runs (small blocks, 2% of the rows) 155 1.005 text 48 5.11 pattern (very few runs) 88 1.55 one byte repeated 2 1.87

Open won exactly where LazyCells already admitted blocks, and nowhere else. LazyCells decides with two tests on a block's record density, its run records R divided by its rows n. A record holds a run of up to 127 rows, so R is close to the number of runs, and the decoder already has it. Open's admission reuses those two lines unchanged: 1/64 ≤ R/n < 0.15, that is, 64·R ≥ n and 20·R < 3·n.

LazyCellsvery few recordsOpenOpen's admission rangeLazyCellsmany records: text1/64 ≈ 1.6%15%0.5%1%5%10%30%record density R/n (log scale)50k records in 900k rows: 5.6%300k: 33% The admission test, on a log axis of record density. Below 1/64 the block is nearly all one letter and LazyCells handles it well; at 15% and above, runs are too short for convoys to pay. The dots are examples: 50,000 records in a 900,000-row block is 5.6%, admitted; 300,000 records is 33%, not.

The test is a cheap predictor, not a guarantee: two blocks with the same density can differ in how their convoys split. The 228 admitted Wikidata blocks hold 98% of the sample's rows, so Open does almost all of Wikidata's work while every other block keeps the kernel it had.

items.title: 5. What did it buy?
items.text:
Getting from the idea to a release took seven steps over two days:

18 NovThe idea, on a 4-CPU cloud VM7–8% faster than LazyCells, 9–21% slower than eager Cells; 39% less heappromising18 NovTen cores, under contention (i9)behind LazyCells' gate: 0.919 of 0.5.6's time at 10 threads; on every block: text 1.73× sloweropens a port19 NovRewritten for productionno unsafe, bounds-checked; Miri, fuzzing, every return arrow audited on small columnssafety PROCEED19 NovWhere does it win? Every block timedfaster only where LazyCells' existing gate admits; up to 5× slower elsewherethe gate19 NovFirst registered test (i9)5–7% faster on Wikidata, but 4 noisy guard cells over 2%, on corpora Open never touchesNOT ADOPTED19 NovSecond test, its rule fixed in advance5–7% faster at 8–20 threads, guards within bounds, 22–24% less memoryADOPT19 NovWorker counts re-measured6 threads moves to the same lazy route; every other setting holds0.5.7 ships From research to release, 18–19 November 2026. The research decoder used unsafe code; the production version has none, and passed Miri, fuzzing and an exhaustive audit of every return on small columns before any timing counted. The first registered test's guard rule compared single estimates with a 2% bound across 39 noisy cells, a rule a change with no effect would fail about 97% of the time. Its verdict stands; the second test, registered separately with its rule fixed in advance, is the one that adopted Open.

The release-on-release run that every mibz2 release gets, on the same i9, agrees with the adoption test:

0.951.001.051.100.5.6's wall time ÷ 0.5.7's, Wikidata (above 1: 0.5.7 is faster)1 thread0.9882 threads0.9914 threads1.0118 threads1.10810 threads1.07312 threads1.08116 threads1.07420 threads1.091 Measured on the i9-10900K, 10 paired rounds (release-scaling/run-20261119T203443Z): 0.5.6's wall time over 0.5.7's on Wikidata, with 95% intervals. At 1–4 threads the intervals span 1. From 8 threads up, 0.5.7 is 7–11% faster. The release's attribution ledger credits the step to Open's merge alone.

What comes next. Open still builds and walks a table of every kept row's return, and that is now where its time goes. A research variant, scalar-cap, measured 2–5% faster than Open at 7–10 workers in the research harness on the same i9. It will need the same block-by-block checks before it can follow Open into a release.

items.title: Research by obligation
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

What changed. mibz2's biggest speed-ups did not come from tuning code. They came from changing what the decoder computes: walking a block's rows one by one gave way to rearranging whole intervals of rows at once, and that gave way to keeping a tenth of the rows and letting the rest travel in groups. This week we set out to find the next change of that size, and spent much of it learning how not to search for one. The result is a written research method, the research charter, whose central idea is simple: keep a register of the obligations, the kinds of work every decoder we have built must pay for, and judge every new idea by which obligation it removes and what it pays instead.

Why obligations, not algorithms. An algorithm is a bundle: it pays for several obligations at once, so when it loses, it is hard to say what lost. An obligation is the part that decomposes: "follow the retained rows one at a time", "build the map that says where each retained row goes next". Candidates come and go; an obligation stays open until something removes it or a proof bounds it. Six candidate improvements to the current kernel lost this week, and every one of them left the register knowing more than before.

What happened today. Two developments sharpened the method after it was written. A measurement traced the expensive work back to the text it produces, and found it sitting in random identifiers. And a mathematician announced a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, found with an AI system, whose account of how it was found gave us a better way to look for new ideas. Section 1 explains the register and section 2 the cycle that uses it. Section 3 reads this week's five research cycles through the register, section 4 describes where new ideas come from, and section 5 what working backwards from the text showed. Section 6 is the adaptation we made today, with a worked toy and a measurement of how to break it.

items.title: Research by obligation: modelling the work, not the algorithms
items.text:
We now track the work any decoder must pay for rather than the algorithms that pay it, and a claimed Riemann proof has sharpened how we hunt.

20 November 2026 · 15 min read · Meta

items.title: 1. The obligation register
items.text:
A short recap of the setting. bzip2 stores each block of text as the last column of a sorted table of the block's rotations. Rebuilding the text means following a path through the table's rows, one byte per step. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form a run, and rows in a wide run move together. mibz2's current kernel, Open, treats wide runs as single units, keeps the rows of narrow runs (about a tenth of all rows), and walks those one at a time.

Profiling Open splits its time into a handful of jobs, and each job is an obligation: something this family of decoders cannot avoid paying for. The register lists them with their measured cost, and beside each, the candidates that tried to remove it:

The obligations, and the candidates they outlived

Following retained rows one by one36–48% of Open's timePipelined emit#656Bit-sliced rank2–3× slowerLanesno gainBuilding the map of retained rowshalf or more of Open's timeFused passes, compressed queues#654Queue-free backward build#659Precomputed jumps#652Finding where runs overlapabout 1.3 transitions per runVia Cells' induction≈1.8 steps per runMetadata held for every run40–100 bytes per runGrammar machinesper-run stateStarting from the decoded columnunexploredopen: no candidate yetWriting every output bytethe floorunavoidable The obligations are from the register; the shares of Open's time are measured (#653). Each grey box is a candidate rejected on native timing or by a decisive count, except for overlaps, where it is the known, costly route.

Reading across a row says what was learned about that obligation. Three candidates attacked the walk over retained rows: a software-pipelined walk (the processor already issues the next load early), a compact rank structure in place of the stored edges (two to three times slower, because one load became four dependent ones), and several walks at once (no gain in our test harness). Three attacked the build: fusing passes, compressing queues, and building the map backwards. The backward build was the most instructive. It removed the queues it targeted, but its second pass over the run records cost about as much as the queues had.

The register also keeps an object apart from the route to it. One cycle found that the structure of where runs overlap is small: about 1.3 transitions per run on our blocks. The only known way to obtain it costs about 1.8 steps per run, which loses. Those are two findings, and rejecting the route must not erase the object: a cheaper way to the same small structure would still be worth having.

When a failure exposes a real obstruction, the register records three things: the concrete witness, the exact scope (which algorithms and cost model it binds), and the escape condition, the assumption a different formulation would have to drop. An obstruction without a stated scope does not count. That rule matters, because after six losses it is tempting to conclude that the walk is a law of nature. It is only a law of the representations tried so far.

items.title: 2. Generate from structure, judge against obligations
items.text:
The register is for judging, not for generating. Early in the week it was used for both, and the ideas it produced were rephrasings of the costs in its own rows: "make the queue smaller", "make the walk shorter". So the method now separates the two, inside a cycle of five phases:

The research cycle

ExploreTriageDeepenConfrontLearngenerate frommathematical structurejudge against the obligation register: what paid work disappears, and what replaces it?Learn writes back the obligation, its witness, scope and escape condition Conceptual. Ideas come from mathematics; the register decides which survive.

Explore generates from mathematical structure. The charter names four routes, as tools rather than quotas. Representation import asks what richer object this is an instance of: both earlier breakthroughs came this way, from seeing the row map as an interval exchange. Obstruction inversion takes a failure's narrowest witness and asks which assumption another primitive could escape. Primitive ablation forbids a dominant operation and checks the cost doesn't reappear elsewhere. Small-instance discovery finds the best exact construction on tiny inputs and looks for the law behind it.

Triage, Deepen, Confront and Learn judge. Every candidate must say which paid work disappears, what replaces it, and how the information it needs is obtained: we call this acquisition first, because several elegant ideas died on the cost of getting their inputs rather than using them. Every cost model is treated as a diagnostic, and with reason. A cache model ranked two of Open's variants the wrong way round, predicting a win for the one that runs 10–16% slower natively. None of the six candidates that passed a model passed native timing.

The cycle asks two separate questions of every candidate. Has the primitive changed, or only how the same operations run? We call the first reorientation and the second traction: Rauzy–Veech induction was reorientation, replacing single steps with operations on whole intervals, while the backward build was traction on Open's existing return map. And has the complete cost fallen? A new representation is not automatically a cheaper computation. The compact rank structure did change the primitive, removing the stored edges entirely, and lost because each step became several dependent lookups.

Two smaller rules hold the process together. A research session pushes its work at every handoff and at least every half hour. The rule has already paid for itself: one session was cut off mid-cycle by a usage limit, and its earlier cycles survived only because they were already published. And new mathematical leads go into an inbox that the researcher reads at a cycle boundary, so a good idea from outside never derails an experiment halfway through.

items.title: 3. Five research cycles, read through the register
items.text:
The register earns its place when a cycle fails, because a failure read against it says which obligation resisted and why. A research model worked through five cycles this week under the charter, after a run of earlier candidates that prompted it. The table lists them all, with the obligation each attacked and what the attempt left behind.

Attempt Obligation it attacked Outcome What it left in the register Precomputed jumps per run record (#652) following retained rows lost building the jumps costs about one whole Open Fused passes; compressed queues (#654) building the map lost the expansion to one entry per retained row is needed, and cheapest done in one sequential fill Pipelined emit (#656) following retained rows not adopted the processor already issues the next load early Tuning the thin/thick limit (#657) both not adopted 16 rows is best; choosing per block gains at most 1%, even with hindsight Cycle 1: contracting the exchange from both ends metadata; overlaps lost on cost the overlap structure is small (1.25–1.37 transitions per run); grammar machines pay 40–100 bytes per run Cycle 2: building Open's map backwards (#659) building the map 1.10–1.15× slower natively the second pass over run records costs about what the queues did Cycle 3: bucketed streaming exchange building the map lost (reported) a claimed limit on keeping the exchange in the last-level cache; not yet audited Cycle 4: contracting an unsplit forest both lost (reported) claimed structure theorems about the run graph; not yet audited Cycle 5: implicit rank in place of stored edges following retained rows 1.7–2.8× slower one dependent load became four; memory fell to 0.36–0.49×

Measured where a PR is cited or a ratio is given; cycles 3 and 4 are as the research model reported them, and are still to be checked.

Two patterns run through the table. Representations that are expensive to build lose on construction; representations that are compact lose on consumption, because recovering each next step takes several dependent operations instead of one load. The fifth cycle shows both sides at once: it cut peak memory to under half and modelled memory traffic by a quarter or more, and still ran two to three times slower, because a smaller description is not a cheaper computation. Neither pattern is a lower bound for the problem. Both are evidence about the families tried, recorded with their scope so the next idea can aim at the assumption that bound them.

The table also shows what the cost models were worth. Every candidate that reached native timing had first passed a model, and every one lost. The register now records each model's track record beside the candidate it scored, in a fidelity ledger, so a model that has mis-ranked before is read with that history in view.

items.title: 4. Where ideas come from: the leads
items.text:
If the register judges, something else has to generate. The charter keeps an inbox of mathematical leads: directions from outside the cycle, which the researcher reads at a cycle boundary and is free to follow or set aside. Three came out of this week, each from asking what richer object a block's runs might be.

A square-tiled surface. Pairing the row map with the plain step to the next row turns the block into a surface glued from unit squares, a branched cover of a torus. Its singular points sit exactly where runs begin and end, and on our six blocks there are only one to eight of them. That is a striking amount of structure, but it forgets the runs' lengths, so it cannot decode a block by itself. The open question is whether directions on the surface, and how points move along them, recover what it forgets (journal).

A train track. The runs can be drawn as a graph, with an arc wherever LF carries one run's rows into another. The arcs number exactly \(2r - 1 - C\), and 88–89% of runs simply pass their rows on to one other run, leaving a branching core of about a tenth of the runs. With the order of strands kept at each junction, this is a measured train track, the object Thurston used to carry tangles of curves on a few weighted branches, and whose basic move is the same as the induction behind our earlier kernel (the train-tracks post). A census found no small separators in the core, and as a set of retained rows it does worse than Open's.

Interval pairings. Agol, Hass and Thurston gave an algorithm that works on huge implicit families of strands through intervals paired by translation, without walking the strands. A block's runs have exactly that shape. Their algorithm counts components, not order; the lead asks whether a version that carries words could recover the text more cheaply.

None of these is a decoder yet, and the charter does not ask them to be. They are where a change of primitive might come from, and the register is what will say whether one does.

items.title: 5. Working backwards from the text
items.text:
The register describes costs in the decoder's terms: rows, runs, passes. Today we asked the same question in the text's terms, prompted by a contrast with the Hutter Prize, which rewards the smallest self-extracting description of Wikipedia and lets decompression take tens of hours. mibz2 sits at the other end: its description is fixed by bzip2, and the goal is the least computation to recover the text. One Hutter winner, STARLIT, won by reordering Wikipedia's articles so similar ones sat together. bzip2 has already done a reordering of its own, sorting every byte by what follows it, and we asked what that exposes.

Tracing every expensive row back to the byte it spells answered it. The repetitive JSON skeleton is already nearly free: keys are about a third of the text and about 1% of the rows that stand alone. Unique random statement IDs, about 5% of the text, hold about 62% of them. Hashes that are reused form small runs, one row per copy. So the obligation "follow retained rows one by one" is, in large part, the obligation to spell random strings (the post).

That reshaped an idea we had been circling: a zoo. Rather than one universal decoder, a repertoire of exact methods, each very good on one kind of structure, with the decoder recognising which applies. Repeated random strings might be copied once one copy is decoded; unique ones might be a true floor for any method that relies on repetition. Recognition has to be cheap, read from what the compressed block already gives us, and the first number to know is how much a perfect choice of method could save. An earlier attempt to tune Open per block found under 1% to gain, which is why that number comes first.

items.title: 6. Adapting the method: toy, missing effect, native surrogate
items.text:
Today Levent Alpöge announced that he believes he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and its generalisation, working with Claude, with the argument formalised in Lean. Nothing here depends on it being right. What interested us is his account of how the argument was found, because it describes a way of searching that our method lacked.

Since then (a note of 21 November): the same day as the announcement, members of the Lean community reported that three independent proof checkers, nanoda, con-leche in its verified mode and pestka, each accepted the Lean development, about 17 million lines, as proving the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. We have not checked it ourselves, and mathematicians are still digesting the argument.

As he tells it, he started from a toy setting where the theorem was already known (the Riemann Hypothesis over function fields) and re-proved it in a new way chosen so the proof might travel. He then named the ingredient that the hard setting lacks: Stepanov's classical argument uses multiplicity, a polynomial vanishing to high order, which over the integers would be "something like differentiating whole numbers". The decisive step was to find a different mechanism, native to the hard setting, with the same effect: chains of theta lifts, each standing in for one order of multiplicity. The human held the analogy; the AI system supplied the technical mastery to build it.

We have a toy setting of our own. When a block's last column has exactly one run per letter, its text is the coding of an especially simple interval exchange; Ferenczi and Zamboni proved that these "perfectly clustering" words are exactly the codings of symmetric interval exchanges, the structure our earlier kernels rest on. With two letters they are the Christoffel and Sturmian words, and their text needs no walk at all.

For the slope \(3/8\), letter \(k\) of the word is \(b\) when \(\lfloor 3(k+1)/8 \rfloor - \lfloor 3k/8 \rfloor = 1\) and \(a\) otherwise, which for \(k = 0, \dots, 7\) gives aabaabab. Sorting its eight rotations and reading the last column gives bbbaaaaa, two runs, the smallest a column can have. A decoder that knew the slope would not need the column at all. It could write any letter of the text directly from its position, in any order, with no step depending on the one before. For an irrational slope \(\alpha\) the same holds with \(\lfloor (k+1)\alpha \rfloor - \lfloor k\alpha \rfloor\): every output position is computed, not reached.

Toy, damaged toy, real block

The toytwo-letter Sturmian wordsletter k = ⌊(k+1)α⌋ − ⌊kα⌋every position computed:no walk at allDamaged on purposea rotation cut in many piecesposition still x + kαbut the runs multiply:width lost, coordinate keptA real blockWikidata JSONno known coordinaterandom IDs: one-row runs,walked step by stepThe question: what object, native to real blocks, gives cheap global coordinates the way kα does? Conceptual. The middle panel's measurements are in the table below.

How a surrogate was tried the same evening, and answered the wrong question

The first version of our transfer went wrong in an instructive way. We named the missing ingredient as run width, since the toy has two enormous runs and the random IDs have none, and tested an obvious surrogate the same evening: walking many independent stretches of the path at once, as mibz2's plain decoder already does. It gave no gain on Open's walk, and more to the point, it was the wrong test. Running walks side by side still follows the same edges; it is a speed-up of the old operation, not a new one.

The correction, which came out of the discussion, is that the toy's real power is not width but cheap global coordinates: a compact number (\(k\alpha\) modulo 1) from which any position's letter follows. In the toy the two coincide, which is why they were easy to confuse.

They come apart if the toy is damaged on purpose. The damage keeps the rotation by \(\alpha\) and both letters but cuts the circle into \(p\) pieces, each lettered \(a\) or \(b\) at random. The coordinate survives untouched: letter \(k\) is the letter of the piece holding \(x + k\alpha\) modulo 1, found by one binary search over the cut points, for any \(k\), in any order. What changes is the column, which we measured on texts of 5,000 letters with the golden-ratio slope:

Pieces \(p\) Runs in the last column Mean run width (rows) 2 26 192 8 44 114 64 218 23 256 802 6.2 1,024 2,018 2.5

Measured (toy2.py, two letters throughout).

Correction, 20 November 2026: the first version of this table gave each piece its own letter, so at 1,024 pieces it had a 1,024-letter alphabet and its run count mostly counted letters. The research line caught it. With two letters the effect is stronger, not weaker.

With a few pieces the column stays wide, so a small cut barely damages the toy. With a thousand pieces the runs average two and a half rows, narrower than the random strings in our real blocks, and the coordinate still answers any position in one search. So a block can be almost all narrow runs and still have a global coordinate that makes the walk unnecessary. Width-based methods, ours included, would find almost nothing to exploit in it.

There is a limit, which the research line also proved. Every text coded from a rotation has zero entropy: a handful of numbers describe it completely. Real blocks are not like that. A block with about 760 random statement IDs holds about 90,000 random bits, and no global coordinate can be smaller than the information it determines. So on real data the coordinate we are looking for cannot be a single number like \(k\alpha\). At best it describes the structured part, and the random strings must be paid for some other way.

That is the precise form of the question for the research line: what object, native to real blocks and cheap to read off the compressed input, gives coordinates the way \(k\alpha\) does, or lets long stretches of the path be composed without walking them? Part of the answer may already exist in outline. For a rotation, the digits of a position in the Ostrowski numeration, built from the continued fraction of \(\alpha\), say where it sits at every scale. For a general interval exchange, the induction that our earlier kernel performs builds a comparable hierarchy, and a position's path down that hierarchy is its coordinate. Our kernels pay to build the whole hierarchy and then write the text from it. Whether a position's coordinate can be read off without paying for the whole build is open, and it is exactly the kind of question the register exists to price.

Ostrowski numeration sets forth a whole number as a sum of the denominators of \(\alpha\)'s continued-fraction approximations, each taken at most as many times as the next partial quotient allows, as decimal writes it as a sum of powers of ten.

items.title: 7. Where this leaves us
items.text:
Three pieces now fit together. The obligation register tells us what our present algorithms pay for. Importing mathematical structure tells us what other operations might exist. Toy-to-hard transfer tells us which missing effects those operations should try to reproduce.

The method in one chain: model the obligations, because they decompose and algorithms don't; generate ideas from mathematical structure; judge them against the obligations, with acquisition counted and models treated as diagnostics; and when a phenomenon makes the problem easy somewhere, find what makes it easy, break it on purpose, and look for a different mechanism that recreates the effect where it is missing.

The method has not yet been shown to produce breakthroughs: five research cycles under it found real structure and no faster decoder. What it has shown is narrower: failed approaches are cheaper to reject, their hidden costs are easier to see, and the mathematics they leave behind is harder to lose.

A new research line is running now, independently, with the geometric leads (square-tiled surfaces, train tracks, interval pairings) as starting points and the toy-transfer lead waiting at its next cycle boundary. Its results come back for independent verification before anything reaches the decoder.

Research records:

  • The research charter: method and frontier and obligation register.
  • Toy, missing ingredient, native surrogate, with the correction and the lanes experiment.
  • Working backwards from the text.
  • Levent Alpöge, Remark (20 November 2026), announcing the proof. On 20 November its Lean formalisation was reported accepted by three independent kernels (nanoda, con-leche --verified, pestka) in the Lean Zulip thread "Discussion: Alpöge Proves the Riemann Hypothesis".
  • S. Ferenczi and L. Q. Zamboni, Clustering words and interval exchanges (2013); S. Mantaci, A. Restivo and M. Sciortino, Burrows–Wheeler transform and Sturmian words (2003).

items.title: Train tracks
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

What a train track is. A curve drawn on a surface, such as a sphere with a few holes or a doughnut, may be long and looping. Many stretches of it then run side by side before they part. A train track replaces all those side-by-side strands with a single branch, and writes on the branch how many strands it stands for. Where strands part or meet, the branches join at a switch, smoothly, like railway points, and the numbers must add up there. William Thurston introduced train tracks in the late 1970s to study curves and the maps that move them on surfaces. With a track, a few branches and a few numbers stand for a curve that might wind around thousands of times. Lee Mosher's three-page note1 is the gentlest way in.

Why it matters to mibz2. Undoing bzip2's Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) means following one long path through the rows of a block until it has visited every row; each step reads one byte. That walk is most of the cost. mibz2's kernels save work by treating whole groups of rows that move together as one unit (A new way back from the BWT, Open Returns). That is the train-track idea, applied to rows. The central operation of train tracks, splitting, is the same operation as the Rauzy–Veech induction behind our Cells kernels. Dunfield and Thurston say so in as many words, and we show their figure in section 3.

What this post does. It explains train tracks from the beginning using figures from the papers that define them (sections 1–3). It then lays a small compressed block over the picture: its runs become branches, and the places where groups of rows merge or part become switches (section 4). It shows the next layer of the theory, maps that write words (section 5), and ends with what the theory gives us already and what is still open (section 6). No new decoder comes out of it yet; this is a map of the territory.

items.title: Train tracks: carrying a tangle of paths on a few weighted branches
items.text:
Thurston's train tracks squeeze a tangle of curves onto a few weighted branches that can be edited directly, and a compressed block's runs form something very like one.

20 November 2026 · 9 min read · Open question

items.title: 1. From curves to branches
items.text:
The name comes from Thurston's own drawings. In his lecture notes2 he asks us to picture a curve on a surface as "many parallel strands in thin, branching corridors". Then: "Imagine squeezing the nearly parallel strands of γ in each corridor to a single strand. One obtains a train track τ (with switches) which approximates γ. Each leaf of γ may be imagined as the path of a train running around along τ."

Thurston's corridors, and the track they squeeze down to

Top: the strands of a curve running side by side in branching corridors. Bottom: each corridor squeezed to one line, a train track, with a train running on it. Reproduced from Thurston, The Geometry and Topology of 3-Manifolds, §8.9 (p. 204 of the notes), for commentary.

The figure below, from Dunfield and Thurston's 2006 paper3, shows two train tracks: one on a sphere with four holes (drawn as a disc with three holes plus the outside), and one on a torus. Each thick line is a branch. Where two branches meet a third, they arrive from the same side and merge smoothly; that junction is a switch.

Two train tracks

Train tracks on a four-punctured sphere and on a torus. Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 16, for commentary.

A track becomes useful once it has numbers. Each branch gets a non-negative weight, the number of strands it carries, and at every switch the weights must balance. In Masur, Mosher and Schleimer's words, a transverse measure "satisfies the switch conditions: for every switch \(x \in \tau\) we have \(w(a) + w(b) = w(c)\)" (2010, p. 4)4. Here \(a\) and \(b\) are the two branches on the narrow side of the switch and \(c\) is the branch on the wide side. So if 5 strands come in on one branch and 3 on the other, the shared branch carries 8.

A weighted track like this stands for a whole curve, or a whole family of curves, without drawing any of them. That is the first idea: many paths that travel together are stored once, with a count.

items.title: 2. Editing the track instead of the curves
items.text:
The second idea is what makes train tracks a tool rather than a notation. The track can be changed by a local move, and the change can be computed on the weights alone, while the curve it stands for stays the same.

The basic move is a split, which acts on a branch that is the wide side of a switch at both ends (a large branch). Two pairs of strands enter it, one pair at each end, and run side by side through it. Splitting pulls the branch apart in one of three ways, depending on which strands end up next to which.

The three splits of a large branch, and a slide

"Top: A large branch admits a right, central, and left splitting. Bottom: a mixed branch admits a slide." Reproduced from Masur, Mosher and Schleimer (2010), Figure 1, for commentary. The inverse of a split is called a fold.

The weights decide which split to make. Two groups of strands enter the large branch on the same side, one from each end. If one group is heavier, the right or left split keeps every strand on the track, according to which; if they weigh the same, the central split does. The branch that now joins them carries the difference of the two weights. Applied again and again, the move shrinks the weights by repeated subtraction, the way Euclid's algorithm shrinks two numbers to their greatest common divisor. On a torus, a sequence of left and right splits spells out the continued fraction of a curve's slope (Mosher 2003).

So a split costs a comparison and a subtraction, however many strands the branch carries, which is the property we care about.

items.title: 3. Interval exchanges are train tracks, and splitting is Rauzy induction
items.text:
mibz2 does not start from curves. It starts from an interval exchange: a line cut into pieces, with the pieces put back in a different order. The BWT's LF map is one (A new way back from the BWT builds it in full): the rows are the line, and each run of equal letters in the BWT's last column is a piece that LF moves as one block, keeping its rows in order.

Dunfield and Thurston show that an interval exchange is a train track with a single switch. In their Figure 17, the left picture is a track on a sphere with five holes whose branches all meet at one point. The right picture thickens it: the shaded bar is the line being cut up, and each loop is a band that carries one piece of the bar's top edge to a piece of its bottom edge.

An interval exchange drawn as a train track

"At left is an interval exchange τ on a 5–punctured S². At right is a regular neighborhood of τ." Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 17, for commentary. The shaded bar is the interval; the bands are the pieces that get exchanged.

How to read these band pictures. The black lines are not paths. The gap between each pair of neighbouring black lines is a band: a strip carrying a whole interval of points side by side. The shaded horizontal bar is the interval itself. A band leaves the bar from one stretch of its edge and comes back to another stretch, and every point carried along the band arrives in the same order it left. The loops that leave and return on the same side of the bar, and look like a pair of rabbit ears, are bands that reverse direction; Dunfield and Thurston allow them. The interval exchanges in mibz2 never have them: every band of LF goes from the top edge to the bottom edge. There is one band per run of the BWT's last column, with the run's width as its weight.

Then they split it. In the next figure, \(t\) and \(b\) are the rightmost bands on the top and the bottom of the bar. Band \(t\) is wider than band \(b\), so \(b\) is cut out of \(t\)'s end and glued on: the new track \((\tau', w')\) has a band \(t'\) of weight \(w_t - w_b\) and a band \(b'\) of weight \(w_b\), and nothing else changes. If \(t\) carries 7 points and \(b\) carries 3, after the split \(t'\) carries 4 and \(b'\) carries 3. No point was dropped; the same points are carried by differently drawn bands.

Splitting an interval exchange

"Splitting an interval exchange." Reproduced from Dunfield and Thurston (2006), Figure 18, for commentary. Their text continues: "The basic operation is called Rauzy induction in the context of interval exchanges, and splitting or sliding in the context of train tracks."

That sentence is the bridge. Rauzy–Veech induction, the operation behind our Cells kernels, is train-track splitting: it compares the two rightmost pieces, subtracts the shorter from the longer, and records which piece followed which. Dunfield and Thurston use the same move to count how many separate closed curves a weighted track carries, without ever drawing one. That is close to our problem, but not the same: they need the number of curves, and a decoder needs the exact order of every byte along one of them.

items.title: 4. A compressed block as a weighted track
items.text:
Here is what the picture looks like for a real (tiny) block. bzip2 turns the text banana$ into the last column annb$aa, with the original text starting at row 4. Grouped into runs, the column reads a, nn, b, $, aa, five runs over seven rows. LF moves each run as a block. Where the image of one run lands in another, we draw an arc between them and give it the number of rows it carries. That gives the run network:

Arc Rows it carries What happens there a → nn 1 row 0 goes to row 1 nn → aa 2 rows 1 and 2 travel together to rows 5 and 6 b → $ 1 row 3 goes to row 4 $ → a 1 row 4 goes to row 0 aa → nn 1 row 5 goes to row 2 aa → b 1 row 6 goes to row 3

Read as a track, the runs are branches and the weights are the row counts. Two switches stand out. At nn, two single strands, from a and from aa, merge into a branch of weight 2, and the order is fixed: the strand from a is on top (row 1), the one from aa below it (row 2). At aa, that bundle of 2 parts again, one strand to nn and one to b. Every switch condition holds: \(1 + 1 = 2\) at nn, and \(2 = 1 + 1\) at aa. Following the strands from row 4 visits rows 4, 0, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3 and spells $ananab, which is banana$ read backwards.

On real blocks the same network is cheap to build: one pass over the runs, with no row-level work. We measured it on six blocks of Wikidata JSON, each about 900,000 rows (the census). It has 1.21 to 1.25 arcs per run. Between 88 and 89 percent of runs are plain stretches of track, with one arc in and one arc out, and merging those leaves a branching core of about a ninth of the runs. So a block's paths really do travel in bundles along a few branches and part at a modest number of switches.

One piece is still missing before this is a train track in Thurston's sense: a track lives on a surface, and the order of strands at each switch comes from that surface. For a BWT block we have one. Pairing LF with the move to the next row glues the rows, as unit squares, into a closed surface whose corners all sit at run boundaries (the origami lift). The run network is drawn on it.

items.title: 5. Maps that write words
items.text:
A second kind of train track, from Bestvina and Handel's work5 on maps of graphs, is closer to what a decoder does. Here the track is a graph, and a map sends each edge not to one edge but to a whole path of edges. Rafiqi and Zeytin's survey (2026)6 gives an example on a surface of genus 2, a doughnut with two holes: a track with four edges \(e_1, \dots, e_4\) meeting at one vertex \(v\), and a map that sends, for instance, \(e_1 \mapsto e_1 e_2 e_3 e_1 e_3\) and \(e_4 \mapsto e_1 e_2 e_4 e_3\).

A track on a genus-2 surface, mapped into itself

"A genus 2 surface with a train track invariant under a pseudo-Anosov map." Reproduced from Rafiqi and Zeytin (2026), Figure 1, for commentary. The map sends each coloured edge to a word in the edges, such as e1 ↦ e1e2e3e1e3.

A pseudo-Anosov map, as the reader may meet it in Thurston's classification, stretches a surface by a fixed factor along one family of curves and shrinks it along another, everywhere save at finitely many singular points. Thurston's classification makes it the typical kind of map of a surface to itself, beside periodic and reducible ones.

Such a map holds two kinds of information. Counting how often each edge appears in each image gives a matrix of non-negative integers, and its largest eigenvalue says how fast paths grow when the map is applied again and again. The words themselves give the order. For a decoder only the second kind is enough: knowing that a stretch of text holds three as and two ns does not say which comes first.

mibz2 already builds such words. Each step of the Rauzy–Veech induction in Cells records which piece followed which, and the result is a grammar whose rules spell the block. In the language of this section, that grammar is the sequence of edge-to-path maps the splits produce.

items.title: 6. What is known, and what is open
items.text:
The table below sets the parts of the theory against what mibz2 already does.

Train-track idea In mibz2 Status Strands that travel together stored once, with a weight Runs, and Open's convoys of rows that move together in use Splitting a weighted track Rauzy–Veech induction in Cells in use; the same move Maps that send edges to words Cells' grammar of return words in use Weights and their matrix Counts of each letter known; cannot give the order The run network as a track on a surface Built cheaply from the runs; surface from the origami lift measured; the census is above Folds, and the "illegal turns" of Bestvina and Handel none open Choosing a different track for the same paths none open

The open rows are where something new could come from. Bestvina and Handel simplify a map of graphs by folding (gluing together two edges that leave a vertex in the same direction) and by tracking which pairs of directions are eventually glued, the illegal turns. Folding is cheap and works on edges, not on the paths they carry. If the run network can be turned into such a map without walking the rows, its illegal turns might single out the few branchings where the order of the text is really decided. That is a question, not a result. Two easy uses of the network have already failed: its branching core has no small cuts to split it at, and walking the rows of the core costs more than Open does (the census).

These leads now sit in the project's list of open mathematical directions, for the research agent working on new decoders to take up. The general point holds whatever comes of them: a decoder gets faster when it stops following paths one at a time and starts editing a small object that carries many of them. Rauzy–Veech induction was the first such operation we found, and train tracks are the theory it belongs to.

Research records: the run network and its census; the origami lift.

Figures from the papers above are reproduced at reduced size for commentary and criticism, each credited in its caption.

❦
