items.title: Where the decoding work goes
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

What we measured. Undoing bzip2's Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) means rebuilding a block's text one byte at a time from a sorted table of its rows. Each byte of the text comes from exactly one row. Some rows are cheap, because they belong to a large group of rows that the decoder moves together. Others are expensive, because they stand alone and the decoder has to visit each of them in turn, waiting on memory every time. Until now we have counted the expensive rows but never asked which text they spell. So we decoded six blocks of the Wikidata dump, followed every row back to the byte it produces, and sorted those bytes by kind: JSON keys, numbers, words, and the long random identifiers that Wikidata attaches to its records.

What we found. The repetitive part of the JSON, which looks like the obvious target, is already nearly free: keys such as "mainsnak" are about a third of the text but about 1% of the rows that stand alone. Those rows belong overwhelmingly to random strings. The 36-character IDs that Wikidata gives each statement are about 5% of the text and about 62% of the lone rows. The 40-character hashes that identify a reference are a different case: each one is used several times, so its rows come in small groups, one row per use.

Why it matters. It says where a better decoder must win, since collapsing repeated structure is what the current decoder already does well. What remains splits into random strings that repeat, which could be copied once one copy is decoded, and random strings that don't, which no amount of recognising structure can help with. This post builds the measurement up from one example (section 1), gives the totals over six blocks (section 2), explains why random strings behave this way (section 3), says why we went looking (section 4), and ends with the questions it opens (section 5).

items.title: Where the decoding work goes: random IDs in repetitive JSON
items.text:
Tracing each costly row back to the text it spells shows that JSON keys cost almost nothing, while random statement IDs claim two thirds of the hardest rows.

20 November 2026 · 9 min read · Open question

items.title: 1. One snippet, character by character
items.text:
A quick recap of the setting, which Open Returns works through in full. bzip2 sorts all the rotations of a block of text and stores the last column of the sorted table. The decoder rebuilds the text by walking that column backwards: from each row, a step called LF finds the row holding the previous byte. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form a run. Because a run's rows move together under LF, mibz2's current kernel, Open, treats a wide run as one unit. The rows of narrow runs it keeps individually and walks one by one. They are about a tenth of a block's rows, and walking them is most of the decode's cost. Below we call a run of fewer than 16 rows thin, which is close to, though not exactly, the set of rows Open keeps.

The figure shows how that looks on real text, in three snippets of block 0. Each character is shaded by the width of the run that holds it, so a wide cell is cheap and a dark cell costs a step of its own.

Three snippets of block 0, each character shaded by the width of its run

JSON skeleton"mainsnak":{"snaktype":"value","property":"P2093"A hash used 6 times"hash":"cbff8d4b3b7b35f905ef3147a7a6cb88845a774f"A statement ID"id":"Q38584699$0EF8A40C-5CE8-4302-BACA-3B0B69926C69"run of 16 rows or more: moves with its grouprun of 2 to 15 rows: a thin runrun of 1 row: walked alone Measured on block 0 of the admitted Wikidata blocks. The JSON keys sit in runs of hundreds to tens of thousands of rows. Every byte of a hash used six times sits in a run of six or seven. A statement ID's characters sit in runs of one or two from its first digit.

The three snippets behave in three different ways:

  • The JSON skeleton ("mainsnak":{"snaktype":"value","property":"P) sits mostly in runs of 763 to 26,407 rows. The same bytes, followed by the same text, appear thousands of times in the block, so their rows lie side by side in the sorted table and travel as one group.
  • A reference hash used six times sits in runs of six (twice seven). Each of its 40 hex digits is followed by the same rest-of-hash in all six places, so the six rows sort together. They form a thin run: six rows, not one, but far from the thousands of the skeleton.
  • A statement ID sits in runs of one or two from its first digit. Its 32 hex digits are random, and no other text in the block continues the same way, so almost every row is alone.

items.title: 2. The totals over six blocks
items.text:
The snippet is one example, whereas the measurement covers every byte of the six blocks, about 5.4 million bytes. A short script (costmap.py) classifies each byte by a pattern: statement IDs, 40-digit hashes, entity IDs such as Q42, other numbers, JSON keys, other letters, and the remaining punctuation. The chart compares each kind's share of the text with its share of the thin-run rows and of the one-row runs.

Share of the text against share of the expensive rows, by kind of text

0%20%40%60%Statement IDs (GUIDs)5%29%62%Hashes (sha1)3%15%6%Entity IDs (Q…, P…)6%10%8%Other numbers8%15%10%Other letters20%21%9%Punctuation and spaces22%8%5%JSON keys36%2%0.9%share of the textshare of thin-run rowsshare of one-row runs Measured; each bar is the mean over the six blocks. The classes are pattern matches, and "thin" means a run of fewer than 16 rows, an approximation to the rows Open keeps. The per-block figures are in the research journal.

The per-block ranges tell the same story as the means. Statement IDs are 3–8.5% of the text in each block but 54–67% of the one-row runs. JSON keys are 33–38% of the text but 1–4% of the thin-run rows. IDs and hashes together hold 32–53% of the thin-run rows. The other kinds, numbers, words and entity IDs, cost at most about twice their share of the text. By contrast, a statement ID's share of the one-row runs is about thirteen times its share of the text.

items.title: 3. Why random strings stand alone
items.text:
The table's rows are sorted by the text that follows each byte. Two rows therefore sit next to each other when their following text agrees for a long stretch. A run of width 6 therefore means six places in the block where the same byte is followed by the same text; a run of width 1 means that combination happens once.

Repeated structure gives wide runs: a key that appears 3,000 times, followed by the same punctuation and the same next key, puts 3,000 rows in one run. That is why the skeleton is cheap, and also why bzip2 compresses this kind of text well: a few wide runs describe many bytes.

A random string does the opposite. A statement ID is 32 random hexadecimal digits. The row of a byte inside it is sorted by the text that follows that byte, which is the rest of the ID. Even four random hex digits allow 65,536 continuations, and the block holds only about 760 IDs, so that following text is almost always unique and the row stands alone. The same is true of a hash the first time it is used. But a hash used six times has six rows for each digit, all followed by identical text, so it forms runs of six. Its cost is in the thin runs, not the one-row runs, which is exactly where the chart puts it: in block 0, 841 hash fields hold only 137 distinct hashes.

Three kinds of text, three kinds of cost

Repeated structureJSON keys, punctuationWide runs: thousandsof rows move as one.Already collapsedby today's decoder.Repeated random stringsreference hashesThin runs: one rowfor each copy.Could be copied onceone copy is decoded.Unique random stringsstatement IDsOne-row runs: eachbyte is its own step.Nothing in the blockrepeats it. Conceptual. The three kinds need three different treatments, which is why one decoder that treats every thin row alike leaves something on the table.

None of this is special to Wikidata. JSON from logs, APIs and database dumps has the same shape: a repetitive skeleton with random identifiers and hashes threaded through it. The measurement uses Wikidata's text, but the conclusion is about that shape.

items.title: 4. Why look at the text at all?
items.text:
The question came from a contrast with the Hutter Prize, which rewards the smallest self-extracting description of a gigabyte of English Wikipedia. Its rules allow decompression to take tens of hours on one core. mibz2 is the opposite case: the description is fixed by bzip2, and the goal is the least computation to recover the text. A short description is not the same as a cheap one to use. Our own research has met that gap directly: an earlier experiment shrank the decoder's lookup table to a compact form and found the decode 1.7 to 2.8 times slower, because each step took several dependent lookups instead of one.

A short description, a compact table even, buys naught at decode time: shrunk to a compact form, the decoder's lookup table made each step several dependent lookups instead of one, and the decode ran 1.7 to 2.8 times slower. A fact about one table, not a verdict on every compact form.

One Hutter winner in particular suggested the question. STARLIT (Margaritov, 2021) did not improve the compressor at all. It reordered Wikipedia's articles so that similar articles sat together, and the unchanged compressor then did better. bzip2's encoder has already done a reordering of its own, sorting every byte by the text that follows it. We asked what that reordering exposes about the text, working backwards from the structure we know the text has to what it costs to decode. The first answer is the one above: the structure we expected to exploit is already exploited, and the cost sits in the parts of the text that have no structure.

items.title: 5. What comes next
items.text:
The measurement turns a vague idea, a "zoo" of decoding methods each suited to a different kind of text, into three concrete questions for the research line:

  1. Repeated random strings. A hash's six copies spell the same 40 bytes. If the decoder could find out cheaply that a thin run's rows are copies of one another, it could decode one copy and write the others. Finding that out from what the decoder already holds, before the text exists, is the hard part, and its cost must be counted.
  2. Unique random strings. Statement IDs have nothing to share, so their one-row runs may be a true floor for any method that works by recognising repetition. Is there an operation on them that is not a step-by-step walk, or can we prove there isn't one, for a stated class of methods?
  3. A method per kind. Before any classifier is built, the first measurement is the best case: if each block, or each part of a block, could use whichever method suits it best, how much would that save? An earlier attempt to tune Open per block found less than 1% to gain even with hindsight, so this is the number to know first.

These are now recorded as a lead for the research line. The measurement script is in the research journal, and anyone can rerun it on the six blocks.

Research records:

  • Working backwards from the text: the discussion, the per-block table and costmap.py.
  • The run network: the runs as a graph, and the longest chains of thin runs.
  • Open Returns: the current kernel, and which rows it keeps.
  • The Hutter Prize and STARLIT.

items.title: Admitting dense blocks to Open
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 is a bzip2 decoder in Rust. Most of its time goes on inverting the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) of each block. Its fastest kernel for that, Open, used to refuse blocks with many short runs. On our Wikidata benchmark it refused five of the 233 full-size blocks, which fell back to an older kernel allocating about 5.6 MiB per worker. That fallback set the decoder's peak memory. In mibz2 0.5.11, Open admits those blocks under a cap on its first pass (#703).

The effect was measured on the i9-10900K we test releases on, which has ten cores and a 20 MiB shared L3. Over ten paired rounds, 0.5.11 against 0.5.10, on the Wikidata benchmark:

threads peak memory (RSS) wall time median peak RSS 8 0.738 [0.710, 0.767] 0.976 [0.965, 0.987] 87.0 → 63.4 MiB 10 0.709 [0.691, 0.728] 0.960 [0.956, 0.965] 93.9 → 66.5 MiB

The output is byte-identical on every block, and #703 is the only decoder change between the two releases. The intervals are 95% intervals of the paired ratio, over this one machine and corpus.

The takeaways:

  • The cause was a routing gap, not the kernel's cost. Open's admission test refused blocks whose density r/n, runs per byte, exceeded 0.15. Five full-size Wikidata blocks sit between 0.151 and 0.206, so they paid for a full-table fallback.
  • A bounded band closes the gap. Blocks with r/n from 0.15 to 0.28 are admitted if Open's first pass stays under a cap on its retained rows and thick strips. All five fit under it.
  • Two short arguments make the port safe. No elimination step ever widens a strip, so the widest initial strip bounds every later step. Three working buffers, in turn, can live inside an array that is dead until a late phase.
  • The memory claim transferred; the speed predictions did not. The research line that proposed the change predicted the dense blocks would take under half the cycles. Natively they take 12–43% longer than on the fallback, on one thread. The speed that does appear on the i9 comes from the smaller working set, not from the kernel being faster on these blocks.

items.title: Admitting dense blocks to the Open kernel: 29% less peak memory
items.text:
A bounded admission band takes five dense blocks off a 5.6 MiB-per-worker fallback, and the decoder runs slightly faster in over a quarter less memory.

21 November 2026 · 10 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.11 (changelog)

items.title: 1. Why did five blocks take the expensive path?
items.text:
bzip2 cuts a file into blocks of up to 900 kB and applies the BWT to each. The transform reorders a block so that bytes with similar contexts sit together, and equal bytes form runs. mibz2 decodes several blocks at once, one per worker thread, and each worker needs its own scratch memory.

Open keeps only the rows of a block's narrow runs and moves each wide run as one strip (Open returns). Since 0.5.10 its scratch is about 1.2 MiB per worker, small enough for seven to ten workers to share the i9's 20 MiB L3. A block with many short runs leaves more rows for Open to keep, so its admission test refused blocks whose density r/n exceeded 0.15. A refused block went to LazyCells and then to Segmented, which builds a full table of the block at about 5.6 MiB per worker.

The benchmark is an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump: 431 blocks, of which 233 are full-size blocks on the route Open serves. Open took 228 of them; the other five have densities from 0.151 to 0.206. A worker that met one of these held the fallback's table, so it was these five that set the worst worker's memory.

Where the 233 full-size blocks go, before and after the dense band

0.000.050.100.150.200.250.30block density r/n: runs per byte of the blockold line 0.15dense band ends 0.280.5.10#703228 blocks: Open(count gates; not plotted)228 blocks: Open(unchanged)5 refused → LazyCells → Segmentedabout 5.6 MiB per worker5 admitted to Open, within the cap199k–232k rows, 568–2,729 strips41, 278, 56, 16527041, 278, 56, 165270 Measured routing on the benchmark's 431 blocks (#703's census). The 228 blocks below r/n 0.15 are admitted by Open's count gates in both versions; their individual densities are not plotted. The five above the line are plotted at their measured r/n. The 150 tiny blocks and the 48 blocks on the column route are unchanged and not shown.

items.title: 2. How is a dense block admitted safely?
items.text:
The band admits a block with r/n between 0.15 and 0.28 if Open's first pass stays under a cap. The cap is min(256,000, 0.3n) retained rows and 16,384 thick strips. The check sits on the queues' cold path, so the first pass's hot loop is unchanged. Once a block passes either limit, a sticky flag stops the pass and the block goes to LazyCells as before. Blocks the old test admitted keep their route, with no cap. The five dense blocks fit, at up to 231,600 retained rows.

A denser block also means more elimination work, so the port needs a bound on it. Open eliminates intervals by Rauzy–Veech steps: each step replaces the wider of two strips with the difference of their widths. No step ever makes a strip wider, so the widest strip at the start bounds every later step. A block whose strips are all at most 32,768 rows wide therefore runs the plain elimination loop unchanged. A block that fails this certificate takes a contracted loop instead. It treats a long spiral, a run of steps that peels one strip against the same partner, as one step, building its word by repeated squaring.

On Wikidata no block fails the certificate, so the contracted loop never runs: it bounds the worst case and is not a speed-up.

items.title: 3. Where do the extra buffers live?
items.text:
Admitting the dense blocks must not bring back the memory it saves. The research line's second idea, EdgesMux, places working buffers inside the edges array, which the kernel does not write until a late phase. Its lifetime argument (Theorem 19.1 of the cycle 19 journal) is that each buffer's last read comes before edges is first written. Its verifier poisons each buffer after its last read, over 1,000 runs, and the output stays exact.

To poison a buffer is to spoil its contents on purpose once its last read is done, whereby any later read would show in the output. The output stayed exact over 1,000 runs; poisoned earlier, as a control, it breaks.

Most of this was already in 0.5.10, which put the elimination's nodes in edges (#692). The port moves the remaining buffer, the strips' image order, into the first words of edges, worth 27–28 KiB a worker. Its tests poison each region of edges after its last read, and the output stays exact; poisoned earlier, as a control, the output breaks.

items.title: 4. What is the measured effect?
items.text:
Two measurements bear on it: the port's own in-process A/B, in a 4-vCPU cloud container, and the release-scaling run on the i9.

The A/B runs master's kernel, unchanged, in the same binary as the candidate, and alternates the two. An A/A control, built from master's own tree, shows the noise floor. There are 12 rounds with 95% intervals.

measure A/A control #703 against master kernel heap, worst worker, 10 workers (KiB) – 6,804.5 → 1,268.8 (0.186×) 1 thread, six blocks Open already took 0.993–1.019 1.003–1.009 1 thread, the five newly admitted blocks 0.987–1.019 1.120–1.427 4 workers, time in the five blocks 1.004 [0.994, 1.015] 0.925 [0.909, 0.942] 4 workers, a whole pass 1.007 [1.000, 1.013] 1.003 [0.991, 1.016] end to end, 8 threads: peak memory – 0.741 [0.714, 0.768] end to end, 8 threads: wall time – 0.978 [0.928, 1.031] end to end, 10 threads: peak memory – 0.783 [0.754, 0.812] end to end, 10 threads: wall time – 1.002 [0.957, 1.050]

Ratios are #703's time or memory over master's. On a fresh kernel, each of the five blocks drops from 5.6 MiB to about 1 MiB.

The worst worker's kernel heap falls to under a fifth because no worker now holds the fallback's table. End to end, the process's peak memory falls by about a quarter. Container wall time does not move beyond noise, because the five blocks are under 4% of a pass and its cache is not the i9's shared L3.

On the i9, the release-scaling run compared 0.5.11 with 0.5.10 from 1 to 20 threads. At 1, 2 and 4 threads nothing changed beyond noise. From 8 threads up, 0.5.10 took 2.5% to 5.6% longer, with every interval excluding no change. Peak memory fell as in the container.

Per-worker memory against each worker's share of the i9's 20 MiB L3

02,0004,0006,0008,000KiB per worker0.5.9: scratch, admitted blocks4,2360.5.10: scratch, admitted blocks1,2000.5.10: worst worker, incl. dense fallback6,804.5#703: worst worker1,268.8share at 7 workers: 2,92610 workers: 2,048 Measured, two measures. The upper pair is per-worker scratch on the blocks Open admits (0.5.10's changelog, from #692). The lower pair is the worst worker's kernel heap over the whole corpus at 10 workers (#703's harness), which includes the fallback's table when a worker meets a refused block. The dashed lines are 20 MiB divided by 7 and by 10 workers.

The wall-time gain on the i9 is consistent with the cache account. With ten workers, each worker's share of the L3 is about 2 MiB. A worker holding a 6.8 MiB fallback therefore evicts its neighbours' working sets, while a worker at 1.3 MiB fits in its share. The container, with a different cache, could not show this, so it is our account of the i9 result, not a measurement of cache misses.

items.title: 5. What transferred from the research line?
items.text:
The change came from Mechanisms, one of our AI research lines. Its cycle 19 built a candidate called AhtEdgesMux16 and measured it in its own harness against mibz2 0.5.8. The harness includes a contention model, a simulator that charges each worker a share of the cache.

The research line's claims against the native measurements

1.61.41.21.00.80.60.40.20.0dense blocks, timeclaim: model, 8–10 workerscontainer: 1 threadcontainer: 4 workersworst worker's heapclaim: vs 0.5.8container: vs 0.5.10, 10 workerswhole decoder, 8 threadscontainer: peak memorycontainer: wall timei9: peak memoryi9: wall timewhole decoder, 10 threadscontainer: peak memorycontainer: wall timei9: peak memoryi9: wall timenew ÷ old (below 1: less time or memory) Ratios, new over old; below 1 is better. Claims are the line's own (cycle 19 journal), against 0.5.8 and from its contention model. Container figures are #703's, against 0.5.10. i9 figures are 0.5.11 against 0.5.10 from the release-scaling run's records, paired by round. Bars are 95% intervals where they exist.

The memory claim held, against a newer baseline. The line measured the ten-worker maximum heap falling from 9,979 KiB to 1,346 KiB against 0.5.8. By 0.5.10, however, the admitted blocks were already at about 1.3 MiB. The gain that remains is the dense blocks' fallback, which no longer allocates its table.

Of a contention model that promised half, and a kernel that came in slower

The speed predictions did not. The contention model predicted the dense blocks would take under half the cycles, with a cache share of about 2 MiB per worker. Natively, on one thread, Open is slower than the fallback on these blocks, because with the cache to itself the fallback's full table is fast. With four workers in the container, Open takes 7.5% less time on them. On the i9 the whole decoder is faster from 8 threads up. That gain comes through the smaller working set, so it is spread over all blocks rather than concentrated in the five. The line's other claims shrank too. EdgesMux was worth 432 KiB against 0.5.8, yet most of it had already shipped in 0.5.10. The spiral contraction, for its part, never runs on Wikidata.

Correctness. Every block of the corpus, and six authenticated reference blocks, decode byte for byte as the plain inverse does. The bzcat example at 4, 8 and 10 threads gives the same SHA-256 as bzip2 -dc. The correctness gate passes its 338 cases, and eight hand-made mutations of the new code were each caught by the tests. CI's paired bench at 1 to 4 threads found no change in Wikidata's wall time beyond noise.

The change shipped in mibz2 0.5.11.

Research records: Mechanisms' cycle 19 journal; the port's journal and its results (#703); 0.5.11's release-scaling records on the i9 and its attribution row; 0.5.10's memory diet.

items.title: Besieging hard problems
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 is a Rust decoder for bzip2, and for months we have searched for faster ways to undo the reordering at its core. This post describes how we are rebuilding that search, and why. A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, built at a scale no person could write and accepted by three independent checkers, has shown what a search can attempt once checking is cheap. Our checks of correctness are already cheap, but our checks of speed are not, so that is where we start.

On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, found working with Claude and written out in full in Lean, a language whose proofs a small program called a kernel can check line by line. By the end of that day, members of the Lean community had reported that three independent kernels, nanoda, con-leche in its verified mode and pestka, each accepted the development. It is about 17 million lines of Lean v4.33.1 in 175,190 files. It proves the Riemann Hypothesis, and its generalisation to Dirichlet L-functions, a family of functions that pose the same question for primes in arithmetic progressions. It does not, however, cover the wider Selberg class.

Three kernels are three programs written apart, each re-checking the exported proof from scratch, whereby a bug in any one checker can't pass the proof alone.

The Riemann Hypothesis was posed in 1859. It says that the zeros of one function, which governs how the primes are spread out, all lie on a single line. It has been the most famous open problem in mathematics for more than a century, and generations of the strongest mathematicians have failed to settle it. A proof of it, of any length, would be an event. This one is checked by machines, and built at a scale no person could write or read. That raises a second question beside the mathematics. What kind of method makes such a proof possible, and what can those of us working on smaller hard problems take from it?

We have not checked the proof. We are not number theorists, and nothing below depends on the argument being right. What we use is its reported shape, chiefly the overview that Chris Birkbeck posted on the Lean Zulip thread "Discussion: Alpöge Proves the Riemann Hypothesis". Nor is a formal check the same as human understanding. Birkbeck himself wrote: "I have not yet understood how these combine to exclude zeros." Where this post reads a mechanism into the proof, it says so.

The takeaways come first.

  • The economics of difficulty have changed. For as long as mathematics has existed, a proof had to be short enough for people to find, check and explain. A route that was valid but needed tens of thousands of pages was out of reach. When machines can build and check such routes, length stops being the dominant constraint.
  • The method is a sequence of moves, not one insight. We read twelve of them in the proof's shape, in four stages. The target is strengthened into a statement about a whole family. The forbidden event is excluded by bounds from different fields on a quantity they can each constrain. The work moves to a richer setting where those bounds exist, and the foundations the route needs are built, not assumed.
  • Search can be wide only where checking is cheap. A kernel's verdict is certain and costs little next to discovery, so the search can afford strange routes. Discovery, verification and understanding become three jobs, done at different times.
  • For mibz2, a fast decoder for bzip2, the binding constraint is performance checking. Our correctness check is cheap and certain; our performance check is scarce and has misled us. Faithful, cheap measurement under realistic load comes before any wider search for new algorithms.
  • The research question sharpens. We want a defined cost model in which lower and upper bounds on decoding can meet. Our latest negative result points at global structure, and the right primitive may not be the one we have spent months tuning.

Section 1 sets out what was achieved and why its scale matters. Section 2 describes how the problem was changed before it was solved, and section 3 why the route looks strange to specialists. Section 4 covers the role of cheap checking, and the three moves that decide the rest. Section 5 applies all of it to mibz2, and section 6 says what comes next.

items.title: Besieging hard problems: cheap checks first, after the Riemann proof
items.text:
A machine-checked Riemann proof shows how far a search can range once checking is cheap, so ours now begins by making speed cheap to check.

21 November 2026 · 16 min read · Meta

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.10 (changelog)

items.title: 1. What was achieved
items.text:
Seventeen million lines is hard to picture. Mathlib, the community library on which most Lean mathematics is built, took years of work by hundreds of contributors to reach a fraction of that. The development uses no axioms beyond Lean's own, so every theorem it relies on is proved inside it. That includes a large part of modern arithmetic geometry, which most papers in the field cite rather than reprove.

Birkbeck's overview gives the structure in five steps, paraphrased here:

  1. The Riemann Hypothesis follows from the statement that no Dirichlet L-function vanishes where the real part of \(s\) exceeds \(\tfrac12\). This step is short and standard.
  2. That non-vanishing follows from three ingredients. One is a growth bound on certain Galois cohomology groups (objects that measure how far a number-theoretic equation fails to have solutions), resembling Tate–Shafarevich groups, over a family of subfields of cyclotomic fields. The second is a covolume bound from arithmetic geometry. The third is a set of statements about theta integrals on unitary groups, with the local Langlands correspondence for \(\mathrm{GL}_n\).
  3. The cohomology bound is an automorphy-lifting argument. It uses Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized, cuspidal automorphic representations of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) over CM fields. Base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel's purity theorem, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the theory of complex multiplication and Deligne–Ribet are all used along the way.
  4. Those Galois representations are not assumed. The development builds them by a geometric construction for unitary groups, with theta lifts between groups. As far as Birkbeck can tell, this is not the route in the literature.
  5. Because nothing is assumed, the infrastructure is proved inside too: resolution of singularities in characteristic zero, the arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel theorem, Moriwaki's bigness theorem, toroidal compactifications of Siegel varieties, Kawamata–Viehweg and Nadel vanishing, Grothendieck–Messing theory and prismatic Dieudonné theory.

Each item in step 5 is a major theorem; several took their original authors years, and some have never been formalised before in any system. Here, however, they are scaffolding, built because the route needed them.

The announcement also describes more than 250,000 pages of generated exposition, which Alpöge chose not to present as a readable proof, and he expects major simplifications. One number theorist, writing on social media, put the strangeness this way: the proof "takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built for a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the destination, and somehow create[s] a wormhole to the original destination." A problem many had assumed would need new theory in arithmetic geometry may instead yield to a long chain of existing, deep results.

A reading project has since published a source-linked atlas of the development, which maps its components to pinned lines of the Lean source and marks which cuts of the argument have been checked separately. Its own summary describes a one-sided bound on sums over primes, supplied by the arithmetic, which analysis turns into a region free of zeros. That is the atlas authors' reading, and we have not checked it either.

Why the scale matters beyond mathematics. The usual picture of a great proof is a single insight that makes a hard problem easy. This development may contain such an insight; no one can yet say. What it certainly contains is an enormous amount of machinery assembled around the problem until the conclusion could not be avoided. That suggests some problems were hard not because the necessary idea was out of reach, but because every known route was far too long for people to build and check. If so, the limits on what can be solved were partly limits of human logistics. They were set by how many concepts one mind can hold, how long an argument a community can review, and how much foundational work its attention can pay for.

items.title: 2. How is a problem changed before it is solved?
items.text:
Read as strategy, the overview suggests twelve moves, which our research journal sets out in four stages. They choose the statement, then the quantity the proof turns on, then the route, and finally run the search. They are our interpretation of the proof's shape, not established descriptions of its mechanism. Where a move names a classical pattern (Deligne's amplification, a Bloch–Kato-style link between cohomology and L-values), that goes beyond what Birkbeck's overview says. As principles for organising a hard search, however, they stand on their own.

Twelve moves in four stages: our reading of the proof's shape

I. The statement1Strengthen it untilthe tools preserve it2Prove a growth rate,not a value3Use inequalities,not formulasII. The quantity4One quantity twotheories can measure5Amplify a defectbefore measuring6Seek quantities thatcan’t be negativeIII. The route7Plan backwards fromwhere tools work8Push difficulty toclassified local cases9Re-optimise when thecost of proof changesIV. The search10Make checking cheap,then search widely11Use a toy to find theingredient, then drop it12Separate correctnessfrom understandinghighlighted: what to constrain (4), where to constrain it (7), how to afford the search (10) Conceptual, and our interpretation: not a dependency diagram of the proof, and not a description its authors have confirmed. The highlighted moves, 4, 7 and 10, decide the others (section 4).

items.title: Choosing the statement
items.text:
The statement is strengthened until the tools preserve it. The development does not attack the Riemann Hypothesis alone. It proves non-vanishing for every Dirichlet L-function, across families of cyclotomic fields. A stronger statement can be easier to prove when the family is closed under the operations the tools need: twisting by characters, base change up a tower of fields, lifts between groups. A single object, by contrast, gives an induction nothing to work with. Pólya called this the inventor's paradox: the original problem is the destination, not necessarily the place where the work is done.

A growth rate is proved, not a value. Across a tower of fields, a hypothetical zero would make an obstruction grow at a measurable rate. Comparing exponents of growth is robust, since exponents survive the constants and error terms that swamp a comparison at any single level.

Inequalities replace formulas. The infrastructure in step 5 (Hilbert–Samuel, bigness, Kawamata–Viehweg and Nadel vanishing) consists of robust inequalities. No exact formula is needed. A chain of inequalities is long but local, since each link can be checked alone. That is part of why seventeen million lines can be checked although no one holds the whole argument.

items.title: Choosing the quantity
items.text:
Two unrelated theories must be able to measure the same thing. This is the most important move. Constructing a mechanism that rules out zeros directly is hard. The alternative is to find a quantity that a hypothetical zero would change, and to constrain it from independent directions. Birkbeck's step 2 names three bounds of different kinds, from algebra, from geometry and from harmonic analysis. Our reading is that they meet like a vice: one bounds a quantity from above, another from below, and a zero would need a value between them that does not exist. One theory gripping the quantity gives a bound; two give a squeeze.

A defect is amplified before it is measured. A single zero may be invisible to coarse tools. Pushed through a family, a tower or a repeated construction, however, it can produce enough obstructions to violate a bound. Deligne's tensor-power argument is the classical model: a bound on \(|\alpha|^{2k}\) for every \(k\) controls \(|\alpha|\) itself.

Quantities that cannot be negative are sought out. Theta integrals, norms and volumes are manifestly non-negative. If a counterexample would force such a quantity below zero, or below a volume, the counterexample is impossible.

The difference between these ways of working and a direct construction matters. A construction gives only an example, whereas bounds that meet give finality. If every zero, or every decoder, must satisfy constraints that leave no room, the question is closed.

items.title: 3. Why does the route look so strange?
items.text:
The third stage chooses the route, and here the development departs furthest from the literature.

The route is planned backwards from where the tools work. Dirichlet L-functions have no geometry of their own. Unitary groups do: their Shimura varieties are spaces with Frobenius maps, cohomology and notions of positivity, where powerful bounds exist. The route runs from that setting back to a chain of transfers (base change, theta lifts) that reaches the original problem. The transfers are the cost, and the destination is the point. In other fields the same move has familiar forms: solving an optimisation problem through its dual, replacing a data structure with one that exposes the needed order, or giving a compiler a new intermediate representation. The richer setting may be far more complicated than the original, yet that is no objection in itself. Complexity that does no work is the problem, not complexity as such.

Difficulty is pushed to local problems that are completely classified. Local Langlands, Clozel's purity theorem and Bernstein–Zelevinsky classify everything at a single prime, and the global argument then combines the local contributions. This works only where a complete local classification exists, and section 5 describes a case of ours where it does not.

The route is re-optimised when the cost of proof changes. Birkbeck's remark that the construction of the Galois representations is "not the route in the literature" follows from the economics. The literature's routes are optimised for human cost. They are short, and they cite large results proved elsewhere, such as Harris and Taylor's construction of Galois representations, as single steps. In a development with no axioms, by contrast, every cited result costs its full formalisation. The cheapest route therefore changes: it may have more pieces, each simpler to build, and pass through constructions a specialist would never choose.

So a route that looks alien may reflect a different cost function, not a worse one. When the cost of a step changes by orders of magnitude, the best architecture of the whole argument changes with it. An established architecture should never be assumed optimal after the costs of implementation, memory, parallelism or verification have moved. For us that rule is concrete: the algorithm at the heart of every bzip2 decoder was designed for one core with cheap random access to memory, and that is not the machine we run on.

items.title: 4. Why must checking be cheap before search can be wide?
items.text:
The fourth stage runs the search. A kernel's verdict on a proof is certain, and it costs little next to the work of finding the proof. The thread records those costs. Building the development took just over an hour on eight 192-core machines. nanoda then checked the exported proof, 61.57 GB of it, in 27 minutes on 80 threads; con-leche took under four minutes on 64 cores, and pestka about nine on 96. A proof that took a long campaign to find was checked, three times over, in an afternoon. Accepting a step does not depend on anyone's judgement. That asymmetry is what lets the search take risks: unintuitive routes, long compositions of results, steps no one has yet understood. A search of that kind pays only where checking is much cheaper than generating, so verification has to be built before the search is widened.

Two further moves follow from this. The first uses a simplified problem to find the missing ingredient, then leaves it behind. The toy proof in Alpöge's remark guided the discovery, but it is not part of the Lean development. His remark describes the transfer: an operation that makes the easy setting work, multiplicity in a Stepanov-style argument, has no obvious counterpart over the integers, and iterated theta lifts were proposed to reproduce its effect. What transfers is the effect, not the operation. The second separates correctness from understanding, so that three jobs once done together can be done apart.

Three jobs, once bundled, now done apart

When people do all three jobsfind the route · check it · explain it — by the same people, at the same timeso a route is viable only if it is short enough for all threeWhen machines checkDiscoverymachine searchlong, strange routes allowedVerificationindependent kernelscheap and certainUnderstandingpeople, afterwardsits own research projectthe length of a route stops being the constraint; the cost of checking it becomes one Conceptual, not a dependency diagram of the proof. Above: when people do all three jobs, a route is viable only if it is short enough to find, check and explain at once. Below: a machine search can try long routes, independent kernels check the result, and understanding becomes later work. In the Riemann development, three kernels accepted it before anyone could say how its three bounds combine.

Discovery finds a route that works, however strange. Verification checks every step independently of whoever found it. Understanding compresses the route into ideas a person can hold, and it can now come afterwards, as a research project of its own. The construction may even be the raw material from which a short proof is later extracted. Rigour is not relaxed: every step is checked. What is relaxed is the demand that a person grasp the whole before it is accepted. We may increasingly have correct solutions before we know why they are the right ones.

Three of the twelve moves decide the rest. The fourth says what must be constrained: a quantity that two independent theories can each bound. The seventh says where those constraints can be obtained: a setting reached by planning backwards. The tenth makes searching the resulting space of routes affordable: checking that is cheap and certain. Together they describe a different kind of enterprise from thinking harder about a fixed problem. It engineers the conditions under which the problem becomes solvable, and then searches them.

items.title: 5. What does this mean for mibz2?
items.text:
mibz2 is a Rust decoder for bzip2. Most of its time goes on undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), a reordering of each block of up to 900 kB that groups similar bytes together so they compress well. Undoing it is classically done by following a map called LF from one row of a table to the next. Each step's address depends on the result of the previous step, so the walk is a chain of dependent memory accesses, and every miss in the cache stalls it. Our recent posts describe the decoder's two ways of running that walk and how they behave on many cores (Fast alone, slow in a crowd). The project's earlier note on research by obligation described how the announcement changed the way we search.

We are not proving theorems, and we should not transplant mechanisms we cannot yet explain. We can, however, adopt the method. The research journal's note on the proof's shape asks of each of the twelve moves what it would mean for us. Four consequences follow.

items.title: The binding constraint is performance checking
items.text:
Our correctness check is already like a kernel's. A candidate decoder must reproduce every byte of the original (parity), pass Miri, Rust's checker for undefined behaviour, and survive fuzzing. All of that runs on CI in minutes, and its verdict is close to certain.

Our performance check is the opposite. The authoritative measurement is a run on one ten-core desktop machine, an Intel i9-10900K, which a person has to start, and which can run one experiment at a time. The cheaper proxies have misled us repeatedly. Our fidelity ledger records, for each candidate that reached a native test, what the cheap prediction said and what happened. A selection from it:

Candidate Cheap prediction Native outcome Packed queues (#654) 8–15% faster 4.6–9.3% slower A backward pass through the table 26–28% less work 10–15% slower on all six blocks Eight interleaved lanes (#675) 13% faster on one thread, natively 5% slower at 8 threads on the i9 A cheaper elimination step alone (#679) about 5% faster on one thread faster at 6 and 8 threads, inconclusive at 10

The eight-lane candidate is the clearest case. It made the kernel 13% faster on one thread because it keeps up to eight memory lookups waiting at once. On the i9 with eight workers sharing one cache and one path to memory, that capacity was already in use, and the gain reversed.

Where our search is limited: the cost of each check

Generate candidatescheap:many per dayCheck correctnessCI:parity, Miri, fuzzingCheap speed proxiesone thread, C models:often wrongThe i9 under loadscarce:one run at a timedecides adoption → the narrowest stage limits the whole search Conceptual. Generating candidates and checking their correctness are both cheap. The check that decides adoption, the i9 run under realistic load, is scarce, and the cheap proxies before it have often ranked candidates wrongly (the fidelity ledger above). Widening the search at the top only lengthens the queue at the bottom.

One distinction from the proof helps here: the complexity of discovering a principle differs from the complexity of executing it. A very long argument can establish that a simple decoding operation is valid, and a short theorem can justify a computationally terrible algorithm. Our checks must judge the second, whatever the first cost.

If we can generate a hundred candidate algorithms but measure only a handful faithfully, our limit is not creativity but experimental throughput. So the first investment is the speed at which bad ideas are rejected, not the speed at which ideas are produced. That means a harness on CI that runs the real Rust code with several workers decoding at once, under the shared-cache contention production has. A candidate's behaviour in a crowd is then screened before it reaches the i9. Research lines also hand over patches against the real code rather than re-implementations, so that every stage checks the same artefact, as the three kernels did.

items.title: Bounds that meet need a defined cost model
items.text:
Today we race algorithms against each other. The proof's second move suggests asking a different question: how close are we to the best that any decoder could do?

Let \(D(x, A)\) be the number of serially dependent memory accesses that decoder \(A\) makes on input \(x\). A meeting of bounds would require two results. First, a lower bound \(L(x) \le D(x, A)\) that holds for every decoder \(A\) in a precisely defined model of computation. Second, a construction \(A^\ast\) with \(D(x, A^\ast) \le U(x)\). Where \(L\) and \(U\) are close, we would have an explanation of near-optimality, not another benchmark winner. Where they are far apart, the gap says what remains unexplained.

Bounds that meet: what any decoder must pay, against what our best decoder pays

no decoder cando better than thisthe gap: whatis unexplaineddecoders thatdo worselower bound L(x)upper bound U(x)proved for every decoder,in a stated cost modelachieved byour best decoder A*D(x, A): serially dependent memory accesses of decoder A on input x →where the two lines meet, the search for this resource is complete Conceptual; no bound has been proved. The lower bound would hold for every decoder in a stated model of computation, and the upper bound comes from a specific decoder. Each resource needs its own pair of bounds, and a bound in a model that ignores the hardware's real bottleneck explains nothing.

None of this is meaningful until the model is defined. Decoding spends several different resources, and each has its own bounds:

  • the number of random accesses to memory;
  • the depth of the serial chain, the accesses that must wait for one another;
  • misses in each level of cache, and the transfers between them under contention;
  • the work and memory spent preparing a structure before decoding;
  • the memory footprint while decoding;
  • the total work across all parallel workers.

There is an obvious candidate for a quantity both sides can bound, because string compressibility has measures on two sides. On the BWT's side is \(r\), its number of runs. On the text's side are measures such as \(z\), the number of phrases in its LZ77 parse, and \(\gamma\), the size of its smallest string attractor. They are tied by inequalities such as Kempa and Prezza's \(r = O(z \log^2 n)\). But an inequality between measures of compressibility is not a lower bound on the cost of computation. The bridge from one to the other has to be built, and building it is the research.

items.title: The latest negative result points at global structure
items.text:
The shape of the proof suggested one concrete lead, which we tested the same day. The local Langlands correspondence classifies the local pieces of the problem completely, so the global argument only has to glue them. Our analogue would be a catalogue: for each local arrangement of runs around a row of the table, a precomputed fragment of output, so that decoding steps from fragment to fragment.

Before the data, the note registered a rule: drop the lead unless at least 50% of the rows the decoder walks fall in arrangements that determine their output, with a catalogue small enough for a core's own cache. On six real blocks of Wikidata, the census (#687) found at best 10.5%. Arrangements of at least two rows that determine their output covered at most 3.3%, so the lead was dropped.

The reason is more useful than the number. The bytes a row emits next are its own sorted prefix, fixed by its position in the global order of the block, not by the shape of the runs around it. Local classification fails because the information the decoder needs is global, which is why attention moves to constructions that recover the global order directly. One is \(\Phi\), the map at the core of the r-index, a compressed text index that steps through text order from \(r\) stored samples. The cost of building those samples, and of reading them under contention, decides whether it can compete.

items.title: LF may be the wrong primitive
items.text:
The walk along LF was the best route under the cost model of its time: one core, and memory access that was cheap relative to computing. Under six to ten workers sharing 20 MiB of cache, the best route may be a different one altogether. Every kernel we have tuned so far descends from that walk. The next large gain may not come from a faster LF kernel; it may come from finding that LF traversal is the wrong primitive to optimise.

That sharpens the research question to one sentence. Can we preprocess the run structure of a BWT block into a compact representation that provably reduces the serial dependency depth of decoding, without paying more in preprocessing, memory traffic or contention than it saves?

items.title: 6. What comes next
items.text:
The order follows from the argument. The crowd harness on CI comes first, so that candidates are ranked under realistic contention before an i9 run. The cost model comes second, with each resource listed above defined well enough that a lower bound can be stated in it. Third come the constructions of global order that avoid LF, beginning with how cheaply \(\Phi\)'s samples can be obtained from the run structure. Each enters with a falsifiable claim and a rule for rejecting it, registered before its data, as the census was.

The chain of the argument is short. A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis has been checked by three independent kernels at a scale no person could write or review. It was reached by strengthening the statement, constraining quantities from several sides, moving to a richer setting and building every foundation it needed. That search could be wide only because checking was cheap and certain. In mibz2, checking correctness is cheap, but checking performance is not, so that is where the work must go first.

The lesson we take is not to imitate a seventeen-million-line proof. It is to find out what becomes possible when the length of a solution is no longer the dominant constraint.

Sources: Levent Alpöge's remark, whose toy proof is not part of the Lean development; the Lean Zulip thread "Discussion: Alpöge Proves the Riemann Hypothesis" (20 November 2026), for the kernel checks, their costs and Chris Birkbeck's overview; the source-linked atlas of the development.

Research records: the proof's shape, as twelve moves applied to mibz2 (#686); the local-factor census (#687); the fidelity ledger.

items.title: Fast alone, slow in a crowd
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Sixteen at a stroke described the one change in mibz2 0.5.8. Inside Open, the decoder's newest way of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), short copies of varying length became fixed sixteen-wide writes, so the processor no longer has to guess where each copy ends. Open got about a fifth faster on one thread, and the whole decoder 5% faster at ten threads on the i9-10900K, the ten-core desktop processor we test releases on. This post follows that change, and the candidate meant to succeed it, from one thread to the whole machine.

bzip2 cuts a file into blocks of up to 900 kB, and mibz2 decodes several blocks at once, one per worker thread. Undoing each block's BWT is most of the work, and mibz2 has two ways to do it. Cells, the older, is the faster for a lone worker. Open keeps only the rows of a block's narrow runs, about a tenth of a Wikidata block, and lets the rest travel in groups (Open Returns). It does more arithmetic than Cells but holds less in memory at once, and that pays when many workers share the processor's caches (Lazy letters measured why). So mibz2 runs Open only with many workers: from 8 on most machines, and on the i9 at 6 threads and from 8 up.

The question matters because a speed-up is cheap to measure on one thread, but production runs Open only when the cores are crowded. Crowded cores share one cache and one path to memory. A gain that holds for a lone worker can therefore shrink or reverse once every core competes for them.

What we found. Four runs on the i9 answer the question for 0.5.8 and its successor:

  • 0.5.8 keeps its gain on the whole machine. It is 7% faster than 0.5.7 at 8 threads and 3–5% faster from 10 to 20, with less processor time. At 1, 2 and 4 threads nothing changed, because Open doesn't run there.
  • Splitting one block across a team of threads still never pays. Teams of two or three were slower at every thread count from 4 to 20.
  • 0.5.8 moved one of the decoder's choices. At exactly 4 threads, Open with four workers now beats Cells by 5.5%, although our cost model had called that cell a near-tie.
  • The successor won alone and lost in a crowd. It walks each block in eight interleaved lanes, and it made Open 13% faster on one thread, as large a gain as 0.5.8's own when the two are timed side by side. On the i9 it was 5% faster with 6 workers, level with 7 and 5% slower with 8, so it was not adopted.

Alone and in a crowd: two changes to Open, by how many Open workers run at once

0.800.850.900.951.001.051.10level with the build beforenew time ÷ old time (below 1: faster)1 workerone thread, kernel time,cloud container6 workers6 threads,whole decoder, i97 workers10 threads (the default),whole decoder, i98 workers8 threads,whole decoder, i90.8870.8720.9220.9500.9471.0120.9741.0490.5.8’s fixed-width writes, against 0.5.7’s Open (shipped)the eight-lane candidate, against 0.5.8’s Open (not adopted) Measured. The first column is Open's kernel time alone, on one thread in a cloud container, over the whole Wikidata sample: 0.5.8's change is the inverse of the build before it at 1.128 (1.074, 1.184), and the eight-lane candidate 0.872 (0.820, 0.928) of 0.5.8. The other columns are the whole decoder's wall time on the i9, 16 paired rounds each, at 6, 10 and 8 threads, where production runs 6, 7 and 8 Open workers. The two kinds of measurement differ, so read each line's slope, not the step across the dashed divider.

Why the larger one-thread gain lost. Open's last step is a walk through a table, and each entry it reads names the next one. A single walk therefore can't start a lookup until the previous one has come back from memory, and while it waits, most of the memory system's capacity sits idle. The eight lanes cut the walk into pieces and step through each in turn, so up to eight lookups are in flight at once. On one thread that capacity was free, whereas with eight workers on the i9 it is shared. The lanes then plausibly compete for it, along with the wider tables the candidate also brought. That is our account, not a measurement (section 4 says what would test it). 0.5.8's change instead removed instructions and wrong guesses, work each core does on its own. Its gain also shrank as workers were added, but it never reversed.

Section 1 gives 0.5.8 against 0.5.7 across the machine, and section 2 the check on teams. Section 3 shows the one choice that moved, beside its prediction. Section 4 takes the eight lanes from one thread to eight, and section 5 sets each recent candidate's result alone beside its result in a crowd. Section 6 says what comes next.

All the i9 figures come from one machine: an Intel i9-10900K with 10 cores and 20 hardware threads, 256 KiB of level-2 cache per core and 20 MiB of level-3 (L3) cache shared by all ten. The workload is the benchmark's Wikidata sample, an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump that decompresses to 210 MB.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: Fast alone, slow in a crowd: which speed-ups survive many cores
items.text:
Walking each block in eight lanes made our newest decoding loop 13% faster on one thread, yet 5% slower once eight workers shared the processor.

21 November 2026 · 12 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.9 (changelog)
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: 1. How did 0.5.8 do on the whole machine?
items.text:
Before each release we time it against the last one on the i9, from 1 thread to 20. Each of ten rounds runs both releases back to back, and their ratio is taken within the round, so slow drift in the machine cancels out. The 95% intervals describe the spread across those rounds, on this one machine and corpus.

0.5.8 against 0.5.7 on the i9, by thread count

Cells only: 0.5.8’s change can’t run hereOpen in use, from 8 workers0.900.920.940.960.981.001.021.041.060.5.8’s wall time ÷ 0.5.7’s, paired by round (below 1: 0.5.8 is faster)no change1 thread0.9942 threads1.0014 threads1.0058 threads0.93410 threads0.95112 threads0.96916 threads0.97420 threads0.964wall time, with its 95% intervalprocessor (CPU) time Measured on the i9-10900K, decoding the Wikidata sample, 10 paired rounds per count. The run's summary records 0.5.7's time over 0.5.8's; the figure shows the inverse, so that below 1 means 0.5.8 is faster. In the upper band the decoder runs Cells only, so 0.5.8's change can't reach it; in the lower band it runs Open.

Below 8 threads, no change was detected, as the decoder's routing predicts. At 1 thread mibz2 decodes serially with Cells, and at 2 and 4 threads it runs that many workers, still with Cells, so 0.5.8's change to Open never executes. Open starts at 8 workers, or at 6 threads on the i9, a count this grid doesn't include. The stage timing traced the routing, and it also explains why CI's benchmark never saw the gain: CI times 1 to 4 threads, where Open never runs.

From 8 threads, every interval lies below 1. At 8 threads 0.5.8 took 0.934 of 0.5.7's time (0.925, 0.943). In the run's own terms, 0.5.7 took 1.071 times as long, and 1.052 times at 10 threads, the default. Processor time fell with the wall time, by 3–7%.

The gain is largest at 8 threads, where the decoder runs 8 Open workers. From 10 threads up it runs 7, the i9's trim: fewer workers than threads, which finishes sooner on this machine (Modelling the cache to rightsize workers). The decoder's wall time hardly moves from 8 threads to 20 (0.079 to 0.084 seconds), so threads past 8 buy no more speed on this machine.

The change's own i9 test, on four copies of the sample end to end, had measured 0.974 at 8 threads and 0.947 at 10. The two runs agree in direction, though at 8 threads they differ by more than their intervals, which cover each run's own rounds only. Peak memory rose by 2–6%, on peaks of about 100 MB, because the new queues stay allocated between blocks. At 2 threads, where nothing changed, the peaks also differ by 2 MB, so part of that is noise. For scale, lbzip2, the established parallel bzip2 decoder, took 6.3 times as long as 0.5.8 at 8 threads.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: 2. Do teams of threads win anywhere yet?
items.text:
A team is several threads that cooperate on one block, instead of one worker per block (mibz2 gets a pit crew). Teams would pay if blocks became slow enough, or the machine wide enough, that cooperating beat working independently. Each release checks that threshold on the i9 at ten thread counts from 4 to 20, with ten paired rounds each. Each figure in the table is that decoder's wall time over the shipped decoder's, so above 1 means slower:

threads teams of 2 teams of 3 one block per thread, untrimmed 4 1.374 2.007 1.016 6 1.438 1.664 1.195 8 1.630 1.888 1.061 10 1.974 1.599 1.054 12 2.184 1.720 1.124 16 2.674 1.981 1.135 20 3.149 2.242 1.160

The counts not shown, 5, 7 and 9, follow the same pattern. The closest any team came was teams of two at 7 threads, at 1.213 (1.190, 1.235). The shipped choice also beat one worker per thread without the trim, or matched it within noise, at every count. Teams therefore stay unused.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: 3. Did 0.5.8 change how many workers the decoder runs?
items.text:
On the i9 the decoder doesn't simply run one worker per thread. For each thread count, and for whether the program is pinned to particular CPUs or free to use all twenty (unpinned), it has a measured choice of worker count and method. A release that changes what a block costs may move those choices, so each release re-measures them. There are 26 cells, 12 pinned and 14 unpinned, and each compares the shipped choice with its neighbours: a worker fewer or more, or the other method. The main corpus is four copies of the Wikidata sample, with generated text and random bytes as guards. Testing many cells at once invites a win by chance, so the rule applies Holm's correction across them before calling any gain.

One cell moved. Unpinned at exactly 4 threads, Open with four workers took 0.945 of the time Cells did (0.923, 0.969), with a corrected p of 1.7 × 10⁻⁴. No change was detected on either guard, and its peak memory was 0.927 of Cells'. Every other cell kept its shipped choice. #678 makes the change for the next release.

Before the run, our cost model froze its predictions. It is a contention model, fitted to the i9's earlier runs, of how worker counts compete for the shared cache and the processor. It predicted that no choice would change, and it named this cell a near-tie at 1.02 (0.97, 1.06). 0.5.7's run had measured Open at 1.073 of Cells here, and 0.5.8's cheaper Open, it reasoned, would close most of that gap.

One cell, three readings: Open against Cells at 4 threads, unpinned

0.900.951.001.051.10Open’s wall time ÷ Cells’, four workers, unpinned (below 1: Open is faster)level0.5.7’s recalibrationmeasured, 19 November1.073: Open slowerour cost model for 0.5.8predicted before the run1.02: a near-tie0.5.8’s recalibrationmeasured, 21 November0.945: Open faster Measured (solid) and predicted (hollow, dashed), on the i9 with four copies of the Wikidata sample, 12 paired rounds per run. The prediction was frozen before 0.5.8's run. The lower interval lies wholly below the predicted one.

The miss is in one input, not in the model's structure. For 0.5.8's gain at 4 workers, the model assumed 0.92 to 0.97, since only the 6-thread figure, 0.922, had been measured. Dividing the two runs' readings, 0.945 by 1.073, puts it nearer 0.88, a figure derived from two separate runs rather than measured. The model had flagged that input as having no basis, and its own scoring rule counts a miss there against the input, not the model. The miss anticipates section 4: a kernel's gain at one worker count is not its gain at another, and here it was larger with fewer workers.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: 4. Why did a 13% one-thread win lose on eight cores?
items.text:
The candidate came from our research line's C harness, which tests ideas on Open's kernel in isolation before they are ported to the decoder (#675). It makes two changes.

The first is the walk in eight lanes. Open's last step follows its table from one kept row to the next, writing each row's word of text as it goes. Every step needs the entry the previous step pointed to, so the walk is a chain of dependent lookups. When an entry isn't already in cache, the core waits for it, and nothing else in the walk can proceed. The candidate cuts the chain into dozens of pieces, marking each cut so that a lane can tell where its piece ends, and walks eight pieces at once, one step of each in turn. While one lane waits for memory, the other seven do their steps.

Why eight lanes help a lone worker: waits that overlap

One walk: each step’s lookup must come back before the next step can startwalk5 steps, 5 waits for memory, and never more than one lookup waitingEight lanes: eight pieces of the walk take turns, so up to eight lookups wait at oncelane 1lane 2lane 3lane 4lane 5lane 6lane 7lane 8In the time the walk takes 5 steps, the lanes take up to 40. A lane can’t write its text in place, since theearlier pieces’ length isn’t known yet, so it writes into spare 4 KiB pages, moved into order at the end.work: read an entry, write a wordwaiting for the next entry to arrive from memory Conceptual timing, not measured values, and idealised: it assumes every lookup misses the cache and that memory can serve eight at once. In practice most lookups hit, and the walk is only part of Open's time, so the gain on one thread was 13%, not eightfold.

The pages add work of their own. Each lane's output goes into 4 KiB pages of output space not yet written, or of an overflow area past its end, and the pages are moved into order once the walk ends.

The second is a cheaper way of building the table, with a wider cut-off. The construction, a new elimination rule that the research line calls R4, stores only a backward link per entry and reuses a field that is no longer needed for coordinates, so it needs one array fewer. It also writes short words, up to 16 bytes, straight into the table instead of a separate store. Alongside it, Open keeps runs of up to 24 rows instead of 16, so it keeps more rows, and its queues are filled 24 rows at a time.

On one thread, natively, the pair made Open 13% faster. In the Rust decoder, on a cloud container, over the whole Wikidata sample, Open took 0.872 of 0.5.8's time (0.820, 0.928). That is eight interleaved runs of each build, paired by run. The lanes alone gave 0.917, and R4 with the wider cut-off 0.925. For comparison, the same timing puts 0.5.8's own change at 0.887 of the build before it (the last post's "about a fifth" came from an earlier set of runs). The candidate also made Open 12% faster than Cells on one thread, where 0.5.8's Open was only 3% faster. Indicative runs of the whole decoder on the same shared container, with Open forced on, already showed the gain thinning: 0.914 at 1 worker, 0.924 at 2 and 0.972 at 4, the last within noise.

The rule for the i9 was registered before any data. The test ran production's decoder, unpinned, at 6, 8 and 10 threads, where it runs 6, 8 and 7 Open workers, on four copies of the sample with 16 paired rounds. The candidate would be adopted only if 10 threads, the default, were faster beyond noise, neither 6 nor 8 slower, and peak memory within 10% everywhere. The registration itself expected the whole-decoder gain to be "smaller with more workers sharing memory bandwidth" (the registration).

The results, as the candidate's time over 0.5.8's, with 95% intervals over the 16 rounds:

threads Open workers wall time processor time peak memory step 6 6 0.950 (0.944, 0.955) 0.953 1.019 faster 8 8 1.049 (1.023, 1.075) 1.009 1.036 slower 10 7 1.012 (0.991, 1.033) 0.980 1.010 no change detected

Of eight lanes that ran swift alone and fell behind in company

Ten threads was not faster and eight was slower, so the verdict was not adopted. A diagnostic run with the worker count fixed agreed: 0.946 at 6 workers and 1.044 at 8. Read by worker count, the results make one sequence, 0.950 with 6, 1.012 with 7 and 1.049 with 8, and each worker added took away more of the gain.

What plausibly happened. On one thread, the lanes used capacity the memory system had spare: it can serve many outstanding requests at once, and a single dependent walk asks for one at a time. With eight workers each walking eight lanes, up to 64 lookups compete for the same L3 cache and the same memory bandwidth, alongside every other part of eight decodes. Capacity that was idle for one worker is therefore already in use. The candidate also widened each worker's working set, because its wider cut-off keeps more rows. On the six Wikidata blocks examined most closely, its overflow pages took 184 to 216 KiB per worker, close to the 256 KiB of level-2 cache each core has. Both effects would plausibly push more data out to the shared L3, where every worker meets.

Fast alone, slow in a crowd: one doorway, shared by every worker

Alone: one workerIn a crowd: eight workersworker8 lanesthe shared doorwayL3 cache (20 MiB) and memory bandwidth8 requests waiting: plenty of roomlanes fill capacity that was idle:13% faster on one threadw1w2w3w4w5w6w7w8the same doorwayL3 cache (20 MiB) and memory bandwidthup to 64 requests, plus wider tablesthe capacity was already in use:5% slower at eight threads Conceptual, a plausible account and not a measurement. The doorway stands for the L3 cache and the path to memory that all ten cores share. The analogy stops holding in two places: a cache serves many requests at once up to a limit rather than one at a time, and each core also has its own 256 KiB level-2 cache that no other worker touches. What it shows is the direction of the effect: capacity that one worker can borrow is already spent when eight need it.

This account fits the order of the results, and the registration foresaw its direction, but we have not counted cache misses or memory traffic on the i9 at these worker counts. That measurement would confirm or refute it. One detail it doesn't yet explain is that at 10 threads the candidate used 2% less processor time while its wall time stayed level.
