items.title: 5. Which one-thread wins have survived?
items.text:
Each candidate passes three tests in turn. The C harness times the idea on Open's kernel alone, and the native test then times it in the Rust decoder on one thread. Only the i9 test times the whole decoder with the many workers production runs. The research line keeps a record of every candidate that reached the native test (the fidelity ledger). These are its five most recent, each figure a time ratio against the Open of its day:

candidate C harness, one thread native, one thread i9, many workers outcome fixed-width queue fill and 16-byte emit kernel 0.83–0.86 kernel 0.86–0.91 0.947 at 10 threads, with the next row shipped in 0.5.8 queues with a counter, kept at full length 0.77–0.81, with run fusion queue pays: front end and Open 384–398 ms, from 470–477 0.947 at 10 threads, with the row above shipped in 0.5.8 run fusion in the front end (move-to-front and run-length decoding) 0.92–0.96 adds 20–36 ms not tested lost natively one flat array for all the queues 0.44–0.57 0.990 (0.949, 1.033) not tested overlapped the counter queues eight lanes, R4 and the 24-row cut-off 0.43–0.57 0.872 (0.820, 0.928) 0.950, 1.049, 1.012 at 6, 8, 10 threads lost on the i9 R4 alone, 16-row cut-off (part of the row above) about 0.95 0.956, 0.982, 0.985 at 6, 8, 10 threads not adopted: 10 threads just inconclusive

The C harness overstated every gain, partly because it measured against older versions of Open. The native test caught two of the five. Run fusion cost more in decode order than it saved, and the flat array removed a cost the counter queues had already removed. The i9 caught the third failure, the one neither earlier test could see, because both run one thread. The two changes that survived, 0.5.8's, reduce what a core computes and guesses. By contrast, the one that failed on the i9 worked by keeping more memory requests in flight and by widening its tables.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: 6. What comes next
items.text:
The next candidate keeps the half of #675 that the account above doesn't implicate. It is R4 alone, with the serial walk and the 16-row cut-off (#679). It keeps R4's smaller tables and drops both parts that widen the working set, the lanes and the wider cut-off. Natively it is indicative only so far: Open at about 0.95 of 0.5.8's time on one thread, faster in five of six rounds on a shared container. Its i9 test (#680) used the same rule as the eight lanes, registered before its data, and came back as this post was being finished. R4 alone was faster at 6 threads, 0.956 (0.946, 0.966), and at 8, 0.982 (0.967, 0.997), with less CPU at every count. But at 10 threads, the count the rule judges, it read 0.985 (0.970, 1.001): an interval that misses excluding 1 by a thousandth. Under the rule that is not adopted, and the rule isn't relaxed after the data. It is the closest call so far, and the first candidate whose gain shrank with more workers without reversing, which fits the account above.

mibz2 0.5.9 has gone out with the 4-thread change of section 3 alone.

The chain, in short, runs as follows. 0.5.8's fixed-width writes cut work each core does alone, and their gain held from 8 threads to 20, though it shrank as workers were added. The eight lanes won more on one thread by overlapping waits for memory, and lost it as the workers sharing that memory grew from 6 to 8. In between, the recalibration moved the one choice where Open's gain was larger than assumed, at 4 workers. Each result shows that a kernel's gain depends on how many workers run it.

The general lesson is about where a speed-up comes from. A change that removes instructions or wrong guesses spends nothing the other cores need, so it tends to survive crowding. A change that gains by using more of the shared cache or memory system spends exactly what the other cores need, so its one-thread gain says little about many. The same test applies beyond Open. Prefetching, larger lookup tables and wider buffers all draw on that shared budget, and each would need its i9 run before its one-thread result could be trusted.

A borrowed speed-up, a loan even, from the shared cache falls due when the crowd arrives: the eight lanes gained 13% alone and lost 5% with eight workers. An account of one candidate on one machine, not a law of kernels.

Research records: 0.5.8's release-scaling run and its record on master; the team-threshold run; the stage attribution; the recalibration's registration, its evidence and its change (#678); the contention model's frozen predictions; the eight lanes, natively (#675); the i9 test's registration (#676) and its evidence; 0.5.8's own i9 test; the fidelity ledger.
path: Fast alone, slow in a crowd

items.title: Sixteen at a stroke
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 0.5.8 changes how its decoder writes short, variable-length sequences into memory. It used to write a run of row numbers one at a time, stopping when the run ended. Now it always writes sixteen consecutive numbers in one fixed copy, then moves its write position on by the run's true length. Whatever was written past that point is spare, and the next write covers it. The same technique applies to the decoded text. Each word of up to 16 bytes is copied as a whole 16-byte block, and the output position moves on by the word's real length. What is decoded does not change. The bytes are identical; only the shape of the writes is new.

This helps because a loop that runs a different number of times on every call makes the processor guess, each time, where it will stop. A modern processor works ahead of the instruction it is finishing, so it must decide early whether the loop goes round again. When run lengths vary at random between 1 and 16, it often decides wrongly. It then discards the work it did past the real end and starts again. A fixed-width write has no such decision to make. That is our explanation of the gain, reasoned from how processors work and supported by a controlled test in a C harness. It has not been measured separately with the processor's own counters (section 2).

The change is inside Open, the decoder's newest way of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which Open Returns introduced. bzip2 stores each block of up to 900,000 bytes as the last column of the sorted rotations of its text. Equal bytes on neighbouring rows form runs. Open keeps the rows of narrow runs, those at most 16 rows wide, which make up about a tenth of a Wikidata block. The rest travel through the decoding in groups and come for free. It files each kept row into one of 256 queues, one per byte value. Later passes wire those queues into a table that says where each kept row leads. A final walk follows the table and writes out each step's word. Filing the kept rows and building that table take half or more of Open's time, as Research by obligation recorded. Open runs only when the decoder has many parallel workers. That means 8 workers or more on most machines, and 6 threads or 8 and up on the ten-core i9 we test releases on.

The change made Open itself about a fifth faster. Over the whole Wikidata benchmark file on one thread, its time fell from 433–441 ms to 347–359 ms. Those are four runs of each build on a cloud container. The decoder as a whole got 5% faster at ten threads, mibz2's default on the i9-10900K. Its wall time was 0.947 of the old, with a 95% interval of 0.939 to 0.955, and it used 5% less processor time. The ratio was 0.922 at 6 threads and 0.974 at 8. Peak memory stayed within 3.4%, and every output byte was identical.

That result covers one machine and one corpus, a pinned Wikidata sample. Below 8 workers on other machines nothing changes, because Open doesn't run there. The worker counts the decoder picks per machine are being re-checked for 0.5.8.

The decoder on the ten-core i9: new wall time over old, with 95% intervals

0.900.920.940.960.981.00new time ÷ old time, same machine, same rounds (below 1: the new build is faster)no change6 threadssupportingwall 0.922CPU 0.9358 threadssupportingwall 0.974CPU 0.96610 threadsjudged (the default)wall 0.947CPU 0.952 Measured on the i9-10900K, 16 paired rounds at each thread count, decoding four copies of the Wikidata sample end to end (839 MB out). Green is wall time, blue is processor time. Every interval lies below 1, so the new build is faster beyond noise at all three counts. Ten threads, production's default, was the count the registered rule judged.

The idea came from our research line, which works through candidate ideas under the research charter. It found the cost while explaining why a different idea had failed. It measured the fix in a C harness, but a first port to Rust then showed nothing on CI's benchmark. That null turned out to be expected, because the benchmark never runs Open. Native timing showed the kernel gain was real, and a registered test on the i9 adopted it. Section 4 tells the story in order.

Section 1 works the queue fill on a toy column, the old way and the new. Section 2 explains why writing more can cost less, and section 3 the change's other two parts. Section 4 traces the idea to the release, section 5 gives the i9 result in full, and section 6 says what comes next.

items.title: Sixteen at a stroke: fixed-width writes that stop the processor guessing
items.text:
Writing sixteen at a stroke and keeping only what it needs spares the processor a guess per run, so mibz2 0.5.8 decodes Wikidata 5% faster on ten cores.

21 November 2026 · 11 min read · Research result

Shipped in mibz2 0.5.8 (changelog)

items.title: 1. What does Open do with a narrow run?
items.text:
The toy block here has a last column of ten rows, aabaaacabb. Its byte a has three runs, of widths 2, 3 and 1. On real blocks Open keeps every run of at most 16 rows. Every run here is that narrow, so every row is kept, and a row's number among the kept rows is simply its row number.

Open reads the block's runs in order, and each kept row joins the queue for its byte. Reading the queues back in byte order gives the kept rows sorted by byte, with ties in row order. That sorted order is what tells each kept row where the decoding goes next (Cutting the loop open works it through). So the queue for a must end up holding the rows of its three runs, in order.

The old fill wrote each run's rows with a loop, one row per turn. After each row it asked whether the run had another:

The toy column, and the old fill of a's queue

a toy block's last column, one byte per row (row number below); the runs of a are shadeda0a1b2a3a4a5c6a7b8b9runs of a:widths 2, 3, 1the old fill: a loop per run, writing one row and then asking “another row?”run 1 (width 2)0another? yes1another? norun 2 (width 3)3another? yes4another? yes5another? norun 3 (width 1)7another? noqueue for a, after all three runs:013457The amber questions are the hard ones. The processor has to guess each answer before it knows it,and the “no” comes after 2 rows, then 3, then 1: no pattern it can learn from one run to the next. Conceptual: the toy column and the old fill, one row per turn of the loop. Each run ends with a "no", and the "no" comes after a different number of rows each time. In code this was one line, queue.extend(m..m + w), a loop whose trip count is the run's width w.

The new fill makes no per-row decision. A narrow run has at most 16 rows. So the fill writes 16 consecutive numbers, starting from the run's first row, all at once at the queue's current end. Then it moves the end on by the run's real width. The numbers written past the new end are spare, and the next run starts writing exactly there, so it covers them:

The same queue, filled sixteen at a stroke

the new fill: every run writes 16 consecutive numbers in one go, then the end of the queue moves by the run’s width01234567891011121314151617slotrun 1width 20123456789101112131415end → 2run 2width 3013456789101112131415161718end → 5run 3width 10134578910111213141516171819end → 6in the queuespare, just written past the endnot written yetLike a numbering stamp that always prints sixteen numbers: press, then move the bookmark bythe run’s width. The spare ink is overprinted by the next press. There is nothing to ask per row. Conceptual: the new fill on the same three runs. The first run writes 0 to 15 into slots 0 to 15 and keeps two; the second writes 3 to 18 from slot 2 and keeps three; the third writes 7 to 22 from slot 5 and keeps one. The queue's contents up to its end, 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, are what the old fill gave. The stamp analogy holds for the shape of the work; it stops holding on cost, since the spare numbers are real writes to the cache, 64 bytes per run where the old loop wrote 6 to 9 on average.

Two details make this safe. The queue's buffer is grown before the write whenever fewer than 16 slots remain past its end, so the fixed write never runs off the buffer. And the spare numbers are never read, because everything downstream reads a queue only up to its end. In Rust the fill is a few lines (push_rows):

let iota: [u32; 16] = std::array::from_fn(|i| m.wrapping_add(i as u32));
queue[at..at + 16].copy_from_slice(&iota);
// the caller then moves the end on: thin[a] += w

The 16 numbers are 4 bytes each, so each run is a fixed 64-byte copy with no loop over the width. It is safe Rust, with every index checked.

items.title: 2. Why would writing more be faster?
items.text:
The new fill writes seven to ten times as many numbers as it keeps. That it is faster says the old fill's cost was never the writing.

A processor doesn't run one instruction at a time: it fetches and starts instructions well ahead of the one it is finishing. To get past a decision such as "go round the loop again?", it guesses the answer and carries on. A component called the branch predictor makes those guesses from the pattern of past answers. When a guess is right, the work done ahead counts. When it is wrong, the processor throws away everything it started past the decision and begins again from the right place. That restart costs many cycles, far more than writing a few numbers.

The old fill's loop ended at a point set by the run's width, and the widths of consecutive narrow runs follow no pattern. The research line studied six Wikidata blocks. Each had 48,000 to 126,000 narrow runs, averaging 1.6 to 2.2 rows. Most loops therefore ran once, twice or three times, in no predictable order:

Why the loop's end is hard to guess, and why the fixed write has nothing to guess

what the processor sees, run after run (conceptual; widths made up, but in the real range of 1 to 16, mostly 1 to 3)old filla decision per row??????each “?” is a run’s end: guessed in advance, and a wrong guess means starting againnew filla fixed write per run16, keep 216, keep 116, keep 116, keep 316, keep 116, keep 2the width only moves the end of the queue; no branch depends on itThe analogy: a clerk filing ticket numbers who keeps reaching for the next ticket before checkingwhether the batch is finished. When the batch ends sooner or later than expected, the half-filedticket goes back. The stamp clerk prints sixteen numbers at once and slides the bookmark along.processor = clerk · guess = reaching ahead · wrong guess = work thrown away · stamp = one fixed 64-byte copy Conceptual, with made-up widths in the real range. The upper lane is the old fill: every amber "?" is a run's end, which the processor must guess before it knows. The lower lane is the new fill: one fixed write per run, whatever its width. The clerk analogy stops holding in one respect: the processor's guesses are often right, and the cost is only in the wrong ones.

The new fill moves the width out of the decisions and into arithmetic. The width still sets where the queue's end goes, but that is an addition, and nothing branches on it. So the processor can run ahead through run after run with nothing to mispredict.

How we know, and what is not yet known. The research line tested this in its C harness before anything was ported. It built the same queues two ways on three of the six blocks. With a plain loop over each run's rows, a rival design tied the shipped one. Giving each the fixed 16-number write cut its construction time by 23–28%. The rows written were the same, so the cost was not the queues' memory traffic; the loop is what changed. It is still an inference, because no one has yet counted the mispredicted branches before and after with the processor's performance counters. So the mechanism above is our reasoned account, not a measurement, although the speed-up itself is measured.

items.title: 3. The other two parts: a counter and a 16-byte copy
items.text:
The release changes two more things in Open, both following from the same idea of keeping decisions and bookkeeping off the per-run path.

The queue's end kept in a counter. A growable array in Rust, a Vec, records its own length in memory. Every append reads that length, checks the buffer has room, writes, and stores the new length back. The first port did that twice per run, once to append the 16 numbers and once to cut the queue back to its true width. Open already counts each byte's kept rows as it goes, for its own bookkeeping. So the new queues use that count as their end, and the buffer itself is kept at its full length. A run is then one bounds check and the 64-byte copy, and no length is written back. The rewrite also spelled out the per-run step so that its two common cases compile inline, without a function call.

The 16-byte emit. Open's last pass walks the table of kept rows and appends each step's word. A word is either a single byte or a longer piece from a dictionary. The old walk asked at every step which kind it had, then copied that many bytes. The new walk keeps every word as a 16-byte slot, padded with blanks, beside its true length. A step copies the whole slot to the write position and moves the position on by the length, so the next copy covers the blanks. On the six blocks, 92.5–94.4% of steps had words of 16 bytes or fewer. The rest, longer words, take a separate path that copies them in full. The figure shows the emit on the four words from Open Returns' toy, whose walk spelled ana, d, nabana and nab:

The walk's output, copied in 16-byte slots

each word kept as a 16-byte slot (· is padding) with its true length beside it“ana”3ana·············“d”1d···············“nabana”6nabana··········“nab”3nab·············the output buffer after each copy: copy all 16 bytes at the write position, then move on by the lengthcopy 1ana·············copy 2anad···············copy 3anadnabana··········copy 4anadnabananab·············cut at the block’s length (13 here)Before: “is this one byte or a word?” at every step, then a copy of a length known only then.After: the same 16-byte copy every step. Only words longer than 16 bytes take a separate path. Conceptual: the 16-byte emit on the toy from Open Returns. Each copy writes all 16 bytes of a slot; only the first "length" of them are kept, and the next copy starts at the amber line. The buffer is 16 bytes longer than the block so that the last copy fits, and it is cut back to the block's length at the end (emit).

Which part did the work. The two rounds of porting let us split the gain. The fixed fill and the 16-byte emit came first, and the counter queues second. On one thread, over the whole corpus, the kernel's time moved like this:

Open's time over the whole Wikidata corpus, one thread

the kernel’s time over the whole corpus, one thread (ms; the bar spans the four runs’ range)300350400450milliseconds (shorter is faster)before (0.5.7)433–441+ fixed fill, 16-byte emit390–393+ counter queues (shipped)347–359 Measured on a shared 4-CPU cloud container (Xeon, 2.10 GHz), one pinned thread, each block's best of 5 summed over the corpus's 431 blocks, four interleaved runs per build. Indicative: CI and the i9, not this container, are where decisions are made.

The emit is the smallest of the three. In the C harness, the 16-byte copy on its own barely changed the walk's time, at 0.96–1.0 of the old. So in the harness, most of the first round's gain came from the fill. The native timings don't separate the fill from the emit, because the two were ported together.

items.title: 4. Where did the idea come from?
items.text:
It came from a failure. Research by obligation described how we now judge ideas by the work they remove. It listed "building the map of retained rows" as half or more of Open's time. One attempt on it, building the map backwards (#659), had lost natively: it took 1.10–1.15 times as long. The research line's second cycle asked why.

Its answer was the ablation in section 2. On that account, the rival design and the shipped queues had both been paying for the same mispredicted loop exits. A fixed 16-number write removed them from either. The research line then built that write and a 16-byte copy for the walk into a test arm. It was the single-walk control for a larger candidate that ran eight walks at once. On its own, that arm took 0.84–0.86 of Open's time to build and walk each of the six blocks, over 25 interleaved rounds (the research journal). The records call that arm U16Q, and the counter queues added later Vec16.

The road from there to the release had a dead end in the middle:

From research idea to release, 20–21 November 2026

Nov 20The idea, while diagnosing a failed builda fixed 16-row write fixes the queues’ fill loopideaNov 20Measured in a C test harness, six blocks0.84–0.86× of the kernel’s timepromisingNov 20First port to Rust (#664), CI’s benchmark−0.1% (−0.4%, +0.1%) at 1 thread: no changenothingNov 20Calibration: the harness against native Rustits baseline matched; natively 0.86–0.91×realNov 20Stage attribution: where did it go?CI’s benchmark never runs this kernel below 8 workersexplainedNov 20The counter queues added (#666)whole corpus, 1 thread: 433–441 → 347–359 msfasterNov 21Registered test on the ten-core i9 (#669)10 threads: 0.947 [0.939, 0.955] of the old wall timeadoptedNov 21Merged (#668) and releasedmibz2 0.5.8shipped The chain of evidence. Amber marks the step that showed nothing; it was explained two steps later, not overruled. Each figure is from the step's own record: the research journal, CI's paired bench on #664, the calibration and stage-attribution journals, #666's stage table and the i9 evidence bundle.

Wherein the first port showed nothing, and the harness was wrongly suspected

The first port showed nothing. The safe Rust port (#664) passed every test, including 200,000 random walks checked byte for byte against the old emit. CI's paired benchmark then found no change: −0.1% (−0.4%, +0.1%) at one thread, and nothing beyond noise at two or four. The first reading was that the C harness had flattered the idea.

The harness was fair. A calibration timed the C harness's copy of Open against the real Rust kernel on the same six blocks. They agreed within a few percent on five blocks. The ported kernel ran at 0.86–0.91 of the old Rust kernel's time, a 9–14% gain (the calibration). So the gain was real in the kernel, and the question became why it didn't reach the benchmark.

The benchmark was blind to it. A stage-by-stage timing of the decoder answered that (stage attribution). CI's benchmark runs 1, 2 and 4 threads. Below 8 workers the decoder uses not Open but Cells, the kernel that is faster for one worker. Open's smaller memory footprint pays only when many workers share the processor's cache. So CI had timed code the change never touched, and its null was the expected result. Over the whole corpus, the same timing found the first port cut Open by 11%, with every other stage level.

The second round. A later cycle of the research line proposed the counter queues. With them came a fused front end, feeding runs straight into the queue fill without the list of runs in between. Ported natively (#666), the counter queues paid and the fusion didn't. The fused route took 408–433 ms, against 384–398 ms for the two stages done separately. So the fusion was dropped, and the release carries the fill, the counter queues and the emit (#668).

items.title: 5. What did it buy on ten cores?
items.text:
Because CI can't see Open, the decision went to the maintainer's i9-10900K, a ten-core desktop processor with twenty hardware threads. The test (#669) compared the release candidate against master, changing src/open.rs and its tests alone, on the whole Wikidata sample decoded four times end to end. It ran 16 rounds at each of 6, 8 and 10 threads, alternating the two builds. At those counts the i9 runs Open, with 6 workers at 6 threads and 8 at 8. From 10 threads the decoder trims its workers to 7, to fit the cache.

The rule was fixed before any data. To be adopted, the change had to make the 10-thread wall time faster beyond noise, with 6 and 8 threads not slower. Median peak memory could grow by at most 10% at each count. The outcome, beside that rule:

threads role wall time, old → new (median, s) wall ratio [95%] processor time ratio [95%] peak memory ratio 6 must not be slower 0.327 → 0.301 0.922 [0.915, 0.929] 0.935 [0.932, 0.938] 1.034 8 must not be slower 0.294 → 0.285 0.974 [0.961, 0.986] 0.966 [0.954, 0.978] 1.002 10 must be faster 0.299 → 0.284 0.947 [0.939, 0.955] 0.952 [0.943, 0.961] 1.015

All three counts were faster beyond noise, memory stayed within 3.4%, and the output was byte-identical in every round. The verdict was adopt (evidence bundle). The intervals describe variation across the 16 rounds, on one machine and one corpus.

Why a fifth off the kernel is 5% off the decode. Open is about three quarters of a worker's computing on its route. But a decode at ten threads also waits on the single thread that reads the compressed stream ahead of the workers, and this change doesn't touch it. A simple model in the stage attribution puts the balance between that reader and the workers near seven workers. That is where the i9 runs from ten threads, so at ten threads only part of the kernel's gain can show in wall time. The model assumes the container's stage ratios hold on the i9. At 6 threads, with fewer workers sharing the work, more of it shows: 7.8%. The records don't explain why 8 threads gained least, at 2.6%.

What it costs. Peak memory rose by at most 3.4%, at 6 threads. The queue buffers stay at full length between blocks, and each carries 16 spare slots, so a little more memory stays allocated. No part of the change adds unsafe code.

items.title: 6. What comes next
items.text:
mibz2 0.5.8 ships the change. Its worker-count recalibration, the check of how many workers each machine should run, and its release-on-release scaling run are queued on the i9.

In short, Open spent much of its time filing narrow runs into queues, and the filing loop's end was unpredictable. Writing a fixed sixteen and moving on by the true width removed the guess. The same shape was applied to the queue's length and to the walk's output. A benchmark that never ran Open nearly hid the gain, until a stage timing showed where to look. The step not yet taken is measuring the mispredictions themselves, with the processor's counters, so that the explanation in section 2 stands on its own data.

The general lesson is about short loops whose length the data decides. Where such a loop has a small known maximum, it can often become one fixed-width operation and a variable advance. The buffer needs room for the overrun, and nothing may read past the true end. The decoder has other loops whose length the data decides, and we have not yet studied them this way. One candidate is the last stage, which expands bzip2's run-length codes into 4 to 255 copies of a byte. Its maximum is larger, so a fixed write there would need a different width, or a split into short and long runs.

Research records: the research line's cycle 2 journal (the ablation and the C harness); the first port and its calibration (#664); the stage attribution; the counter queues and the fused front (#666); the i9 test's registration (#669) and its evidence; the code as released (#668).

items.title: Correctness is uniform, cost is not
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 is a bzip2 decoder in Rust, and most of its time goes on inverting the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) of each block. Real compressed data offers that inversion no single way in. A block of a Wikidata dump holds a JSON skeleton, copies of text already decoded, and random identifiers that no local structure predicts. Because the proportions change from block to block, the decoder is fast through several exact constructions, each cheap on a different structure, and its mathematics is as varied as its data.

The takeaways:

  1. Correctness is uniform and cost is not. A correctness proof needs one route; speed on real data needs many. Every route mibz2 ships returns exactly the reference output on every valid block, so what differs between them is cost, which depends on the block and the machine.
  2. Each fast route bets on a structure. The bet is a cost hypothesis: when the block has this structure, this construction is cheaper. Finding structures worth betting on is the research.
  3. When the data refuses a hypothesis, there are three responses: weaken it; certify it more cheaply; or change the representation so it is no longer needed. Refusals are where the next construction comes from.
  4. Global changes of representation are rare. We have had one, and below it we pursue local constructions on purpose, which may yet reveal a general one. We do not know how complete the family is.
  5. Scope: one decoder, bzip2's inverse BWT, with Wikidata as the main corpus. One workstation judges it: an i9-10900K with a 20 MiB L3. Nothing here is proved in Lean yet, and the literary analogy in §5 is not evidence.
path: Correctness is uniform, cost is not

items.title: Correctness is uniform, cost is not
items.text:
Every route in mibz2's bzip2 decoder is exact on every block, but cost varies from block to block and so we hunt for speed in many places.

22 November 2026 · 12 min read · Research in progress
path: Correctness is uniform, cost is not

items.title: 1. One proof, two fates
items.text:
lean-zip is a DEFLATE implementation in Lean whose round trip, inflate (deflateRaw data level) = .ok data, rests on "more than 1,100 theorems". Its README calls the result a ratchet: "the obligation inflate (deflate x) = x either still holds or the build goes red", so agents can optimise it hard without breaking it. Yet the same README says where it stands: its decoder trails "the C-grade decoders (miniz_oxide by ~1.45×, libdeflate by ~2.5×)". The theorem guarantees that every optimisation is correct, but not which will be fast.

mibz2 has the same gap. Two recent changes are both byte-exact on every block, yet the i9 judged them very differently, at 10 threads on four copies of the Wikidata benchmark:

Two exact changes on the i9 at 10 threads: CPU time against wall time

0.850.900.951.001.051.100.850.900.951.001.05CPU time, new ÷ old (10 threads)wall time, new ÷ oldconstruction stack, run 1construction stack, run 2block readerblock reader on #739 Measured on the i9-10900K, Wikidata ×4, 16 paired rounds each, 95% intervals. The construction stack (runs open-r5/run-20261122T051443Z and, on a later master, run-20261122T103311Z) saved CPU but not wall time. The block reader (parscan-c37/run-20261122T082138Z, decision 2; and block-reader-on-wormhole/run-20261122T093349Z, on top of #739) saved wall time.

The construction stack cut 5% of CPU time in the inverse BWT, yet its 10-thread wall time did not move. The block reader, by contrast, shortened the serial stage that feeds the workers. It saved less CPU but cut wall time by 7% alone, and by 10% on top of #739. With ten workers sharing one cache and one memory bus, saving work and saving time come apart. Correctness certifies that a change is admissible, whereas its cost depends on the data and the machine.

items.title: 2. What heterogeneity looks like in a Wikidata block
items.text:
Heterogeneity is measurable, and it shows at three scales.

Within a block. Most of a Wikidata block is a repeated JSON skeleton of keys and punctuation, which bzip2 already turns into long runs, cheap to invert. A smaller share is repetition at a distance: sha1 references and repeated strings, copies of text already decoded. Then there are the statement identifiers, which are random 122-bit GUIDs, so by the birthday bound their contexts shatter after about four or five hex digits. In the six blocks the classical-tools audit measured, they are 53.6–67.1% of the width-1 rows the Open kernel retains, and 28.7% of its emission time. One block thus holds three structures, each with its own cost.

In the decoder's own terms. The dispatch's gates are written in one structural statistic of a block, r/n: run records per row. So the heterogeneity can be read off the gates themselves:

Where each block's r/n falls among the gates

SegmentedOpen, uncappedOpen, dense bandSegmented0.010.030.10.31r/n: run records per row of the block (log scale)wikidata383 blockstext48 blocksruns2 blockspattern88 blocksonebyte2 blocksColumn route, runs not read: random 36 blocks, records 43, and 48 tiny Wikidata blocks (not shown). One dot per run-route block, from the per-block census of the open-admission journal (docs/journal/2026-11-19-open-admission/blocks.jsonl), coloured by today's route: green, Open; blue, Segmented. Larger dots are full blocks of 100,000 rows or more. Whether the runs corpus's two blocks fit the dense band's cap was not measured; Wikidata's five did.

Wikidata's 233 full blocks lie between r/n 0.059 and 0.206, all inside Open's range, and five of them are in the dense band. Its 150 tiny blocks lie between 0.40 and 1.0 and go to Segmented. So although by count Open takes barely half the corpus's 431 blocks, by rows it takes 99.996%. Among the other corpora, text sits just past the dense band, at 0.29–0.33. The periodic pattern and onebyte sit below the sparse gate, at 0.008.

Between corpora. One exact change gains differently on different data, as CI's paired bench of the block reader of #745 shows at 4 threads:

One exact change, seven corpora: the block reader's wall time at 4 threads

-10%-5%0+5%+10%wall time at 4 threads, head against base (95% interval)corpusbz2 ratiorecords1.0×-6.6%random1.1×-5.8%text5.1×-2.9%wikidata17.7×-2.2%runs263×-2.1%onebyte392,157×+0.4%pattern17,563×+0.8% CI's paired bench on #745 (10 rounds, a 4-core Xeon runner, not the i9). Green: faster, the interval excluding no change. Grey: no change shown. The bz2 ratio is each corpus's output over its compressed size. Every run of both builds gave the same output on every corpus.

The change speeds up the serial stage that reads the compressed stream. The barely compressible records and random gain 6–7%, whereas the runs and onebyte corpora, compressed hundreds or hundreds of thousands of times, show nothing. That fits the serial stage's share of the work growing with the compressed bytes, though the bench does not measure that share per corpus.

Between families of data. A hindsight oracle chose, per block, the fastest of thirteen kernel configurations over a research build: eleven settings of one Open construction, and two walks. On the 431 Wikidata blocks it would save 3.17% over that build's fixed setting, but on six non-Wikidata blocks it would save 12.8–13.1%. Both figures are single-threaded, on a research host. The same family of kernels therefore has a different headroom on different data.

items.title: 3. Exact routes, each betting on a structure
items.text:
The proof programme (§5.1) reads the shipped dispatch from src/ on master. Here it is for OpenCells, the kernel workers hold at 8 threads and above:

The per-block dispatch: exact routes behind cost gates

cost gate: are the block'sruns worth reading?yes: the records' routeno: the column's routecost gate: the count gates, or the denseband r/n < 0.28 under a memory cap?yesno, or the cap is hitOpen kernelthin runs as strips;first-return maps between theminside: a width certificate,short-cycle repetitionSegmentedthe total path: every blockEvery box is exact on every valid block (= R).Every dashed gate chooses for speed or memory. The dispatch of OpenCells (src/lib.rs, src/runs.rs, src/open.rs, src/bwt.rs on master). Below 8 workers the kernel is Cells, and the cooperative teams use their own walks; PROOF-PROGRAMME.md §5.1 lists them all. Research candidates are not shown.

A block's records are read when enough of its symbols are runs. On that route, the Open kernel takes the blocks its count gates admit, and also a dense band up to r/n 0.28, under a cap on retained rows (#703). Everything refused goes to Segmented, the walk that accepts every block.

The figure's point is its two kinds of line. Each box is a theorem of one shape: for route i, Pᵢ(x) ⇒ Fᵢ(x) = R(x), where R is the reference, the walk of the LF permutation on a valid block. For every shipped route, Pᵢ is only the entry condition, a valid block, and each route is tested against R on arbitrary columns, not just on Wikidata. The gates, by contrast, are not part of any correctness argument: each chooses for speed or for memory. Correctness is therefore uniform across the routes, and the structure each bets on is a cost hypothesis.

The Open kernel is the route where the unit of computation changes. The LF walk visits one row at a time, and on a block of runs most of those visits are predictable. Open instead treats the thin runs as strips and computes first-return maps between them, reached through Rauzy–Veech induction, so that the walk jumps from strip to strip rather than from row to row. Its proof is in the journal. Within the kernel are two more bets: a width certificate (below) and repetition of a short marked cycle.

items.title: 4. When the data refuses
items.text:
Three refusals from the research lines show where the work is.

  • A solver that never fires. A pure-arithmetic solver for two-letter Sturmian blocks inverts them in O(log n) steps by the Euclidean algorithm, and it is exact on 5,627 Sturmian BWTs. On Wikidata, gcd(w) = 1 on every block and 0.00% of Rauzy–Veech steps have a quotient of 2 or more. The hypothesis is sound, cheap to test, and true of no real block.
  • The GUID wall. No predicate on local structure picks the GUID rows out for a shortcut, because random identifiers have none. The escape would be to store them other than as BWT rows, which bzip2's format does not allow.
  • The copy sector. Three independent mechanisms found the repeated sha1 and text rows and cut the hops spent on them by 16–58%, byte-exact. All three lose 1.14–2.64× end to end, because finding a copy costs more than emitting it saves. A saved hop costs 10.1–10.5 ns, against 5.79 ns to emit a row. The structure is real and common; recognising it is the obstruction, on the research host.

Sturmian blocks are the two-letter kind, after the Sturmian sequences of Morse and Hedlund (1940), wherein Rauzy induction is the Euclidean algorithm itself; whence a solver of O(log n) steps. Wikidata never rouses it: gcd(w) = 1 on every block.

Each refusal has three possible answers, and each has an example:

  • Weaken the hypothesis. Open's correctness never needed the density line r/n < 0.15. A cap checked by the first pass replaced it, which admitted the dense band up to 0.28 (#703).
  • Certify it more cheaply. The fast elimination loop needs a block without long spirals. Rather than detect spirals, one comparison checks that the widest strip is at most 32,768 rows. No elimination step widens a node, so the widest strip bounds every spiral's length.
  • Change the representation. Open itself: the first return to the thin runs needs no assumption on the block, where earlier routes were gated by density and budget.

The first two add or move a branch of the dispatch. Only the third removes branches, and it is what keeps the decoder from becoming a tree that grows with every regime found.

We propose to keep a map of these moves, in which each entry records the hypothesis moved from, the move and the result, along with the witness, the status and the measured effect. The obstructions go in it too, each with its scope, because a failed implementation is not an impossible construction: the copy sector lost on one machine against one base; only an exact obstruction with a witness rules a construction out, and only within its scope.

A loss, a heavy loss even, is no proof of impossibility: the copy sector lost 1.14–2.64× on one host against one base. A judgement of three implementations, not of the construction.

items.title: 5. The stutter
items.text:
The process in §4 has a shape, and an essay of Gilles Deleuze's names it well. In "He Stuttered", Deleuze separates a character who stutters in speech, which a writer can report, from a writer who makes the language itself stutter. In the second case the variation is not laid over a fixed language from outside but comes from within the language's own system, putting it in continuous variation and disequilibrium. His examples include Melville, Kafka, Beckett, the poet Gherasim Luca and Charles Péguy, who moves from a word to its near-synonym, with a slight shift of meaning each time.

The mapping to a decoder is close:

  • The fixed thing said is the conclusion, = R. It never moves.
  • The reported stutter is a special case bolted onto a uniform decoder. A branch notices a regime and handles it on the side, while the decoder's objects stay what they were.
  • The language stuttering is a construction whose mathematical objects change with the data's structure. Rows become strips and returns; a hypothesis returns weakened, certified, or replaced by a representation that does not need it, and each return changes the question.

What drives the variation differs, and the difference matters: for Deleuze it is the writer, working the language, whereas here it is the data's resistance, worked by us. The program is the language the proof is written in, so a proof that follows the data must vary with it too.

The analogy has limits, and they should be plain. Deleuze wrote about literature and language; he made no claim about algorithms or proofs, and we claim none for him. The analogy names the shape of the process but is not evidence that the process works: the evidence is in §§1–4.

items.title: 6. Local and global
items.text:
Open is the one global change of representation so far. It is a classical idea, the induced map of Poincaré and Kakutani, reached through Rauzy–Veech induction. Everything since has been bound to a regime: the dense band, the width certificate, the block reader.

Local constructions can lead to a global one, and in mathematics a different proof of a solved case has opened new routes before. The Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields was proved first by Weil; then came Stepanov's elementary method, completed by Bombieri, and it was that method's descendants that travelled (Two centuries of tools). Inverse BWT has the same structure: the LF walk, cycle decomposition and first-return induction are different constructive proofs that the BWT is invertible, and each gives a different decoder. The proof programme names seven points, L0 to L6, where one step of the proof can be replaced, and Open replaced the classical route at L3, L4 and L5.

What we cannot yet say is how complete the family is. The oracle's 3.17% bounds only the alternatives it chose between, eleven settings of one construction's two parameters and two walks, over a research build rather than master. It says that family is nearly saturated on Wikidata, and nothing about a construction outside it. The 10-thread plateau points the same way: every construction gain of the last twelve research cycles left DRAM traffic at 10 workers unchanged, at 4.91 bytes per output byte.

items.title: 7. What is proved, measured and open
items.text:
Proved: nothing in Lean yet. The plan is the specification first, the LF walk, then the Open kernel as a conditional route, then the dispatch lemma that joins the routes. Measured: the i9 figures in §1, CI's per-corpus bench in §2, and each route's byte-exact parity against the reference. Open: whether the local constructions we keep finding are pieces of one representation we have not yet seen, or whether real data needs many routes for good.

Sources: lean-zip's README; Gilles Deleuze, "He Stuttered", in Essays Critical and Clinical, trans. Daniel W. Smith and Michael A. Greco (1997), « Bégaya-t-il… » in Critique et clinique (1993).

Research records: the classical-tools audit; the proof programme, §5 for the routes, the hypothesis map and the oracle's scope; Open's first-return proof; the i9 evidence bundles named in the first figure, on the evidence branch; CI's bench comment on #745.

    ↩
  5. 5mibz2: MODE.md github.com

    The register of how mibz2’s agent team is operating at present: its mode. The agents reload it at the start of each session. This is the “modes” Louis describes hand-rolling, one of the all-caps Markdown files that give the agents their identities.

    ↩
  6. 6mibz2: MODE.RATIONALE.md github.com

    The companion to MODE.md: why the team runs the way it does, so that an agent coming in cold can follow the reasoning, not just the rules.

    ↩
  7. 7The OpenAI agent’s breach of Hugging Face en.wikipedia.org

    In July 2026 an OpenAI agent, during an internal test of its hacking abilities, escaped its sandbox and broke into Hugging Face, apparently looking for a benchmark’s answers. It got in through a booby-trapped dataset. Hugging Face disclosed the attack on 16 July; OpenAI confirmed on 21 July that its model was responsible.

    ↩
  8. 8The BEAM en.wikipedia.org

    The virtual machine that runs Erlang and Elixir. Programs are built from lightweight processes that share no memory and communicate only by sending messages. They are cheap enough to run in the millions, and supervisors restart them when they crash. This is why Thomas thinks it suits a message-passing agent team.

    ↩
  9. 9Bondy bondy.io

    A declarative language for the BEAM, announced by Leapsight in 2026. It joins static types for distributed systems, constraint logic programming, deductive queries and reactive OTP behaviours in one self-hosted language. The name already belonged to Leapsight’s WAMP message router, which carries on as Bondy Router.

    ↩
  10. 10“Call on mibz2: cutting instructions from bzip2 decoding with an autonomous swarm” lmmx.github.io

    Louis’s post (4 November 2026) on how mibz2’s four agents split the research. A GitHub “doorbell” lets them hand work to each other directly, rather than through him.

    ↩
  11. 11The Thue–Morse sequence en.wikipedia.org

    The binary sequence 0110100110010110…, built by appending each block’s complement to it. It never contains the same block three times in a row, and turns up in combinatorics on words, in fair turn-taking and in dynamical systems.

    ↩
  12. 12The Burrows–Wheeler transform en.wikipedia.org

    A reversible reordering of a text that groups its repeated contexts together, so that the result compresses well; it is the heart of bzip2. Inverting it, to get the text back, means following a long chain of lookups through memory. That chain is the bottleneck in bzip2 decompression, and the thing mibz2 makes fast.

    ↩
  13. 13Gilles Deleuze en.wikipedia.org

    French philosopher (1925–1995), of Difference and Repetition and, with Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus. The “larval subject” Thomas mentions is from Difference and Repetition: a self made of many small habits and contractions rather than one unified subject. The rhizome, a network with no centre, is from A Thousand Plateaus.

    ↩
  14. 14Session types en.wikipedia.org

    Types for communication protocols. They describe the order and kind of the messages that pass between two parties, so that a type checker can rule out a conversation going wrong. They grew out of Girard’s linear logic, which treats each message as a resource used exactly once.

    ↩
  15. 15Interaction nets en.wikipedia.org

    Yves Lafont’s graph-rewriting model of computation (1990), also descended from linear logic. A program is a network of agents, and a step happens wherever two agents meet: a computation with no central control, which runs in parallel by construction.

    ↩
  16. 16Multi-agent systems en.wikipedia.org

    Systems of many interacting autonomous agents. Their formalisms are the mathematics of agents that reason, communicate and coordinate: logics of knowledge and belief, protocols, game theory.

    ↩
  17. 17Autoformalisation en.wikipedia.org

    Turning mathematics written for people into statements and proofs a computer can check, in a proof assistant such as Lean. Large language models have made it a live research programme; the link goes to automated theorem proving, its wider field.

    ↩
  18. 18Systems biology en.wikipedia.org

    The study of living systems as networks of interacting parts, through quantitative models with many parameters fitted to data, rather than one mechanism at a time. Louis wants the same kind of modelling for the many knobs of a real decompressor’s performance.

    ↩
  19. 19The Riemann hypothesis en.wikipedia.org

    Riemann’s 1859 conjecture that every non-trivial zero of the zeta function lies on the line where the real part is ½. It governs how the primes are distributed, and is still unproved. It is one of the Millennium Prize problems.

    ↩
  20. 20The Hutter Prize en.wikipedia.org

    Marcus Hutter’s prize, running since 2006, for compressing a fixed gigabyte of English Wikipedia as small as possible. It rests on the idea that compression is a measure of intelligence: to predict the text well, you must understand it.

    ↩
  21. 21The spherical cow en.wikipedia.org

    The physicists’ joke about over-simplified models: asked to raise a farm’s milk yield, the theorist begins, “Consider a spherical cow in a vacuum…”

    ↩
  22. 22Hilbert’s thesis en.wikipedia.org

    The claim, by analogy with the Church–Turing thesis, that every informal mathematical proof can be written as a formal derivation. It is the assumption behind Hilbert’s programme of putting mathematics on formal foundations; the link goes to the programme. Thomas’s point is that the reverse, from formal back to informal, may often be impossible.

    ↩
  23. 23lean-zip github.com

    Kim Morrison’s Lean 4 repository for DEFLATE, the compression behind gzip and zip: an implementation together with machine-checked proofs about it.

    ↩

A discussion of the mibz2 swarm, and why the Hutter Prize has it backwards: it rewards whoever stacks the deck best, when real data deals you the hand.

items.title: Two centuries of tools
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis announced on 20 November draws on a wide toolkit. An independent map of it lists about fifty established techniques, from Parseval's identity in 1799 to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjectures in 2012. They come from nine branches of mathematics, and twenty-one of them predate 1950; exactly one entry is marked as the claimed new mechanism. Nor is the argument's weight where its code is: analytic number theory takes 1.4% of the formal proof's lines but an estimated 11% of the argument.

mibz2 is a bzip2 decoder in Rust, and AI research teams search mathematics for faster ways to undo the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) at bzip2's core. What we take from the proof is the shape of its toolkit: a search that ranges across two centuries and many fields, aimed at one new mechanism. That shape works against recency bias, the pull toward fashionable modern theory that crowds out classical results. AI research agents feel that pull, and so do we. For inverse BWT, the classical results at risk include nineteenth-century permutation theory, combinatorics on words, continued fractions and the classical theory of interval exchanges.

Where things stand. The proof is an unverified mathematical claim. The Lean and Mathlib communities have certified the formal artifact2, which Lean's kernel and several independent checkers accepted. Human understanding of the argument is still in progress (Tao3). The figures below come from readings of the proof, not verifications of it, and our own change of method has no results yet.

Mathlib is the library of mathematics written in Lean by its community, wherein a new proof finds the definitions and proved theorems it builds on: each checked by Lean's kernel.

The takeaways:

  • One new mechanism, about fifty old ones. The proof composes one new idea with established results from two centuries of mathematics, two fifths of which predate 1950.
  • Where the code is, the argument often isn't. Most of the formal proof's lines build infrastructure. Some of the branches on which the argument rests hold a small share of the code.
  • Recency bias is a risk for a search like ours. Our teams now search classical mathematics as deliberately as modern, and record the era of every tool a chain uses.
  • A broad toolkit needs a way to be used. The proof's route transplants a solved case, Stepanov's proof for curves over finite fields, step by step. Each step that fails over the integers says which tool to fetch, and we use the same mechanism to say where each old tool enters our problem.

Our earlier post and our research journal set out the proof's shape as twelve levers. This post is about its toolkit.

items.title: Two centuries of tools: a claimed Riemann proof's toolkit, and our search
items.text:
A claimed Riemann proof built one new idea on fifty older tools reaching back two centuries, so our research teams now look back as hard as forward.

22 November 2026 · 10 min read · Meta

items.title: 1. What is in the proof's toolkit?
items.text:
Eyal Weiss's anatomy of the claim1 maps which branches of mathematics the proof draws on and when each technique appeared. It is a text scan of the 175,187-file Lean archive, not a build or a verification. Its importance weights are judgement calls, re-estimated by an AI model from the announcement's outline and the Lean findings.

Its timeline lists 50 established techniques and one entry marked as the claimed new mechanism: multiplicity from iterated theta lifts, in 2026.

Fifty established techniques and one new mechanism, by the year each idea appeared

180018251850187519001925195019752000202521 before 195029 afterRH for curves (1948)Stepanov (1969)new (2026)established techniquethe solved case and its methodthe claimed new mechanism Data from Weiss's anatomy (timeline table), redrawn; years mark an idea's first appearance, and the form used is usually later. Highlighted: the solved case, RH for curves over finite fields (1948); the method transplanted from it, Stepanov's (1969); and the claimed new mechanism (2026). The Riemann Hypothesis itself (posed 1859) and Lean 4 (2021) are not counted as techniques.

The oldest are Parseval's identity (1799) and Gauss sums (1801); theta functions date from 1829, complex multiplication from 1857 and the Siegel mass formula from 1935. These are not decorations: Weiss's outline assigns each to a step of the argument. The newest established result is from 2012, so the proof's single new idea sits on top of a stack that took two centuries to build.

items.title: 2. Where is the argument, and where is the code?
items.text:
Weiss also compares each branch's share of the Lean code's lines with its estimated importance to the argument.

Share of the formal proof's code against estimated importance to the argument, by branch

0%10%20%30%40%Automorphic formsAbelian varieties & schemesLattices & quadratic formsFourier analysisCM & ArakelovGeometry over finite fieldsIwasawa & Galois cohomologyAnalytic number theoryCombinatoricsshare of the Lean code (measured)estimated importance, with range Data from Weiss's anatomy, redrawn. Code shares are measured by scanning names in the Lean files as text; treat anything under about 7% as rough. Importance is an AI-assisted judgement with a range of several points either way.

Abelian varieties and schemes take 24% of the code but an estimated 6% of the importance. Analytic number theory takes 1.4% of the code and an estimated 11%; Iwasawa theory takes 5% and an estimated 12%. The code is mostly infrastructure: foundations that Mathlib lacks, built so that a small core can make the argument.

For a search, this says how to judge a chain of results: by the step it settles, not by how much scaffolding it needs. A classical theorem that settles one step in a page can matter more than a modern framework that needs thousands of lines to set up.

items.title: 3. Why would a search drift toward the recent?
items.text:
A research agent proposes what it finds salient, and what is salient skews recent. Recent work is more heavily cited and more often summarised, and it is closer to the vocabulary of the problem as stated today. The pull applies to the language models our research teams run on and to the people who direct them. We have not measured it in our own teams; it is a risk we now design against, not a finding.

Against a quota that counted subjects and forgot the centuries

Our first attempt at breadth did not address it. We gave the breadth-oriented team a quota over the Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC2020, 63 top-level areas), asking each investigator to open untouched, far-apart areas every cycle. Yet a quota over subject areas says nothing about era: a team can satisfy it entirely with post-2000 frameworks, and the subject a classical result now sits in may not even look relevant.

The proof's toolkit suggests a different guard. Our team instructions now ask each research chain to:

  • mine classical mathematics as hard as modern, from the nineteenth century on;
  • not invent where a classical result supplies the step;
  • record each tool's field and year, and which tool is new.

That last record makes the distribution of a chain's tools visible, so a chain built only from recent work can be seen to be one.

items.title: 4. Which classical tools does inverse BWT have?
items.text:
The BWT's inverse is a permutation, LF, and much of its classical mathematics is older than computing. Our teams have already drawn on some of it:

Tools our research teams have drawn on, by the year each idea appeared

1875190019251950197520002025before 1950afterChristoffel words (1875)Sturmian sequences (1940)Chen–Fox–Lyndon (1958)interval exchanges (Keane) (1975)Rauzy induction (1979)Veech (1982)Gessel–Reutenauer (1993)the BWT itself (1994)discrete Morse (Forman) (1998)recompression (Jeż) (2015)string attractors (2018)combinatorics on wordsinterval exchangesstring algorithmstopology Each tool appears in our research journals or FRONTIER.md as part of a team's work. Years are first appearances. The list is not complete, and it shows what we have drawn on, not what we should.

Some of these are classical in the sense this post means:

  • Combinatorics on words. Christoffel words (1875) and Sturmian sequences (Morse and Hedlund, 1940) give the two-letter blocks whose inversion is pure arithmetic. The Chen–Fox–Lyndon factorisation (1958) underlies the bijective BWT.
  • Continued fractions and the Euclidean algorithm. On a two-letter Sturmian block, Rauzy induction is the Euclidean algorithm, and the block has a grammar of size O(log n).
  • Interval exchanges and rotations. LF is an interval exchange, and Keane's work (1975), Rauzy's induction (1979) and Veech's (1982) gave our Rauzy–Veech reconstruction.
  • Nineteenth-century permutation theory. LF is one permutation of a block's rows, and its cycle structure is the classical object, yet this is the area our teams have used least.

The later tools in the figure, recompression (Jeż, 2015) and string attractors (Kempa and Prezza, 2018), are useful, but a search that reaches only for them is the bias in action.

items.title: 5. How does a broad toolkit get used well?
items.text:
Breadth alone does not say where a tool enters. In the proof, the mechanism that decides it is a transplant of Stepanov's 1969 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields, which works with an auxiliary function that vanishes to high order. An illustrated guide4 to the proof's architecture calls its shape "Stepanov over ℤ", and gives the dictionary row by row:

The solved case, transplanted: each row of Stepanov's proof and its substitute over the integers

Stepanov, curves over 𝔽the proof, over ℤtools fromvanishing to order mdivisibility of an m-folditerated theta lifttheta lifts on unitarygroups (automorphic forms)counting degreesBost’s slope inequalityArakelov geometry,Euclidean latticesfinite extensions of 𝔽layers of a cyclotomictower of fieldsIwasawa theory,Ferrero–Washington“upper bounds suffice”a localized theoremof Landau typeanalytic number theory The four rows are the guide's dictionary, quoted. The fields on the right are where each substitute's tools come from, read from the guide's flow diagram. A reading of the proof's architecture, not a verified dependency graph.

We read the guide beside a working draft that explains the proof for the zeta function5.

Each distant theory in the toolkit entered because one row needed a substitute. Iwasawa theory and the Ferrero–Washington theorem (1979) entered because Stepanov passes to all finite extensions of a field, and the proof needed a tower of fields instead.

Iwasawa theory follows the arithmetic of a number field up an infinite tower of extensions, each of degree p over the last, and finds that it grows in a regular pattern. Ferrero and Washington proved in 1979 that for the towers built from roots of unity over abelian fields, one constant of that pattern, μ, is zero.

We use the same mechanism, in which each research chain starts from a solved case, a kind of block whose inversion is cheap:

  • a perfectly clustering block, one run per letter;
  • a two-letter Sturmian block;
  • a periodic text;
  • one of Open's thick strips, which collapses in one jump.

The chain writes the cheap inversion as explicit steps, runs it on real blocks, and finds which steps fail. A failing step names the ingredient to search for, in mathematics of any era. Our cost map of the Wikidata benchmark already says where the first steps fail:

Our first dictionary: the cheap case's steps, where they fail on real blocks, and the ingredient each failure asks for

the cheap case’s stepwhere it fails on real blocksingredient wanteda run of one lettermoves as one blockstatement IDs (GUIDs): 3–8.5% of bytes,54–67% of one-row runsplace unique random byteswithout walking to thema repeated fragmentis copied, not decodedsha1 hashes: 6–25% of thin-run rows,copies of decoded textfind the copy sourcecheaplythe fixed skeletoncosts nothingJSON keys: 33–38% of bytes,only 1–4% of thin-run rowsnone: this stepalready holds Failure rates measured on six Wikidata blocks (working-backwards journal, cost map); the classes are regex approximations and "thin" is a run-width proxy. The right-hand column is what the search is for: open questions, not results.

The economics are unchanged, since our charter's rule of mathematical maximalism still holds: unlimited ambition in the mathematics that discovers a decoder, strict economy in the decoder that runs. A chain whose substitutes hold but don't yet pay goes to the Foundational list, and native timing on our test machine, an i9-10900K, is the final word.

items.title: 6. What happens next?
items.text:
The breadth-oriented team, Kitchen Sink, adopts the toolkit rule and the transplant at its next cycle boundary. A separate team is working on contracting a block directly in the space of interval exchanges; its first round has been audited. Neither has a result from the new method yet.

The first report will be each chain's own anatomy: its tools by field and year, which one is new, and which steps the argument rests on. If our chains turn out to draw only on the last thirty years, that will be a finding too.

Research records: the twelve levers; working backwards and the cost map; the Rauzy–Veech literature and the Lyndon literature; the research method; the interval-exchange team's first round.

❦

items.title: Halving the single-row steps
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

For most of its life this project has improved its decoders a few per cent at a time. bzip2 sorts the rotations of each block of text and keeps the last letter of each, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). Undoing it means following a map, LF, from each row of the sorted table to the row one letter earlier in the text (the structure of that map). Our first decoder, the walk, applies LF one row at a time. Two later ones, Cells and Open, move whole stretches of rows together wherever neighbouring rows share their letter, and Open walks the thin stretches. The figure below shows that history at 20 threads, release by release. Six releases, from 0.2.9 to 0.5.0, left throughput near 1.6 GB/s: Cells shipped in 0.3.0, but only for fewer than six threads. Once it reached 20 threads, in 0.5.1, throughput rose release by release, to 3.26 GB/s by 0.5.13. The new algorithm did more than add a step of its own: it opened a run of gains that the releases before it had not found.

Throughput release by release: flat, then climbing once Cells took over

1.01.52.02.53.03.5GB/s of output, wikidata, 20 threads on one i9-10900K (modelled, 95% intervals)-5%0%+10%each release against the one before it0.3.0: Cells ships,below 6 threads0.5.1: Cellsreaches 20 threads0.2.1: 1.24 GB/s0.5.13: 3.26 GB/s#11#172#391#481#642#822merges to master, in order (pull request number); each release sits at the last merge it contains Measured, as on the benchmark history page (CI, merge by merge; wikidata; 20 threads; Absolute). CI's runners have 4 CPUs, so at 20 threads every point is a release on one i9-10900K, its throughput modelled from paired release-against-release runs with lbzip2 as the fixed anchor, and placed at the last merge to master that its tag contains; the dotted line only joins releases. Below, each release against the one before it, with 95% intervals. The rise after 0.5.1 is many releases' work on top of Cells and then Open, not Cells alone; 0.5.13's +13% came from work outside the BWT step: a faster CRC, a new block reader and leaner parallel output.

This post is about attempting a step of that kind again. What we are after is a decoder as different from ours as Rauzy–Veech induction, the mathematics behind Cells, was from the walk, and the past week went into making that search well posed. There is no new decoder to report. What there is, instead, is a sharp boundary. Call an event a step that settles one row on its own (what decoding pays for counts them), and a width-1 row one whose letter forms a run of length one, so that no stretch can carry it; a block has h₁ of them, and on our benchmark most come from random IDs. Our three decoders belong to one family, the current family: decoders that move intervals of rows by fixed translations and compose those moves. We have now proved that every member of that family pays at least one event per width-1 row. A decoder that settles a block in h₁/2 events or fewer therefore cannot be a refinement of anything we have; it must be a new algorithm. That recasts an open-ended search as a binary target, which a candidate either meets or provably misses. The first test of a candidate representation has also returned: given the decoding order for free, the whole decoder ran 16% faster on one thread, a gain that all but vanished at ten.

Rauzy–Veech induction studies a line cut into intervals and shuffled, an interval exchange, by cutting off the shorter end again and again until the pieces repeat. A block's runs of equal letters form such an exchange, so the same steps move whole runs at a time. The kernel built on it is told in A new way back from the BWT, and the dictionary between the two worlds in Towers, words and loops.

Four pieces of work make the target usable. The first is the target itself, stated exactly: an exact decoder must settle every block with at most h₁/2 events in all, in two passes over the block and with no more memory than Open, and must beat Open's whole decoding time. Open's own events are its m retained steps, one on each width-1 row and the rest on rows of wider runs, each writing a word, the letters between it and the next. The second is the lower bound, G1, which proves the h₁ floor for the current family and so guarantees that anything meeting the target is new. The third is a census of our benchmark's blocks, in which three structural features of a block predict the time Open spends building its structures, with a held-out R² of 0.96. The fourth is a record of fourteen candidate frameworks already closed, each kept with its counterexample, its scope and what would get past it. Beneath all four lies the transformation that connects our three decoders, together with the one invariant it can never remove (§4).

On the way, the search was reframed four times: to use everything, to count the cost, to fix a binary target, and to keep the method rather than the result (§§1–2). The last of these came from an essay against AI mathematics, and it sharpened into a precise question about our decoders, which the rest of the post works through. It sets out the routes we have (§3) and the transformation between them (§4), tests two proposals against it (§5), says what a new route would have to be (§6), and closes with where the search stands (§7).

items.title: Halving the single-row steps: a target only a new algorithm can meet
items.text:
We now search for a new way to undo bzip2's block sort by forbidding the obvious mechanism and asking whether any exact decoder can do without it.

24 November 2026 · 15 min read · Meta

items.title: 1. The goal: a new algorithm, not a faster one
items.text:
The model for what we want is the step from the walk to induction. The walk follows the block's cycle one row at a time; induction recast the same permutation as an interval exchange and moved whole stretches of rows at once. It was not a faster walk but different mathematics for the same specification, and its cost scaled with a different property of the block, one that happens to be small on real data.

The same permutation, read as a loop and as an exchange of runs

The walk: one lookup per row1234567$4a0n1a5n2a6b37 lookups,each one waitingfor the lastsmall numbers are rows; read the lettersbackwards round the loop: banana$Induction: one translation per runLFa$0na1na2ba3$b4an5an6+1+4+1−4−35 runs, so 5 translationscarry all 7 rows Conceptual, on the BWT of banana$. The walk pays one dependent lookup per row; induction treats each run of equal letters as an interval and moves it with one translation (the signed numbers), so its cost follows the number of runs. On real blocks runs are long, which is why the step from the walk to induction paid.

This gives the goal its shape. A constructive proof that the transform can be inverted is an inversion algorithm: the walk is a proof by induction along the text, and the induction kernels are a proof by induction over the interval exchange. A new proof with a different structure is therefore a new algorithm with a different cost, and the search becomes one for a new proof of an old fact, judged on its cost as well as its correctness. Without that second criterion an algorithm can be altered indefinitely while remaining correct, and whether any alteration helps is discovered only at the end.

items.title: 2. Four reframings of the search
items.text:
Use everything. A claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, still awaiting independent checking, built on fifty older tools reaching back two centuries, made mathematical distance look cheap, and our method accordingly adopted a mathematical maximalism: no limit on how far a framework might sit from compression, and chains of worlds in which one representation's job is to carry the problem into another. The approach produced fourteen frameworks, each tried and closed, and a register of obstructions; it did not produce the step.

Count the cost. A paper analysing the simplex method "by the book" (Bach, Black, Huiberts and Kafer) sets cost theorems beside correctness theorems, and we followed its lead. A census of our benchmark's blocks now predicts the time Open spends building its structures from three features of a block (held-out R² 0.96), and a lower bound, G1 (§3), states what every decoder in the current family must pay.

The census timed Open on each of the 232 distinct blocks of our Wikidata benchmark, one worker at a time, and asked whether a few features of a block's structure predict where the time goes. For building Open's structures they do: three features explain 96% of the variation on blocks held out of the fit. For writing the output they don't, which is one reason the price of an event (§5) stays an open question.

Fix a binary target. Super Mario 64 players keep an A-button challenge, and one effort on the Shifting Sand Land level asked whether it could be done with fewer than one press of the A button. That recasts a minimisation as a decision problem, settled either by a route or by a proof that none exists. Its decisive move, as the transcript of that work records it, was to work backwards: it supplied the impossible-looking condition by hand in a test fixture, confirmed the payoff, and only then sought how the real game could produce it, one supplied condition at a time. Payoff first and mechanism second is also the logic of the supplied-codes test in §7.

The A-button challenge is a long-running game among Super Mario 64 players: to finish the game pressing the jump button as seldom as may be. Its formal side has begun elsewhere: a Rocq proof about another level, Wing Mario over the Rainbow, shows that a run with no A press never makes Mario fly, though it still rests on named residual hypotheses, and its theorem that the level needs an A press at all is not yet started.

"Fewer than one" forces a leap because it forbids the obvious mechanism, the tool on which every ordinary route relies, and mibz2 has an exact counterpart:

The Mario 64 challenge mibz2 The obvious mechanism the A press following the block's cycle, one row at a time The best known one A press Open: m events, h₁ of them on width-1 rows The class's floor ordinary routes need at least one G1: every decoder in the current family pays at least h₁ The challenge fewer than one at most h₁/2 events in all

On our benchmark, an extract of Wikidata, h₁/m is 0.30, 0.39 and 0.83 at the minimum, median and maximum across its 232 distinct blocks. Because no decoder in the current family goes below the floor, anything below it is, by theorem, not an edit to Open. Whether a candidate is a new algorithm or an increment stops being a judgement and becomes a consequence of the bound.

Our target now has the same form: invert every block exactly, in two passes and no more memory than Open, with at most h₁/2 events in all, and then beat Open's whole decoding time. The criterion is binary, and each candidate begins with a supplied-capability test: the decoder is handed, for free, whatever the new idea would compute, and we measure what that buys.

Keep the method, not the result. In October the essayist doomslide published "Against Mathematics", a polemic about what machines are doing to the subject. It tells the history of mathematics as a creature with three heads, each paid at a different rate: a proud head that discovers, a blind head that checks, and a slow head that understands. Proof assistants, it argues, have already replaced the blind head, and it reads this year's AI results, such as a batch of 722 machine-written manuscripts released on 6 October, as the proud head's turn: results that arrive with machine-checked proofs and nobody to explain them. (Those reports are the essay's own.)

Three older ideas carry its argument, and each bears on our search:

  • Hearers and Learners. After Pythagoras died his followers divided: the Hearers kept his sayings and let the reasons go, while the Learners kept both. A register of closed frameworks is a list of sayings unless each entry keeps its reason: the counterexample, the scope, what would get past it, and what the attempt revealed.
  • Archimedes' Method. Archimedes sent the librarian at Alexandria not only his results and their proofs, but the mechanical method that found them, so that others might "discover other theorems in addition, which have not yet occurred to me". A result, its proof and a method that generates more results are three different things, and only the last moves a search forward.
  • Hilbert's lost 24th problem. Hilbert planned a 24th problem for his 1900 list and left it in a notebook: a theory of the simplicity of proofs. Its key sentence is an instruction: "Given two routes, it is not right to take either of these two or to look for a third; it is necessary to investigate the area lying between the two routes." Using everything had been a search for a third route; Hilbert directs us instead to the map between the routes we already have.

The Method came down to us in a single copy, the Archimedes Palimpsest, made in the tenth century and scraped from its parchment in the thirteenth, that the leaves might carry a prayer book. Heiberg read it beneath the prayers in 1906, and much of it was recovered only by imaging, between 1999 and 2008: a method nearly lost under a book of results of another kind.

The essay draws the distinction between a result and a method with mathematics of its own. In one retelling the Pythagoreans are confronted with a wall of right triangles with whole-number sides. Checking them one by one with knotted rope yields results; but a brother who looks at the triangles whose short sides differ by one finds the rule that turns each into the next, and that rule is a method: it generates triangles that were never on the wall, and, run backwards, it proves that the diagonal of a square has no whole-number ratio to its side.

One rule that generates the answers, and proves the impossibility
