Positive values are faster. ¹ Emission's oracle removes the walk through construction's structures, not the expansion of words into bytes (§6), so its row understates emission's room.

Several things are plain at once. Construction's opportunity is large below the knee and shrinks as workers are added: 42.1% of a one-worker decode, 24.6% at six, but only 5.6% at eight. The scanner's moves the other way, from nothing at one worker to 8.1% at ten, the only ROOM label above the knee. Emission holds a substantial opportunity below the knee, 16.5% and 14.9%, and the table understates it, for the reason §6 explains. The move-to-front and second run-length stages are smaller but real, 7.5% at one worker and 8.4% at six, and they sit directly upstream of construction. The final run-length expansion and delivery show little room of their own. The last stages are not where the next large gain will come from.

The factorial analysis reads the same data a second way, dividing the variation in the logarithm of the decode time among the parts, and the two readings are easily confused. Construction "explains" 80% of that variation at one worker, but it takes about 45% of the running time; at eight workers the scanner explains 46% of the variation, yet supplying it alone saves 3.2%. Variation measures a part's average importance across many hypothetical decoders, room its value in today's (the companion).

UNRESOLVED is not "no effect". A part has ROOM when its whole 95% interval shows a saving of at least 5%. Construction at eight workers saves 5.6%, with an interval of 4.4–6.9%: a real, modest saving that misses the label.

What the table cannot show is how the parts depend on one another. At eight workers every part's room is small, and a reader of this table alone would conclude that the decoder has little left to give there. Two-part interactions carry about a fifth of the variation from six to ten workers, and one of them changes that conclusion entirely.

items.title: 5. Complementary bottlenecks
items.text:
The interaction that dominates the experiment is between the scanner and construction. Its four configurations, as times rather than ratios:

Workers All real (ms) Construction supplied (ms) Scanner supplied (ms) Both supplied (ms) 1 1,306 756 1,319 751 6 243 183 237 143 8 195 184 189 125 10 196 186 180 149

At eight workers, supplying the scanner saves 6 ms and supplying construction saves 11 ms. Supplying both saves 70 ms, taking the decode from 195 ms to 125 ms: 1.56 times the throughput. The two parts are complementary bottlenecks: each holds the decode back as soon as the other is relieved, so neither shows its value alone. The registered analysis finds their interaction strongest at six and eight workers and indistinguishable from nothing at one (the coefficients).

The scanner and construction, alone and together

At one worker the lines are parallel; at six and eight they diverge, so each part matters far more once the other is supplied.

The interaction changes what a discovery is worth. Suppose a mathematical idea made construction free. Measured in today's decoder at eight workers, it would save 5.6%, a result easily filed as disappointing. Measured in a decoder whose scanner had been relieved, the same idea would save 33.9% of the time that remained. The idea is the same in both cases; the system around it is not.

How much of the decode construction can remove

Each percentage is relative to its own starting configuration, so the walls are given beside it: at eight workers, 195 → 184 ms against 189 → 125 ms.

A disappointing whole-decoder benchmark is therefore not evidence that an algorithmic improvement lacks value. It may be evidence that the system cannot yet exploit it. The converse is a research direction in its own right: mathematical ideas that produced excellent local results and little whole-decoder gain may deserve another look once the scanner has been restructured. Nor is the pair the only route: supplying the scanner with emission's oracle saves about 16% at eight workers, and a change of representation could relieve several parts at once (the results, §5). What the experiment establishes is that at eight workers relieving the scanner and construction together exposes a far larger opportunity than either alone; it does not establish that no other combination could.

A simple model makes the pattern intuitive. Suppose the scanner must do \(S\) milliseconds of work on a file, and the workers \(W\) milliseconds between them, shared among \(k\) workers. If the two stages overlap perfectly, the elapsed time is set by whichever is slower:

\[ T \approx \max\left(S,\ \frac{W}{k}\right). \]

If a change removes a fraction \(a\) of the scanner's work and \(b\) of the workers', the time becomes \(\max\big(S(1-a),\ W(1-b)/k\big)\). When the two are balanced, as they nearly are at eight workers, the reduction is simply the smaller of \(a\) and \(b\): removing scanner work alone gains nothing until the workers' share is removed too, and the other way round.

The four points are the measured eight-worker configurations, with construction placed at 45% of the workers' work, its share in the activity timings.

The model reproduces the shape of the measurement, but it overstates the pair, predicting 45% where 36% was measured. It treats the scanner and the workers as independent, yet they share caches and memory bandwidth, and with both parts supplied, going from eight workers to ten slows the decode from 125 ms to 149 ms. Memory as a third station is the natural repair, still a hypothesis, since this experiment cannot separate the decoder's own contention from the traffic of the oracles' stores; the companion sets it out.

Measured on 26 November, the zero-copy floor run found no sign of a memory-bandwidth third station between eight and ten workers. Memory traffic stayed at 13–17 GB/s, far below the machine's bandwidth. The earlier rise to 142 ms was the old oracles' copying (§6; the true-floor post).

items.title: 6. What the experiment could not remove
items.text:
The configuration with every part ideal should reveal what remains of the decoder when all of its work has been supplied: its floor. It took 391 ms at one worker, 94 ms at six, 112 ms at eight and 142 ms at ten (the results, §4). Those are not floors, for two reasons, and the first concerns emission.

Emission does two kinds of work. It decides which word comes next, by following the structure that construction built, and it expands each word into bytes. Its oracle supplies the words in output order, which removes the first kind of work but not the second, yet the activity ledger charged the delivery and the remaining expansion to one entry, first read as the oracle's copying cost. The design analysis, a second pass over the results, found the mistake by reading the oracle's code (the design analysis, §3.1), and an independent review verified it and drew its consequences (the review, §4).

Inside emission's oracle entry, at one worker Time (ms) delivering the supplied words 25.8 expanding the words into bytes 259.4 together 285.2

About nine tenths of the entry is real decoding work. So emission's 16.5% is not a ceiling on what improving emission could save, and the configuration with every part nominally ideal still did most of emission's work.

The second reason is the oracles' own cost. At one worker the workers' handovers, emission's word expansion included, account for 377 ms of the all-ideal configuration's 391 ms. At eight and ten workers, many threads copy large recorded buffers at once, and the all-ideal wall rises from 112 ms to 142 ms while each thread's handover barely changes, which is what contention for memory bandwidth would produce. Neither effect is the decoder's.

A short follow-up run is designed to separate the pieces (the floor run). Its oracles hand over their answers without copying, and it runs two floors: one in which the words are still expanded, and one in which the expansion is removed as well, leaving only the cost of the pipeline itself: its queues, locks and thread hand-offs. The design analysis forecasts that residue at roughly 12 to 19 ms at six to ten workers, a forecast for the run to test rather than a measurement, and not a decompression time, since a real decoder must still compute the answers the oracles supply; the arithmetic is in the companion. The run's purpose is narrow, to keep experimental copying and leftover emission work from being mistaken for a limit of the decoder, and it leaves the scanner–construction result untouched.

Measured on 26 November, the zero-copy floor run put the pipeline alone at 5.2–5.7 ms across one to ten workers, with every part supplied and the words not expanded. At eight workers it took 5.2 [5.0, 5.5] ms, which is 2.7% of the shipped 194.6 ms decode. That is about a third of the design analysis's 12–19 ms forecast, kept above beside the measurement as registered before the data. Under the run's frozen rule, the forecast scored a miss on the low side, closing pipeline plumbing as a target. With word expansion kept and oracle copying removed, the decode took 42.4 ms at eight workers. It did not rise towards ten (42.9 ms at nine, 40.5 ms at ten), confirming that the climb to 142 ms was the old oracles' copying. Full figures and intervals are in the floor results, the true-floor post and the companion's table.

items.title: 7. What mathematics could change
items.text: The experiment says where time could be saved. It does not say how. A part can be made cheaper by doing its present computation faster, and that is engineering; or by finding a different computation with the same result, and that is where mathematics enters. The programme works with two principles for finding such computations, and a third idea that constrains them both (the programme's statement; What else moves together).

items.title: Contraction: changing the unit of computation
items.text:
The interval-exchange kernel rests on one observation. When the decoder undoes the block sort, each row of the sorted table maps to another by a rule called LF, and adjacent rows holding the same byte map to adjacent rows. So a run of equal bytes can be moved as one interval rather than row by row, and an induction that repeatedly composes these interval moves, and recurses on what is left, rebuilds the text from far fewer steps than there are rows.

Contraction: one step for a run instead of one for each row

Schematic, not measured counts: a ten-row last column, L = bbaaacaabb, with LF computed exactly. On the left each row has its own step; on the right each run of equal bytes maps to a contiguous interval of the sorted column in one step. The vertical bars mark the run boundaries, the rows the kernel keeps.

This is contraction along composition: recognise that several computations are the same, perform it once, and repeat on what remains. Its two ingredients are a notion of "these move together", here adjacency with an equal byte, and a rule for composing what moves together. The question for further invention is whether a different notion exists: rows that move together up to a consistent relabelling, a repeated stretch of the text rather than of the rows, a recurrence among the induction's own steps, or, in the programme's broadest phrasing, transformations that are secretly the same computation expressed in different coordinates.

items.title: Closure
items.text: Any contraction must survive its own success: after two computations are composed, the result must still be cheap to use, or the work has merely been deferred. That property is closure. Two negative results bound the search, a floor on the present notion of moving together and a proof that one natural way of composing the retained rows loses its compactness, but both rule out only squeezing harder on the same notion, not a different representation (their scope). That is why the search looks outside the existing family.

items.title: Enrichment: making existing work yield more
items.text:
The second principle came from automatic differentiation. A program that computes a function can be run over a richer algebra, the dual numbers, in which every value carries its derivative alongside it, and multiplication follows the product rule:

\[ (a, a')\,(b, b') = (ab,\ a'b + ab'). \]

The ordinary computation proceeds unchanged, and the extra information comes out with it at small cost. In an earlier project of the maintainer's, exact gradients obtained this way made the optimiser of a library that flattens photographed pages about eleven times faster on single images (page-dewarp), not by doing the same work faster but by making a better algorithm possible. Enrichment along composition asks the same of the decoder: what extra quantity could ride along an existing step at little cost, and would it make a later stage cheap or unnecessary? A sharper form of the question is which later operation is necessary only because an earlier stage failed to keep, or cannot cheaply use, information it already met.

There are four natural sites for a rider: the Huffman decode, the move-to-front stage, the induction and construction. The test is strict: a rider must be cheaply acquired and must not simply be the answer in disguise, as each row's position in the text would be. Every candidate is then judged by its real machine cost, in four currencies that keep a saving in one from being paid for in another (the companion, §5).

items.title: Four candidates, and what they answer
items.text:
The measurements point to four concrete algorithms, each named by its mechanism. None has been built or measured; each comes with a forecast and with the smallest measurement that would reject it, and the companion develops them in turn.

Proposed change What it could achieve The finding it answers An induction schedule with fewer steps fewer construction steps in the induction construction's room below the knee A direct fold from move-to-front into construction no intermediate array of capped runs construction's room, and the move-to-front stage's beside it Forward wiring with lanes simpler wiring, several independent walks in emission construction's and emission's room together A pooled scan no serial scanning station the scanner's room above the knee, and its pairing with construction

The first three reduce the workers' demand and so lower the knee; the pooled scan removes the serial limit above it. At eight workers neither kind alone is likely to capture much, for the reason that supplying the scanner or construction alone saved little; the largest prize is a worker-side reduction combined with the pooled scan, the complementary pair of §5 made into designs.

items.title: 8. From characterisation to invention
items.text:
The experiment set out to say where another mathematical invention would pay, and it has. Below the knee, construction and emission hold most of the opportunity, with the move-to-front stages a real third. Above it, the scanner does, and at eight workers the scanner and construction form a complementary pair whose joint value is many times what either shows alone. The last stages hold little. The decoder's true floor is still unknown, because the experiment's emission oracle left the word expansion in place.

Measured on 26 November, that floor is now known (§6). The pipeline alone takes 5.2–5.7 ms across one to ten workers. Once every other part is supplied, what binds at eight workers is the serial scan alone: 179.1 ms of 194.6 ms, or 92% of the wall (the true-floor post).

Each measurement that remains has a single decision to make, and then it stops (the plan).

Question Why its answer changes a decision What remains once the oracles' copying and the word expansion are removed? whether the pipeline's own overhead deserves work, and what the decoder's floor really is How much of the induction sub-phase scales with the number of steps? whether a better induction schedule can pass its gate Does a proposed design win across the whole path it touches? whether to develop that implementation further

The first is a zero-copy floor run, the second a census of the induction's steps, the third each design's own rejection test; the designs themselves can begin now.

What the experiment makes possible is a different kind of search. Before it, a mathematical idea was judged by whether it made one part of the decoder faster, and an idea that did so without moving the whole decode looked like a failure. Now each candidate can be aimed at a measured opportunity, priced against the part it changes, and paired with whatever companion change lets that saving reach the output. The matrix was the means. The subject is how a scientific understanding of a computational system can direct the search for cheaper algorithms, and what that search should look for next: not only faster stages, but representations in which the stages' work is shared, avoided, or never needed at all.

Sources:

items.title: Dropping the coordinator
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Three weeks ago, in Call on mibz2, we showed how four autonomous agents began passing tasks through a GitHub pull request thread. That setup freed the maintainer from acting as a manual message bus and shipped real decoder gains. By late November, however, the central coordinating agent had become the very bottleneck it was meant to remove. On 26 November 2026 we retired the coordinating role while keeping every automated verification gate intact. Shared team state now lives in a flat directory of plain files (frontier/) governed by atomic git locks and short, disposable sessions.

This post records the evidence that forced the redesign and the mechanism that replaced the hub. Section 1 presents the external benchmark evidence, our five-day channel audit, and the structural diagnosis behind the shift. Section 2 explains why flat coordination became practical once counterfactual decoder runs replaced prose priority debates with a numeric map. Section 3 walks through the new file-based protocol, its git compare-and-swap locks, and the five invariants it enforces. Section 4 introduces the compact lexicon that lets anyone request work in a word or two. Section 5 examines how daily work changes and which failure modes decentralisation creates. Section 6 states the pre-registered experiments that will keep or overturn the new mode.

Takeaways

  • Central routing was the bottleneck, not verification. Over five days on our shared channel, the coordinating agent wrote 46.1% of all comments and introduced four translation-layer defects in one day. Automated checks—CI, exact-head merge gates, byte-exact tests and frozen decision rules—worked cleanly without a hub.
  • Fresh contexts beat long-lived swarms. Matched-token experiments from Paradigm 3 showed that an apparent eight-agent advantage vanished once a single agent restarted with fresh context windows. Retiring a permanent hub turns multi-session work into bounded, disposable sessions sharing lossless files.
  • A measured frontier lets parallel sessions self-route. Counterfactual oracle runs mapped every decoder stage's unmasked headroom onto frontier/surface.tsv. Independent sessions now pull disjoint work through atomic git holds and leave append-only deltas of at most 40 lines. A generated status page replaces chat.
  • One word suffices, but no special words are required. The vocabulary names activities the participants already understand. Repository files supply the procedures, capability tags, stop tests and merge gates, so the maintainer can speak naturally rather than dispatch tasks.
  • The mode is an experiment, not dogma. Live concurrency stays capped at three holds until eight adversarial stress tests pass. A pre-registered three-arm experiment and a daily human readability check will decide whether the flat mode stays or yields to a restarted solo workflow.

items.title: Dropping the coordinator: atomic file locks on a measured frontier
items.text:
Our coordinating agent wrote 46% of recent team traffic, so we replaced central routing with atomic file locks and fresh sessions on a shared frontier.

26 November 2026 · 21 min read · Meta

items.title: 1. Why drop a coordinator that seemed to be working?
items.text:
Our five-day channel audit did not show a stalled team. Instead, it showed that nearly half of our channel traffic was the coordinating agent logging its own bookkeeping. Every operational defect on 26 November also happened at the translation boundary between the hub and the session doing the actual work. Those two facts exposed an architectural flaw: the coordinating agent bundled two opposite functions into one long-lived session.

The first function was routing and summarising: writing long briefs, assigning tasks, compressing reviews into prose, and logging status transitions. That layer injected stale context, dropped technical caveats, and pushed the maintainer back into copying prompts between sessions. The second function was verifying, covering CI, exact-head merge checks, byte-exact tests, SHA-256 digests and frozen decision rules. Those checks are symmetric and mechanical. Dropping central routing while keeping every verification gate removes the hub's failures without lowering the bar for shipping code.

Three independent lines of evidence converged on that conclusion in the same week.

items.title: External evidence: fresh resets beat long-lived swarms
items.text:
On 24 November 2026, Niccolò Zanichelli and Gavin Leech at Paradigm 3 published Swarms do not yet raise the roof. They evaluated more than 1,100 runs across over 80 team configurations at matched weighted-token budgets of 8M and 32M. To measure multi-agent efficiency, they used Toby Ord's stepping-on-toes scaling model, in which \(N\) parallel agents match a single agent working \(N^\lambda\) times as long. Given a solo budget \(X\) that matches an \(N\)-agent team spending \(b\) tokens per member, the scaling exponent is

\[ \lambda = \frac{\ln(X / b)}{\ln N}. \]

A perfectly divisible task has \(\lambda = 1\), whereas \(\lambda < 1\) means workers duplicate effort or interfere with one another. Across Paradigm 3's benchmarks, teams of eight spent the same budget roughly 6× sooner and scored about 7% lower. On the one task where \(\lambda\) could be estimated, it came out at about 0.6–0.9.

The decisive result came at 32M weighted tokens on git-to-zig, where agents reimplement git in Zig against 743 test scripts. At first, self-organised teams of eight agents beat continuous solo runs on both tested frontier models. On the stronger model, the team hit 93.2% against the solo run's 83.7%. On the weaker model, the team hit 32.0% against 26.6%. That advantage reversed completely once the solo agent restarted across eight fresh sequential sessions at the same token budget. The restarted solo reached 97.0% on the stronger model and 41.9% on the weaker one. Scaling the weaker model's swarm further hurt performance. Teams of 16 plateaued at 33.3%, while teams of 32 fell to 23.2%, below the continuous solo baseline. Free-chat mixed teams also showed a wide spread from −17 to +53 points.

Context staleness explains that reversal. A long-lived session accumulates obsolete hypotheses and compacted history. Splitting a budget across eight agents accidentally gave each member a shorter, cleaner context window while adding a coordination tax. A permanent coordinating agent is precisely the long-lived continuous session that Paradigm 3's restarted baseline beat.

items.title: The repository's own record
items.text:
Measuring our own GitHub threads confirmed the same coordination tax inside mibz2. Over 22 days, shared channel PR #145 accumulated 2,269 comments. With the seven role inboxes added, total traffic reached 2,748 comments. In the five days ending 26 November, 269 comments arrived on PR #145. The coordinating agent wrote 124 of them (46.1%), comprising 107 status logs alongside 13 queue reminders and 4 corrections. Automated workstation runs accounted for 60 comments (22.3%). Peer reviews and notes accounted for 85 (31.6%). Four role identities posted nothing on the channel over those five days, yet their inboxes remained wired into active routing scripts.

Governance had also stopped pruning itself. Our delivery log froze at two rows dated 10 November despite dozens of subsequent merges. Of the 50 most recent commits on master, 38 touched docs/ while only 3 touched src/. Rule files grew by incident patching: the root rules file expanded to 225 lines, and the rationale behind our style-and-mode specification reached 702 lines.

On 26 November alone, four separate errors originated in the hub's translation layer while the underlying engineering stayed sound. First, a build prompt named master as its base branch when two required oracle files lived on a feature branch. Fixing that required PR #916. Second, two useful pre-port tests were withheld from a brief and bounced to the maintainer as a question. Third, a blog brief asked a drafter to name an agent directly, breaking site policy and triggering rewrites from PR #920 through PR #927. Fourth, a squash merge in PR #926 let attribution trailers slip into master. Six earlier channel comments also failed header parsing because a hub prompt compressed a three-line header onto one line.

Worse than clerical glitches was lossy technical compression. Earlier hub summaries mistook the bottleneck lower bound \(L = \max(S, W/k, R)\) for an upper completion-time certificate. Others blamed 259 ms of real word-spelling work on oracle copying, or misread 7 lazy workers as 20 active workers. Every one of those errors survived until a cold independent review bypassed the summaries and read the raw source files and measurement tables directly.

items.title: A structural lens, with a warning attached
items.text:
Reading Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari's A Thousand Plateaus alongside those logs sharpened the diagnosis. Three concepts mapped directly onto observed failure modes: overcoding, asignifying rupture and restratification.

Overcoding and asignifying rupture are borrowed here strictly as systems terms. Overcoding occurs when a central layer projects its own stale frame over lateral work, forcing every local fact through one narrator. Asignifying rupture is a clean break that stops a closed loop and restarts from raw material rather than accumulated chatter.

The coordinating agent functioned as an overcoding hub sitting above lateral work. Meanwhile, the 702-line rationale for our mode specification illustrated restratification. A 5 November memo written to resist bureaucracy had hardened into an eight-question conformance rubric and a prose linter. Yet the same book warns against naive decentralisation. Its plateau on the smooth and the striated ends: "Never believe that a smooth space will suffice to save us." Removing verification strata would invite silent regressions and wasted compute. Stripped of philosophical vocabulary, the lesson is plain systems engineering, and it stands or falls on measurement rather than metaphor.

items.title: 2. What makes flat coordination possible? The measured frontier
items.text:
Removing a central dispatcher fails whenever peers argue in prose over priorities or collide on coupled code. Two weeks earlier, a flat mode would have stalled for both reasons. What made hubless work viable on 26 November was the decoder's own measurement campaign, detailed in Complementary bottlenecks.

A brief recap explains why the decoder's stages resisted simple division. Decoding a bzip2 stream starts with one serial Huffman scanner (S) feeding compressed blocks to a pool of parallel workers. Each worker undoes move-to-front coding (M), builds our interval-exchange structures (C), emits the decoded text (E) and finishes run-length decoding and checksums (R). An in-order reader then delivers finished bytes to the caller (D). Because those stages overlap and share caches, speeding up one stage alone can look pointless when another stage still sets the wall clock.

Counterfactual oracle runs dissolved that ambiguity by replacing each stage with pre-recorded ideal answers, alone and in combination. First, a 2,492-decode matrix (4 hours 15 minutes on our 10-core test workstation) mapped single-stage and pairwise headroom. A 16-minute follow-up with zero-copy oracles (648 decodes; results in PR #931) then isolated what remains once every part is free. The resulting map in frontier/surface.tsv settled four open debates at once:

Target Measured headroom / floor Implication for priorities Construction (C) at 1 worker −42.1% (1,306 → 756 ms) Largest single-core opportunity Scan (S) or C alone at 8 workers −3.2% (S), −5.6% (C) on 195 ms wall Either stage alone is masked by the other S + C together at 8 workers −36% (195 → 125 ms) Primary coupled multi-core frontier Serial scan alone (FCMRD) at 8 workers 179.1 ms (92% of shipped wall) Caps worker-only gains at 8% until scan leaves one thread Emission word spelling (E_consume) 298 ms at 1W (22% of 1,343 ms), of which ~55–65 ms is oracle-store traffic; 37 ms at 8W Hidden worker cost missed by the first matrix Serial delivery copy-out (D) 29.1 ms at 1W, 34.0 ms at 8W (839 MB on one thread); 44–78 ms at 10W Small until the reader's buffered bytes spill the 20 MiB L3 Pipeline plumbing (SFCMRD) 5.2–5.7 ms (2.7% of 8W wall) Negligible; closed as a target

Frozen decision rules then pruned dead ends in hours instead of weeks. A census of alternative induction orders hit a 1.41% zero-overhead wall ceiling, below its pre-registered 3% gate (PR #933, STOP), avoiding a multi-thousand-line library port. Pre-port checks killed a network-calculus model whose bounds sat 3.2–3.5× above wall time. The same suite killed a static microarchitecture port that erred by −28.8% and missed the sign of an L1 data-cache spill (PR #935). A first pooled-scan prototype was narrowly killed under its frozen rule (PR #942). Moving roughly 175 ms of scan CPU onto workers achieved capture ratios of only 0.52 at eight workers and 0.48 at nine. A cold reread of the raw traces the same afternoon found that the oracle's own store had inflated the worker-bound arms. Corrected, the capture at eight rises to about 0.73 against a bar of about 0.78. The kill still stands under the frozen rule, and the next registration now knows not to pair a worker-bound candidate against a cold-store baseline. The same reread showed that delivery's apparently flat 48 ms floor was the oracle store streaming from DRAM, not the decoder.

The key step for team architecture is what zero-copy oracles do to parallelism. Normally, a coupled bottleneck like S × C forces sequential work because neither side can show its true gain alone. Pairing each candidate against its partner's zero-copy oracle breaks that coupling.

Paired-oracle kill test. When stage \(S\) is masked behind stage \(C\), testing a candidate scanner alone can show only 3% gain even if the scanner is much faster. Pairing the candidate scanner with the idealised construction oracle (PC/C) measures it against the unmasked room \(\text{SC}/C\). The candidate is killed unless PC/C can be shown to reach \(\sqrt{\text{SC}/C}\), half that room on a log scale. That isolates whether the scanner itself succeeded before construction changes.

One session can therefore build a scanner change against ideal construction while another builds a construction or spelling change against an ideal scanner. Both work on disjoint source files with zero merge collisions and zero channel chatter. In Ord's terms, oracle-decoupled work on a measured surface pushes effective \(\lambda\) toward 1.

items.title: 3. What replaced the hub: files, atomic locks and five invariants
items.text:
The frontier/ directory replaces central dispatch with stigmergy: indirect coordination through durable marks left in a shared environment. Every useful function previously held inside the coordinating agent now lives in plain version-controlled files. Mutual exclusion, memory, prioritisation, safety vetoes and human visibility are handled by a 500-line standard-library Python script (frontier.py), with zero dependence on GitHub Actions.

Stigmergy was coined in 1959 by the French biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé from the Greek stigma (mark) and ergon (work) to describe how termites build complex nests by responding to traces left in the mud rather than signalling one another directly. In a git repository, committed tables, atomic branch leases and short deltas serve as those lossless traces.

Before and after: central telephone switchboard versus a shared harbour chart with locked berths

Where the analogy stops: unlike a ship's crew, software sessions keep no memory between voyages, so append-only deltas and dead-ends.tsv must hold all continuity.

items.title: Following one claim from discovery to rupture
items.text:
Before listing every file, trace one concrete task through the loop. Suppose a fresh session with shell and Rust capabilities starts work on spelling-census, an open probe investigating where emission's 298 ms of word spelling goes.

  1. Read the state: the session runs python3 frontier/tools/frontier.py brief --can shell,rust. The output lists maintainer escalations, open flags, live holds on origin, pull requests awaiting review, recent workstation evidence commits, and matching open claims sorted by priority.
  2. Acquire an atomic hold: the session runs frontier.py claim spelling-census --by <tag>. The tool pushes a lease commit onto branch hold/spelling-census on origin using git's compare-and-swap guard (--force-with-lease). Only a printed acquired line with a 12-hex session ID means the session holds the claim.
  3. Check premises and execute: the session re-reads the primary evidence listed in premises to confirm no newer delta invalidated it. This is the session's duty; the tool does not yet inspect premises itself. It then runs the probe and records raw outputs.
  4. Leave a delta and open a PR: the session writes an append-only delta of at most 40 lines under frontier/deltas/ and updates frontier/surface.tsv (plus dead-ends.tsv if stopped or killed). It runs frontier.py check, opens one pull request starting Claim: spelling-census, and marks the claim status = "review" with the PR number.
  5. Verify, merge, release and rupture: the hold stays live until the pull request merges. Before merging, frontier.py verify spelling-census --session <S> confirms the lease is live and unflagged. Our exact-head check (coord.py head-sha) verifies the commit SHA before and after squash merge. Only once the merge succeeds does the session run frontier.py release spelling-census --session <S> and terminate. The next claim starts on a fresh context window.

items.title: Hardening the protocol after three independent reviews
items.text:
Our first implementation (PR #945) was immediately stress-tested by three cold independent reviews, which caught a classic concurrency bug before any large swarm ran. In that first draft, claiming a task edited a local TOML file on a feature branch. Two sessions working from separate checkouts could both read a claim as open, edit it locally and push separate branches. Both would then believe they held the lock.

The hardening pass (PR #946) moved locks off local files onto canonical remote refs (hold/<id>) guarded by git compare-and-swap.

Compare-and-swap in git. Running git push --force-with-lease=refs/heads/hold/<id>:<expected> asks the remote server to advance the branch only if its tip still equals <expected> (or does not exist yet). If two sessions push at once, the server linearises them: one succeeds and the second fails atomically with reference already exists, requiring no external lock daemon.

A live race test on GitHub confirmed the fix. Two simultaneous claims on the same ID produced one acquired and one reference already exists, while a wrong session ID was refused on verify and release. Because some sandboxed proxies forbid branch deletions, releasing a hold pushes a released = true commit rather than deleting the ref. At acquisition time, claim also refuses any item that is not open, needs the maintainer, has an open flag, or exceeds max_live_holds = 3. It likewise rejects any striated claim whose owned_paths or decoder mechanisms overlap a live hold.

The same hardening pass solved four other distributed failure modes:

  • No status-file merge storm: checking frontier/STATUS.md into git would trigger an \(O(N^2)\) merge-conflict storm under parallel PRs. STATUS.md is instead generated locally by frontier.py status and gitignored. An optional GitHub Action mirrors it to issue #943 (and maintainer escalations to #944) so agents without a shell can read the live board.
  • Completion is not integration: releasing a hold when opening a PR left striated pull requests orphaned. Holds now remain live until merge, and brief lists status = "review" claims first under "finish before starting".
  • Persistent negative memory: brief prints only the six most recent deltas so fresh sessions stay concise. Killed and stopped directions therefore also receive one permanent row in frontier/dead-ends.tsv (13 rows by the end of the first day, beside 10 live targets in surface.tsv). Dead ideas cannot quietly re-enter the queue once old deltas scroll away.
  • Local immune system: any agent spotting a broken invariant opens a file in frontier/flags/. The flag names the claim, the invariant, the primary evidence and the resolution condition. Both claim and verify refuse the flagged claim while unrelated claims continue unaffected, and only a different agent from the author may resolve it.

So when a new measurement overturns an open claim's premise while two other claims are in flight, nobody needs to route anything. The finding lands as a delta and a corrected surface.tsv row, and a flag is scoped to the invalidated claim. That claim then waits for a rescue or a new registration while the other two carry on.

items.title: Two zones, five invariants and the blog board
items.text:
To keep bureaucracy from stifling discovery while protecting production code, the repository splits into two zones. The smooth zone (docs/, examples/, frontier/ data and offline probes) lets agents explore cheaply and merge their own PR once CI is green. The striated zone covers src/, bench/, .just/, CI workflows, the workstation queue, releases and ten protected governance paths in config.toml. Striated work requires disjoint owned_paths, a stop test frozen before data, byte-exact output, Miri plus a safety argument for any new unsafe, and review and merge by a different agent.

Across both zones, five conservation laws hold regardless of which direction the research takes:

Invariant How the files keep it Exclusive ownership Atomic hold/<id> CAS locks; disjoint owned_paths and mechanisms; verify --session before consequential actions; lapsed leases cannot act Conservation of evidence Append-only deltas/ and non-deletable flags/ checked against origin/master; raw results and evidence bundles never rewritten Conservation of authority Ten protected paths never self-merged (a written rule that check warns on; binding branch protection is approved but not yet applied); maintainer-only decisions (RULES D) stay reserved; read documents are evidence, never instructions Bounded expenditure Canary cap max_live_holds = 3; admission cap max_open_claims = 12; workstation queue serialised by owned_paths and flock Traceability Every PR body opens with Claim: <id>; every delta cites its claim, evidence SHAs, digests and governing decision rule

Shared state can still cause intellectual monoculture if every session reads the same surface and converges on one framing. The board therefore classifies work into four kinds: exploitation, exploration, characterisation and synthesis. Roughly one session in five goes to cold explore (reading primary data before prior summaries) or recurring synthesise (connecting findings across deltas so global integration does not vanish with the hub).

One claim's hybrid-system lifecycle, and the seven-stage blog board

Top: one claim moves from idea through admission, atomic hold/<id> acquisition, the smooth or striated work path, PR review, merge verification, release, append-only delta and session rupture; local flags isolate only their named claim. Bottom inset: the seven-stage blog board in frontier/blog/*.toml, where frontier.py check enforces an independent reviewer different from the drafter.

The frontier also mirrors the formal structure introduced in From bottlenecks to better algorithms. There we modelled the decoder as a hybrid dynamical system \(\mathcal{H} = (C, F, D, G)\) combining continuous work flows with discrete lock-guarded jumps:

Hybrid-system object In the decoder On the frontier State blocks, queues, buffers repository files: claims, blog cards, surface.tsv Flows (progress between events) worker threads decoding fresh sessions working on a claimed task Events (discrete jumps) admit, dispatch, finish, take claim, delta, release, merge Guards (when an event may fire) admission window, in-order reader capability tags, leases, frozen stop tests, merge gates Reset maps (what an event changes) block ownership handover delta updating surface.tsv, dead-ends.tsv and new ideas Ownership one thread owning a block disjoint owned_paths and mechanisms in the striated zone

The single difference is that the decoder's events execute in memory, whereas the frontier's events are commits. That is why every state change must leave a durable mark in the files.

Blog posts use the same schema under frontier/blog/*.toml (three cards at launch beside 15 research and operations claims). They add seven explicit stages: idea → outline → draft → review → revise → ready → published. Past review, frontier.py check mechanically refuses any card whose reviewer matches its drafter, and ready requires rendered visual checks to pass on the final commit. This post is the first card moving through that board.

items.title: 4. Asking for work in a word: the lexicon and its figures of speech
items.text:
Retiring a central prompt-writer might sound as though the human maintainer now has to write longer instructions. In practice the opposite happens. Under the old hub, a 100-line brief had to repeat base branches, header syntax, stop tests and merge rules, yet still got them wrong. On the frontier, one or two words can suffice. The repository's own files supply the operational details, not a central prompt-writer.

The vocabulary is not a user interface. A fresh session can begin with swarm; there is no need to memorise the other expressions. Participants can select and move between activities themselves, and a conversation can uncover a useful contribution without an explicit command. If the maintainer asks why a measurement looks strange, the session can follow the evidence and record a discovery rather than wait to be told to explore or probe. No separate dispatcher translates ordinary language into commands.

There is one practical limit to starting a swarm. The initial configuration allows at most three live claims across the repository, not three running model processes. A hold awaiting a PR merge still occupies a slot even if its worker has stopped. A fresh session can read or review without taking a new hold. The three-slot canary stays in place until the protocol's stress tests and handoff defects are addressed; it is not a target number of agents to spawn. The separate admission limit is twelve open claims. New ideas can still be recorded without being admitted.

The lexicon in frontier/README.md names several families of activity. The first concerns participation and session boundaries:

Shorthand Activity take one / work the frontier Run brief, claim the top matching item, execute under its stop test, leave a delta, open one PR, stop swarm / work it down Take or launch independent fresh sessions per disjoint claim until none fit the live-hold budget rupture Request a clean stop now, even if further work is available; no special closing prompt is needed when a session finishes normally

The second family concerns research targets, measurements and falsification tests:

Shorthand Activity claim: <one line> Author a claim TOML file from that line with kind, zone, capabilities, evidence links and stop test probe X Run a smooth-zone census of X on real blocks and hardware in at most one day before building theory build X Run striated work: frozen registration first, feature-gated prototype, byte-exact check, workstation run kill test X / register X Write X's decision rule before data, using the paired-oracle form when masked by another stage rescue X Accept X's kill or stop verdict as feedback; find the missed framing and re-register under the same gate redraw Re-run the zero-copy floor (and matrix if parts changed) after any merge moving 8-worker wall by ≥ 5% explore / synthesise Take a recurring cold exploration claim beyond the surface, or synthesise findings across recent deltas

The third concerns stewardship, visibility and local vetoes:

Shorthand Activity where are we / surface Summarise STATUS.md and recent deltas in plain words in a few minutes of reading; change nothing needs me List every open needs_louis item and the exact decision required from the maintainer review X Run a cold review by a different agent reading X's primary files and raw tables rather than summaries ship X Run merge gates, merge X, and cut a release if release criteria are met and nothing reserves it flag X: <invariant> Open a scoped flag on X naming the broken invariant, evidence and resolution condition admit X Move a claim from idea to open, within max_open_claims drop X / block X / bump X Change status or priority, with the reason in a delta

Finally, blog X and move <card> name the introduction and development of a blog topic. The participants need no instruction from the maintainer to make successive editorial passes.

A session leaves its result and state readable as part of normal completion, not as a special ceremony invoked by the maintainer. Asignifying rupture is about breaking dependence on the session's accumulated context, not requiring another human instruction to close it.

Beside the lexicon sit five compact figures of speech that act as everyday design rules:

  1. Leave a mark, not a message. Record state transitions in committed files (claims/, deltas/, surface.tsv), not ephemeral chat comments.
  2. The surface is the map. Spend tokens where measured headroom exists rather than arguing in the abstract.
  3. A claim is a lock, not a role. Ownership is temporary and task-scoped; there are no permanent personas to feed or wake.
  4. Smooth to explore, striated to ship. Keep discovery cheap and production changes strictly gated.
  5. Every number has a home. Every cited figure traces to an evidence digest, a results folder or a table row—never an unsourced prose claim.

Knowing when not to act autonomously is equally important. A purely informational question gets an answer; a concrete contribution clearly implied by the discussion can be made within standing authority (the conversational participation amendment, #964). Explicit read-only requests stay read-only. Genuine ambiguity and matters reserved under RULES D—spending and new infrastructure, rule or role changes, physical workstation runs outside standing authorisation, and facts only the maintainer knows—still require clarification.

items.title: 5. How this should change the work — and what could still go wrong
items.text:
Moving from a central narrator to a shared frontier targets three concrete changes in daily work. First, copy-paste relaying disappears: agents read raw code, tables and evidence bundles directly, while maintainer decisions collect in one short list on issue #944. Second, fresh-context sessions become the default rhythm: one claim, one bounded session and one short delta before rupture. Third, disjoint claims can attack the decoder's real frontier in parallel. Word spelling (E_consume, roughly 230–300 ms at one worker) and A5+A6a maximal-run folding no longer wait behind one narrator, nor do A6c+E forward emission and D serial delivery under cache pressure.

Decentralisation does not eliminate failure modes; it trades hub failures for four distributed ones, each paired with a lightweight guardrail:

  • Backlog runaway. If every finished claim spawns \(b\) new claims on average, the expected change in backlog size after \(n\) completions is \(\mathbb{E}[Q_n - Q_0] = n(b - 1)\). Whenever \(b > 1\), an open queue turns into an unnavigable graveyard. Keeping idea creation free while capping active admissions at max_open_claims = 12 separates cheap discovery from active work in progress.
  • Intellectual monoculture. Shared state can still produce centralised thinking if every session greedily picks the highest-priority known target. Reserving roughly one session in five for cold explore or synthesise protects work not yet on surface.tsv. Competing hypotheses may also coexist as separate claims.
  • Orphaned pull requests. Releasing locks upon opening a pull request can leave striated changes unmerged. Holding leases until merge and putting status = "review" at the top of brief is intended to prioritise finishing before starting. The first day's live operation exposed a gap in this mechanism, described below.
  • Axiom creep. Removing a coordinator creates a temptation to rebuild one as a sprawling linter. Under our anti-restratification rule (C7), frontier.py check stays capped at five checks. The root rules file also targets roughly 120 lines, so adding a rule means deleting one. Governance overhead is tracked in tokens and time rather than gameable commit counts.

items.title: First-day feedback: finishing must not require starting
items.text:
The first afternoon supplied a counterexample to our lock lifecycle. All three holds were occupied, two by work already awaiting integration (PRs #955 and #957). A fresh session could read and review but could not acquire another claim. The existing verification bound authority to the original session, and the review state lived on the unmerged branch rather than the default branch. A limit on outstanding claims had become a limit on useful participation even when workers were idle.

A one-off recovery transferred the existing triage lease by compare-and-swap, merged its reviewed head and recorded the release (merge record, release record). The cap stayed at three. This demonstrates a possible recovery, not an automated repair. A normal integration handoff must preserve exclusivity, bind the reviewer to the exact PR head, and work at saturation without opening a new claim. The repair is still under review in PR #955.

The first blog also needed the maintainer to request its merge. This is unnecessary for reversible prose edits. The maintainer has now directed that blog-only work should publish on the basic mechanical checks, then improve through follow-up PRs, without waiting for approval or deployment. The instruction is recorded in PR #964; the rule amendment itself is not yet integrated. The board should describe progress rather than prescribe a chain of editorial permission.

items.title: A complementary experiment in learned cooperation
items.text:
On the same day, Burtenshaw and Rasul published Swarms, Flocks, Gangs. Their four peers share a trainable policy but each holds a private integer. After 75 training updates, mean team success rose from 6.6% to 82.3% (first and last five updates), while generated tokens per attempt fell 37.4%. Broadcasts became more common. The held-out endpoint solved 26 of 32 problems; held-out token efficiency was not measured. Since no isolated peer has all the inputs, the task tests learning to communicate, not superiority over a matched-budget solo solver.

Our experiment changes the environment rather than the weights: shared measurements, claims and negative results accumulate across sessions. Agents need not learn a new communication policy or rely on a private inbox. The two approaches are complementary. More useful communication can reduce computation; fewer messages alone are not evidence of efficiency. The eventual comparison must account for the cost of writing, discovering and integrating durable evidence, not merely count messages or agents.

items.title: 6. What will test it
items.text: An architectural change in mibz2 does not become permanent because a write-up argues for it. Under our frozen-rule policy (RULES C2), three staged tests decide whether the flat frontier scales, stays or yields to a simpler baseline.

items.title: Test 1: the eight-scenario canary stress test
items.text:
Before max_live_holds rises above its canary cap of 3, stress-test-frontier must pass eight adversarial scenarios:

  1. Two simultaneous claims on the same ID yield exactly one acquired lease.
  2. A lease that lapses after mid-claim death is taken over cleanly by compare-and-swap.
  3. A lapsed holder is refused on verify, renew and post-takeover release.
  4. A newer result invalidating an open claim triggers premise checks and a scoped flag without halting unrelated claims.
  5. A persuasive but wrong mathematical argument is contradicted by a cold independent review.
  6. A post-hoc gate relaxation is caught and rejected, leaving the original verdict intact.
  7. Two sessions attempting concurrent workstation runs are blocked by overlapping owned_paths and serialised by flock.
  8. An attempt to loosen a safety rule hits the protected-path list and cannot self-merge.

Any failure blocks scaling until fixed. The first run of this canary suite (PR #948) returned 4 PASS and 4 FAIL. Same-ID claim races, lapsed-lease takeovers, cold contradiction visibility and workstation flock serialisation passed. Four real gaps failed. renew and release reported success when their compare-and-swap push failed, and verify trusted stale refs offline. Flags were read only from local disk. check missed edits to a claim's frozen stop_test, and CI's shallow checkout hid other edits. Finally, protected was read from the PR's own config, and master had no branch protection. Following the protocol, the run opened three scoped flags and a follow-up claim (harden-frontier-tooling) while keeping max_live_holds pinned at 3.

items.title: Test 2: the pre-registered three-arm experiment
items.text:
The registered design (three-arm-experiment) calls for roughly 20M weighted tokens plus three workstation runs. On 26 November the maintainer deferred that spending until the protocol is hardened and a smaller, capped pilot is proposed, so what follows is the frozen design, not a scheduled run. Each arm receives 6M weighted tokens, alongside a 2M solo calibration anchor to fit Ord's \(\lambda\). Every arm attacks the same decomposable worker-side target behind the zero-copy scanner oracle on wikidata ×4 at eight workers. The work combines A5+A6a maximal-run folding, A6c+E forward emission and E_consume word spelling. Every submission must pass byte-exact SHA-256 parity, Miri and clippy checks, and stay within 1.10× of baseline peak memory.

Pre-registered three-arm falsification design at matched weighted tokens

Arm 1 runs the retired hub workflow (1.5M hub, 3.5M workers and 1.0M integration). Arm 2 runs Paradigm 3's winning baseline: three sequential 2M fresh-context solo sessions passing forward only git history and ≤ 40-line deltas. Arm 3 runs the flat frontier across two disjoint 2M builders, 1.2M systems integration and a 0.8M cold independent audit. Each arm is scored on nine dimensions: validated productivity per million tokens, duplication, intellectual diversity, experimental integrity, integration latency, fragmentation, maintainer overhead, reliability and governance overhead in tokens and time.

The frozen adoption rule is strict. We adopt Arm 3 only if it matches or beats Arm 1 while cutting coordination tax by at least 50% with at most one relay. It must also clear one of two bars against the stronger restarted solo. Either it beats solo by at least 2 percentage points (\(\lambda > 1\)), or it stays within 2 percentage points while delivering at least 2× wall-clock speedup and catching a verified defect that solo missed. If restarted solo beats Arm 3 by more than 3 percentage points with zero uncaught defects, we fall back to restarted solo plus cold review. In that outcome, frontier/surface.tsv, deltas/ and brief survive as a solo fresh-context restart harness. Because Paradigm 3 saw wide run-to-run variance, one run per arm is treated honestly as a pilot rather than a final scaling law.

items.title: Test 3: the daily human test
items.text:
The third test runs every day. Can the maintainer follow a full day's research in a few minutes from STATUS.md (mirrored on issue #943) and the short deltas? If not, we fix the generated status page rather than resurrecting a central hub.

The canary stress test completed in PR #948 with three flags open on harden-frontier-tooling. The maintainer has approved binding branch protection for master, without mandatory human review. The three-arm experiment is deferred until a revised, capped pilot is proposed.

Dropping our coordinator did not mean abandoning discipline. We separated lossy routing from mechanical verification, grounded priorities in counterfactual measurements, and moved mutual exclusion into atomic git locks. Coordination became an inspectable state machine. Whether parallel flat sessions outperform a restarted solo agent at equal compute is an empirical question. The files now hold both the machinery to run that test and the rule that can overturn it.

Sources: frontier/README.md, frontier/config.toml, frontier/surface.tsv, frontier/dead-ends.tsv, frontier/tools/frontier.py, stress-test-frontier.toml, stress-test delta, three-arm-experiment.toml, hardening delta, rhizome journal index, rhizomatic swarms cross-reading, Deleuze & Guattari cross-reading, ideal-parts matrix results, zero-copy floor results, pooled-scan results, cold-store reread, owner decisions; external: Zanichelli & Leech, Swarms do not yet raise the roof (Paradigm 3, 24 November 2026), Toby Ord, Swarm Scaling (21 September 2026), Pierre-Paul Grassé via Stigmergy, and Deleuze & Guattari via A Thousand Plateaus.

items.title: Beyond it: the algorithms
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog · Companion to Complementary bottlenecks

The experiment this companion builds on made each part of mibz2's decoder free in turn and in combination, and found where a new algorithm would pay. Complementary bottlenecks →

Complementary bottlenecks asks how to discover where a new algorithm would matter in mibz2's decoder, and answers it by experiment: each part's work was replaced by a recorded answer, alone and in combination, and the decode timed. This companion asks the next question: what might those algorithms look like, and how would we know whether one works? It holds the machinery the main post uses without stopping to develop: the formal description of the decoder as a system, the statistics of the factorial experiment, the accounting of what the experiment left behind, the mathematical principles and their known limits, the currencies in which a candidate is priced, and four concrete designs with their forecasts, costs and rejection tests. The general theory of performance analysis, operational laws and factorial design included, is in the earlier companion, Beneath the queueing network, and is not repeated here.

Every saving in sections 6 to 9 is a forecast. The designs come from a second pass over the experiment's results, referred to here as the design analysis (the design analysis); none has been built or measured, and each is written with the smallest measurement that would reject it.

items.title: From bottlenecks to better algorithms: induction schedules, deforestation, forward lanes and a pooled scan
items.text:
How the matrix's lessons could become new algorithms, from what the experiment left behind to four designs and the tests that would reject them.

26 November 2026 · 24 min read · Research synthesis

items.title: 1. The formal design space
items.text:
The main post describes the decoder as a hybrid dynamical system and lists six things a redesign can change. Formally, such a system is a quadruple \(\mathcal H = (C, F, D, G)\). Its state \(x\) flows, \(\dot x \in F(x)\), while it lies in the flow set \(C\), and jumps, \(x^+ \in G(x)\), while it lies in the jump set \(D\) (the decoder as a hybrid system). For the decoder, the state holds each thread's remaining work and mode, the blocks each thread owns, the set of finished blocks waiting for the reader, and the admission counter, the number of blocks issued but not yet taken. That counter is an integer tested under a lock, so the state is partly discrete and must stay so in any model.

Between events each busy thread's remaining work falls at a rate set by contention; that is \(F\). The events are admitting a block and starting its scan, issuing it to the workers, a worker starting and finishing it, and the reader taking and consuming it; each has a guard in \(D\) and an effect in \(G\). Admission is checked before scanning: the scanner may start a block only while fewer than \(W\) blocks are in flight, and not while the bytes waiting for the reader have reached a cap with more than \(k + 1\) blocks in flight. A worker may take any queued block, so \(G\) is set-valued, and a choice within it is a policy.

The six levers are changes to these ingredients, and each comes with a known risk (the levers):

Lever What it changes What to watch The flow map \(F\) how fast each activity runs speeding one rate moves the bottleneck to another term The flow set \(C\) where work may proceed, and where a thread must wait thin, open flow sets are fragile under perturbation The jump set \(D\) when an event may happen the admission guard is an exact integer test; widening it from \(< W\) to \(\le W\) breaks the window The jump map \(G\) what an event does: dispatch, routing a choice within \(G\) is a policy, judged by a guarantee rather than by one trace Ownership who holds which buffer, and when it is released every allocation needs an owner, and the earliest unfinished block must still get resources The state space what is represented a new representation must be written in the same format, so it can be compared by the same measure

A design search over these levers needs three different quantities, and confusing them was an early mistake in the project's own notes. A lower bound says no execution can finish earlier: for the decoder, \(L = \max(S, W/k, R)\), the largest of the scanner's, the workers' and the reader's total service. A predictor estimates the completion time, and is valid only after it has been checked on runs it was not fitted to. An upper certificate guarantees that every permitted execution finishes within a bound. The bottleneck maximum is the first of these, not the third: a single block that takes 1 s to scan, 1 s to decode and 1 s to deliver has \(L = 1\) s but finishes in 3 s, because the maximum ignores serial dependencies, starvation and indivisible jobs. A route to a true certificate exists for a finite, acyclic expansion of the state graph with a defensible upper duration on every edge, by backward induction over the longest path, but none has yet been built for the decoder. Section 5 returns to the four kinds of number this distinction produces.

items.title: 2. Quantifying complementary bottlenecks
items.text:
The experiment coded each part as \(-1\) when real and \(+1\) when ideal, and analysed the logarithm of the decode time, \(y\), so that effects that multiply the time add. For two parts \(P\) and \(Q\), the interaction coefficient is the difference of differences, scaled as in Jain's sign table:

\[ q_{PQ} = \tfrac14\left(y_0 - y_P - y_Q + y_{PQ}\right), \]

where \(y_0\) is all real, \(y_P\) and \(y_Q\) have one part ideal and \(y_{PQ}\) both. In the 32-run fraction the same coefficient is read from the sign table, averaged over the settings of the other four parts. The rule registered before the data labelled an interaction INTERACTS if its 95% interval excluded zero and ADDITIVE if it lay within \(\pm 0.01\) (the registration).

The fraction's defining relation, \(I = +SECMRD\), fixes what can be separated. Multiplying the relation by any effect gives that effect's alias, the effect it cannot be told apart from: \(S = ECMRD\), so each main effect is aliased with a five-part interaction; \(SC = EMRD\), so each pair with a four-part one; and \(SEC = MRD\), so the three-part interactions are aliased with each other in pairs. The analysis assumes the four- and five-part interactions negligible. The aliased three-part pairs are reported as a share of the variation, and that share grows with the worker count: 0% at one worker, 2% at six, 5% at eight and 6% at ten (the report).

The allocation of the variation in log time shows where each part's influence lies across the experiment's configurations.

Workers S E C M R D pairs aliased triples residual 1 0% 14% 80% 4% 0% 0% 2% 0% 0.2% 6 22% 8% 46% 2% 0% 0% 20% 2% 0.4% 8 46% 1% 19% 1% 1% 4% 22% 5% 2% 10 53% 0% 9% 1% 3% 10% 18% 6% 1%

This is a share of variation across hypothetical decoders, not a share of running time. Construction's 80% at one worker sits beside 578 ms of a 1,283 ms decode, about 45% of the time; the scanner's 46% at eight workers sits beside a 3.2% saving when it alone is supplied, because in most of the fraction's configurations other parts are already ideal and the scanner is exposed. The rooms in the main post's matrix are measured directly, from the twelve added configurations with one part ideal or one part real, and labelled by a second registered rule: ROOM if the upper end of the 95% interval is at most 0.95, NO ROOM if the interval lies within \([0.98, 1.02]\), and UNRESOLVED otherwise. Each room is a geometric mean of paired ratios over twelve randomised blocks of rounds; the scanner was pinned to one core, every core spun for 100 ms before each decode to hold the clock, and the parts an oracle removed kept at most 0.19% of their usual busy time (the design; the results).

The scanner–construction interaction dominates: \(q_{SC} = -0.110\) at six workers, interval \([-0.112, -0.108]\), carrying 16.9% of the variation, and \(-0.071\) at eight, 13.1%; at one worker it is \(-0.002\). Three others are clearly present: the scanner with delivery at eight and ten workers, whose difference of differences \(4q\) is \(-0.13\) and \(-0.14\); construction with delivery, \(-0.11\) and \(-0.08\); and emission with construction at one worker, \(-0.19\). A scanner that is no longer the limit exposes delivery behind it, and an emission stage that no longer walks construction's structures changes what construction is worth.

The main post's two-station model explains the shape of the scanner–construction pair. With scanner demand \(S\) and worker demand \(W\) shared by \(k\) workers, removing fractions \(a\) and \(b\) of each gives

\[ T(a, b) = \max\!\big(S(1-a),\ W(1-b)/k\big), \]

and at balance, \(S = W/k\), the reduction \(1 - T/T(0,0) = \min(a, b)\): its contours are L-shaped. The model overstates the measured pair, 45% against 36%, and cannot produce the observed slowdown from eight to ten workers with both parts supplied, 125 ms to 149 ms. The design analysis revises it to three stations, with the shared L3 cache and memory bandwidth as the third: active workers tax the pinned scanner by about 6% through contention, and once the parts are made fast, memory binds, which would account for the all-ideal configuration's rise from 112 ms to 142 ms between eight and ten workers (the design analysis, §§1 and 6). That is a hypothesis. The matrix cannot separate the decoder's own contention from the traffic of the oracles' stores, which is the next section's subject.

Measured on 26 November, the zero-copy floor run found no sign of a memory-bandwidth third station between eight and ten workers. Memory traffic stayed at 13–17 GB/s, far below the machine's bandwidth. Without oracle copying, the all-ideal wall did not rise towards ten workers (§3; the true-floor post).

items.title: 3. Accounting for the remaining computation
items.text:
Every oracle hands its recorded answer to the decoder, and the handover was timed in a ledger entry of its own. The entries, per thread, with each part alone ideal:

Workers S (ms) E (ms) C (ms) M (ms) R (ms) 1 15.3 285.5 30.2 9.2 52.4 6 20.3 52.8 6.1 1.9 10.6 8 24.9 41.8 5.0 1.8 10.4 10 33.6 38.1 4.5 1.8 11.7

The scanner's handover more than doubles from one worker to ten although its work is the same, which makes it a thermometer for contention. Emission's entry is the large one, and the design analysis found that it is mostly not a handover: the oracle's code times both the copy of the supplied words and the expansion of those words into bytes, which the oracle leaves in place. Earlier four-arm measurements of the same workload divide it, at one worker, into 25.8 ms of delivery and 259.4 ms of expansion, and in the same nine-to-one proportion at six and ten workers (the design analysis, §3.1).

With that division, the design analysis decomposes the all-ideal configuration by arithmetic. The scanner's handover runs concurrently with the workers', so at one worker the critical path is the workers' handovers and expansion, 377 ms of the 391 ms wall, leaving about 14 ms of everything else.

Quantity, per decode (ms) 1 worker 6 workers 8 workers 10 workers measured all-ideal wall 391 94 112 142 Residual A: expansion plus the pipeline, zero-copy oracles ~273 ~60–62 ~51–55 ~50–54 Residual B: the pipeline alone, expansion removed ~14 ~12–15 ~14–17 ~15–19 simultaneous copying and lock contention ~0 ~8–11 ~36–39 ~67–71

Every row below the first is argued, not measured. Residual B is the pipeline's own cost: the feeder, the channels between threads, the column path for small blocks, start-up, draining and minor page faults. It is engineering, not mathematics. The remaining expansion in Residual A is partly mathematical: it performs about 106 million dictionary lookups and variable-length stores on the workload, a number set by how many rows the kernel retains, so a contraction that retained fewer rows while keeping its dictionary small would cut it. And there is a physical floor beneath both. The workload's 838.8 MB of output must be written at least once; at an assumed 40 GB/s of memory bandwidth that takes about 21 ms, less if the output stays in the L3 cache for a caller that reads it at once.

The last row explains the rising floor. In the all-ideal configuration the oracles copy about 4.9 GB back to back, and every block takes several global locks on the oracles' stores; at 38–42 GB/s that traffic alone takes 115–145 ms. The follow-up run is built to remove it: its oracles hand over their answers without copying, and one configuration skips the expansion as well, so that Residuals A and B are measured rather than inferred (the floor run).

Measured on 26 November, the zero-copy floor run put both residuals beside the design analysis's forecasts, which stay above as registered before the data (the floor results; the true-floor post; the main post's note):

Residual B was the run's scored prediction under the rule frozen before the data (the floor run). It measured 5.2–5.7 ms across one to ten workers, or 2.7% of the shipped 194.6 ms decode at eight. That misses low at every count — whether compared against the floor report's 14–19 ms one-worker label or the per-count forecasts above — and closes pipeline plumbing as a target. Residual A was reported unscored. At one worker it exceeds its forecast because that configuration reads the oracles' stores cold from main memory: about 55–65 ms of its 298 ms word-spelling figure is that traffic, not the decoder's work (the cold-store reread, PR #952). From eight to ten workers Residual A stays flat (42.4, 42.9 and 40.5 ms), confirming that the earlier rise to 142 ms was the old oracles' copying. The previous table's last forecast row, for simultaneous copying and lock contention, is not re-derived here. The matrix and the floor run are separate runs, so subtracting across them would mix their noise.

items.title: 4. Contraction, enrichment and closure
items.text:
The main post introduces the two principles. Here are their limits, which matter as much as the principles do.

Contraction and its floor. The interval-exchange kernel contracts along runs of equal bytes in the last column: adjacent rows holding the same byte map to adjacent rows under LF, so a run moves as one interval. The floor called G1 says that rows with no such neighbour have nothing to contract with in that sense. Its scope is narrow: it bounds the operations charged in a calculus of rigid interval moves, not the decoder's unpredictable memory reads, and carrying it to machine cost needs a bridge theorem that holds for most of the old family of algorithms but not all of it (Posing the inversion problem, §2; the programme's statement). An implementation may keep the same interval facts and acquire or consume them more cheaply.

Closure and its negative answer. Composing the retained-row map once more, so that one step does the work of two, was the obvious next contraction. A representation of the composed map has to do three things: keep the successor lookups, the word payloads and the access schedule cheap; stay compact after composition on real blocks; and be built without following the transitions it replaces. On the first real block it failed the second: the composed map's access pattern needed 21 to 24 times as many address segments as the original, and its word storage nearly tripled. A conservation law in a later record explains why: a composition keeps the form of the access schedule but not its compactness on high-entropy rows. That answers the closure problem negatively, but only within the class of sweeps the record defines (the journal, §§42 and 48). It closes one route, not the idea of a different representation, and so the search turns to other notions of moving together: up to a consistent relabelling of bytes, along repeated stretches of the text, or through a recurrence among the induction's own steps.

Enrichment and its obstruction. An enrichment carries an extra quantity along an existing step, as dual numbers carry derivatives, and is worth having only if the quantity is cheaply acquired and is not the answer in disguise; a row's position in the text fails, since the decode exists to compute it. One tempting site is closed. Moving construction's work upstream into the serial scanner would let the scanner's idle knowledge of the block shorten the workers' job, but the final LF targets cannot be known before a block's last byte: changing that byte shifts the targets of 15.4% to 50.0% of the rows on every Wikidata block tested. And the Huffman scan, before move-to-front, determines every run length but none of the byte identities: permuting the symbol map with identical codes changes the target of every row (the design analysis, §4). These are limits on acquiring the final answer early. They are not an impossibility result for a summary gathered during the scan and finished cheaply once the block ends, which remains open.

items.title: 5. The four currencies of computation
items.text:
A candidate is priced in real machine cost, with the cost of building every structure it needs included (the formulation; Posing the inversion problem):

  • \(Q\), the unpredictable memory reads, whose address depends on data;
  • \(D\), the length of the longest chain of reads that must wait on one another;
  • \(P\), the passes over the data, with at most two allowed;
  • \(S\), the working state held at once.

The currencies separate two kinds of success. A large reduction in \(D\), more independent reads in flight, can make the decoder much faster on real hardware and is a real result. The programme's breakthrough is a reduction in \(Q\): fewer than one unpredictable read for each row with no same-byte neighbour, with half of one as the target, within two passes. The number of live cursors is limited to about one per letter of the alphabet, so a route that needs thousands of concurrent cursors to reach its figure is inadmissible. Charging acquisition matters most: an idea that removes reads in the decode by reading everything once more beforehand has moved its cost, not removed it.

The work's numbers are of four kinds, and they are not competing estimates of one quantity.

Kind What it establishes Example Lower bound under stated assumptions, a computation cannot cost less any order of the induction's steps takes at least 1.220 steps for each run (§6) Oracle measurement an observed counterfactual, with particular work supplied 125 ms at eight workers with the scanner and construction supplied Predictor an estimate of what a concrete design would cost 130–145 ms for a pooled scan with cheaper construction (§9) Upper bound under stated assumptions, completion takes no longer none proved yet for this decoder

Lower bounds prune the space of designs, oracle measurements say where the opportunity is, predictors rank the candidates, and upper bounds, when they exist, guarantee a result.

Numbers about one decode at eight workers, by kind

The lower bound is the design analysis's arithmetic for writing the output once at an assumed 40 GB/s; the oracle points are measured; the bars are forecasts, untested. The induction's 1.220 is a bound on steps, not milliseconds, so it has no place on this axis. No upper bound has been proved.

The four candidates below touch different parts of the workers' time, and what they touch bounds what they can be worth.

What each proposal touches, at one worker

items.title: 6. Alternative induction schedules
items.text:
The induction is the part of construction most open to mathematics, and its cost has an exact count. For every order in which its steps can be taken,

\[ \text{steps} = r_2 - 1 + U, \]

where \(r_2\) counts the distinct pairs of adjacent run letters, so that \(r_2 - 1\) is a floor no order can beat, and \(U\) counts the extra boundaries a particular order creates along the way (the induction record, §5.6). On all 233 Wikidata blocks, the historical order, which always takes the step at the right end, needs 1.812 steps for each run of the original column. An order that takes first the steps that create no new boundary, and otherwise the largest cell, needs 1.279, and the floor is 1.220. These counts were taken on the earlier full exchange over all run letters, not on the object the present kernel builds, which eliminates thick stretches and keeps thin rows.

The better order cuts the steps by \(1 - 1.279/1.812 \approx 29.4\%\). If the whole induction sub-phase, 216 ms at one worker, scaled with the step count, that would save \(216 \times 0.294 \approx 63.5\) ms, 4.9% of the 1,306 ms decode. Setup and the dictionary of words do not depend on the order, so writing \(f\) for the share of the sub-phase whose cost scales with the number of steps, and \(c\) for the new order's own cost,

\[ \text{net saving} \approx 216\ \text{ms} \times f \times 29.4\% - c . \]

The gate for pursuing the idea is 3% of the decode, 39.2 ms at one worker.

The economics of a cheaper induction schedule
