It assumes the historical cut transfers to the present kernel's object and that the reducible work scales in proportion to steps. The gate is crossed at 62%, 70% and 77% of the sub-phase for 0, 5 and 10 ms of scheduling overhead; at most 63.5 ms can be saved.

The schedule passes its gate only if at least about 62% of the sub-phase is step time that falls in proportion, before paying for the scheduling; with 5 ms of overhead the threshold is 70%. A short census measures that share on the object the decoder actually builds, and the idea stops if the share times the cut is under 3% (the census). A schedule with fewer steps can also lose the memory locality and the cheap sweep order of the present one, which the census's timings would show. This is the narrowest of the four proposals and its ceiling is modest, but the census that settles it is cheap.

items.title: 7. Deforestation across stages
items.text:
The move-to-front stage produces the block's runs capped at 127 bytes each, and construction's first pass immediately joins them back into maximal runs. Between the two sits an intermediate array, written in full and read back.

The direct fold: removing an intermediate representation

TodayMTF, RLE2decodes the symbolscapped runs, ≤ 127 eachwritten out, then read backconstruction, first passrejoins the maximal runs3,990–5,284 extra records a block, 3.5–10.2% of the runsabout 360 MB written and read back over the workloadThe direct foldMTF, RLE2emits each maximal run onceconstructionaccumulates the runs as they arrivedirectlyForecast (the design analysis): 110–145 ms at one worker; one pass and 180 KB a worker fewer.Rejection test: if the first pass's queue pushes, not the rejoining, take most of its time, stop. Design, not measured: today's three stages and the proposed two. The extra records and the traffic are the design analysis's counts on the Wikidata workload; the saving is its forecast.

The fold removes the intermediate representation where the fast path allows it: the move-to-front loop emits each maximal run once, and construction accumulates it directly into the counts and queues its later phases need, splitting only the run that contains the block's original-row pointer. Functional programmers call this deforestation, eliminating the intermediate data structure between two transformations. The present two-pass path stays as the fallback for blocks the kernel declines.

The capped runs add 3,990 to 5,284 records a block, 3.5–10.2% of the runs. Removing them saves one pass and about 360 MB of reads and writes over the workload, and 180 KB of state per worker. In the four currencies, \(Q\) and \(D\) are unchanged, since the move-to-front permutation is the same serial chain, and \(P\) and \(S\) fall. The forecast is 110–145 ms at one worker, about 8.5–11% of the workers' time, most of it in construction's first pass. The risk is branch misprediction in the move-to-front loop on the test for short runs, mitigated by how lopsided the run lengths are: in the workload's hexadecimal groups 83–85% of runs have length one, and in its template groups 98% exceed sixteen. The rejection test is a ten-minute profile that splits construction's first pass: if pushing rows into the queues takes more than 70% of it and the capping and rejoining take under 50 ms, the fold is dropped in favour of the wiring (the design analysis, §5).

items.title: 8. Forward wiring and multi-lane emission
items.text:
Construction's last sub-phase wires the retained rows into a cycle, and emission walks that cycle to write the text. Today each link is stored as the XOR of its two neighbours, \(\text{link}(i) = \text{prev}(i) \oplus \text{next}(i)\), which saves memory and lets emission walk from one mark in both directions at once. But a step along an XOR link must know where it came from, so each walk is a chain of dependent reads, only two of them in flight at a time, and wiring the links costs some 106 million scattered read-modify-writes on the Wikidata workload.

The proposal stores the successor alone, \(\text{link}(i) = \text{next}(i)\), which can be written sequentially, and walks the cycle forward only, in several lanes at once. The cycle is cut at \(K\) anchors chosen uniformly at random; each lane walks one arc from its anchor to the next, and a lane that finishes takes the next unvisited anchor. The arcs come out in the wrong order, so a final pass stitches them together and performs the run-length expansion and checksum segment by segment.

Two ends of one cycle, against forward lanes from many anchors

Today: two ends of one cycleforward from the mark over half the cyclebackward from the mark over the other halfthe mark: both walks start heremarkforwardand backwardXOR-linked: each link is prev ⊕ next,so a step must know where it came from;two chains of dependent reads at onceProposed: K anchors, forward lanesarc of 7% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 1arc of 14% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 2arc of 5% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 3arc of 22% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 4arc of 7% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 3arc of 16% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 1arc of 22% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 3arc of 7% of the cycle, walked forward by lane 2an anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts herean anchor: a lane starts hereK = 8 anchorsL = 4 lanesforward links only: link = next;a lane that finishes its arctakes the next unvisited anchorthe lanes, in time1lane 1: 0.07 of the cyclelane 1: 0.16 of the cycle2lane 2: 0.14 of the cyclelane 2: 0.07 of the cycle3lane 3: 0.05 of the cyclelane 3: 0.07 of the cyclelane 3: 0.22 of the cycle4lane 4: 0.22 of the cycledone at 0.34 man even split: 0.25 mLongest of K arcs,on average: m HK / KK = 8: 0.340 mK = 32: 0.127 m8 lanes, even: 0.125 m Conceptual: one cycle of retained rows. Right, an illustrative draw of eight anchors walked by four lanes; the timeline shows each lane's arcs. With only twice as many anchors as lanes, one lane still finishes well after an even split, which is why the design takes four times as many. The expected longest arc is the order-statistics result in the text.

There is real mathematics in choosing \(K\). Uniformly placed anchors cut a cycle of length \(m\) into uneven arcs, and the walk is not finished until its longest arc is. In the continuous-spacing model the expected longest of \(K\) arcs is

\[ \mathbb{E}[L_{\max}] \approx m\,\frac{H_K}{K}, \]

where \(H_K = 1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1K\) is the \(K\)-th harmonic number. With as many anchors as lanes, eight of each, the longest arc averages \(0.340\,m\), nearly three times an even share, and the eight lanes behave like three. With four times as many anchors, \(K = 32\), it falls to \(0.127\,m\), almost exactly the even share of \(m/8\). That is why the design takes many more anchors than lanes.

One change relieves several costs. Construction's wiring becomes sequential; emission gains several independent chains of reads to overlap, which the design analysis estimates lifts the reads in flight from about two to between six and seven; the backward expansion of words disappears; and the final pass can consume the segments directly. The forecast is about 120 ms from the wiring, 110–140 ms from the walk and 52–78 ms from the forward expansion, 280–340 ms in all at one worker, 21–26% of the workers' time, at the price of 1.0–1.5 MB of scratch per worker. In the four currencies, \(D\) falls by about a factor of three while \(Q\) is unchanged. The rejection test is a standalone harness on the 932 blocks of the workload that the kernel decodes: if the new path does not save at least 190 ms at one worker, because memory bandwidth saturates with four lanes, say, or because managing the segments eats the wiring's gain, it is dropped for a simpler prefetch on the present links (the design analysis, §5).

This proposal crosses a stage boundary, and it illustrates the experiment's lesson in miniature: a different consumer allows a cheaper structure to be built. It also illustrates the currencies. A walk in several lanes can make the decoder much faster without reducing the number of unpredictable reads, and if it does, the research question about reads remains open. Both outcomes deserve to be recorded as what they are.

items.title: 9. Dissolving the serial scanner
items.text:
The scanner oracle deleted the Huffman work from the decode. A pooled scan would not delete it; it would change where it is done. Today one thread decodes every block's Huffman codes in turn and hands the symbols to the workers through a queue. Pooled, a fast pass first finds where each block starts, and each worker then scans its own block before rebuilding it.

The pooled scan: the same work, redistributed

Today: one scanner thread, then the workerscompressedfilescanner threadHuffman, block after blocksymbolsqueueworker 1M · C · E · Rworker 2M · C · E · Rworker kM · C · E · Rreaderin orderPooled: each worker scans its own blockcompressedfileboundary finder48-bit block markerworker 1scan · M · C · E · Rworker 2scan · M · C · E · Rworker kscan · M · C · E · Rreaderin orderThe same Huffman work, spread over the workers' cores instead of one; the symbols queue, about 400 MB oftraffic, disappears. A wrong boundary is caught because each block must end where the next begins. Design, not measured. The pooled scan removes the serial station and the queue between it and the workers; the Huffman work itself remains, spread across the workers. A false marker inside compressed data is caught because each block must end exactly where the next begins.

Finding the blocks. A bzip2 block begins with a 48-bit marker, the digits of \(\pi\) in binary-coded decimal, but blocks are not byte-aligned, so the search runs over all eight bit alignments of the compressed file. The design analysis estimates 1–2 ms on the 47 MB workload with vector instructions, and bounds the chance of a false match by \(8\,|B|\cdot 2^{-48}\) for a file of \(|B|\) bytes, about one in a million here. A false match is caught rather than trusted: each block's decode must end exactly where the next block's marker begins, and on any mismatch the decoder falls back to a serial continuation from the true end.

Redistributing the work. Eight or nine workers each own a small scanning scratch and a window of a few megabytes of compressed input, and run scan, move-to-front, construction, emission and the final expansion locally before publishing their block; the count stays below ten to keep the working set inside the 20 MiB L3 cache. The symbols queue between scanner and workers, about 400 MB of traffic over the workload, disappears.

Why it interacts with construction. If a block costs \(s\) on the scanner and \(w\) on a worker, a serial scanner caps the throughput at \(1/s\) blocks per unit time however many workers there are, while \(k\) pooled workers, each doing both jobs, complete about \(k/(s + w)\). The knee puts \(w\) at about \(7.5\,s\), so at eight or nine workers, where the two stations are nearly balanced, pooling alone gains little in this model. As construction gets cheaper, though, \(w\) shrinks and the pooled rate rises, while the serial cap does not move. The pooled scan and cheaper construction are the main post's complementary pair, made into designs.

Why not enrich the scanner instead. Pushing construction's work into the serial scanner would lengthen the station already on the critical path; a fused Huffman and move-to-front scanner tried earlier slowed the scan from 74.5 ms to 107.9 ms and the whole decode by 18.5%. And §4's obstructions forbid computing the final LF targets before a block ends. Dissolving the boundary is the one move that touches both the scanner and construction; the induction and the wiring must still be attacked inside the workers (the design analysis, §4).

The forecast is 172–175 ms at eight or nine pooled workers on its own, 10–12% below today's 195 ms, and 130–145 ms combined with cheaper construction. The measured 125 ms with both parts supplied makes that a sensible scale to aim at, though it does not validate the forecast. The rejection tests are a five-minute timing of the marker search, which fails above 10 ms single-threaded, and a minimal prototype at eight and nine workers, which fails unless it beats 195 ms by at least 7% while keeping peak memory under 75 MB.

items.title: 10. Comparing the candidate algorithms
items.text:
Proposal Changes Forecast saving Extra cost Rejected if Induction schedule the order of the induction's steps at most 63.5 ms at one worker; gate 39.2 ms the schedule's own bookkeeping step share × cut < 3% of the decode Direct fold MTF and construction's first pass 110–145 ms at one worker branch mispredictions in the MTF loop queue pushes dominate the first pass, and capping and rejoining take < 50 ms Forward wiring with lanes wiring, emission, final expansion 280–340 ms at one worker 1.0–1.5 MB scratch a worker; stitching the arcs saves < 190 ms at one worker Pooled scan where the Huffman scan runs 172–175 ms at eight workers; 130–145 ms with cheaper construction the marker search; a compressed look-ahead window marker search > 10 ms, or < 7% faster than 195 ms

All four are forecasts by one analysis, with different degrees of support, and the one-worker figures say nothing directly about eight workers, where the scanner limits. Read with the experiment, they sort themselves. The fold and the forward wiring reduce the workers' demand and so lower the knee; the pooled scan removes the serial limit above it; and the largest prize lies in combining a worker-side reduction with the pooled scan. The induction schedule is narrow, but its census is the cheapest of the four measurements to run.

Three mathematical questions remain open behind them. The first is closure: whether some representation of composed retained-row transitions stays compact after composition, which §4's negative result rules out only within one class. The second is a notion of moving together other than equal adjacent bytes, which would change what the induction contracts along. The third is a deferred summary: a quantity gathered during the scan and finished cheaply once a block ends, which §4's obstructions leave open. A candidate that answered any of them would be priced in the four currencies of §5 and aimed, through the main post's matrix, at the part of the decoder where it could pay.

items.title: The decoder's true floor and a pooled scan
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 already decompresses at 4.31 GB/s on our eight-worker Wikidata benchmark, and almost none of the remaining cost is in the pipeline's plumbing. Queues, synchronisation and hand-offs account for only about 3% of the current 194.6 ms wall time when we isolate them with zero-copy stand-ins. Main-memory bandwidth is not yet the limiting factor on this machine, although L3 cache capacity matters. The implication is that the next substantial speedups must come primarily from making the algorithms themselves cheaper, rather than rearranging how they are coordinated.

This is the practical payoff of our hybrid-systems model and its design levers: distinguish the work done between events from the rules that move work between threads. Pooling the scan redistributes computation without eliminating it. The experiments instead expose a previously underestimated cost in spelling dictionary words into bytes, alongside opportunities to fuse construction and reduce cache traffic. The next milestone is to demonstrate a path towards 6 GB/s (about 140 ms for the same 838.8 MB of output, or 39% higher throughput). Supplying both scan and construction with idealised answers has already produced 135.3 ms, equivalent to 6.20 GB/s, but that is a diagnostic measurement, not a production speed or a promise that the target is attainable. The task now is to turn that measured headroom into real algorithmic gains.

In Complementary bottlenecks, we replaced each stage of mibz2's bzip2 decoder with a pre-recorded stand-in called an oracle. That factorial experiment showed where new algorithms could still speed up decoding. Its technical companion, From bottlenecks to better algorithms, turned those measurements into four candidate designs, including a pooled scan. Together, those two posts left two empirical questions open before any large redesign could start. First, how much of the earlier all-ideal floor belonged to mibz2's pipeline rather than to oracle copying? Second, would moving the serial Huffman scan into the worker pool unlock the 36% gain measured when scanning and construction improve together?

A short recap grounds both questions for a reader arriving cold. Decoding a bzip2 file moves each compressed block through six stages. One serial thread decodes Huffman symbols (S). A pool of parallel workers then undoes move-to-front coding and zero-run encoding (M) and builds the interval-exchange structures (C). Each worker walks those structures and expands their words into bytes (E, called emission in Open Returns), then finishes run-length expansion and checksums (R). Finally, an in-order reader copies completed blocks to the caller (D). As shown in The decoder as a queueing network, adding workers speeds decoding up until the bottleneck knee near 7.7 workers on earlier code. Below the knee, workers set the pace. At eight workers, where mibz2 ships on our 10-core Intel i9-10900K machine, the serial scanner and the workers are almost evenly matched.

Both open questions now have direct measurements on the same four-stream Wikidata file. That workload holds 47.4 MB compressed and expands to 838.8 MB uncompressed. Removing oracle copying and emission's leftover word expansion drops mibz2's all-ideal floor to roughly 5 ms at every worker count. It also refutes the suspected DRAM-bandwidth bottleneck between 8 and 10 workers, while revealing that 20 MiB L3 cache capacity does bind there. At the same time, it uncovers two large costs the first matrix could not see. Emission's word spelling is measured at 298 ms at 1 worker (an upper bound inflated by cold oracle reads; roughly 230 to 245 ms in situ). Real serial delivery starts near 29 ms on warm blocks, then climbs to 44–78 ms at 10 workers as unread blocks crowd the L3 cache. Testing the pooled scan behind ideal construction then ends in a narrow kill under its pre-registered gate. Pooling fails to remove scanning CPU; it merely moves that work onto workers that are already busy below nine threads.

This post reports both experiments and their consequences. Section 1 separates pipeline plumbing from oracle copying and settles the DRAM-bandwidth versus L3-capacity question. Section 2 measures each stage alone real and quantifies the newly exposed spelling, delivery and RLE1/CRC costs. Section 3 explains the prototype and why we tested it behind ideal construction. Section 4 presents every gate from the kill-test run. Section 5 derives the queueing arithmetic behind the 10-worker crossover and diagnoses cold-store bias in the paired-oracle test. Section 6 explains why the frozen verdict stands and sets out what we build next.

Takeaways

  • Pipeline plumbing is negligible. With zero-copy stand-ins replacing every stage and word spelling removed too, decoding takes 5.2 to 5.7 ms across every worker count. That is 2.7% of the shipped 194.6 ms wall at 8 workers. Queues, locks and hand-offs need no work.
  • DRAM bandwidth did not bind from 8 to 10 workers, though 20 MiB L3 capacity does. Removing 4.9 GB of oracle copying flattened the all-ideal wall with spelling kept to 42.4 ms at 8 workers and 40.5 ms at 10. Live memory traffic stayed at 13 to 17 GB/s. The earlier rise from 112 to 142 ms was a copying artifact; however, L3 capacity still binds at 8 to 10 workers for delivery and RLE1/CRC.
  • The serial scan caps worker-only gains at 8% at 8 workers, and two hidden costs scale in opposite directions beneath it. Keeping only the scan real takes 179.1 ms at 8 workers, or 92% of the shipped wall. Beneath it sits emission's parallel word spelling, measured at 298.2 ms at 1 worker (a cold-store upper bound; roughly 230 to 245 ms in situ) and shrinking to 37.2 ms at 8. Delivery's real serial copy-out goes the other way: traced at 29.1 ms at 1 worker and 34.0 ms at 8, it climbs to 43.7–77.9 ms at 10 workers as unread blocks evict L3.
  • The pooled scan missed its frozen gate narrowly, despite clean plumbing. All 10 exactness tests passed with zero dropped blocks and zero fallbacks. Peak memory stayed within 1.4% (passing K3), and the AVX2 marker finder took 4.82 ms at 9.84 GB/s (under half of K4's limit). Behind ideal construction, pooling captured 52% of the scan's room at 8 workers and 48% at 9. Its 95% confidence ceilings missed K1's half-capture bar by 0.009 and 0.042.
  • Pooling moves scanning CPU onto workers instead of removing it, so it wins only from slack. Pooled workers spent 173 to 193 ms scanning, matching the serial scanner's 171 to 190 ms. That extra load slowed standalone decoding below nine workers and broke even at 9 (1.000). Only at 10 workers, where shipped workers sat 20.2% idle, did pooling win (6.4% by geometric mean, P/none = 0.936; median wall fell 5.3% from 197.6 ms to 187.2 ms).

items.title: The decoder's true floor and the limits of a pooled scan
items.text:
Zero-copy stand-ins drop mibz2's plumbing floor to 5 milliseconds and uncover hidden spelling and cache costs, while pooling the scan pays off only from slack.

26 November 2026 · 19 min read · Research result

items.title: 1. How much of the first matrix's floor was the decoder's?
items.text:
In the first 44-arm matrix, making all six parts ideal left a steep residual wall. It took 391 ms at 1 worker and 94 ms at 6, then climbed from 112 ms at 8 to 142 ms at 10. Two artifacts contaminated those readings. First, the original oracles copied about 4.9 GB of pre-recorded answers into the decoder under global locks (Section 3 of the companion post). Second, the emission oracle skipped the graph walk yet left word-to-byte expansion running inside each worker. Because those costs were mixed together, the first matrix could not tell whether mibz2's pipeline plumbing was slow. It also could not tell whether main memory formed a third bottleneck above 8 workers.

To separate plumbing, copying and word spelling directly, we built zero-copy borrow oracles in PR #921. We then ran a 16-minute floor diagnostic, archived in PR #931 (the floor results). Instead of copying recorded buffers, each borrow oracle hands the next stage a borrowed slice. We also added a setting F (E_full) that skips word spelling alongside the graph walk.

Zero-copy borrow oracle. Rather than cloning recorded buffers under a lock for each block, a borrow oracle hands the downstream stage a read-only reference to pre-recorded memory. That strips replay traffic off the memory bus, though the downstream stage then reads cache lines that the real upstream stage would have warmed.

The run executed 648 decodes on the i9-10900K at six worker counts (1 and 6 through 10). Each cell ran across 8 randomised blocks, with traces on the first 4 and the scanner pinned to CPU 6. Every validity check passed. Every decode produced byte-identical output, and the scanner pin held in all 216 pinned traces. Removed parts kept at most 0.15% of their real busy time, well under the 5% void threshold. No F arm called word spelling, and live memory-controller counters stayed active throughout.

Second, DRAM bandwidth did not bind between 8 and 10 workers, though 20 MiB L3 cache capacity does. Arm SECMRD removes oracle copying while keeping word spelling (Residual A). Its wall time falls from 54.0 ms at 6 workers to 46.7 ms at 7. From 8 to 10 workers it stays flat at 42.4 ms, 42.9 ms and 40.5 ms. Live hardware counters confirm why. That extra traffic nudges SECMD's wall slightly upward (55.0 → 55.2 → 56.6 ms) while SECMRD stays flat (40.8, 42.4, 39.7 ms). That same L3 spill also slows real delivery copy-out, as Section 2 shows next.

Measured data (zero-copy floor run, i9-10900K, wikidata ×4; first-matrix baseline from the 44-arm run; traced delivery copy_out and A9 CPU from the pooled-scan traces). Visual analogy: taring a scale removes the shipping crates (4.9 GB of oracle copies and unremoved word spelling), revealing how light the tray itself is (5.2 ms) and how heavy each stage is alone. Where the analogy stops: pipeline stages overlap in time rather than summing like static weights (179 + 98 + 84 ms exceeds the 195 ms shipped wall), zero-copy borrowing leaves construction's store cache-cold for emission's walk, and traced delivery activity is not directly comparable to floor-arm wall differences.

items.title: 2. What remains when one stage at a time is real?
items.text:
Once the scale is tared down to 5.3 ms, enabling one real stage at a time exposes its isolated cost. The table below lists median wall times at 8 workers and 1 worker beside the shipped decoder. Where cold oracle stores or wall differences mask the live cost, traced real figures sit beside them.

Single real stage (all else free) Arm Median wall at 8 workers Median wall at 1 worker Shipped decoder (all real) none 194.6 ms 1,342.7 ms Scan FCMRD 179.1 ms (92% of wall) 169.7 ms Emission (walk + spelling; cold-store caveat) SCMRD 98.1 ms 694.2 ms Construction SFMRD 83.6 ms 609.5 ms Delivery (cold oracle store) SFCMR 52.3 ms (34.0 ms traced) 54.7 ms (29.1 ms traced) MTF / RLE2 SFCRD 20.1 ms 141.1 ms RLE1 / CRC (wall difference) SECMD − SECMRD 14.2 ms (104.0 ms traced CPU) 65.8 ms Nothing (plumbing alone) SFCMRD 5.3 ms (2.7% of wall) 5.8 ms

One caveat belongs right beside emission's row. Arm names list the ideal parts, so in construction's isolated arm (SFMRD), emission and its walk are free (A7 is 0.0 ms at every count). The cold reads happen in emission's isolated arm (SCMRD), where emission runs real against a zero-copy borrow of construction. In the shipped decoder, real construction warms its structures in the worker's caches right before emission walks them. In SCMRD, the walk (A7) reads construction's store cold from main memory. It takes 98.9 ms per worker at 8 workers against 72.4 ms as shipped, and 697.9 ms against 545.2 ms at 1 worker. Emission's isolated row (SCMRD) therefore overstates its standalone cost by roughly that warm-cache benefit. The serial scan's row (FCMRD) has no cross-stage cache distortion.

Four findings from this table and its companion traces reshape our priorities.

First, the serial scan imposes a hard ceiling at 8 workers. Running only the Huffman scan real (FCMRD) takes 179.1 ms at 8 workers. That is 92% of the shipped 194.6 ms wall. Even if every worker-side stage became free, 8-worker decoding could drop by at most 8% while scanning stays on one thread. This sharpens the first matrix's S × C result into a strict ordering rule. Worker-side optimisations cannot show their full gain at 8 workers until scanning leaves its serial station.

Second, emission's word spelling is a major hidden worker cost, though its oracle number is an upper bound. Subtracting Residual B from Residual A isolates E_consume, the loop that expands dictionary words into bytes. At 1 worker it measures 298.2 ms. It accounts for 98% of SECMRD at 1 worker and 87 to 90% from 6 workers up. The trace ledger matches directly at 299.7 ms for 1 worker and 39.8 ms per thread at 8 workers. Because workers run spelling in parallel, its wall time drops cleanly to 37.2 ms at 8 workers and 35.2 ms at 10. However, a cold-store check the same day (PR #952) showed that 298.2 ms is inflated by cold oracle reads. In SECMRD, workers spell from C's 120.6 MiB store and 425.1 MiB of recorded u32 codes. At 1 worker that reads 504.3 MiB from DRAM against 151.1 MiB for the entire shipped decode. In the first matrix's arm E, where construction is real and warm, consume_ns is already 41.5 ms lower (300.9 → 259.4 ms). Estimating across runs puts true in-situ spelling near 230 to 245 ms, or roughly 17 to 18% of the 1,342.7 ms 1-worker wall.

Third, delivery's real serial copy-out starts cheaper than the floor run suggested, then grows exactly as workers speed up. The floor run's flat 47.3 to 49.3 ms (SFCMR − SFCMRD) was a cold-store artifact corrected the same day (PR #952). There, the reader copied from the R oracle's 209.7 MiB store, over ten times the 20 MiB L3. Every worker count paid 5.1 million LLC load misses and 853.5 MiB of DRAM reads at roughly 17 GB/s. On real blocks in the pooled-scan bundle's traces (n = 3 per cell, ledgers on, medians), delivery behaves very differently. These are traced reader activity times rather than wall differences, so they are not directly comparable to the floor table's columns:

Workers Shipped none copy_out Fast workers PC / SC copy_out Ready-queue high-water (none / SC) 1 29.1 ms — 0.9 MiB / — 6 27.6 ms 29.8 / 29.0 ms 5.1 / 6.0 MiB 7 30.6 ms 33.7 / 32.5 ms 5.2 / 7.7 MiB 8 34.0 ms 40.0 / 39.5 ms 6.9 / 8.6 MiB 9 43.2 ms 51.5 / 54.9 ms 12.0 / 10.3 MiB 10 43.7 ms 67.4 / 77.9 ms 14.6 / 16.3 MiB

Delivery is cheap while workers are slow, and gets dearer precisely as they speed up. At 9 to 10 workers, the ready queue (READY_BYTES = 12 MiB) holds 12 to 16.3 MiB of unread blocks inside a 20 MiB L3. Those ready blocks spill to DRAM, where the single reader then competes with all ten workers.

Fourth, RLE1/CRC's modest wall difference hides a growing worker cost. Subtracting SECMRD from SECMD gives 14.2 ms at 8 workers and 65.8 ms at 1 worker as wall differences. In the pooled-scan traces, however, RLE1/CRC (A9) spends 104.0 ms of worker CPU at 8 workers in none, or 7% of worker CPU. At 10 workers that climbs to 133.0 ms in none, and to 191–216 ms in PC and SC. Whenever a block expands during run-length decoding, unrle_in_place runs four full-buffer passes, including two full writes. Under 8 to 10 workers, those writes spill dirty lines out of the 20 MiB L3 alongside ready blocks.

items.title: 3. Designing a pooled scan and testing a masked stage
items.text:
With the floor settled and the 179.1 ms serial scan confirmed at 8 workers, our first build target was clear. We set out to dissolve the serial scanner into the worker pool, as sketched in Section 9 of the companion post. Before writing code, we audited three earlier parallel-scan attempts recorded in the registration (§2). The first (bench-par-scan, 10 November) proved SIMD marker finding nearly free at 9.3 GB/s, or 0.19% of decode. On 10-worker level-9 Wikidata it stalled at 0.981 while workers were still slower than the scanner. The second (PR #741) beat shipped speed at 8 and 10 workers (0.935 and 0.883), yet slowed two to six workers (1.11–1.13). Its peak RSS also climbed to 1.28× at 10 workers and 1.99× at 20, probably from buffering the full input and holding \(4 \times \text{threads}\) blocks in flight. The third (PR #770) bounded memory with a lead scanner and two helpers, but serialised them behind one chain head. That nearly doubled scan CPU, slowed 8 to 20 workers by 54 to 61% (1.605× at 8 workers), and left workers roughly 40% idle.

Our new prototype (PR #932) avoided all three traps. As compressed chunks arrive, the feeder thread runs an AVX2 nibble filter to locate candidate block markers in bounded memory. No scanner thread, helper scanner or joiner thread exists. Each worker claims one candidate inside the shipped admission window and runs scan · M · C · E · R end to end. That eliminates the 190.6 MiB symbol queue between scanner and workers. The in-order reader accepts whichever ready block starts at the chain's exact next bit offset. On any false or missed marker, the reader falls back serially so exact bytes and exact errors always hold. At 1 worker, the prototype keeps the shipped path unchanged.

48-bit block marker. Every bzip2 block opens with the first twelve digits of \(\pi\) in binary-coded decimal (0x314159265359). Because blocks are bit-packed rather than byte-aligned, a boundary finder checks all eight bit shifts. The AVX2 nibble filter screens non-matching bytes at nearly 10 GB/s, and the reader verifies every decoded block against the exact bit-offset chain.

Testing this prototype fairly meant avoiding a measurement trap explained in Masked bottlenecks in a two-stage decoder. The design analysis had proposed killing any pooled scan that failed to beat shipped 8-worker decoding by 7% standalone. That test was impossible by construction. Even an ideal zero-cost scanner saves only 3.2% alone at 8 workers, because construction still limits the workers.

Instead, we froze a paired-oracle kill test in the registration before writing any code (also discussed in Dropping the coordinator). We paired the pooled scan P with construction's zero-copy oracle C, giving arm PC. We then compared PC/C against an ideal zero-copy scan behind C (SC/C). On a log scale, this asks whether pooling captures at least half of the multiplicative speedup that an ideal scan achieves once construction is free:

\[ \text{capture} = \frac{\ln(C / PC)}{\ln(C / SC)}, \qquad \text{K1 kills if } \text{UB}_{95\%}\!\left(\frac{PC}{C}\right) > \sqrt{\frac{SC}{C}}. \]

Log-scale capture. Because speedups multiply rather than add, half the room between C (ratio 1) and SC (ratio \(SC/C\)) is the geometric mean \(\sqrt{SC/C}\) rather than the arithmetic midpoint. Requiring the 95% confidence ceiling of PC/C to stay at or below \(\sqrt{SC/C}\) asks for statistical evidence of at least 50% capture, not merely a favourable point estimate.

Three companion gates guarded against earlier failure modes:

  • K2 (standalone cost). Kill if the 95% confidence floor of P/none exceeds 1.03 at a judged count.
  • K3 (memory). Kill if median peak RSS of P/none exceeds 1.10 at any count from 6 to 10.
  • K4 (finder speed). Kill if the single-threaded finder takes over 10 ms on the 47.4 MB input.

Section 1's floor run automatically set two switches in the registration before any prototype code ran. Because Residual A stayed flat from 8 to 10 workers, both 8 and 9 became judged counts. Both had to pass K1 and K2. Because Residual B was 2.7% (under 10%), capture remained capped rather than treating plumbing removal as extra scan capture.

items.title: 4. The kill test's verdict: KILL, narrowly, on K1
items.text:
The kill test ran 480 decodes across 12 randomised blocks on the i9-10900K in 15 minutes (the pooled-scan results). The first 3 blocks were traced unpinned, and an 11-pass pinned benchmark timed the finder alone. Every validity check passed. All 10 exactness tests passed on the test machine. Every pooled decode at 2 or more workers was wholly pooled, with zero dropped blocks, zero fallbacks and zero degraded decodes.

Every resource and plumbing gate passed as well. Peak memory stayed within 1.4% of shipped across 6 to 10 workers (0.988 to 1.014), passing K3 cleanly. On CPU 4, the AVX2 marker finder scanned the 47.4 MB input in a median 4.82 ms (interval [4.81, 5.00] ms). It processed 9.842 GB/s and located all 1,724 block markers plus 48 stream-end markers, under half of K4's 10 ms limit. Standalone cost passed K2 at both judged counts. At 8 workers P/none was 1.052, yet its 95% confidence floor (1.023) remained under 1.03. At 9 workers P/none hit exact break-even (1.000). In traces, candidate copying moved 45.2 MiB in 4.32 to 7.24 ms against a ~5 ms estimate. In-decode marker finding took 4.97 to 7.35 ms. The 190.6 MiB symbol queue disappeared, and at 8 to 10 workers the worker idle share (job_wait / life) fell from 6.5–20.2% in none down to 1.2–2.5% in P.

Yet K1 fired at both judged counts, killing the prototype narrowly under the frozen rule.

The margin was tight. Behind ideal construction at 8 workers, pooling cut median wall time from 183.2 ms down to 158.1 ms, against 135.3 ms for an ideal scan. Its point estimate captured 52.1% of the scan's room. Even so, its 95% ceiling (0.8758) sat 0.009 above the 0.8670 bar. At 9 workers (C = 184.2 ms, PC = 159.9 ms, SC = 140.2 ms), capture fell to 48.1%. Its ceiling (0.9058) missed the 0.8636 bar by 0.042. Only at 10 workers did pooling clear the bar cleanly. There it achieved 62.7% capture behind C and a 6.4% standalone win by geometric mean (P/none = 0.9357; median wall fell 5.3% from 197.6 ms to 187.2 ms).

Standalone walls also missed the companion post's unscored forecast. The design analysis had projected 172 to 175 ms at eight and nine workers. Measured block means were 207.5 ms at 8 workers (206.5 to 208.6 ms) and 195.2 ms at 9 workers (192.3 to 198.1 ms).

items.title: 5. Why pooling was not enough
items.text:
At first glance, missing K1 by 0.009 at 8 workers looks like noise or a small implementation tax. The per-thread traces show a much clearer picture. Pooling worked as engineered, with zero duplicated work, tiny worker idleness and roughly 5 ms of chain overhead. Two effects explain the results in Section 4: a conservation law on CPU time drives the standalone crossover, while an asymmetric cold-store bias distorted the paired-oracle capture denominator.

In traced decodes, the workers' summed scanning CPU (A2 + A3) in P matched the dedicated scanner's CPU in none at every worker count:

Workers Pooled workers' scan CPU (P) Dedicated scanner CPU (none) Worker idle share (none → P) 6 172.9 [172.2, 173.6] ms 171.3 [170.2, 172.3] ms 1.4% → 0.9% 7 174.1 [172.5, 175.7] ms 170.6 [170.3, 171.0] ms 1.9% → 1.2% 8 177.7 [175.1, 180.3] ms 177.5 [148.2, 206.8] ms 6.5% → 1.2% 9 182.8 [171.9, 193.8] ms 173.4 [160.6, 186.3] ms 10.1% → 1.6% 10 192.7 [181.9, 203.6] ms 189.6 [184.1, 195.2] ms 20.2% → 2.5%

Unlike PR #770, which nearly doubled scanning CPU, this prototype wasted nothing. It simply moved roughly 178 ms of scanning CPU off the dedicated scanner core and spread it across the \(k\) worker cores.

That move turns the two-station bottleneck model from Section 9 of the companion post into a sharp wall-time comparison. Let \(s\) denote total scanning CPU per decode and \(w\) denote total parallel worker CPU. Let \(\epsilon\) denote the small residual from marker finding, candidate copying and tail imbalance:

\[ T_{\text{serial}}(k) \approx \max\!\left(s,\ \frac{w}{k}\right), \qquad T_{\text{pooled}}(k) \approx \frac{s + w}{k} + \epsilon. \]

The model's first-order arithmetic accounts for the direction and the crossover. It is only a first-order guide, because \(w\) itself grows with \(k\). In none, total CPU climbs from 1.714 s at 8 workers to 2.007 s at 10. Likewise, S's wall implies \(w\) rising from roughly 1,480 ms at 8 workers to 1,700 ms at 10. Part of that climb is RLE1/CRC (A9) under L3 pressure. Its traced CPU in none rises from 89.5 ms at 6 workers to 104.0 ms at 8 and 133.0 ms at 10. Holding \(w\) constant therefore overpredicts the 10-worker gain.

Below the knee (\(w/k \ge s\)), pooling must lose. Workers already set the wall clock. Adding \(s/k\) of scanning to each worker lengthens the decode by 22 to 30 ms. Deleting the 190.6 MiB symbol queue cannot offset that, because Section 1 proved that all inter-stage plumbing costs only ~5 ms. In this run, the S arm (ideal scan, real workers) took 184.9 ms at 8 workers against \(s \approx 178\text{ ms}\). Workers therefore still bind at 8 workers here. Adding \(s/8\) onto that 184.9 ms worker load gives about 207 ms, matching the measured 207.5 ms mean. Standalone P slowed 6 and 7 workers by 10% and slowed 8 workers by 5.2%.

Above the knee (\(w/k < s\)), pooling wins only when workers have slack to absorb \(s/k\). Setting \((s + w)/k < s\) yields the zero-overhead break-even point:

\[ k > 1 + \frac{w}{s}. \]

From this run's S arm at 8 workers (\(w/8 \approx 184.9\text{ ms}\) against \(s \approx 178\text{ ms}\)), the knee sits at \(w/s \approx 8.3\). That puts zero-overhead break-even near \(k \approx 9.3\). The earlier 25 November queueing post measured \(w/s \approx 7.67\) on older code, putting break-even near 8.7. Both agree within a worker: pooling loses at 8 workers and breaks even near 9, where P/none measured 1.000. At \(k = 10\), shipped workers sat 20.2% idle waiting on the serial scanner. Absorbing \(192.7 / 10 \approx 19.3\text{ ms}\) of scanning per worker fit inside that slack. Worker idleness fell to 2.5%, delivering a 6.4% win by geometric mean (P/none = 0.9357). Median wall time fell 5.3% from 197.6 ms to 187.2 ms.

Behind ideal construction, \(s/k\) explains the PC − SC gap, while a cold-store bias depressed capture. Making construction ideal (C) shrinks \(w\) enough that PC beats C by 14% at 8 workers. An ideal scan (SC) deletes scanning CPU completely, whereas a pooled scan still pays \(s/k\). At 8 workers, adding \(177.7 / 8 = 22.2\text{ ms}\) to SC's 135.3 ms predicts 157.5 ms against a measured PC of 158.1 ms. At 9 workers, adding \(182.8 / 9 = 20.3\text{ ms}\) to SC's 140.2 ms predicts 160.5 ms against PC at 159.9 ms. Both PC and SC pay that difference cleanly. Yet the ~50% capture figure itself was depressed by an asymmetric cold-store bias uncovered in PR #952. Zero-copy C forces the emission walk (A7) to read construction's store cold in every C arm. At 8 workers, traced A7 rose by +220.4 ms (PC − P) and +196.2 ms (SC − S). At 9 workers those jumps reached +293.9 ms and +257.7 ms. PC and SC are worker-bound (job_wait just 3.6 and 0.2 ms per worker at 8), so their walls pay that entire bloat. C alone is scanner-bound (job_wait 50.6 ms per worker at 8 and 91.8 ms at 9), so its wall absorbs the bloat completely. That asymmetry shrinks the C − SC denominator that capture divides by. Subtracting the traced bloat shifts 8-worker capture from 0.52 to roughly 0.73. That diagnostic bound shows pooling is not structurally capped near 50%, though it is not a re-grade of K1.

Where the analogy stops: CPU cores share a 20 MiB L3 cache, pay ~5 ms each for boundary finding and candidate copying, and still commit finished blocks strictly in order.

items.title: 6. Keeping the verdict and what comes next
items.text:
Even knowing that cold-store C biased K1 downward, honouring the frozen KILL verdict is both sound method and the right engineering decision.

Pre-registered kill test. Freezing the decision rule before running the benchmark stops a team from moving the goalposts after seeing data. When a prototype misses a frozen gate or uncovers a measurement bias, the right move is to diagnose the cause and register a better test or design, not to re-grade the old run.

Even setting K1 aside, standalone P/none measured 1.052 at 8 workers. Shipping the prototype behind an 8-worker flag would therefore ship a 5% slowdown where mibz2 defaults. Dissolving the dedicated scanner forces \(k\) workers to absorb \(s\) on top of \(w\), which taxes any worker count without slack. The same rule governs any streaming pipeline with a dedicated serial parser costing \(s\) and a worker pool costing \(w\). Removing the parser breaks even at \(k^* = 1 + w/s\) before overhead. It loses whenever \(k < 1 + w/s\) and wins only when \(k > 1 + w/s\). To win on both sides of the knee, a pipeline has two clean options. It can shrink \(w\) until \(1 + w/s\) drops below the target worker count. Alternatively, it can keep the dedicated parser alive and let workers help only from idle slack. There is also a clear experimental lesson for future gates. A paired-oracle kill test must not set a worker-bound candidate against a scanner-bound cold-store baseline, or asymmetric cache bloat will bias capture against the candidate.

Together, the zero-copy floor run, the pooled-scan kill test and the cold-store analysis close three blind alleys and lay out a clear order for our next work:

  • Closed targets. Pipeline plumbing (~5 ms, 2.7% of wall) needs no attention. The three-station DRAM-bandwidth hypothesis is not supported at 8–10 workers, though 20 MiB L3 capacity does bind for delivery and RLE1/CRC. Unconditional full pooling stops as built under its frozen K1 verdict.
  • Shrink worker demand \(w\) first. Lowering worker CPU speeds up 1–7 workers at once and pulls \(1 + w/s\) below 8 workers so scanning relief pays off where mibz2 ships. Four worker-side targets are open. Emission's word spelling (~230–245 ms estimated in situ) leads the list; its parts have since been measured by the spelling census (PR #951) and the Rauzy output census (PR #958). Beside it sit folding move-to-front into construction's first pass and forward wiring with multi-lane emission. The fourth target is single-pass RLE1/CRC to end unrle_in_place's four-pass L3 spill (104 ms of traced CPU at 8 workers).
  • Test a slack-only hybrid scanner under a warm paired baseline. Keep the dedicated scanner thread so saturated workers at six to eight cores never pay a scanning tax. Let workers claim look-ahead candidates with the proven 4.82 ms AVX2 marker finder only when they would otherwise wait in job_wait. Scanning CPU is then spent strictly from slack. Full pooling can also be re-tested under a fresh registration once worker-side cuts lower \(w\) and a warm baseline removes cold-store bias.
  • Contain L3 eviction in delivery and consider exposing zero-copy lending. Real delivery copy-out already climbs from 34.0 ms at 8 workers to 67.4–77.9 ms at 10 when faster workers pile 12–16 MiB of ready blocks into the 20 MiB L3. Zero-copy block lending already exists internally at StreamDecoder::read_block (src/parallel.rs:880, #[doc(hidden)]) and publicly through BzReader's BufRead (characterised in PR #966). The immediate no-API lever is tightening the READY_BYTES working-set cap so ready blocks stay L3-hot. Exposing read_block publicly remains an open API decision beside it.

Sources:

  • Zero-copy floor (PR #921, PR #931): floor results, report and raw table.
  • Pooled-scan kill test (PR #932, PR #942): registration, results and report.
  • Cold-store and L3 analysis (PR #952, PR #954, PR #966): cold-store and RLE1 LLC report, delivery characterisation, spelling census and Rauzy output census.
  • Earlier parallel scans: PR #741 and PR #770, summarised in the registration.

  • Earlier decoder posts: The decoder as a queueing network, Masked bottlenecks, Open Returns and Huffman decoding.
  • Reproducible figures and measured surface: figures_floor_and_pooled_scan.py, surface.tsv and dead-ends.tsv.

items.title: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Two measurements from primary traces sharpen where mibz2 should spend its next engineering effort. First, moving off our Wikidata benchmark exposes a blind spot. Across seven other corpora, 84% of full blocks bypass the Open inverse-BWT kernel completely, and every block in Open's dense admission band is refused after paying for a failed first pass. Second, replaying per-block timestamps at eight workers on Wikidata explains the 8 to 9 millisecond gap between shipped wall time and the bottleneck lower bound. Most of that gap is either already targeted by our seam-window patch or part of an irreducible queueing floor, leaving no hidden 3% lever in pipeline coordination.

Both findings follow directly from The decoder's true floor and the limits of a pooled scan. That post established that on our 10-core Intel i9-10900K machine, decoding four copies of Wikidata (838.8 MB uncompressed) at eight workers puts the serial Huffman scanner (S) and the eight workers (W/8) in a near-exact tie near 185 ms, while shipped wall time sits at 192.9 to 194.6 ms. Two natural questions remained open: how much of our Wikidata-tuned worker surface actually runs on ordinary files, and whether the 8 to 9 ms coupling gap at the eight-worker tie hides an unowned speedup.

This post answers both from primary evidence. Section 1 reports the off-Wikidata route census and the exact cost of dense-band refusals. Section 2 corrects a common accounting mistake about our 5.2 ms plumbing floor and validates a discrete-event replay of the parallel decoder. Section 3 isolates the two mechanisms driving mid-stream stalls and prices the remaining floor at a future 150 ms tie. Section 4 sets out the concrete changes these measurements justify.

Takeaways

  • Off Wikidata, Open runs on only 16% of full blocks. Across seven local corpora (107 full blocks), 90 blocks run the Segmented fallback instead of Open, and all 25 blocks in Open's dense band (\(r/n \in [0.15, 0.28]\)) are refused after running Open's first pass to its cap.
  • Dense-band refusals cost 13 to 48% extra inverse time on refused blocks. On ordinary prose, that wasted pass makes production 1.09 to 1.32 times slower than Segmented alone. A single pass over the run records predicts every refusal before Open begins.
  • Do not subtract 5.2 ms of empty-pipeline plumbing from the eight-worker tie gap. When real work runs, per-block handoffs overlap behind active stages. Unoverlapped handoff overhead is only 1.12 to 1.16 ms.
  • Chunk maintenance amplifies the eight-worker tie by about 2.15 ms. Eleven discrete 0.53 to 1.54 ms copy-and-drain stalls in ChannelSource::view skew the scanner across the four corpus copies. Removing them via a reused seam buffer recovers that coupling loss on top of its 10 to 11 ms direct scan reduction.
  • No standalone 3% lever hides in the remaining coupling gap. Post-seam at a balanced 150 ms tie, about 4.5 ms is an irreducible queueing, startup and handoff floor. The remaining unowned levers (runt-exempt slots and a smaller initial read chunk) cap near 2.5 ms combined, or 1.6% of wall time.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie: route refusals and coupled stalls
items.text:
Off Wikidata, 84% of full blocks bypass our Open kernel and pay dense refusals while trace replay decomposes the eight-worker tie.

27 November 2026 · 8 min read · Research result
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 1. What happens when the decoder leaves Wikidata
items.text:
Almost every worker-side speedup we have measured so far targets the Open Returns inverse-BWT kernel (OpenCells). On our Wikidata benchmark (corpora/wikidata.bz2, 431 blocks), all 233 full blocks enter Open because their run-to-row ratio \(r/n\) sits near 0.068. To test how often Open actually runs on other data, we ran a route census across Wikidata and seven container-built bzip2 -9 corpora spanning prose, source code, JSON, binaries, DNA and random bytes.

Each full block (\(n \ge 100{,}000\)) takes one of three routes:

  1. Column route (Segmented): move-to-front keeps the flat BWT column because runs are too short to compress into run records.
  2. Open route (OpenCells): run records pass admission and stay within Open's retained-row and thick-strip caps.
  3. Run-route fallback (Segmented): run records enter the run path, fail Open's gates or its dense-band cap, and fall back to Segmented inversion.
Corpus Full blocks Column (Segmented) Open Run-route fallback (Segmented) \(r/n\) p10 / p50 / p90 wikidata 233 0 233 0 0.063 / 0.068 / 0.115 prose 8 0 1 7 0.162 / 0.170 / 0.175 pysrc 11 1 1 9 0.226 / 0.294 / 0.314 rustsrc 16 0 8 8 0.053 / 0.158 / 0.229 json 16 5 7 4 0.053 / 0.070 / 0.217 elf 33 27 0 6 0.232 / 0.261 / 0.413 dna 14 13 0 1 0.724 random 9 9 0 0 —

The split is stark. Off Wikidata, Open admits only 17 of 107 full blocks (16%). The column route takes 55 blocks and the run-route fallback takes 35, putting 84% of non-Wikidata full blocks onto the Segmented kernel. Where Open does admit a block off Wikidata, it wins cleanly: 0.38 times Segmented on json (\(r/n < 0.15\)) and 0.76 times on rustsrc, matching its 0.48 ratio on Wikidata.

The real surprise sits in the dense band (\(r/n \in [0.15, 0.28]\)). In Admitting dense blocks to Open, we added a bounded cap (Cap::dense: at most \(\min(256{,}000, 0.3n)\) retained rows and 16,384 thick strips) fitted to Wikidata's five dense blocks. All five Wikidata blocks pass that cap and finish in 0.78 times Segmented's time. Off Wikidata, however, all 25 blocks in the dense band fail the cap — after Open has already executed its first pass up to the limit.

Corpus and dense-band outcome Blocks Production inverse (ms) Segmented inverse (ms) Ratio prose (refused) 7 21.0 17.1 1.23 rustsrc (refused) 8 28.0 20.6 1.36 json (refused) 4 17.6 11.8 1.48 elf (refused) 4 16.4 14.5 1.13 pysrc (refused) 2 7.0 6.9 1.02 wikidata (admitted) 5 11.4 14.6 0.78

(Single-thread timings on a 4-vCPU Xeon VM, production vs Segmented on the same blocks; shares and ratios are diagnostic, not workstation adoption evidence.)

Those 25 refused blocks waste about 19 ms (~0.8 ms per block), or 13 to 48% on top of the fallback's own inverse time. On the whole prose file, production finishes 1.09 to 1.32 times slower than running Segmented directly. Yet the refusal is completely predictable before Open allocates or scans anything. Retained rows are simply the rows belonging to maximal runs of at most 16 bytes, plus the marked row. Summing thin runs across the run records in one cheap pass separates the two populations cleanly: every refused block exceeds 256,000 retained rows (the smallest is 257,495 on elf, and prose spans 311,318 to 380,411), while every admitted Wikidata block lies between 199,189 and 231,600. Thick strips never bind (at most 8,081 against 16,384).

This reveals a sharp corpus asymmetry. Serial Huffman scanner improvements benefit every corpus equally because every route reads the same compressed bitstream. Open-kernel worker speedups cover 100% of Wikidata's full blocks but only 16% off Wikidata. Fixing the dense-band pre-check and dissecting the unowned Segmented fallback are therefore essential for ordinary text and source code.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 2. Why the eight-worker tie leaves 8 to 9 ms on the table
items.text:
Turning back to eight workers on Wikidata (wikidata ×4, 1,724 blocks, 838.8 MB output on our i9-10900K), the operational lower bound is

\[ L = \max\!\left(S,\;\frac{W}{k}\right), \]

where \(S\) is total serial scanner busy time and \(W/k\) is mean worker busy time across \(k = 8\) workers. Across three primary i9-10900K evidence bundles — character stage 1 (48 grid runs plus 4 complete nanosecond per-block traces), the zero-copy floor (cc8ba137), and the pooled-scan run (c71c4a56) — shipped wall time exceeds \(L\) by 7.6 to 9.1 ms (4.0 to 4.7% of wall):

Primary i9-10900K bundle (k = 8, medians, ms) Untimed wall Traced wall scan_busy wkr_busy/8 wall − max slot_wait (waits) in_wait job_wait/8 character-stage1 grid none (\(n = 48\)) — 192.27 184.45 182.67 7.57 3.25 (13) 1.39 8.41 character-stage1 traced r0–r3 mean — 195.61 184.99 185.64 9.13 5.20 (19) 1.43 9.57 zero-copy-floor none (pinned CPU 6) 194.57 194.36 184.35 186.35 8.01 6.10 (24) 1.26 6.94 pooled-scan none (unpinned) 192.93 193.72 184.79 184.86 8.86 4.11 (14) 1.34 8.50 pooled-scan S (scan ideal, workers bind) 184.88 185.35 1.61 184.19 1.16 180.14 (1,342) 0.00 0.22 pooled-scan SC (scan + construction ideal) 135.31 133.30 1.46 132.18 1.12 129.15 (1,256) 0.00 0.23

That table immediately corrects a tempting accounting error. It is easy to subtract our all-ideal SFCMRD plumbing floor (5.2 ms) from the 9.1 ms gap and assume only ~3.9 ms is queueing loss. That subtraction is wrong. In SFCMRD, all 5.2 ms sit exposed because no real decoding work runs alongside them. As soon as real worker stages run (S and SC above, or SFMRD at 0.88 ms and SECMRD at 0.69 ms), per-block handoffs (issue 0.65 ms, pool+publish 0.07 ms per worker, and mutex acquisitions of 0.3 ms scanner / 0.06 ms worker) overlap behind real compute. The true unoverlapped handoff residual above \(L\) is only 1.12 to 1.16 ms.

To break down the rest of the 9.13 ms gap without guessing, our coupling dissection built a discrete-event simulator implementing the exact admission guard (Shared::full), FIFO job queue (Jobs), \(k\)-worker pool, and in-order Ready ring from src/parallel.rs. Fed the recorded per-block service times from all four traced rounds (blocks-r00 to blocks-r03), the replay tracks real wall time to within 0.94 to 1.36 ms (mean +1.15 ms, matching S and SC's handoff residual):

Round (k = 8) \(S\) (ms) \(W/8\) (ms) \(L = \max\) Real wall (slot_wait) Replay wall (slot_wait) Real − Replay r0 183.99 188.31 188.31 198.89 (9.61) 197.53 (8.72) +1.36 ms r1 183.24 182.58 183.24 192.02 (3.27) 190.93 (2.56) +1.09 ms r2 184.13 181.43 184.13 192.33 (2.18) 191.11 (1.46) +1.21 ms r3 188.59 190.24 190.24 199.21 (5.74) 198.27 (5.10) +0.94 ms Mean 184.99 185.64 186.48 195.61 (5.20) 194.46 (4.46) +1.15 ms

Because the replay reproduces real wall time and slot_wait closely across all four rounds, toggling one pipeline rule at a time isolates each physical source of delay.
