items.title: 3. Chunk maintenance stalls and runt-diluted slots
items.text: Four mechanisms explain the entire gap above \(L\).
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 1. Stop-the-world chunk maintenance creates a mid-decode phase inversion (~2.15 ms coupling bonus)
items.text:
Whenever a block's lookahead crosses a 4 MiB input chunk boundary, ChannelSource::view (src/parallel.rs) drains the buffer and copies the incoming chunk on the serial scanner thread (in_maint: 10.1 to 11.2 ms at eight workers). In the per-block traces, that 10.1 ms is not smooth overhead. It arrives as 11 discrete stop-the-world stalls of 0.16 to 1.54 ms, heavily front-loaded across the four identical 431-block copies as the window buffer grows and faults pages:

\[ \text{in\_maint}(c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3) = (3.81,\; 3.09,\; 1.86,\; 1.40)\;\text{ms}. \]

That slope pulls scanner time from 48.74 ms on copy 0 down to 44.61 ms on copy 3, while worker time changes far less (47.95 to 45.22 ms). On copies 0 and 1, the scanner falls behind and starves the workers. On copies 2 and 3, the scanner surges ahead and hits the admission window. In the exact-tie replay (\(S = W/8\), zero startup), removing in_maint drops the mid-stream coupling gap from 6.61 ms to 4.46 ms — a 2.15 ms coupling bonus that our seam-window patch captures automatically on top of its 10 to 11 ms direct scan cut.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 2. Runt blocks dilute the 32-slot window (1.21 ms at a 150 ms post-seam tie)
items.text:
Wikidata is not clustered into bursts of full blocks and bursts of tiny runts. Its 233 full blocks (~900 KB) and 198 runts (median 8 to 30 bytes) alternate almost everywhere (F.F.F.F…; max runt streak is 2). Yet Shared::full counts every block equally against SLOTS_PER_THREAD × k = 32 slots. As a result, 15 to 16 of the 32 slots always hold tiny runts, leaving only 15 to 17 full blocks of slack.

Meanwhile, READY_BYTES (12 MiB) never fires at eight workers: slot_cap is 0.00 ms across all 48 grid runs, and median peak ready bytes is only 6.01 MiB. Every single slot_wait at eight workers is a 32-slot head-of-line stall caused by one slow executing block (such as block offsets 56, 171, 278, and 389, taking 2.1 to 3.4 ms). While that single worker finishes, the scanner runs 32 places ahead (offsets 88, 203, 310, and 421) and blocks.

Importantly, slot_wait and worker job_wait are sequential, not simultaneous. Intersecting the exact nanosecond intervals in blocks-r00 through blocks-r03 shows mean worker idle time during slot_wait is only 0.033 to 0.042 ms in rounds 1 to 3 (matching pooled-scan's 0.04 ms). Every worker is busy while the scanner waits, and the lost scanner time reappears downstream as worker starvation once the slow block clears.

Expanding the window to 64 slots — or exempting tiny runts from the 32-slot count — captures 100% of the infinite-window wall saving. Today (with in_maint still present) that saves 2.10 ms (1.08%); at a future 150 ms exact tie after the seam window lands, it saves only 1.21 ms (0.77%). Trying to inline runt decoding onto the scanner thread makes wall time worse (+1.12 ms) because it adds worker CPU directly onto the tied serial scanner.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 3. Startup and the 4 MiB initial read chunk (2.62 ms total; 1.35 ms recoverable)
items.text:
Startup accounts for 2.41 ms median across 48 runs (2.62 ms mean in r0–r3), split into two pieces:

  • 1.22 ms spawning k + 2 OS threads before the scanner starts block 0 (a one-shot per-stream cost that amortises to zero on larger inputs);
  • 1.40 ms of block-0 in_wait (1.26 to 1.40 ms across all three bundles), because the feeder thread (src/read.rs) allocates a fresh 4 MiB buffer and reads all 4 MiB before pushing chunk 0, while the scanner and all eight workers sit idle waiting for a ~25 KiB first block.

Starting with a smaller first chunk (for example 256 KiB before ramping to 4 MiB) recovers about 1.35 ms (0.68% today; 0.86% at a 150 ms tie), once per stream.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 4. The irreducible queueing floor and cross-talk
items.text:
Even with infinite slots, zero startup, and zero in_maint, a balanced 150 ms tie still pays 2.19 ms (1.44%) above \(L\): about 0.7 ms for one-block fill and drain, 0.6 ms from full-vs-runt size bimodality, and 0.9 ms from within-class block-time variance and eight-worker end-of-stream finish spread. Adding thread spawn (1.22 ms) and unoverlapped handoff overhead (~1.1 ms) gives an irreducible floor near 4.5 ms.

Cache cross-talk between the scanner and workers is also smaller than it looks at first glance. Comparing pinned none against scan-alone FCMRD at eight workers (zero-copy-floor) shows scanner active time rising by +9.67 ms: +4.16 ms is in_maint memory contention (already removed by the seam window), +1.50 ms is the 4.95 → 4.90 GHz all-core turbo step, and +4.46 ms in Huffman decode (A3) is a one-worker cross-core free_syms coherence handoff that is already present at \(k = 1\) and stays completely flat (746 to 752 Gcycles) from 6 to 10 workers. Worker-side cross-talk from the scanner is only +0.67 ms (S vs none).

Component of the 8-worker coupling gap Today (r0–r3, ~195.6 ms) Future 150 ms tie (post-seam, ~157.5 ms) Status / ceiling in_maint coupling amplification ~2.15 ms 0.00 ms Covered by seam-window patch 32-slot HOL window (runt dilution) ~2.10 ms 1.21 ms (0.77%) Unowned; runt-exempt 32 slots Block-0 in_wait (4 MiB first chunk) 1.40 ms 1.35 ms (0.86%) Unowned; one-shot startup OS thread spawn (t_first_scan_start) 1.22 ms 1.22 ms (0.77%) Irreducible per decode call Indivisible-block variance & drain tail ~1.11 ms 2.19 ms (1.39%) Irreducible queueing floor Handoff / wakeup residual (Real − Replay) 1.15 ms ~1.1 ms (0.7%) Closed plumbing residual Total coupling gap 9.13 ms (4.67%) ~7.5 ms (4.8%) Combined unowned ceiling: ~2.5 ms (1.6%)
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: 4. What changes next
items.text:
Together, these two measurements close a dead-end temptation and open a neglected axis of real performance work:

  1. Do not chase a standalone coupling project at eight workers. Once the input seam window removes in_maint and its 2.15 ms coupling bonus, the remaining unowned coupling mechanisms cap near 2.5 ms (1.6% at a 150 ms tie). Reaching our 6 GB/s (~140 ms) research milestone still depends on algorithmic cuts to both the scanner and the workers.
  2. Keep READY_BYTES distinct from SLOTS_PER_THREAD when tuning L3 cache pressure. Because READY_BYTES never fires at eight workers while 32 slots already suffer runt-diluted head-of-line stalls, shrinking SLOTS_PER_THREAD below 4 would regress eight-worker throughput unless runts are excluded from the slot count. Bounding READY_BYTES alone protects 9-to-10-worker L3 residency without hurting eight workers.
  3. Fix dense-band refusals and map the Segmented fallback. A one-pass thin-run pre-check removes the 13 to 48% dense-band regression on prose and source code with zero Wikidata impact, and a dedicated phase dissection of Segmented now targets the 84% of non-Wikidata blocks that our Wikidata-only surface never showed.
  4. Land the seam window first on the workstation queue. It removes 10 to 11 ms of serial in_maint copy work plus 2.15 ms of coupling distortion, giving both the worker-side fold test and the combined scanner improvements a clean, stationary baseline.
path: Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie

items.title: Reopening Open's middle and off-Wikidata
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Four merged results show how research persistence works in both directions. Off Wikidata, we shipped a safe cap precheck that removes wasted work on refused dense blocks. We also dissected the Segmented fallback into a zero-memory stack that cuts prose and source decoding by 15.4 to 16.1%. Back inside Wikidata's Open kernel, redesigning all three sub-phases of its middle stage together reopens a phase that earlier isolated tweaks could not push past 3%. In parallel, a rescue of contracted return-map constructors trimmed real waste yet stopped cleanly once a bare pointer-chasing floor exceeded the budget.

This post builds on Off Wikidata and inside the eight-worker tie and Complementary bottlenecks. One evidence boundary matters up front. The dense-band cap precheck (#1040) is already merged into production and measured on pinned CI hardware. The Segmented dissection (#1042), the A6b redesign (#1046) and the contraction rescue (#1038) are diagnostic VM probes with exactness verified on every tested block. Both passing probes now move to production build pull requests and 10-core Intel i9-10900K workstation confirmation.

Section 1 covers the shipped dense-band precheck, Segmented's three-lever comeback and why a two-step LF² table failed. Section 2 explains how combining all three A6b sub-phases cuts A6b by 27.4 to 28.8% with zero unsafe. Section 3 contrasts that win with #1038's scoped stop on contracted return-map constructors. Section 4 sets out the admitted follow-on builds and workstation checks.

Takeaways

  • Dense-band refusals off Wikidata are gone (#1040, shipped). Checking the dense-band cap from run records cuts median refused-block inverse time from 1.536× to 1.027× with zero unsafe. On pinned CI hardware, four-thread text runs 3.7% faster and Wikidata stays unchanged.
  • Segmented fallback drops 15.4 to 16.1% on prose and source (#1042, PASS). Sequential LF construction, AVX2 reverse assembly and invariant-checked run fills speed all 78 off-Wikidata Segmented blocks by 18.4 to 18.5% at zero extra memory. A 2-step LF² table blows up construction 3.9 to 4.2×.
  • Reopening C-A6b needed all three sub-phases together (#1046, PASS). Fused setup, safe fixed-size Box<[T; 65536]> u16-link inline15 SoA steps and generation-tagged caches cut A6b by 27.4 to 28.8%. Full C+E drops 5.4 to 7.6% with zero unsafe and zero A7 regression.
  • Layout and deduplication both matter in A6b. Structure-of-arrays beats 24-byte and 32-byte array-of-structures layouts by 4 to 7 ms. Dropping contents deduplication inflates dictionary entries by 73.3% and regresses downstream emission.
  • Persistence includes knowing when a floor binds (#1038, scoped STOP). Cleaning up contracted return-map construction cut contraction by 9.0 to 13.9% and fixed runs.bz2. Even so, bare 4-lane pointer chasing alone takes 30.6 ms and already exceeds the ~24 to 25 ms VM budget.

items.title: Reopening Open's middle and the off-Wikidata decoder
items.text:
A safe fixed-size redesign cuts Open's middle stage by 28% and a fallback stack speeds off-Wikidata blocks by 16%, while contraction hits a floor.

27 November 2026 · 8 min read · Research result

items.title: 1. Off Wikidata: dense-cap precheck and Segmented's 16% comeback
items.text: Our previous post showed a stark corpus split. On Wikidata, every full block enters our Open Returns kernel. Off Wikidata, most full blocks fall back to the Segmented inverse-BWT decoder. Worse, every off-Wikidata block in Open's dense band (\(r/n \in [0.15, 0.28]\)) paid for a failed first pass of Open before falling back.

items.title: Eliminating dense-band refusal penalties (#1040)
items.text:
The first fix is already shipped in src/open.rs and recorded in the dense-cap-precheck delta. A safe single-pass helper called within_cap counts retained thin-run rows and thick strips straight from the run records. It runs only in the dense admission band (cap.m != u32::MAX) and adds zero unsafe code.

We measured 24 dense-band refused blocks across five local corpora (prose, pysrc, rustsrc, json and elf) over seven interleaved repeats. The median per-block ratio against direct Segmented fell from 1.536× to 1.027×. The summed inverse-time ratio fell from 1.404× to 0.984×, leaving every corpus at 1.040× or below:

Corpus (refused dense blocks) Blocks Before (prod / Segmented) After (prod / Segmented) prose 7 1.486× 0.950× pysrc 3 1.164× 0.888× rustsrc 3 1.445× 1.040× json 3 1.492× 0.873× elf 8 1.432× 1.036× Median of block ratios 24 1.536× 1.027× Summed inverse ratio 24 1.404× 0.984×

(Diagnostic VM repeats using ROUTE_SHADOW=1 on the same 24 dense-band refused blocks.)

Wikidata pays almost nothing for this check. Guarding Wikidata's five dense blocks adds about 0.27 ms in total, or 0.03% of single-worker wall time. All 233 full Wikidata blocks still enter Open. On CI's pinned AMD EPYC runner across ten paired rounds, one-thread wikidata wall time shifted −0.2% (−1.0% to +0.6%, rising from 666 to 672 MB/s). On the same runner, four-thread text ran −3.7% faster.

items.title: Dissecting the Segmented fallback (#1042)
items.text:
Removing wasted refusals still leaves Segmented running on most off-Wikidata blocks. The Segmented fallback dissection tested six bzip2 -9 corpora totalling 82.18 MB raw. Across those files, 78 of 86 full blocks (90.7%) ran Segmented, split into 48 RunsFallback blocks and 30 Column blocks. That covered all 25 blocks of ab gen text and 50 of 51 blocks across prose and source code.

Profiling those 78 blocks exposed where the time goes. Inverse BWT takes 52.5 to 65.8% of worker time on text, prose, source and JSON, and 42.3% on ELF binaries. Within inverse BWT, building the navigation table (build) alone takes 35 to 46% of the stage.

Three zero-memory mechanisms stack into one winning arm called C_trustfill+rev. It matched bwt::walk byte for byte on all 78 blocks and touches zero Wikidata blocks:

  1. Sequential LF column construction (A_col_lf). Replacing the 256-stream random-scatter \(\Psi\) build with a sequential LF pass plus an 8-byte equal-run fast path (w == w.rotate_left(8)) removes scattered writes. On the 30 Column blocks, this cuts steal-free thread CPU by −23.4% baseline and −24.8% native.
  2. AVX2 32-byte reverse assembly (B_col_lf+avx2rev). Walking LF emits each segment backwards. Reversing chunks with AVX2 pshufb and vperm2i128 (with an 8-byte scalar swap_bytes fallback) cuts baseline assembly from 13.68 ms to 7.54 ms (−45%).
  3. Invariant-checked runs::fill_avx2 (C_trustfill+rev). When run records come from runs::front, the buffer bounds and alphabet limits are already established in \(O(1)\). Skipping redundant per-run tiling checks and lim[256] guards cuts the 48 RunsFallback blocks by −13.5% baseline and −14.0% native.
Off-Wikidata Segmented fallback: steal-free CPU reduction with C_trustfill+rev (7 interleaved VM repeats) Baseline x86-64 Native text (25 blks) −11.7% −15.9% prose (8 blks) −21.8% −20.5% pysrc (9 blks) −16.2% −13.6% rustsrc (8 blks) −15.2% −10.5% json (9 blks) −15.5% −12.0% elf (19 blks) −26.4% −24.4% Primary (50 blks) −15.4% −16.1% All 6 corpora (78) −18.4% −18.5% 0% −10% −20% −30% −40% steal-free thread CPU reduction vs shipped Segmented (more negative is faster) Source: docs/journal/2026-11-27-explore/segmented-fallback-dissection.md (#1042, 7 interleaved repeats on a 2-vCPU Xeon VM). Primary comprises text, prose, pysrc and rustsrc (50 Segmented blocks).

On the primary prose/text + source suite of 50 blocks, C_trustfill+rev cuts steal-free thread CPU by −15.44% baseline (195.57 → 165.37 ms) and −16.05% native (189.88 → 159.40 ms). Both builds show non-overlapping spreads. Across all 78 blocks in the six corpora, the saving reaches −18.43% baseline and −18.54% native with zero extra memory.

The same probe also ruled out a classic literature idea: Kärkkäinen–Kempa–Puglisi 2-step LF² stored in Vec<u64>. That D_lf2_u64 arm costs an extra 3.6 MiB per worker. Walking two bytes per pointer chase did cut walk time by −15.0 to −15.7% (120.85 → 101.89 ms baseline, 115.14 → 97.87 ms native). Yet build_lf2 blew up 3.9 to 4.2× (75.1 → 289.4 ms baseline, 73.4 → 308.4 ms native). Total inverse time ran +104.5 to +121.4% slower, and the negative result now lives in frontier/dead-ends.tsv.

items.title: 2. Reopening Open's middle stage with a safe 64K redesign
items.text:
Back on Wikidata, the ideal-parts matrix priced Open's middle stage — endpoint induction (C-A6b, in src/open/endpoint.rs). On our 10-core i9-10900K, C-A6b takes 216.0 ms on one worker (16.54% of the 1,306 ms wall) and 30.4 ms/worker at eight workers. Earlier isolated Round 2 tweaks fell short of our 3% whole-decoder gate. In isolation, inline7_node20 projected +2.48% and no_contents_dedup projected +0.99%.

The whole-A6b redesign probe (#1046) redesigned all three sub-phases of A6b together: setup, steps and dict. It priced the full C + E pipeline (A6a + A6b + A6c + A7) under both shipped bidirectional emission and matched forward emission.

The winning design, comb_nobc_soa_gen, uses zero unsafe. It passed byte-exact verification against bwt::walk on all 431 of 431 Wikidata blocks:

  1. A6b-setup (26.5 → 15.4 ms, −41.7%). A single forward pass over strips_raw fuses strip-order building with strip and domain-gap creation. Scattering a packed u64 into image_order64 turns image-gap construction into a sequential scan with zero random gathers. Sentinel-0 list appends remove branches and direct u16 links replace bit-packed read-modify-write updates.
  2. A6b-steps (64.2 → 43.8 ms, −31.1 to −31.8%). Step time falls from 24.1 to 16.4 ns/step by storing the structure-of-arrays tables in reusable Box<[T; 65536]> arenas indexed by usize::from(u16). Because every u16 is statically below 65,536, LLVM removes 100% of bounds checks in safe Rust and saves roughly 8 ms over dynamic Vec. An inline15 u128 handle keeps short joins in registers and cuts rule allocations by −54.6% (1,647,746 → 747,845), while equal-width steps (aw == bw, 36.98% of steps) update in place.
  3. A6b-dict (40.7 → 34.8 ms, −13.5 to −14.5%). Short dictionary entries build straight from u128 handles without pairs lookups. Persistent generation-tagged L1d-hot caches (contents[4096] at 16 KiB and pairs[1024] at 8 KiB) eliminate 24 KiB of per-block zero-fill. Dead stats counters are gated behind the census feature.
A6b sub-phase ablation ladder on 233 admitted Wikidata blocks (baseline x86-64, shipped bidirectional emission) setup steps dict shipped_baseline 26.6 64.5 40.5 131.7 ms setup_u16_fused 15.3 58.4 35.7 109.6 ms (−16.8%) combined_soa_gen (Vec) 18.9 52.4 35.6 107.8 ms (−18.2%) comb_nobc_soa_gen 15.5 44.5 34.8 95.1 ms (−27.8%) 0 40 80 120 ms pinned 2-vCPU Xeon VM medians (7 interleaved repeats; sub-phase medians may differ from total median by 0.2–0.3 ms) Source: docs/journal/2026-11-26-explore/a6b-combined-redesign.md (#1046). Moving from dynamic Vec (combined_soa_gen) to safe Box<[T; 65536]> (comb_nobc_soa_gen) removes roughly 8 ms of bounds checks in steps with zero unsafe.

We timed all four build × emission cells across seven interleaved repeats on a pinned 2-vCPU Xeon VM. In every cell, comb_nobc_soa_gen cuts A6b by −27.4 to −28.8% (0.712×–0.726×) and full C + E by −5.4 to −7.6% (0.925×–0.946×). Spreads are disjoint on both wall clock and thread CPU in all four cells:

Build × emission cell A6b baseline → redesign (ms) A6b ratio C + E baseline → redesign (ms) A7 Δ i9-anchored 1W Δ (%1W) Modeled 8W Δ Baseline × shipped bidi 131.66 → 95.08 0.722× 566.31 → 533.05 +0.32% +48.7 ms (+3.73%) +8.2 ms/w Baseline × forward 1-lane 130.41 → 94.71 0.726× 508.05 → 473.78 +0.01% +55.5 ms (+4.25%) +8.3 ms/w Native × shipped bidi 131.58 → 94.89 0.721× 593.72 → 561.47 +0.15% +51.7 ms (+3.96%) +8.4 ms/w Native × forward 1-lane 131.00 → 93.26 0.712× 522.68 → 483.24 −0.44% +67.7 ms (+5.18%) +9.1 ms/w

(Diagnostic VM probe timings on 233 admitted Wikidata blocks. The i9-10900K columns are projections anchored to the 1,068.0 ms C + E baseline, not direct i9 runs yet.)

Two structural ablations explain why comb_nobc_soa_gen beat its sibling designs:

  • SoA beats AoS by 4 to 7 ms. Keeping links (8 B/node, ~78 KiB live) and widths (4 B/node, ~39 KiB live) separate from 16-byte u128 words keeps neighbour edits compact in L2. Both 32-byte AoS32 and 24-byte AoS24-inline7 pull wider cache lines on every link update.
  • Generation-tagged deduplication beats dropping dedup. Dropping contents dedup (comb_nobc_soa_nod) shaves another 5.5 ms in A6b-dict (34.8 → 29.3 ms). Yet it inflates dictionary entries by +73.3% (246,680 → 427,381) and regresses A7 emission by +1.47 to +2.10%, breaching our 1.0% guard. Generation-tagged caches preserve dictionary compactness (246,683 vs 246,680 entries, 64,314 long entries and 9,888.3 KiB of spelling) while keeping A7 neutral (−0.44% to +0.32%).

One real caveat remains for the production build. Three Box<[T; 65536]> arenas reserve 1.75 MiB of virtual memory per worker. On Wikidata, each block touches only 0..nodes (about 273 KiB average and 420 KiB max) and drops those arenas before A6c and A7. Verifying RSS and 8- to 10-worker L3 cache scaling on the i9-10900K is an explicit gate for the follow-on build.

items.title: 3. Honest contrast: when rescue hits a structural floor
items.text:
Reopening a stage only stays trustworthy if failed rescues are priced just as strictly. Alongside #1046, we ran a constructor rescue (bwt-contraction-constructor-rescue, #1038) on #1013's contracted return-map idea. That approach removes low-cost F-buckets from Open's edge graph to shorten emission A7. Every arm used #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and passed 8,406 of 8,406 byte-identical exactness checks across both builds.

Cold dissection on the training split (blocks 0..117) found real contingent waste in #1013. Of its 37.6 MiB of spelling writes, 72.4% (27.3 MiB) were redundant re-copies of already-stored LONG prefix words. In addition, the 15.2% of chains longer than 8 hops carried roughly 69% of all eliminated hops.

Fixing that waste helped substantially. The cleaner 1-lane redesign (r1_clean1_2part) cut contraction time by −9.0% baseline (108.69 → 98.86 ms) and −13.9% native (111.44 → 95.94 ms). An \(O(1)\) pre-construction guard (m >= 32,768, elim_frac >= 0.55) also removed #1013's runs.bz2 regression (1.586× → 1.015× baseline, 1.375× → 1.018× native).

Yet on held-out Wikidata across 116 blocks and seven interleaved repeats, neither pre-registered redesign approached forward emission:

Held-out arm (116 Wikidata blocks) contr (ms, base / nat) A7 (ms, base / nat) C + E (ms, base / nat) vs 1-lane fwd (base / nat) vs 4-lane oracle (base / nat) ctrl_fwd_1lane 0.0 / 0.0 108.5 / 121.4 242.3 / 278.0 1.000× / 1.000× 1.138× / 1.163× ctrl_fwd_4lane_ora 0.0 / 0.0 79.1 / 83.9 212.4 / 237.5 0.878× / 0.860× 1.000× / 1.000× ref1013_fb75_L16 108.7 / 111.4 38.3 / 42.8 283.8 / 311.9 1.171× / 1.127× 1.336× / 1.310× r1_clean1_2part 98.9 / 95.9 41.6 / 44.6 275.2 / 299.2 1.142× / 1.079× 1.299× / 1.261× r2_mlp4_buf_bump 104.6 / 111.2 44.0 / 47.7 285.3 / 315.5 1.177× / 1.140× 1.346× / 1.317×

On 24 forced blocks of text.bz2, r1_clean1_2part still regressed 1.327× baseline and 1.257× native against 1-lane forward. Worse, the 4-lane MLP arm (r2_mlp4_buf_bump) ran slower than 1-lane r1 on both builds. Variable chain lengths from 1 to 219 hops end a lane on 67.7% of 4-lane iterations, causing branch mispredictions that flush out-of-order memory-level parallelism.

Why post-A6c contraction hits a structural floor (baseline x86-64 VM ms; dashed line = max budget vs 4-lane oracle) budget ~24.5 ms prep_tag + pure_chase4 (bare) 30.6 ms (zero byte/dict work) prep_tag + pure_chase1 (bare) 55.0 ms r1_clean1_2part (held-out) 98.9 ms ref1013_fb75_L16 (original) 108.7 ms 0 30 60 90 ms bare chase measured on train[0..117]; full arms measured on held-out[117..233] Source: docs/journal/2026-11-24-algorithm-level/bwt-contraction-rescue/results.md (#1038). Even with zero byte extraction, dictionary hashing or spelling writes, bare 4-lane pointer chasing (30.6 ms) already exceeds the entire ~24 to 25 ms VM budget needed to clear the +39.18 ms i9 gate over 4-lane forward emission.

The stop verdict is therefore structural rather than a missed micro-optimisation. Fusing elimination into A6c breaks Reader::wire's SIMD loop, adding +3.7 to +16.1 ms to save 3.4 ms of tagging. Running elimination after A6c hits a 30.6 ms bare 4-lane chase floor (prep_tag 3.4 ms plus pure_chase4 27.2 ms) with zero byte work, dictionary hashing or spelling writes. That bare floor already exceeds the ~24 to 25 ms VM budget.

Put #1046 and #1038 side by side and the boundary is sharp. A6b reopened because removable bookkeeping, bounds checks and allocations dominated three coupled sub-phases. Post-A6c contraction stopped because its irreducible chase floor exceeded what emission could give back.

items.title: 4. What ships next
items.text:
These four merged results leave a clean, prioritized engineering queue. Every VM probe stays clearly separated from shipped production code and i9-10900K adoption gates:

  1. Already shipped (#1040). The within_cap dense-band precheck is live in src/open.rs. It stays neutral on Wikidata and speeds four-thread CI text by −3.7%.
  2. Admitted build — segmented-fallback-build (#1049). Port C_trustfill+rev into src/bwt/ and src/runs.rs at zero extra memory. Confirm the gains across pinned CI corpora and the i9 workstation.
  3. Admitted build — a6b-endpoint-build (#1051). Port comb_nobc_soa_gen into src/open/endpoint.rs with zero unsafe. Verify RSS and 8- to 10-worker L3 cache scaling on the i9-10900K, where A6b sits on the worker half of the eight-worker tie.
  4. Admitted probe — forward-4lane-anchor-probe (#1050). #1038's own control table exposed a +110.7 to +129.0 ms i9 gap between 1-lane forward emission and 4-lane oracle forward emission. This probe tests whether cheap in-A6b/A6c anchors can capture that 4-lane emission win without contraction's pointer-chase tax.

items.title: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Five freshly merged studies turn mibz2's ideal-parts matrix into one coherent 6 GB/s architecture. On our 10-core Intel i9-10900K, shipped mibz2 decodes 839 MB of Wikidata (wikidata ×4) in 192.9 to 194.6 ms at eight workers. That is 4.31 GB/s. Reaching 6 GB/s means finishing the same workload in 140 ms. No single stage can carry that drop alone. Five designs fit end to end across the worker pipeline and the eight-worker schedule. Together they pair sampled-anchor four-lane forward emission and vectored RLE1+CRC fusion with a zero-copy boundary, L1-batched MTF folding and slack-only hybrid scanning.

This post builds on Reopening Open's middle and the off-Wikidata decoder and The decoder's true floor and the limits of a pooled scan. One evidence boundary belongs up front. The i9-10900K baselines (1,306 ms single-worker and 192.9–194.6 ms eight-worker) are direct workstation measurements. The four stage studies (#1057, #1045, #1058, #1055 and #1048) are steal-free probes on a 2-vCPU Haswell Xeon VM. Every arm passed byte-exact parity on every tested block. The eight-worker trajectory (#1056) replays src/parallel.rs deterministically against primary i9-10900K traces. Every projection below awaits production builds and direct 10-core i9-10900K confirmation.

Section 1 shows how 16 scalar anchor tags unlock 4-lane forward emission without breaking SIMD wiring. Section 2 explains why zero-scratch tiled fusion beats both 1-lane emission and contiguous stitching. Section 3 prices a 160-byte vectored ReadyBlock across six real consumer paths and memory budgets. Section 4 diagnoses why direct MTF folding spilled registers and how L1 batching rescues it. Section 5 maps how slack-only helper scanning clears the 140 ms wall without regressing below the knee. Section 6 summarizes the combined architecture and its workstation gates.

Takeaways

  • Four-lane forward emission is paid in full (#1057, PASS). Tagging 16 uniform BWT-row anchors in bit 31 keeps unmodified SIMD wiring and cuts A6c + A7 thread CPU by 31.0 to 35.8% with zero unsafe. Native L3-cold runs reach 97.4% of a prebuilt oracle and project +208 to +235 ms saved on one i9 worker.
  • Fusion only pays off if delivery stays vectored (#1045, PASS / scoped STOP). Zero-scratch in-place tile compaction with 64 KiB PCLMULQDQ CRC32 cuts E + A9 writes by 53.4%. It projects +31.8 to +49.9 ms saved on one i9 worker, whereas contiguous stitching moves 74.9% of the output and erases the win.
  • Vectored delivery costs nothing at the boundary (#1058). An inline 160-byte ReadyBlock keeps all six consumer paths at 0.86× to 1.01× of contiguous delivery while holding RSS at 1.017× with zero Wikidata overflows.
  • L1 batching and guard zones rescue MTF folding (#1048, #1055, PASS). Direct per-run folding spilled runs::front_avx2's 15 live registers and regressed up to +4.3%. A 2 KiB L1d batch plus a 496/512 OutQ16 guard zone cuts push_slow 6.22×. Together they drop A5 + A6a by 12.1% baseline and 19.1% native.
  • Slack-only hybrid scanning crosses 6 GB/s (#1056). Offloading candidate finding to the 91.6%-idle reader thread and scanning only from worker job_wait slack pushes eight-worker wall time to 131.8 ms (6.36 GB/s) at W'/8 = 125 ms. Below the knee, k = 6 stays at 0.997× to 0.999×.
End-to-end 6 GB/s decoder architecture assembled from five merged studies INPUT & SCAN PLANE (#1056) mibz2-read (91.6% idle) AVX2 Finder → Arc<Chunk> OnceLock cands (0 ms tax) Serial Scanner (Policy A) skip helper-verified blocks 11 seam blocks on serial path Slack-Only Helpers prio-1 decode, prio-2 scan local L2 scratch · full_only PER-WORKER OPEN PIPELINE (×8 WORKERS, #![forbid(unsafe_code)] IN NEW KERNELS) A5 + A6a (#1055) 2 KiB L1d run batch OutQ16 496/512 guard A6b (#1046) 64K u16-link SoA gen-tagged dict A6c + A7 (#1057) SIMD Reader::wire S=16 bit-31 · 4 lanes Fused RLE1+CRC (#1045) zero-scratch 4K tiles 64K CRC + GF(2) combine ZERO-COPY VECTORED DELIVERY BOUNDARY (#1058) 160 B ReadyBlock { buf, ranges: [(u32, u32); 16], count, total_len } → BzReader / Python / decode_parallel · RSS 1.017× Each stage removes a separate currency: random-scatter stalls and register spills in A5+A6a, bounds checks in A6b, XOR wiring and 1-lane dependency chains in A6c+A7, full-block re-reads in A9, and serial-scan idle slack across 8 workers.

items.title: The architecture of a 6 GB/s bzip2 decoder
items.text:
Five merged studies show how four-lane forward emission, fused slices and batched MTF pair with slack-only scanning to reach 6 GB/s.

27 November 2026 · 10 min read · Research synthesis
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: 1. Sampled-anchor four-lane forward emission (#1057)
items.text:
The single largest worker prize in mibz2 sits inside A6c + A7 (651.7 ms on one i9 worker, or half of total single-worker time). Earlier work showed why shipped bidirectional emission is expensive. To walk two lanes per edge without knowing endpoints in advance, wire_xor stores XOR-linked adjacency in A6c. That scalar XOR wiring breaks SIMD throughput. Forward 1-lane emission removes XOR wiring yet pays a long pointer-chasing dependency chain across A7.

The sampled-anchor 4-lane probe (#1057) resolves that tension cleanly with #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. Every arm matched byte for byte across all 11,961 checks on Wikidata and synthetic edge cases.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Keeping SIMD wiring untouched
items.text:
First, A6c keeps the unmodified SIMD outq::Reader::wire loop. On the VM, SIMD Reader::wire takes roughly 30 ms warm and 40 ms L3-cold across the 233 Open-admitted Wikidata blocks. Shipped wire_xor takes 91 ms warm and 108 ms cold. That is 2.7× to 3.0× slower.

Second, the probe checks bit 31 of edges[u]. Every Wikidata Open block packs a destination index (max_bits = 18) and a dictionary index (max_dict = 1,712). Because \(18 + 11 = 29 \le 31\), bit 31 is free on all 233 blocks.

Third, after Reader::wire finishes, the probe marks \(S\) uniform BWT-row anchor indices:

\[a_k = \left(\text{mark} + \left\lfloor \frac{k \cdot m}{S} \right\rfloor\right) \bmod m, \qquad k = 0, \dots, S - 1\]

Tagging \(S = 16\) anchor entries takes just 16 scalar writes per block. That adds roughly 30 nanoseconds per block, or 7 microseconds across all 233 blocks.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Why \(S = 16\) beats \(S = 4\) by order statistics
items.text:
Choosing \(S\) uniform BWT-row indices partitions the single cycle of length \(m\) into \(S\) random segments whose lengths behave like independent exponential spacings. With only \(S = 4\) segments, four parallel lanes must wait for the longest of four exponential pieces. Its expected length follows the fourth harmonic number \(H_4 = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{4} = 2.083\times\) the mean segment length. Measured across Wikidata at \(S = 4\), the longest segment is indeed \(2.081\times\) the mean, leaving three lanes idle for over half the tail.

Oversampling to \(S = 16\) fixes load balance dynamically. Four lanes pull from the queue of 16 segments as each segment ends. Whenever any lane hits an anchor edge, a single sign-bit check catches all four lanes at once:

if ((ed0 | ed1 | ed2 | ed3) as i32) < 0 { /* retire hit lane, pull next anchor */ }

That branch fires only ~16 times per block (0.014% of iterations). At \(S = 16\), the longest single segment shrinks to \(0.818 \times (m / 4)\) and effective lane parallelism rises to eff_K = 3.153 across the whole block (including the 3 → 2 → 1 drain). Each segment writes into a 32 KiB slab-continuation arena (max_arena = 992 KiB, averaging 41.6 ordered slices per block regardless of \(S\)).

(Diagnostic VM medians of steal-free thread CPU across 7 interleaved repeats; 100% disjoint spreads against shipped_bidi. Modeled i9 columns scale VM ratios to the 651.7 ms A6c + A7 i9-10900K baseline.)

The cold-cache result is striking. Under L3-cold pressure, fwd_4lane_sampled_S16_vec reaches 1.000× of the prebuilt oracle on baseline (323.61 vs 323.46 ms). On native it reaches 1.026×, or 97.4% of the oracle (303.41 vs 295.66 ms). That projects +208 to +235 ms saved on one i9 worker. That is 16.0% to 18.0% of single-worker time, or +29 to +33 ms/worker at eight workers.

items.title: 2. Upstream vectored RLE1+CRC fusion (#1045)
items.text: Once emission runs forward in four lanes, A9 (RLE1 expansion plus CRC32) sits right behind it. On one i9 worker, A9 takes 66.6 to 74.4 ms. Earlier standalone post-emit work (#988) stopped because a separate pass over the output buffer hit a 72.3% L1d-hot compute floor. Moving RLE1+CRC upstream into the 4-lane emitter seemed promising. Yet the fusion probe (#1045) showed that three of four candidate designs fail. Only one clears the gate. Every arm passed all 13,360 exactness checks across Wikidata and edge-case corpora.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Why three designs stopped
items.text:
1. 1-lane fused (fused_1lane — STOP). Fusing RLE1+CRC into a single forward lane surrenders 4-lane memory-level parallelism. It regresses by −92 to −186 ms projected on one i9 worker.
  2. Inline per-step FSM (fused_4l_fsm — STOP). Running the RLE1 state machine byte-by-byte inside the 4-lane pointer-chase loop bloats WordMeta and spills live lane state. It regresses by −126 to −205 ms projected on one i9 worker.
  3. 4-lane contiguous stitched (fused_4l_tile4096_stitch — STOP). Even when each lane fuses RLE1+CRC cleanly in 4 KiB tiles, compacting the four output segments back into one flat Vec<u8> destroys the win. On Wikidata, 86.4% of lanes change length after RLE1 expansion. Re-packing lanes 1 to 3 moves 74.53 of 99.56 MiB (74.9% of all output). Across wikidata ×4, that copies 598.9 MiB of extra bytes. Write savings drop from −53.4% to −18.6% (1,718.2 → 1,398.8 MiB), leaving timing flat at −23 to +11 ms projected.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Why fused_4l_tile4096_vec passes
items.text:
The winning arm (fused_4l_tile4096_vec) keeps the 4-lane pointer-chase loop clean and delivers vectored slices without stitching:

  • Zero-scratch single-pass in-place tile compaction. Each lane emits raw BWT bytes straight into its own output slice until it fills a 4 KiB tile. Then it expands RLE1 in place. Because 89.4% of Wikidata 4-byte runs have extra == 0 (four equal bytes followed by a zero repeat count), expansion shrinks the stream so dst <= src. Only when a rare long repeat causes net growth does the tile spill its short suffix to a tiny scratch buffer. Across all 431 Wikidata blocks, zero RLE1 runs straddled a lane boundary.
  • L2-hot 64 KiB PCLMULQDQ CRC32 + GF(2) combine. Every 64 KiB of finalized lane output feeds hardware-accelerated CRC32 while still hot in L2 cache. At block end, four crc32_combine calls over \(\text{GF}(2)\) fold the four lane CRCs into the exact bzip2 block CRC in microseconds.

(Diagnostic VM medians of steal-free thread CPU across 7 interleaved repeats. On warm runs fused_4l_tile4096_vec beats even the zero-RLE1 separate-CRC floor because 64 KiB tiled CRC stays L2-hot. On cold runs it matches the floor to 0.00 ms.)

items.title: 3. The zero-cost vectored delivery boundary (#1058)
items.text: Both #1057 and #1045 point to the same architectural need: stop forcing workers to stitch emitted slices into one flat Vec<u8>. Before touching src/parallel.rs, we priced the vectored delivery boundary in a dedicated probe (#1058). It uses #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and tests 200 MiB of real Wikidata blocks plus synthetic guards (runs, onebyte, max16).
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: A 160-byte inline ReadyBlock
items.text:
Instead of heap-allocating a Vec<Vec<u8>> per block, a worker hands the reader an inline 160-byte struct:

pub struct ReadyBlock {
    buf: Vec<u8>,
    ranges: [(u32, u32); 16],
    count: u8,
    total_len: u32,
}

It allocates zero extra heap buffers. When the consumer finishes draining the last range, into_buf() recycles buf directly into free_out with zero changes to pool accounting, while Ready::size tracks logical total_len.

items.title: Zero consumer tax and bounded RSS
items.text:
We timed six real consumer paths across contiguous, stitched, 4-lane vectored and 16-segment vectored delivery. Those paths cover zero-copy fill_buf_hash, read_64k and read_256k (both single-slice and scatter-fill) and decode_parallel:

Consumer path (native L3-cold, 200 MiB Wikidata) contiguous_1slice vectored_4lane vectored_16seg stitched_4lane fill_buf_hash (zero-copy BufRead) 1.00× 0.92×–1.00× 0.94×–1.00× +33%..+80% read_64k / read_256k (scatter-fill) 1.00× 0.86×–1.01× 0.88×–1.01× +33%..+80% decode_parallel (parallel sink) 1.00× 0.95×–1.00× 0.96×–1.01× +33%..+80%

(Stitched 4-lane adds +16 to +22 ms per 200 MiB, or roughly +64 to +88 ms across wikidata ×4. Vectored 4-lane and 16-segment stay at parity with contiguous delivery.)

Python's single-copy read(size) path (#1033) also stays clean. At K = 4, single-fill_buf call counts rise +0.0% at read(256K) (1,130 calls) and +13.5% at read(64K). At S = 16, scatter-fill inside Read::read keeps calls completely flat at 3,200 (64K) and 800 (256K).

Slab sizing turned up an equally important guard against naive headroom. A flat +25% (span / 4) per lane inflates Wikidata RSS to 1.178× (1,100 KiB per block), breaching our <= 1.05× budget. Worse, it still overflows pathological runs (2.07×) and onebyte (51.8×). Keeping shipped +6.25% + 64 B gives zero Wikidata overflows at 1.0002× (K = 4) and 1.0010× (S = 16). Adding 4,096 B per lane for in-place tile headroom (+16 KiB per 900 KB block) holds peak RSS at 1.017× with zero overflows, cleanly inside the <= 1.05× gate.

items.title: 4. Rescuing MTF folding with L1 batching and guard zones (#1048, #1055)
items.text: Earlier in the programme, mtf-fold (#1010) tried to remove the 1 MiB runs buffer between A5 (runs::front_avx2) and A6a (Open::from_runs). It streamed each run straight into an inline FoldSink. In theory, folding should remove memory traffic. In practice, our cold dissection (#1048) caught that direct folding regressed A5 + A6a. Baseline ran +1.61% slower across all seven repeats, and native ran +4.33% slower.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Why direct folding regressed
items.text:
Disassembling runs::front_avx2 exposed three compounding costs hidden inside the hot loop:

  1. Register exhaustion (15 live x86-64 GPRs). Standalone runs::front_avx2 is a tight 22-instruction loop that already occupies all 15 general-purpose registers. On baseline, inlining FoldSink + Pass::take + OutQ16 spilled the sink pointer (reloaded 10 times per literal) plus seven GPRs. On native, it spilled the hot MTF-front registers f0 and f1 on every literal.
  2. Zero-hit dead check. Direct folding ran a c == self.c merge check on every emitted run that triggered 0 times in 15,141,602 runs.
  3. Tail-overrun push_slow storm and vzeroupper. OutQ16 called push_slow 417,041 times across 233 Wikidata blocks. 84.3% of those calls (351,722) were pure end-of-chunk f + 16 > 512 tail-overrun guards, not genuine thick-strip overflows. On baseline x86-64, every cold call across the AVX2 boundary also paid vzeroupper.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: The two-part rescue (#1055)
items.text:
The L1-batch rescue probe (#1055) fixed both halves together:

  • L1d-resident [u32; 512] packed run batch (2 KiB). front_avx2 stays completely decoupled, emitting packed maximal runs (c << 24) | total into a 2 KiB L1d stack buffer with second_cold kept out of line. That produces a 24-instruction hot loop with zero f0/f1/GPR spills and zero vzeroupper. When the 512-run batch fills, flush_batch_direct consumes it from L1d with m, in_out and f.runs hoisted in registers.
  • Power-of-2 OutQ16 guard zone (496 / 512). Reserving 16 guard slots at the end of each 1,024-byte chunk (CHUNK = 496, STRIDE = 512) lets the 16-wide SIMD write land unconditionally until f >= 496. That cuts push_slow calls 6.22× (417,041 → 67,001), driving tail_guard and ovf_chunks to zero with zero A6c readback regression.

(Diagnostic VM medians of steal-free thread CPU across 7 interleaved repeats; 100% bit-exact output and disjoint spreads on both builds. Both halves are required. L1d batching alone reaches only +1.60% 1W on baseline, below the 2.5% gate. Adding guard496 clears +3.08% baseline and +4.87% native, or +5.7 to +9.1 ms/worker at 8W.)

items.title: 5. Closing the loop to 6 GB/s with slack-only hybrid scanning (#1056)
items.text:
Stacking the four worker wins (#1046, #1057, #1045 and #1055) pulls per-worker compute \(W'/8\) below the post-#1031/#1034 serial scan floor (\(S' \approx 145\text{–}150\text{ ms}\) on the i9-10900K). At that point, the serial scanner caps throughput around 150.9 ms (5.56 GB/s). Workers sit idle in job_wait for 10.9 to 20.4 ms/worker.

Our earlier pooled-scan prototype (#942) tried to break that ceiling by having workers scan unconditionally. It failed because helper scanning stole cycles below the knee (1.105×–1.149× slower at k = 6..7). It also paid 5.27 ms of pool_copy overhead plus 4.82 ms of candidate finding.

The slack-only hybrid scan study (#1056) replayed src/parallel.rs deterministically against primary i9-10900K traces (character-stage1 r0..r3 and pooled-scan c71c4a56). It found that 63.1% to 70.2% of post-worker job_wait idle time arrives in continuous bursts at least one full-block scan wide.
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: The realized 8-worker wall-time law
items.text:
Workers drain job_queue at priority 1. Only when job_queue is empty do they pull speculative scan candidates at priority 2. That lets the serial scanner and eight workers share scanning at 9-way capacity:

\[\text{wall}_{8\text{W}} \approx \frac{8 \cdot (W'/8) + S'}{9} + 4.85\text{ ms}\]

The 4.85 ms coupling residual breaks into 2.62 ms startup, 1.15 ms validated handoff residual and 0.83–1.18 ms scheduling and drain tail. Using a smaller initial chunk 0 drops in_wait to 0.05 ms and trims the residual to +3.50 ms.

Breaking 6 GB/s (\(\le 140.0\text{ ms}\)) at \(S' = 145\text{ ms}\) requires \(W'/8 \le 133.9\text{ ms}\), or \(\le 135.4\text{ ms}\) with small chunk 0. With L1-batched MTF (W'/8 = 125 ms), eight-worker wall time reaches 131.82 ms (6.36 GB/s). That clears the 6 GB/s target with +8.18 ms to spare.

Coupled eight-worker wall time on wikidata ×4 (839 MB): trace-replay trajectory across the 6 GB/s line 6 GB/s (140 ms) Shipped mibz2 (i9 meas.) 194.6 ms · 4.31 GB/s Workers + serial scan (S'=145) 150.9 ms · 5.56 GB/s Slack hybrid, no MTF fold 141.1 ms (139.7 small c0) Slack hybrid + MTF fold 131.8 ms · 6.36 GB/s 0 50 100 150 200 ms BELOW-THE-KNEE GUARD (k = 6 WORKERS, RATIO VS SERIAL SCAN; 1.000× = PARITY) Killed pooled-scan (#942 P) 1.105× (regressed +10.5%) Slack-only hybrid (#1056) 0.998× (3–4 helper blocks, 0.5–0.7 ms) Source: docs/journal/2026-11-27-explore/slack-hybrid-scan-feasibility.md (#1056). Shipped baseline is directly measured on the 10-core i9-10900K; post-worker and hybrid bars are discrete-event replays of src/parallel.rs driven by primary i9 traces at S' = 145 ms and W'/8 = 135 ms (no fold) or 125 ms (with L1-batched MTF).
path: The architecture of a 6 GB/s decoder

items.title: Zero-plumbing design and below-the-knee safety
items.text:
Four concrete design choices eliminate every overhead that killed #942:

  1. Offload AVX2 Finder to the 91.6%-idle reader thread (0.00 ms tax). Primary per_k.tsv traces show mibz2-read is active for just 12.34 ms and sleeps in feed_wait for 134.10 ms at k = 8. Wrapping each read chunk in Arc<Chunk { base, bytes, cands: OnceLock<Vec<Cand>> }> lets mibz2-read push chunk 0 immediately and populate K4's 4.82 ms AVX2 Finder (9.84 GB/s) while waiting on backpressure.
  2. Eliminate pool_copy by skipping seam blocks (5.27 → 0.00 ms). Fewer than 0.7% of blocks (11 of 1,724) straddle a 4 MiB chunk boundary. Helpers simply skip seam-straddling candidates and leave them to the serial scanner's existing seam window (#1031).
  3. Priority-1 decode draining plus full_only filtering. Helpers touch scan candidates only when job_queue is empty. At k = 6, that runs just 3 to 4 helper blocks (0.5–0.7 ms). Wall time across k = 6..7 stays at 0.997× to 0.999×, versus #942's 1.105×–1.149×. Filtering gap >= 512 B (full_only) cuts helper handoffs by −35% to −41%.
  4. Policy A jump-ahead scanner and worker-local scratch. Instead of stalling on speculative validation (#770's +1.2–2.3 ms serial_wait), the scanner verifies completed helper bit-chains asynchronously and jumps straight past validated blocks. Each worker keeps a thread-local ScanScratch and Vec<u16> (~200 KiB, L2-hot), avoiding cross-core free_syms coherence ping-pong (#1034).

items.title: 6. How the five pieces fit and what builds next
items.text:
Viewed together, the five studies expose a clean architectural stack where each win amplifies the next:

Stage / boundary Primary study Mechanism VM / replay finding i9-10900K gate A5 + A6a #1048, #1055 2 KiB L1d run batch + OutQ16 496/512 guard −12.1% base / −19.1% native (A5 + A6a) ≥ 2.5% 1W, 0 A6c regression A6b #1046 Fused setup + safe 64K SoA + gen-tagged dict −27.4%..−28.8% A6b, −5.4%..−7.6% C+E RSS & 8–10W L3 scaling A6c + A7 #1057 SIMD Reader::wire + S=16 bit-31 + 4 lanes −31.0%..−35.8% A6c+A7 (97.4% of oracle) +208..+235 ms 1W, 0 unsafe E + A9 #1045 Zero-scratch 4K tiles + 64K CRC + GF(2) −53.4% writes, +31.8..+49.9 ms 1W proj. Vectored only (no stitch) Delivery #1058 160 B inline ReadyBlock, +16 KiB tile slab 0.86×–1.01× consumers, RSS 1.017× ≤ 1.05× RSS, 0 overflows 8W scan #1056 mibz2-read Finder + slack-only Policy A 131.8 ms (6.36 GB/s) @ 8W, 0.998× @ 6W ≥ 6 GB/s @ 8W, ≤ 1.005× @ 6W

The dependency order for production builds is equally crisp. First, ship the independent worker kernels (a6b-endpoint-build, opt-in forward-emission and mtf-l1-batch-build) alongside the vectored ReadyBlock boundary (#1058). That lets upstream RLE1+CRC fusion (#1045) land without paying stitching's 74.9% copy tax. Second, verify on the 10-core i9-10900K that the worker stack pulls \(W'/8\) below the post-#1031/#1034 serial scan floor. Then enable pooled-scan-hybrid (#1056) to turn newly exposed job_wait slack into 6 GB/s throughput with zero below-the-knee regressions.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2 as libbzip2 1.0.8 defines it, byte for byte, with every check libbzip2 makes, and decodes several blocks at once.

  • Why 32 couriers beat one: memory-level parallelism, the decoder's premise. One courier waits at every stop to learn the next address; 32 couriers' waits overlap. The lanes, the prefetch, the per-step cost that binds next, and the measurements.
  • What is checked, and when: block CRCs, stream CRCs, what an error reports, and the four inputs mibz2 refuses where libbzip2 does not.
  • How it works: the one sequential phase (the scanner), the workers, and the inverse BWT walked as 32 interleaved chains.
  • Prior work: libbzip2; Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi (DCC 2012); lbzip2 and pbzip2.

items.title: Block CRCs, before the block's bytes
items.text: Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned. A block whose CRC does not match returns none of its bytes: the error comes instead. The bytes returned before an error are exactly the stream's up to the bad block.

items.title: Stream CRCs, at the stream's end
items.text:
Each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. The bytes of a stream's blocks are returned as each block is verified, before the stream's own CRC has been read. So a streaming caller has the whole stream verified only once a read reaches its end without an error: until then, what it has read is provisional.

In Python, BZ2Reader.verified turns true only when a read returns the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched.

items.title: Where an error was found
items.text:
An error says where decoding failed: in Rust Error { kind, block, bit }, in Python the DecodeError message. That is which block, and the bit it starts at. A damaged bit can be found later than where it lies, since the input is only known to be wrong once something it encodes fails a check.

The error kinds (ErrorKind):

  • the input: Empty, NotBz2, Truncated, TrailingData;
  • each of libbzip2's block checks: BadBlockMagic, BadOrigPtr, NoSymbols, BadGroups, BadSelectors, BadSelector, BadCodeLength, BadHuffmanCode, SelectorOverrun, RunTooLong, BlockTooLong, RunUnfinished;
  • BlockCrc and StreamCrc, with the stored and computed values;
  • this decoder's refusals: Randomised, BlockTooLarge;
  • Io (from a BzReader's source), RangeOvershoot, Cancelled, and Internal (a caught panic: a bug).

items.title: What is decoded, and what is refused
items.text:
The format is libbzip2 1.0.8's, with every check it makes: bzip2 1.0 and later output. Four choices differ from it, and each has its own error:

input libbzip2 mibz2 randomised blocks (written only by bzip2 0.9.0 and earlier, before 1999) decoded refused (Randomised) bytes after the last stream that do not begin another stream ignored an error (TrailingData): nothing after a stream is silently dropped an oversubscribed Huffman code pointing past the alphabet a stale table entry read an error a block whose compressed form passes 64 MiB (a real block is at most about 4.2 MB) decoded an error (BlockTooLarge)

items.title: Why 32 couriers beat one: understanding memory-level parallelism
items.text:
Most of a bzip2 decode is one loop, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform's walk, and that loop spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 doesn't make memory any faster. It keeps many of the walk's memory requests in flight at once, so the waits overlap. That is memory-level parallelism (MLP), and it is the library's basic premise.

This page explains it with couriers and a dispatcher, then gives the mechanism behind each part of the picture, and the measurements so far. How it works has the threads around the walk, and Prior work the work it builds on.

items.title: One courier, one chain
items.text:
A motorcycle courier learns each delivery address only on arriving at the previous one: open the envelope, read the next address. The third destination can't be known before reaching the second. The bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next.

That is the ordinary inverse BWT:

  • The table. After Huffman decoding and move-to-front, a block's last column becomes the T-vector: one 32-bit entry a row, holding the row's byte (bits 0–7) and the next row (the bits above). A block holds up to 900,000 bytes, so the table is up to 3.6 MB, larger than most cores' L2 cache.
  • The walk. Start at the block's primary index. Each step loads the current row's entry, writes its byte, and takes the next row from the same entry. The next row is anywhere in the table, so the load usually misses the cache.
  • The wait. The step after can't start until that load returns, because its address is in the load's result. A chain of dependent loads keeps one miss in flight, and the core idles through each one.
courier 1the corewaiting for the next address (a cache miss)idle: nothing to do until the address comes backa steptime → One courier. Each step (dark) is a few instructions; most of the time goes on waiting for the next address (light). Schematic, not to scale.

The walk was measured as latency-bound directly, on the machine where mibz2's prototype was built: walking 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 independent chains through one block, the cost fell from 28.5 to 4.4 cycles a byte of output (compute frontier, section 2). Memory bandwidth was nowhere near its limit. The walk was waiting, not moving data. libbzip2 and lbzip2 walk the one chain.

items.title: 32 couriers, 32 independent journeys
items.text:
Give each of 32 couriers a different delivery chain. While courier 1 waits for its next address, couriers 2, 3, 4… make progress. That is memory-level parallelism: the couriers don't travel faster, but there are enough independent journeys that waiting on one doesn't stop the rest. One courier is limited by the time it takes to get each new address; 32 keep many requests in flight.

courier 1courier 2courier 3courier 4the coreslots for couriers 5 to 32each courier's step, one after anothertime → Four of mibz2's 32 couriers. Each still waits as long for its address, but the waits overlap, and the core takes the other couriers' steps in the gaps. Schematic, not to scale.

The correction that keeps the picture faithful

The CPU doesn't employ 32 workers, and the lanes aren't threads. One core interleaves the instructions of 32 traversal chains, and its out-of-order machinery overlaps their memory requests. The better image is one dispatch centre managing 32 motorcycles, each getting its next destination only when its last delivery returns an address.

What counts is deliveries a second for the whole centre, not how fast one bike finishes its route: sustained throughput, not the latency of any one load. Every load still takes as long as before.

Several threads are several dispatch centres, one a block: mibz2's workers decode whole blocks in parallel (How it works). The lanes are the parallelism inside each one.

items.title: Where the independent journeys come from
items.text:
A block has one chain, not 32: the T-vector is a single cycle through every row (or, for a periodic text, a few). bzip2 carries no metadata to start a walk anywhere but the primary index. mibz2 makes the journeys itself:

  • Random starts. 511 pseudo-random rows, plus the walk's own first row, become segment starts. A random row is a random position in the text, so the cycle is cut into 512 segments of about equal length. (Evenly spaced rows clustered in the text and stalled the lanes.)
  • Flagged starts end a segment. Each start is flagged in bit 31 of its own T-vector entry, which links never use. A lane that reads a flagged entry has run into the next segment's start: its segment ends there, recording which start it ran into, and the lane takes the next unwalked segment.
  • 32 lanes walk in lockstep. Each round, every lane takes one step, writing its byte into its own segment's buffer.
  • The segments are stitched together afterwards. From the first row's segment, each segment is followed by the one it ran into, until the block's length is reached. The output is exactly the plain walk's, byte for byte, including a periodic block's several cycles. The flags are cleared before the walk returns.
  • Short blocks walk plainly. Under 64 KiB, the segments' bookkeeping costs more than the waits it hides; only a stream's last block is ever that short.
one chaincut at startsjoinedthe plain walk: one courier, row after row, from the primary index to the block's endA · lane 1B · lane 3C · lane 2D · lane 4E · lane 2F · lane 1G · lane 4H · lane 3▼ a start row, flagged in its own entry: the segment before it ends there, and a lane takes the nextA, then the segment A ran into (B), then C… until the block's length: exactly the plain walk's bytes One chain cut at flagged starts into segments, walked by four lanes in whatever order the lanes take them, then joined in order. mibz2 cuts each block into 512 segments for 32 lanes.

items.title: Prefetching: phoning ahead
items.text:
Lanes alone weren't enough. Without help, a lane's next load is issued only when its instructions enter the core's reorder buffer, which is full of the other lanes' steps. So the misses in flight were bounded by how many steps that window holds, and adding lanes didn't add misses.

mibz2 issues a software prefetch of each lane's next entry as soon as its row is known (prefetcht0 on x86-64, prfm pldl1keep on aarch64). A prefetch retires without waiting for its data, so every lane's miss starts at once. In the picture, the dispatcher phones each request through the moment an address is read, rather than when that courier's turn comes round on the board.

Try the counts yourself in this schematic. It has one dispatcher, whose paperwork for a step takes a tick or two, and each address takes 31 ticks to come back. The timings are made up for the picture.

The schematic needs JavaScript.

items.title: The dispatcher becomes the bottleneck
items.text:
There is only so much road, and one dispatcher. Add enough couriers and every wait is covered. Then the limit is the dispatcher: each step's paperwork, done for each courier in turn. Add more couriers past that point and the dispatcher spends more on coordination than the extra journeys earn.

In the core, the dispatcher's limits are these:

  • Instructions a step. Every lane's step is a handful of instructions: the load, the flag test, the byte's store, the write pointer's advance, the buffer-end check, the prefetch. With the misses overlapped, the walk runs at the rate the core can issue those instructions.
  • Register pressure. One lane's state (its row, its write pointers, its segment) fits in registers, but 32 lanes' state doesn't. It lives in the L1 cache, and every step loads and stores some of it.
  • Cache contention. The lanes' table lines, the 512 segments' buffers and the lanes' own state share the same caches. At four threads, four walks share the L3.
  • Outstanding misses. A core tracks only so many misses at once (its line fill buffers, and the L2's own queue). Beyond that, more lanes only queue.

The record shows both sides. Without the prefetch, 16 lanes were within noise of 12, and 24 or 32 were slower (PR #21). With it, 16 to 32 lanes were about 26–28% faster than 12 lanes without it, and within noise of each other at one walk. With four walks at once, 32 lanes won clearly. So mibz2 runs 32 lanes and 512 segments (the measured points).

It also explains why a cleverer-looking algorithm can lose. Once 32 misses are in flight, the walk is bound by instructions a step, not by the latency of each load. A change that saves steps but makes each one dearer loses. A change that keeps the steps and makes them cheaper wins.

items.title: Make the dispatcher efficient
items.text:
Once there are enough couriers, cut the paperwork a step. That's how the walk got faster:

  • The flagged walk (#12). It replaced the first segmented walk, which tested every step's row against a separate bitmap of the starts (12 lanes, 256 segments). The flag moved into the entry the step loads anyway, bytes went out through raw per-lane pointers instead of a growable vector's push, and the test for idle lanes left the hot loop.
  • The prefetch, with 32 lanes and 512 segments (#21): every lane's next miss starts at once, as above.
  • The shared-offset walk, after libsais's chain decode (#37, the default walk since 0.1.5). libsais 2.12's decode_chains runs room rounds of every chain at a shared output offset, where room is the fewest bytes any chain's buffer has spare. Within a pass, a lane's byte goes to its buffer's base plus the pass's offset, so the per-step pointer store and buffer-end test are gone. The lanes, the prefetch and the segments are unchanged, so the same misses are in flight. Only the instructions a step drop: one dispatcher's paperwork, done in batches.

Two cleverer-looking ideas from the literature were built, measured and dropped. Both changed the journeys themselves, and both lost to their extra cost a step:

  • The pair walk, ψ² (#34, after libsais and Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's super-alphabet). Each entry holds the row two steps on, so the walk takes half the steps, two bytes at each. But each step costs about twice as much: the second byte comes from a first-byte lookup. With the prefetch keeping 32 misses in flight, halving the dependent loads bought almost nothing, and the pair table took about three times as long to build. Envelopes holding two addresses mean fewer stops, but twice the paperwork at each, and the envelopes take three times as long to fill.
  • Precopy (#36, after Kärkkäinen and Puglisi). Where a stretch of the walk repeats one already walked, its bytes are copied instead of walked. It copied 31.5% of the Wikidata blocks' bytes, and was slower all the same. The repeat check ran on every step, and the steps it skipped were the cheap ones, whose table lines were already in cache. The cost is in the scattered steps, which repeats never cover. A courier who checks the logbook for a repeated stretch at every stop loses more time than the short, nearby stretches it saves.
flagged walk (the default before #37): a step's journey, then its bookkeepingshared-offset walk (#37, the default): the same journeys, less bookkeeping a steppair walk, ψ² (#34, lost): two bytes a step, about twice the work a stepPrecopy (#36, lost): a repeat check on every step; the copies skip only cheap stepsthe journey: load the entry, take its bytebookkeeping: flags, pointers, buffer ends, checksa byte out The core's time once enough misses are in flight, schematically: the bytes out in the same time. The shared-offset walk keeps the journeys and cuts the bookkeeping. The pair walk halves the steps but doubles each one's work, and pays again in its build. Precopy adds a check to every step to skip a few cheap ones.

items.title: The measurements
items.text:
Read these as indicative

These are the walk alone, on one thread, mostly on shared development machines. Each comparison holds only within its own row: the rows differ in machine, clock, corpus and repeats. The implementations differ in more than their lane count, too: the bitmap or the flag, the vector push or the raw pointers, the prefetch, and the segment count. Only the CI benchmark decides what merges.

items.title: The walk alone
items.text:
Cycles a byte of output (c/B), the walk on its own, one thread:

items.title: By lane count: the measured points
items.text:
Only measured points are drawn, each chart on its own axes and naming its source: two sweeps so far, on different machines, corpora and walks, not to be read against each other. A finer sweep of lanes and prefetching is planned. Its points will go into assets/data/lane-sweeps.json, one panel a sweep, and appear here.

Loading the measured sweeps…

items.title: The whole decoder, on CI
items.text:
The walk is about 53–60% of a decode, so a walk change moves the whole decoder by less. Whole-decoder figures come only from the CI benchmark: paired rounds of a pull request's head against its base on one runner (methodology). The walk's changes, on the Wikidata blocks (wall time, head over base, with its 95% interval; − is faster):

change 1 thread 4 threads bench the flagged walk (#12) −10.7% (−11.3%, −10.2%) −16.6% (−18.2%, −15.0%) #12 32 lanes, 512 segments, the prefetch (#21) −13.2% (−13.8%, −12.5%) −8.3% (−11.5%, −5.0%) #21 the pair walk, ψ² (#34, not merged) +40.6% (+40.1%, +41.1%) +24.3% (+22.8%, +25.8%) #34 Precopy (#36, not merged) +18.0% (+15.9%, +20.1%) +6.0% (+5.0%, +6.9%) #36 the shared-offset walk (#37) −10.3% (−10.6%, −10.0%) −9.1% (−12.2%, −5.9%) #37, its first run (EPYC 9V74); its last, on a Xeon 6973P-C: −5.8% (−7.3%, −4.2%) and −2.7% (−4.1%, −1.3%)

Each row is its own runner and its own base, so the rows don't add up. Master's figures over its commits are on the History page, and mibz2 beside the other bzip2 decoders on Alternatives.

items.title: The picture, term by term
items.text: in the picture in the decoder a courier a lane: one traversal chain, walking one segment at a time a delivery address, read on arrival the next row, in the entry the step just loaded waiting for the address a cache miss on the T-vector a delivery chain a segment, from a flagged start row to the next start the dispatcher one core's instruction stream, interleaving all the lanes' steps the paperwork for each step the instructions a step: the flag test, the byte's store, the pointer and buffer bookkeeping phoning ahead the software prefetch of each lane's next entry the road, the board's size the core's limits: outstanding misses (line fill buffers), the reorder window, the caches deliveries a second for the centre bytes of output a second: throughput, not one load's latency several dispatch centres worker threads, one block each

items.title: Threads
items.text:
• The scanner. One thread reads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbols in order. This is the one sequential phase: a block's end is known only once its symbols are read. It finds blocks exactly, not by searching for the block magic, so a magic inside a block's data is never taken for a block. It is roughly a tenth of a decode on well-compressed text, more on poorly compressible data.
  • The workers. Each worker finishes a block: move-to-front, the T-vector, the inverse BWT walk, RLE1 and the CRC.
  • The reader takes the blocks in order. A block's error reaches the reader only once every block before it has been read.
  • Memory is bounded: at most slots blocks are in flight (by default twice the threads), and the buffers are reused from block to block.

With one thread, the same phases run in order on the calling thread.

items.title: The walk
items.text:
The inverse BWT is a chain of dependent loads: each step's row is the previous step's load. A plain walk keeps one load in flight. The default walk (bwt::walk_segments_room, the flagged walk in passes) keeps many, one a lane (Why 32 couriers beat one explains why, and where it stops paying):

  • 512 pseudo-random rows, the walk's first among them, are segment starts;
  • each start is flagged in its own T-vector entry, which ends the segment before it;
  • 32 lanes walk segments in lockstep, each taking the next segment when its own ends, and each lane's next entry is prefetched as soon as its row is known;
  • the lanes step in passes of room rounds, room the fewest bytes any lane's buffer has spare, each byte written at its lane's base plus the pass's offset, so a step has no pointer store or buffer-end test (after libsais's chain decode, #37);
  • the segments are joined in order.

It equals the plain walk on every list, lists of several cycles included: the join follows the segments' links until the block's length is reached. The flags are cleared before the walk returns. Blocks under 64 Ki are walked plainly. The kernel is behind bwt::InverseBwt (Segmented, the default; Plain), so a walk can be swapped and timed as part of the whole decoder.

items.title: Kernels
items.text: Kernels::detect() chooses at run time: AVX2 (with BMI1) for move-to-front and RLE1, and PCLMULQDQ for the CRC. Each has a scalar twin, used on any other CPU and on aarch64 (Kernels::scalar()). The walk's gain is scalar code, memory-level parallelism, so it holds on any CPU.

items.title: Prior work
items.text:
• The format and its checks are libbzip2's (Julian Seward, bzip2 1.0.8, decompress.c). mibz2 follows its decoding rules and makes each of its checks, in its terms. Its Huffman decode tables are built as BZ2_hbCreateDecodeTables builds them, so a stream libbzip2 refuses is refused here too. It is a separate implementation in Rust, not a port of libbzip2's code. The tests use libbzip2 itself (the bzip2 crate's bundled 1.0.8) as the oracle.
  • Interleaving several traversals of one BWT inversion on one thread, so that out-of-order execution keeps their loads in flight, is Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's idea: "Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion", DCC 2012, pp. 99–108.
    • They also use a super-alphabet (an LF² table: two characters a dependent lookup) and "Precopy" for repetitive data. Neither is used here: both were built in mibz2 and lost (why).
    • What is particular here is only how the traversals are found in an existing bzip2 file, which carries no metadata for them: the random starts, the flagged starts that end each segment, and the joining in order.
  • libsais (Ilya Grebnov), 2.12's cyclic inverse BWT, "as used by bzip2": its RUN_LANES store, 16 equal last-column bytes linked at once, is in mibz2's T-vector build. Its chain decode's shared-offset passes are mibz2's walk since 0.1.5 (#37).
  • Block-parallel decoding is lbzip2's (Mikołaj Izdebski) and pbzip2's approach.
  • pbz2 (Soof Golan) arrived independently at a segmented, multi-chain walk too; the bake-off that found it is in the journals.

items.title: Python
items.text:
mibz2 needs Python 3.10 or later. It has no Python dependencies.

pip install mibz2

or with uv:

uv add mibz2

Wheels are built for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows (x64). Each uses the stable ABI (abi3), so one wheel covers every Python version from 3.10.

items.title: Rust
items.text:
cargo add mibz2

The library depends on std only. Its minimum supported Rust version is 1.80. The python feature builds the Python extension module, and is only for maturin.

items.title: Python
items.text:
Write a .bz2 file with the standard library's bz2, to have one to read:

import bz2

with bz2.open("sample.bz2", "wb") as f:
    for i in range(10_000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n".encode())

A whole file in memory, decoded on every CPU this process may use, or on one thread:

>>> import mibz2
>>> compressed = open("sample.bz2", "rb").read()
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(compressed)
>>> data == bz2.decompress(compressed)
True
>>> mibz2.decompress(compressed, threads=1) == data
True

A file read as it is decoded: open takes a path or a binary file object, and returns a buffered binary file. Its raw.verified turns true once a read has reached the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched:

>>> with mibz2.open("sample.bz2") as f:
...     first = f.readline()
...     before = f.raw.verified
...     rest = f.read()
...     after = f.raw.verified
>>> first, before, after
(b'line 0\n', False, True)

A bad input raises mibz2.DecodeError, a ValueError, from decompress or from the read at which it is found. The message says which block and bit decoding failed at:

>>> damaged = bytearray(compressed)
>>> damaged[len(damaged) // 2] ^= 0x10
>>> try:
...     mibz2.decompress(bytes(damaged))
... except mibz2.DecodeError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, isinstance(e, ValueError))
DecodeError True

items.title: Rust
items.text:
use std::io::Read;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // a whole .bz2 in memory (its streams one after another): on this thread, or on 4
    let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
    let text = mibz2::decode(&data)?;
    let same = mibz2::decode_parallel(&data, 4)?;
    assert_eq!(text, same);

    // any Read, as a Read: on this thread, or block-parallel on 4 worker threads
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    mibz2::BzReader::parallel(std::fs::File::open("file.bz2")?, 4).read_to_end(&mut out)?;
    Ok(())
}

A bad stream is an mibz2::Error (its kind, block and bit), or from a BzReader an io::Error of kind InvalidData wrapping it. The Rust reference lists the rest: the push decoder, the block scanner and the decoding of a range of blocks.
